No. WBW827 by the latter mentioned vehicle, which vehicles and trailer 
belong to the Rankrishna Mission Social Kducation Organisers’ Training 
Centre and are used for purposes of social education ;

২010 Act, the (rtovernor is pleased to exempt the snid motor vehicles from

No, 4816W.T.—29th July 1957 —The following draft of amendments 
which, in exercise of the power conferred by seetion 68 of the Motor Vehicles 
Act, 1939 01৮ of 1939), the Governor propuses to make in the Bengal Motor 
Vehicles Rules, 1940, published under notification No. 1930P1., dated the 
1151 September 1940, at pages 2656-2829 of Part I of the Calcutta Gazette 
of the 10th October 1940, as subsequently amended, is hereby published, as 
required by sub-section (1) of section 138 of the said Act, for information of 
persons likely to be affected thereby. 


2. The draft will be taken into consideration on or after the 17th August 
1997 and Bey objection or suggestion with respect thereto which may be 
received by the undersigned betore that date shall be considered :— 


Draft Amendments 
For rule 52 of the said rules substitute the following rule :— 
"52. State Transport Authori!y.—(u) The State Government shall 
appoint an officer in the service of the State Government to be 
the Secretary of the Authority. 


(b) In the State Transport Authority the number of members whose 
presence shall constitute a quorum 81১1] be— 


(i) in the case of an Authority consisting of not more than three 
members, the total number of members constituting the 
Authority, or 

(21) in any other case, three. 

(c) Where the State Transport Authority consists of more than three 
members, the Authority may, at its first meeting, elect one of 
the members to be the Deputy Chuirman, At any meeting of the 
Authority where a quorum is present, the Chuirman shall preside 
aud if the Chuirman is unable to uttend, the Deputy Chairman 
shall act as the Chairman of the meeting, and in the absence of 
both the Chairman and the Deputy Chairman, the members 
present shall elect one of their number to act as the Chairman of 
the meeting. 

(d) The Chairman or the Deputy Chairman or any member acting as 
Chairman of a meeting under sub-rule (c) shall have a second or 
casting vote in all cases of equality of votes. 


(e) The State Transport Authority shall meet at such times and at such 
places as the Chairman may appoint: 


Provided that the Authority shall meet not less than once in each of the 
periods of three months of January to March, April to June, July 
to September, and October to December unless the State Govern- 
ment otherwise directs. 

(f) Not less than ten days’ notice shall be given of any meeting of the 
State Transport Authority. 

(zg) The period of appointment of the State Transport Authority shall 
ordinarily be three years: 


Provided that the State Government may, if it considers necessary to 
do so, reconstitute the Authority at any time before the expiry of 
the said period of three years or extend the said period to more 
than three years. 

(h) The State Government may, at any time, after giving any member 
of the State Transport Authority an opportunity of being heard, 
remove him from office for— 


(i) misconduct in the discharge of his duties, or 

(11) any disgraceful conduct, or 
(iii) persistent failure to attend meetings of the Authority, or 
(iv) any other cause deemed sufficient by the State Government. 


(i) When a member of the Authority dies, or is removed from or vacates 
his office, the ®tate Government may appvint another member in 
his place who shall, subject to the provisions of the proviso to 
sub-rule (g) and sub-rule (h), hold office for the remainder of the 
term of the Authority. 


(j) A member of the State Transport Authority shal] receive a daily fee 
of fifteen rupees for every day on which he attends a meeting of 
the Authority and shall] further be entitled to receive travelling 
and halting allowances at the scale and on the conditions appli- 
cable to members of the West Bengal Leyislature, and any such 
member performing any journey in connection with the business 
of the Authority, otherwise than to attend a meeting of the 
Authority, shall, with the sanction of the Chairman, be entitled 
to receive travelling and halting allowances likewise: 


Provided that ‘the daily fee of fifteen rupees for attending meetings of 
the Authority shall not be admissible to an official or to a member 
of Parliament or of the State Legislature.’’ 


By order of the Governor, 
J. N. TALUKDAR, Secy.

Explanatory note.-—Regarding ‘goods for use 
in manufacture or in the execution of contracts’’ 
the fallowing code letters have been used to 
indicate the meanings noted against each :— 


(A) Other raw materials. 


(B) Plant, machinery, spare parts, accessories 
and consumable stores. 

(C) Building or plumbing materials or fixtures 
required for construction, fitting out or 
repair of any building.

Public Health 


NOTIFICATION 


Hooghly. —No. P.H./3267/2R-68/56.—16th July 1957.—In exercise of 
the power conferred by section 506 of the Bengul Municipal Act, 1932 
(Bengal Act XV of 1932), the Governor is pleased to confirm the following 
set of rules framed by the Commissioners of the Champdany Municipality 
in the district of Hooghly under section 75 of the said Act. 


In addition to the duties imposed upon the Sanitary Inspector by any 
law or order for the time being in force regarding public health, he shall 


perform the following duties: 


1. Under the general supervision and instruction of the Commissioners 


or Health Officer, he shall perform the duties imposed 


upon him by the 


Health Officer or the Commissioners or by any rules, regulation or by-law 
framed under the Bengal Municipal Act, 1932, in respect of any matter 


uffecting public health. 


2. Under the وی‎ supervision and instruction of the Commissioners 


or Health Officer, 


e shall execute and enforce rules and orders relating to 


public health, which may be enacted, made or issued by a competent 


authority. 


3. He shall attend the meetings of the Commissioners when specially 


required. 


4, Matters affecting public health.—As far as practicable he shall keep 


himself informed of all matters affectin 


or likely to affect injuriously the 


public health. For this purpose he shall visit the several areas or localities 
within his jurisdiction both systematically at certain periods and at intervals, 
us occasion may require or as may be directed by the Commissioners or the 


Health Officer. 


5. Dangerous diseases.—He shall enquire into and ascertain as for as 
practicable, the cuuses, origin and spread of any dangerous disease and also 
of other infectious diseases within his jurisdiction when directed by the 


Commissioners or the 


Health Officer, and ascertain to what extent they 


depend on conditions capable of removal] or mitigation. 


6. Notification of epidemic outbreaks.—He shal] give immediate notice 
to the Health Qfficer or Commissioners of the occurrence of any infectious 
or epidemic disease within his jurisdiction. 


7. Epidemic management.—On receiving information of the outbreak 
of any dangerous or epidemic disease within his jurisdiction, he shall visit, 
without delay, the locality where the outbreak has occurred and enquire 
into the causes: and circumstances of such outbreak, and in case he is not 
satisfied that all due precautions are en taken he shall report to the 

t 


Health Officer or the Commissioners as to 


@ measures which appear to him 


to be required to prevent the spread of the disease and shall take such 
measures for the prevention of the disease as he may be authorised to do. 

8. Isolation.—He shall, when required by the Health Officer or the 
Commissioners, remove or superintend the removal of patients suffering from 
infectious diseases to an infectious disease hospital or temporary treatment 
camp and shall perform or superintend the work of disinfection after the 
occurrence of cases of infectious disease in a building. 


9. If directed hy the Health Officer or the Commissioners to do so, he 


shall, from time to time, enquire into and report upon the accommodation 
available in hospitals or dispensaries, either maintained by or receiving aid 
from the Municipal Fund, for the isolation of cases of (a) cholera, (b) small- 
pox, (c) plague, (d) cerebro-spinal meningitis, (e) diphtheria and other 


infectious and dangerous diseases occurring in the area within his jurisdic- 
tion and upon any need for the provision of further accommodation.

10, Removal of nuisances.—If directed by the Health Officer or the 
‘onmmissioners to do so, he shall superintend and see to the due execution 
of all local works, which may be undertaken by the Commissioners for the 
suppression or removal of nuisances within his jurisdiction. 


11. Gonservancy staff.—Subject to the instruction of the Health Officer 
or the Commissioners he shall direct or superintend the work of vaccinators, 
conservancy staff and other subordinate public health staff. 


12. Verification of vital events.—He shall verify occurrences of all 
births and deaths registered in the course of his round and shall report 
unregistered births Hei deaths detected by him to the Registrar of Births 
and Deaths. 


13. Water-supply.—He shall pay particular attention to the water-supply 
of the «rea under his jurisdiction, especially if it is derived from public 
wells, tube-wells or reserved tanks. He shall report to the Health Officer or 
the Comminxsioners whenever uny public well, tube-well or tank is not found 
to be kept in good repair and whenever any reserved tank is not properly 
fenced und kept free from contamination, and he shall render every 
assistance to ensure the purity of the water-supply. He shall also report to 
the same ofticer the insanitary condition of defects in the water hydrants and 
the name of any person, who wastes public water-supply. 


14. Malaria.—In order to facilitate the adoption of measures for reducing 
the prevalence of malarial fever, he shall make a careful survey of the 
distribution of malaria in the different areas under his jurisdiction. When, 
us a result of this survey, he has obtained an uccurate knowledge of the 
distribution and relative intensity of malaria existing in different parts of 
the town or the area under his jurisdiction, he shall prepare a detailed 
report of the existing malarial condition, and submit it to the Health Officer 
or the Cominissioners. 


When directed by the Commissioners or the Health Officer, he shall 
systematically carry out anti-larval and anti-mosquito measures and assist 
in the distribution of quinine to malana patients. 


1h, Fairs.—tHe shall personally attend 21) fairs and religious festivals, 
agricultural and industrial exhibitions and other large gatherings held in 
his jurisdiction and arrange for the erection of temporary latrine acecommoda- 
tion and the protection of the water-supply in order to guard against the 
occurrence of any water-borne diseuse. 


16. Offensive trades.—He shall report to the Health Officer or the 
Commissioners any noxious or offensive trade, business or manufactory 
established within his jurisdiction and the breach or non-observance of any 
by-law or regulation made in respect thereof. 


17. If he is of opinion that any trade or occupation or the keeping of any 
goods or merchandise in uny particular urea by reason of its being injurious 
or prejudicial to the public health should be suppressed or removed or prohi- 
bited or that uction should be taken regarding any public nuisance, he shall 
report the matter to the Health Officer or the Commissioners, so that action 
may be taken under provisions of Chapter XXI of the Bengal Municipal 
Act, 1932, or under section 133 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, or 
any other provision of law. 


18. Railway and steamer stations.—Whenever necessary or advisable 
or whenever directed to do so by competent authority, he shall inspect the 
sanitary condition of railway stations and steamer ghats within his jurisdic- 
tion and shall report the result of hig inspection to the Health Officer or the 
)ٌ0 8:8. 


19. Propaganda.—Subject to the instructions und orders of the Health 
Officer or the Commissioners he shall educate the pablic within his jurisdic- 
tion in matters relating to public health by means of popular addresses with 
or without the aid of the magic Jantern or any other appliance. 


20. School inspections.—If directed by the Health Officer or the 


Commissioners to do so, he shall carry out sanitary inspection of school 


premises. 


2]. Records of inspection.—He shall keep such records of his inspection 
and of other uction taken by him in such manner ag may be directed by the 
Health Officer or the Commissioners. 


22. Weekly epidemic reports.—On every Saturday he shall forward to 
the Health Officer or the Commissioners such reporta as may be directed by 
the Commissioners showing the number of cases of any dangeroug disease 
with mortality therefrom reported to him during the week, «nd mentioning 
the preventive steps taken for the control of the spread of the infection. 


23. Conservancy.—He shall keep a note book in such form as the Health 
Uflicer or the Commissionera may specify, in which he shall record the 
particulars of such defeots in private privies or latrines as require action by 
the owners and of the action actua!ly taken to remove them.

Note.—The Sanitary Inspector shall not merely order work to be done

30. Cowsheds and dairiés.—He shall make regular inspections of cow- 
sheds and dairies and report whether they are in a sanitary condition. He

infection through milk. If in course of such inspection or at any other time 
he detects or becomes cognizant of any infectious disease among the mileh 
cattle, especially tubercular disease of the udder, he shal) report the fact to 
the Health Officer or the Commissioners and, shall take such precautions as 
may he necessary. 


31. Places for the disposal of the dead.—tTe shall visit places for the 
disposal of the dead once a week, if any exist within his jurisdiction, and 
enquire into the number of bodies disposed of there since his Just visit. 
From time to time he shall inform the Health Officer or the Commissioners 
the mensures which should be taken for the improvement of the place. ~

the proper disposal.

steps which should be taken to improve them.

No. 2612-I.R. /IR/1A-14/57.—19th July 1957. 
—Whereas*the (tovernor is of opinion that the 
application of the provisions of section 9A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947) 
(hereinafter referred to as the said Act), in respect 
of the matters specified in items Noa. 4, 6 and 
11 of the Fourth Schedule to the snid Act, to the 
Tea Plantation Industry in West Bengal affects 
the employers in relation thereto 80. prejudicially 
that such application may cause serious repercus- 
sion on the said industry and that public interest 
80 requires; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the power con- 
ferred by section 9B of the 8016] Act, the Governor 
18 pleased hereby to direct that the provisions ot 
section 9A of the said Act shall apply to the Tea 
Plantation Industry in West Bengal, subject to 
the conditions that, for a perind of three yéars 
from the date of publication of this notification 
in the Calcutta Gazette, no notice referred to in 
the said section 9A shall be required in respect 
of the matters specified in items Nos. 4, 6 ond 
11 of the Fourth Schedule to the said Act.

OFFICE OF THE ACCOUNTANT-GENERAL, WEST BENGAL 
NOTIFICATION 


Subject: Submission of rent demand statements 


No. T.M./626.—17th July 1957.—In terms of the instructions issued by 
the Accountant-General, Central Revenues, New Delhi, the Central Publ 
Work Divisional / Estate Officers are required to issue the rent demand 
statements (in form 48 of the (3, P. W. A. Code) in trtplicate in all cases, 
that 18 in the case of both gazetted and non-gazetted Central Government 
servants. Two ae of such demand statements are required to be attached 
with the pay/establishment bills by the Treasury Officers/other Disbursing 
Officers the third copy being returned by them to the Divisional | Estate 
Officer concerned after recording thereon n certificate to the effect thut 
recovery hus been made and the emoluments are correct. Under this 
arrangement two copies of the rent demand atatements in respect of the 
Central Government servants under the audit contro] of this office are 
required to be attached with the pay/esablishment bills, so that one copy 
thereof with the requisite certificate recorded thereon may be passed on 
by this office to the Audit Officer of the Divisional /State Officers, viz., the 
Accountant-General, Central Revenues. It has, however, been noticed that 
only one copy (instead of two) of the rent demand stutements is received in 
this office at present. 


2. All Disbursing Officers of the Central Government under the audit 
control of this office and all Treasury Officers in West Bengal are, therefore, 
requested to ensure that two copies of the rent demand statements are 
invariably sent to this office along with the relevant bills in tuture. 


3. The gazetted Central Government aervants drawiug pay from thia 
office are also requested to attach all the three copies of the rent demand 
statements (received by them from the Divisional / Estate Officers) with their

pay bills submitted to this office for payment.

DISTRICT MACISTRATE’S OFFICE, HOWRAH 
NOTIFICATION 
The 28rd July 1957 

Whereas it hus been reported by the local people 
of the locality that the plying of transport vehicles 
on He in Munshi Lane, Howrah, is causing 
considerable inconvenience to the qeople of the 
lovality; 

And whereas on local enquiry, I am_ satisfied 
that it is necessary in the interest of public safety 
and convenience to prohibit the plying of all 
transport vehicles over this road; 

], therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred 
on me by the State Government under section. 14 
of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 (Act IV of 1939), 
ax amended by Act 100 of 1956, do prohibit, until 
further orders, the plying of all transport vehicles 
over the Hamijuddin Munshi Lane, Howrah. 


B. B. MANDAL, 
District Magistrate, Howrah.

Presidency Division—Jalpaiguri 
No. 13311.8.~¢.—23rd July 1957.—The following by-laws for regulat- 


ing the sanitation of restaurants, eatin 
have been adopted by the District 


houses, tea shops and lodging houses 
oard, Malda, under section 139 of 


the Bengal 14009] Self-Government Act, 1885 (Bengal Act ITI of 1885). As 
it is proposed to confirm the said by-laws under section 139 of the Act, the 
draft of the by-laws is published for the information of the persons likely 


to he affected thereby. 


2. The draft by-laws will be tuken into consideration on or after the 15th 
September 1957 and objections or suggestions, if any, received by the under- 
اہ‎ ۱ ۱ through the District Magistrate, Malda, before that date will be duly 


considered, 


BY-LAWS 
1. For the purpose of these by-laws— 


(a) ‘lodging house’? means a house in which pilgrims or other persons 
are lodged on hire and where there is arrangement for both eating 


and sleeping; 


(b) “eating house’’ means a house or other accommodation where people 
meet, to partake of food or drink on payment but where there 
id no accommodation tor sleeping or rest on payment, and includes 


a restaurant; and 


(c) ‘‘tea ''رمطد‎ 09809 a shop whiere liquid refréshment, such as ‘tea, 
coffee, cocoa, aerated water or other drinks either hot or cold 
are mainly sold and served for- consumption at such shop. 


9 


2, Every keeper of a tea shop, eating house or lodging house shall affix 


‘or put up in front of or within the compound thereof and in a conapicuous 
place a signboard in English and im the local vernacular language or such 
other vernacular languages as may be required by the District Board stating 
the purpose for which such premises are intended for and used. The name 
of the keeper shal] be written on the signboard. 


Part T] 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, ATGUST 1, 1957 


3. Structures used or intended to be used as a tea shop, eating house 
or lodging house shall be constructed of such materials as may be specified 
in that behalf by the District Board, provided that no part thereof shall be 
constructed of inflammable materials and the floor of such structures shall 
a meee impervious and shall be drained to the satiafaction of the District 

oard, 


4. Kvery tea shop, eating house or lodging house shall be provided by 
the keeper thereof with such— 


(n) means of ventilation and lighting in each room, 

(b) supply of water, 

(c) receptacles for the deposit of garbage and refuse of all kinds, 
(d) drains and latrines, and 


(6) in the case of a lodging house, bathing and sleeping accommodation, 
as may be approved or directed by the District Board in each 
case: 


Provided that arrangements shall be made for the use of latrines, buthing 
places and sleeping rooms by males and females separately. 


5. Every keeper of a tea shop, eating house or pe pee house shall make 
urranpgement to prevent smoke from the kitchen from having a direct access 
into the sleeping 85۰ 


6. Every keeper of a lodging house shall put up a notice in each sleep- 
ing room showing the dimensions thereof and the maximum number of 
persons to be Iodged therein and shall not allow any room therein to be 
occupied at any time by a larger number of persons that may be accommo- 
dated with a floor space not less than 40 square feet and a cubic space of 
400 cubic feet for each adult person, two children under ten years of age 
being counted as one adult person. 


7. In every tea shop, eating house or lodging house— 


(u) all floora shall be thoroughly cleaned and washed and al] deposits 
of garbage and refuse removed from the receptacles provided for 
such deposita at least once in every twenty-four hours, 


(b) the inner surfaces of all walls and ceilings shall be lime washed 
biennially in the months of April and October or oftener if so 
required by the District Board, 


(c) all drains shall be maintained in good working order and 01) a proper 
state of repair, and 


(d) the premises shall génerally be kept clean and free from jungles 
and undergrowth. 


8. No keeper of a restaurant, tea shop, eating house or lodging house 
shall employ lepers or persons suffering from an open sore or any loathsome 
or infectious disease to serve in such premises. 


(A.xplanation.—Leucoderma or white skin will be regarded as a loath- 
some disease for the purpose of this by-law.) 


9. Every keeper of a lodging house shall give or cause to be given imme- 
diate notice to the District Board of the outbreak of any infectious disease 
in the premisés and shall comply with such orders and instructions as the 
istrict Board may give regarding the prevention and control of the spread 
of infection and shall not receive or allow to be received in such premises 
any 10016] without the written permission of the District Board. The keeper 
may refuse admission to any person suffering or reusonubly suspected to be 
suffering from any loathsome or infectious disease into the premises. 


Explanation.—(FE) For the purpose of this by-law informf&tion given to 
the Sanitary Inspector of the District Board shall be deemed as information 
sent ae the District Board within whose jurisdiction the lodging house is 
situated , 


(2) Permission 01 the Health Officer of the District Board concerned to 
receive lodgers shall be deemed to be permiasion of the District Board, 


10. The keeper of a tea shop, eating house or, lodging house shall allow 
such tea shop, eating house or lodging house to be inspected at any time by 
the Health Officer of the District Board or his representative. 


11. Whoever commits a breach of any of the above by-laws shall be 
punishable with fine which may extend to fifty rupees; and in case of a 
continuing breach with a further fine which may extend to five rupees for 
every day during which the breach continues after the offender has been 
convicted of such breach.

ANNEXURE 
In the matter of an industrial dispute existing between Messrs. Walford 
Transport Ltd., 72 Park Street, Cafcutta, and one of their workmen Shri 
Kushal Singh, represented by Bengal Motor Industry and Transport 
Workers’ Union, 14 Motisil Street, Calcutta-13. 


BEFORE THE SECOND INDUETRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL. 


PRESENT کر‎ 
সিরাত 0. P. MUKHERJEE, Judge, Sécond. Industrial Tribunal. 


A ppearances : 
For the workman: Shri N. D. Manna, Counsel 
for the Company: Shri 8, C. Sen, Advocate. 


AWARD 


This reference made by the Government of West Bengal, Labour Depart- 
ment, under order No. 5306-I.R./D/40-44/56, dated 12th December, 1956, 
relates to the ا ا‎ of Shri Kushal Singh, a Salesman of : ۵۸۰ 
Walford Transport Ltd. 


The issue as contained in the schedule to the order of reference ita as 
tollows:— 


Whether the discharge of Shri Kushal Singh was justified? To what 
relief is he entitled? 


The contention of the Union 1s that Shri Kushal Singh was discharged 
with effect from Ist February 1956 hecause of his Union activifies. The 
said discharge is an instance of unfair Jabour practice. It was made in 
violation of the principles of natural justice. So reinstatement with back 
hy og in the alternative, compensation with retrenchment relief has heen 
claimed. 


2760 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 1, 1967 [Paar I 


a RN | ۔ے--دد---١‌+۔--٠"۹٭‎ 


In reply, the Company stated that Shri Kushal Singh had to be dis- 
charged as it was found uneconomical to keep him im service. It was noticed 
for some time past that the volume of sales introduced by him fell far below 
the standard. He was warned to improve his sale standard. But the ا‎ 
ing had no effect. So another actice was given to him thereafter drawing 
his attention in this respect. Yet he did not and could not improve his sale 
performance. So at last the Company had no other alternative but to 
discharge him. In the circumstances the discharge of Shri Kushal Singh 
was justified. 


The Company has raised two legal objections 9190. The first objection is 
that it is not an industrial diapute but an individual dispute. The second 
objection is that Shr: Kushal Singh was not a workman as defined in the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, Hence it is contended on behalf of the 
Company that the reference is bad in law and that the Tribunal is not 
competent to decide the same. As the legal objections which the Company 
has pressed relate to the jurisdiction of the Tribunal to decide the present 
dispute, the Tribunal finds itself bouns to record its findings on the said 
objections. If, as u matter'of fact, it be found that it is an individual 
dispute and that Shri Kushal Singh was not a workman, the dispute under 
reference ceases to be an industrial dispute. [In such event Shri Kushal 
Singh, the employee 45010611060) cannot get the aid or benefit of the Act 
nor can the Tribunal proceed to adjudicate the issue framed in this case, 
despite the reference made by the Government. 


Now I take up the legal objections, one by one, and record my findings 
with reasons thereon. 


As stated already the first objection whieh the Company pressed, ia 
that it is an individual dispute hetween the employer: on ‘the one hand and 
one of the employees’ in question on the other. Learned Advocate for the 
Company dgew my attention te the order of reference in this respect. He 
has argued that the fact of representation of the employee concerned by 
the Union which has been mentioned in the order of reference cannot have 
the effect of converting the present dispute which was fundamentally an 
individual dispute into an industrial dispute. It means only that the Union 
represented the employee just to help him in conducting the case before 
the Tribuna]. It does not indicate or prove that the Union has espoused 
the cause of the employee as its own and has identified itself totally with 
this employee. The Union, on the other hand, contends that it in the 
present case had expoused the cause of thé employee long before the date 
of reference. So, even the dispute was originally an individual dispute, 
it became later on converted into an industrial dispute by the intervention 
of the Union. I have given my most anxious consideration to the conten- 
tions put forward by both parties. Considering the matter in 91] its bearing 
and going into evidence [ am of the view that long before the reference 
the Union had espoured and taken up the cause of the employee and foughs 
against the Company. Annexure KI, dated 19th May 1955, to the written 
statement of the Company sbows that Shri W. THlussan, the General 
Secretary of the Union addressed a letter to the Genera] Manager of this 
Company regarding the discharge of Shri Kushal Singh and _ requested 
him to reinstate Shri Kushal Singh immediately and pay him hia dues. 
Annexurt E] is the reply of the Manager to the ات‎ Secretury on 7+ 
May 1956. Shri Hassan, the General Secretary, has also deposed before 
the Tribunal. He is P. W. 3. He has stated in 1019 evidence that 
Shri Kushal Singh is a member of the Union and that the Union had 
taken up his cause. Thus it is abundantly clear that it is not a case of 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 1, 1957 2761 
তা تس حو ہرس حصسود ہر .. بی د2 ہت‎ 
mere representation by the Union but it is a case of the Union making 
the cause of this Salesman as ita own against the Company. In this 
case it cannot be considered to be a case of individual dispute. What 
wns originally an individual dispute was converted into an industrial 
dispute by the intervention of Union which teok up and espoused the 
cause of the employee, Shri Kushal Singh. Learned Advocate for the 
Company has voiced an argument that unless it cau be shown that all 
the workmen, or at least the bulk of workmen of this concern bad 
identified themselves with the cause of Shri Kushal Singh, it cannot be 
an industrial dispute. But I am unable to accept this proposition of 
luw in view of the recent decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Indiu 
in the case of Central Province Transport Services Limited, Nagpur, 
versus Raghunath Gopal Patwardhan, repotted in the (1956-57) 11 ٠. J. BR, 
at page 298. Their Lordships have observed “Notwithstanding that the 
definition of ‘industrial dispute’ iu section 2(k) of the Industrial Disputes 
Act, 1947, is wide enough to cover a dispute between an employer and 
single employee the scheme of the Act appears to contemplate that the 
wachinery provided therein should be set in motion to settle only disputes 
which involve the rights of workmen as a class and that a dispute touching 
the individual rights of a workman is not intended to he the subject of 
adjudication under the Act when the same has not been taken up by the 
Union or a number of workmen’’. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case 
of newspapers Limited versus The Industrial Tribunal, ,تا‎ P., and others, 
has confirmed the above observations and the said decision is reported in 
(1967-58) 12 F.J.R. at page 129. From those decisions it is 7 that 
{hough ‘“‘individual dispute’? may net come under the definition of 
“industrial dispute’, atill such dispute cannat be ousted from the scope 
‘of the definition of the ‘industrial dispute” if the Union or a number 
of workmen take up that dispute. As in the present case before me the 
Union has espoused the cause of the employee concerned, the dispute was 
no longer an individual dispute ond it became an industrial dispute. The 
first legal objection pressed hy the Company therefore fails. 


The next objection as urged on behalf of the Company ia that the 
employee concerned, Shri Kushal Singh, was not a workman within the 
meaning of section 2(s) of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, which runs as 
follows :— 


““Workman means any person employed (including an apprentice) in 
any industry to do any skilled or unskilled manual or clerical work 


for hire or reward. 117 টন 


Before entering into the merits of this objection I am to dispose of a 
point raised on behalf of the Union. JTearned Counsel appearing on behalf 
of the Union has argued before that the uhove definition of workmen has 
‘been amended completely and redrafted by the Industrial Disputes (Amend- 
ment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1956, and that the present case is 
to be decided on the basis of new definition of ‘“‘workmen’’ because the 
section containing such definition of workmen came into force from 29th 
August 1956, which was long before the present reference. By the said 
Act, section 2(s) has been substituted as follows: — 


Workmen means any person (including an apprentice) employed in any 
industry to do any skilled or 3180س‎ manual, supervisory, 
technical or clerical work for hire or reward...........0.. re 


I have given my best consideration to this argument of the Jearned 
Counsel for the Company, but 1 am unoeble to accept it. In my view, it is 
not a correct proposition of law. It is n fact, no doubt, that the present 
reference was made to the Tribunal by the Government on 1961) December 


9762 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 1, 1957 {Parr I 


1956, that is long after the new detinition of workmen as made by 
the Industrial Disputes (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 
1956, came into force. But in the present case the employee concerned was 
admittedly discharged by this Company on 3lst January 1955. In the 
circumstances he is to be governed by the law as it stood on that date. Fur- 
thermore, he was not in the em)loyment of the Company when the new 
definition of workmen came into 10106 or when the reference was made to the 
Tribunal by the Government. He ceased to be an employee of the Company 
then. Therefore, he cannot take advantage of the law which came into 
force subsequently unless it was made retruspective. Shri Kushal Singh is 
not accordingly entitled to get the benefit of new definition of workmen as 
made by the Amending Act of 1956. My view, therefore, 18 that the 
question whether Shri Kushal Singh was a workman or not should be 
decided in the light of section 2(s) of the Act as it stood before the amend- 
ment and substitution as made by the Industrial Disputes (Amendment and 
Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1956. 


Shri Kushal Singh was appointed as a Salesman of this Company and 
was getting basic pay of Rs, 250 plus Rs. 00 D.A. and | per cent. com- 
mission on sales effected by him. He was also allowed car allowance of 
Rs. 100 per month. It has been repeatedly held that in deciding whether 
a particular employee is a workman or not designation does not matter and 
is not of great moment. What is of importance is the nature of his duties. 
So the relevant question is whether he performed clerical or manual work 80 
8৭ to place him under category of ‘‘workman’’ under the Act. The approach 
should therefore be not from the angle of testing whether the employee is 
an officer but from that of examining the duties to be performed by the 
employee and deciding whether they are in the mam clerical or manus] 
This is ultimately a question of fact At best it 15 one of mixed facts and 
Inw. Now let me approach the question from the atandpoint of the duties 
of this employee. IT shal) now discuss the nature of duties of Shri Kushal 
Singh which has emerged from the evidence. Shn Kushal 
Singh himself deposed in the case, and he is P.W 1. Another Salesman 
of this concern has been examined by the Union. He is P.W. 2, K. ۰ 
Chakravarty, P. W.1 Shri Kushal Singh has said ‘‘my_ principal 
duty as Salesman was to contact customers, convince them and 
also to induce them 10 buy the vehicles, .ظط‎ W. 2 K. P. 
Chakravarty has deposed ‘“‘the principal duty of a Salesman is to come in 
contact with customer and convince him and also to induce him to purchase 
ear’’, Thus it is manifestly cjear that the principal duty of the Salesman 
including that of Shri Kushal Singh was to come in contact with the 
customers and convince and induce them to purchase vehicles. As Sales- 
man his main duty was to push on the sale of the vehicles. In my view 
that was the major part of work of Shri Kushal Singh as a Salesman. It 
required initiative and display of intelligence. Shri Kushal Singh has 
stated, no doubt, in his evidence -that the nature of duties was both manual 
and clerical. As he was required to write down ordera of the customers and 
calculate particulars regarding sales of the vehicles he had to do clerical 
work. As he was required to give demonstration of the vehicles to intend- 
ing customers and to show the machineries of the vchicles and explain how 
they worked his work was manual, P. W. 2 Shri K. P. Chakravarty another 
Salesman of this concern has also deposed on the same line. From the 
evidence it appears that writing down of the orders of the customers meant 
only filling up printed Contract Form like Ext. B. Such filling up the 
Contract Form was rather insignificant and ancillary to the main duties 
which a Salesman had to do. It has transpired from the evidence that out 
of 24 Contract Forms executed by Shri Kushal Singh in 1955, 22 Contract 


Pant I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 1, 1957 2763 
মিট 


Forms ure not in his handwriting. So practically Shri Kushal Singh had 
no clerical work to do while employed as a Salesman. If as a Salesman he 
was required to give demonstration of the vehicles to the intending customers 
and explain the machineries to them it cannot be said that he had to do 
mainly manual work. It was a part of his duties as a Salesman. If he had 
to do anything by his own hands by way of testing or demonstrating, it 
cannot be said to be manual work. 


The Tribunal therefore holds that Shri Kushal Singh was not a workman 
within the meaning of the Act. So second legal objection raised on behalf 
of the Company succeeds. 


In the result the Tribunal comes {o the conclusion that Shri Kushal 
Singh cannot be considered to be 8 workman within the meaning of the 
Act. The nature of his duties in the main was neither clerical nor manual, 
That being so, the present dispute betwe2n parties does not fall within the 
ambit of the expression ‘‘induetrial dispute’? aa defined in section 2(k) 
of the Act. Accordingly, the employee is not extitled to invoke the aid of 
the Act nor has the Tribunal jurisdiction to adjudicate on the issue referred 
to it. In this view of the matter it is not necessary for the Tribunal te 


enter into the merits of the case cr tc express any opinion regarding the 
discharge of Shri Kushal Singh.

The case of the Union in short is that the Company Messrs. Ifenry

So reinstatement is sought on their behalf. 


‘The Company traverses the material allegations in the written 6>

DECISION 


This Company was started in September 195] and there is nothing ٥ 
show that it ia a very big business. There is no dispute that these three 
dismissed workmen excepting Gobardhan are unskilled labour and they 
were temporarily employed as mere learners on the basis of ‘no work, no 
pay’. There js also no dispute that all of them except Gobardhan were 
discharged on 15 November 1956 and none of them did put mm service for 
wore than a year. Rameswar was employed on 7th August 1996, Rampher 
employed on 1861) June 1956 and Jagadumba employed on 26th May 0 
and all of them were discharged on Ist November 1956. So none of them 
worked for a year. So it is clear that the provision of aection 251i of 
[udustrial Disputes Act ix not attracted in this case. 


It is a prima facie right of the Management to determine ite labour 
force and the Management would be the best judge to determine who 
would become surplus on the ground of rationalisation, economic or other 
reasons on which retrenchment can be sustained and if the Management 
acting in a bona fide manner effects the retrenchment, the Court should 
not interfere with the retrenchment which the Management may effect. 
At the same tine, it should not be lost sight of that victimisation or unfair 
labour practice in effecting retrenchment would be instances of improper 
motive, such retrenchment the Court must scrutinize with great care. If 
the Court comes to the finding that any retrenchment is actuated by unfair 
motives on the part of the Company, the Court must interefere. This is 
the law as 11010 down in the case of Viswamitra Press reported in 1952 
T.A.C., pages 20-383. In the instant case, the Company’s evidence is that 
in the year 1955 they got a stable order from the Ceylon Government worth 
Rs. 83,000 and these workmen had to be employed and the Company 
expected a similar business in the vear 1906, but their expectations were 
not fulfilled. So these workmen were not needed and the Company 1196 
to retrench them as surplus. I have no reason to disbelieve the evidence 
of the Superintendent in this behalf. As aguinst this evidence there is 
nothing on the side of the Union to enable me to hold that the Company 
really needed the services of these workmen for due performance of the 
volume of work in the factory. Mere oral testimony of one or two work- 
men does not convince the Court that they were retrenched mala tide. 
The Company in effecting the retrenchment, it appears, acted within their 
limits and there is nothing to show that they were actuated hy any 
mala fide or improper extraneous considerations. These workmen were 
employed poi ed as mere learners and so the Company did not trans- 
gress the limits of their rights in discharging these workmen as they were 
not needed for the purpose of this Company in the year 1996. 


The Union has made another attempt to show that within a few ۰ 
of the dismissal of these workmen, the Company employed one >۰. 
The evidence of the Superintendent, O.P.W. (1), is that they emplov 
08809] workers as and when necessary but these workmen did not turn up 
for re-employment. So the action of the Company is not open to much 
criticism for their not employing these dismissed workmen. 


As regards the plea of the Union that these workmen were discharged 
on account of their Trode Union activities, there is not the necessary 
cogent evidence to establish it. Of course, a charter of demands was 
ا‎ to the Company which was settled on 14th November 1906 as per 

xt. A, evidencing the fixation of pay-scale and laying down some rules 
for confirmation, etc. I am not satisfied of the contention on behalf of 
the Union that these workmen were dismissed for their Trade Union 
activities. Therefore, the Union has failed in making out a prima facie

case for reinstatement of these three workmen, namely, Rameswar, Rampher 
and Jagadamba. It is therefore found that these workmen cannot be 
reinstated. 


So far as Gobardhan is concerned, he, however, 82008 on 9 different 
footing. The evidence of the Superintendent is that -Gobardhan was 
employed as a gardener permanently on 6th March 1956 and he was not at 
all discharged and that the Company is ready and agreeable even now to 
take him in provided he agrees to work as a gardener. (mn behalf of the 
Union an attempt has been made to show that Gobardhan was also taken 
in #8 an unskilled labour along with the other three dismissed workmen 
but the evidence of Gobardhan s own countryman 0.P.W. 2, who brought 
him from his native village, negatives the case of Gobardhan. Aocepting 
the testimony of O.P.W. 2, I find that Gobardhan was employed permanently 
as a gardener and that he was not discharged by the Company, but he 
made a common cause with the other three workmen who were dismissed. 
It is therefore open to Gobardhan to report himself for duty to the Company 
on any day within the period mentioned below whereupon the Compan 
pier re-employ him as stated before the Court by the Superintendent in his 
evidence. 


To sum up, the three workmen, namely, Kameswar, Rampher and 
Jagadamba are not entitle to be reinstated and they are not entitled to any 
81181, The Company will offer to employ Gobardhan by issuing a notice 
to him within a month of the publication of this award. If he does not 
report for duty within a week of the receipt of the letter of the Company, 
he forfeits his claim to reinstatement. 


This is my award.

AWARD 


The case of the Union is as follows ہے‎ 


Shri Kailash Ram was employed as a_gate-keeper in the Majestic 
Talkies and was suddenly discharged on 15th October 1956 without any 
notice, reason, enquiry or justification. This is a case of victimisation 
for his Trade Union activities and an unfair labour practice and opposed 
to the principles of social and natural justice. The Union therefore seeks 
his reinstatement with full back wages. 


The Company denies the material allegations im the written statement 
of the Union and contends that this dismissed workman was employed on 
a temporary basis on the 110) March 1955 and was retrenched on 10৮1) 
October 1956 as he proved surplus to the requirements of the Company. 
The Company opposes the workman’s prayer for reinstatement but admits 
liabilities for notice-pay and compensation as provided for in section 251° 
of the Industrial Disputes Act. 


DECISION 


The point for decision is whether the termination of service of this 
workman is justified. On behalf of the Union much stress has been laid 


2788 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 1, 1957 [Pant I 


সস ২ 


upon the unfair labour practice resorted to by the Company for the work- 
man's taking up the cause of the other members of the staff as the Manage- 
ment was not granting them usual leave, increment and bonua, ete. In 
other words, the Union means to say that his espousal of the cause of the 
aggrieved workman of the Talkies alienated the sympathy of the Manage- 
ment which therefore sacked him in order to put a stop to their activities. 
But beyond the evidence of this workman there is no convincing ‘evidence 
on his side to establish the Union’s contention that this was a case of 
victimisation us contended on their behalf. The evidence on record rather 
establishes the contention of the Company that he was discharged aa he 
proved surplus. For the Management the evidence مز‎ that including this 
dismissed workman there were 10 yato-keepers who are quite adequate to 
the needs of the Talkies. Adyaittedly there are 884 seats for the audience 
in the whole House but the parties did not agree in their evidence as to 
the number of gate-keepers and pointers in the whole House. According 
to the Union there are 2 gate-keepers and 2 pointers in the Ist class, there 
is one gate in the 2nd class which is kept closed, there is one gate in the 
3rd class and for that there are one gate-keeper and one pointer. There 
is a pointer for the 2nd class gate. There ure 4 classes in the upper storey 
in which there are one gate-keeper and one pointer. Thus according to 
the evidence of the Union there are 4 gate-keepers and 5 pointers. Accord-

pointmen. Thus the evidence on the side of the Union is different from:

that there are now 1) gate-keepers of whom 2 ordinarily reinain on ۵٥ 
and 7 gute-keepers are sufficient. On the other hand, the evidence of the

it is said that at some previous time there were even 14 = gate-keepers 
according to the evidence of the P.W. (2) Abdul Khaleq, but having regard 
to the gates in the whole House numbering 4 or 5, I think, the present 
number of 9 gate-keepers seems to be quite adequate us urged on behalf 
of the Company. The contention on bebalf of the Union is that this 
workman was not at all aurplus and that by reason of the retrenchment 
the workload on the existing gate-keepers increased, In order to prove 
this, the Union produced a photograph, Ext. 4, to show that one Mahendra 
(Darwan) was on one occasion found checking the tickets of the audience. 
This might be a solitary instance and from this it cannot be generalised 
that the Company always utilise the services of the gate-keepers for other 
purposes. ‘The Union next made an attempt to show that the action of the 
Company was ۲ mala fide one and that is all the more so because the 
Company after discharging this workman employed another gate-keeper 
named Chandeswar who is much junior to him. So the Company departed 
from the principle ‘‘last come, first go’? and the Union insisted om 
reinstatement of the present workman. 


Now, I come to the point of law. It will be useful m thia connexion 
to refer to the American Law on the subject. Under the American Law, 
rights and practices of the Management recognised as Management's 
functions exerciseable by the Company without prior approval of the 
Union have heen classified as (1) methods of plant operation, (2) 
subcontracting of work, (3) determination of supervisory force, (4) plant 
discipline, (5) overtime work, (6) incentive wage plans, (7) job content 
and job evaluation, and (8) determination of employee competence (vide 
Management Function Under Collective Bargaining by the Ludwig 
Teller, pages 34-49). The Management has a right to discharge employees 
for a cause. The views of the Hon'ble Labour Appellate Tribunal of 


Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 1, 1957 2769 


a a rr ne مم‎ manera errr ar as aed 


India on the same subject will appear discussed in the 08889 of Viswamitra 
Press reported in 1952 L.A.C., pages 20-33, and may be quoted aa followa:— 


‘‘It is the prima facie right of the Management to determine 9 
labour force and the Management would be the best judge to 
determine the number of workmen who would become surplus on 
the-ground of rationalisation, economy or other reasons on which 
retrenchment oan be sustained. Where in effecting the retrench- 
ment, the Management acta in a bona fide manner the number 
retrenched by it ought to be accepted. It is not possible or 
desirable to give an exhaustive list of the cases that would be 
covered by the second class. The increase of workloud 01) the 
workmen retained would be an instance of extraneous considern- 
tion, Similarly, victimisation or unfair labour practice in effecting 
retrenchment, would be instances of improper motive. When the 
Management is influenced by extraneous considerations or improper 
motives, the Tribunal must scrutinise the matter with great 
circummspection and must confine the number of retrenchment 

within the limits of actual requirement. In such cases,‏ و 

the Management must justify by evidence the extent of the 

retrenchment. 


If the first question is answered in favour of the Management and the 
extent of the retrenchment determined in accordance with — the 
principles indicated above, the next question would be the 
personnel who would fall under the axe. Here the rule is well- 
established. Other things being equal, ‘the last come must first 

’, If that rule has been departed from, the Management must 
justify the departure and the last question for consideration would 
be the mesure of compensation to be given to persons whose 
retrenchment is upheld by the Tribunal.’ 


The same principles have been enunciated by the Hon'ble Labour 
Appellate Tribunal in the case of Sudaraan Banerji and others vs, Mcleod 
& Co. reported in 19538 .A.C., pages 702-711. In this case also the learned 
Judges reiterated the principle that the authority charged with the duty 
of giving permission would also have to consider the question whether the 
rule of ‘“‘last come, first go’’ has been followed in the proposed retrench- 
ment and if departed from, whether the evidence so led would prima facie 
support the case of departure from that rule. Bearing these principles Im 
mind I proceed to discuss the facts in this case. According to the 
Management the number of 9 gate-keepers is sufficient, and as the Manage- 
ment has prima facie rightly exercised this right in the labour force, 1 
do not think the Court will be justified in interfering with their decision. 
So the firat question is answered in favour of the Munagement. The next 
question is on which personnel should the axe fall. On behalf of the 
Union an attempt has been made to show thut one Chandeswar who joined 
the service in June-July 1956 was employed after this workman was 
retrenched but this allegation is negetived by the evidence of P.W. (4) 
Md. Ibrahim. His evidence is that Chandeswar was in service for about 4 
or § years and then he left the job for some time and rejoined in June or 
July 1956. So it is not a fact as urged by the Union that he was junior 
to the dismissed workman who was employed only on 1161) March ۰ 
Thus it is established thut the Management has not departed from the 
principle of ‘‘last come, first go’’. This workman is the juniormost and 
reasonably the axe fell on him. If the Union could prove that the rule of 
“last come, first go’’ was*departed from, it was upon the Management to 
Justify the departure but in this case the principle has not been departed 
rom,

the workman is entitled to one month’s notice-pay and one month’s pay 
as retrenchment benefit under section 25F of the industrial Disputes Act. 
He put in 1984 months’ service roughly from 11th March 1955 to 15th 
October 1956 and so he is entitled to one month’s pay as compensation. 
Thus he is found entitled to 2 months’ full pay at the rate of Rs. 45 per 
mensem, i.e., Ha. 90 plus back wages, if any. The Company must pay 
Re. 90 ء ںام‎ back wages, if any, to the workman within a month of the 
publication of this award.

Whether the dismissal of Shri Ram Daresh Singh, driver, has heen

AWARD 


The case of the Union is that this driver Ram Daresh Singh was 
summarily dismissed without uny charge-sheet or enquiry on 23rd April 
1956. This dismissal is arbitrary, unjustified and an unfair laboun 


practice. The Union therefore seeks his reinstatement together with 
back wages. 


The case of the Company is that he took an advance of Ra. 300 from 
the Managing Director while he went home on receiving the news of hia 
mother’s illness. 


DECISION 


The Union examined the driver alone. The driver stated in his deposition 
that he was summarily dismissed without any charge-sheet or anything of 
the kind. No. enquiry was held. He has further denied to have 
received an advance from the Managing Director of a sum of Rs. 800 as 
alleged on behalf of the Company. fhe evidence of the driver is practically 
unchallenged. It therefore establishes the case of the Union. On the other 
hand, there is no evidence adduced on behalf of the Company. As regards 
the advance of Rs. 300, it is stated in the written statement of the Company 
that this amount was advanced by the Managing Director himself. There 
is no receipt in token of the advance. The Managing Director does not 
come to prove the advance. 


At the prayer of the Company to secure the presence of the Managing 
Director in order to give a denial to the plea of the driver that he did not 
really take an advance of Ra. 900) an opportunity was given to the Company 
to produce the Managing Director and another date was fixed for hearing 
but on this date (5th July 1957) also the Managing Director did not appear. 
So the plea of advance to the workman fails. 


In the circumstances, I must find that the dismissal of the driver has 
been quite unjustified and mala fide without any semblance of enquiry. 
Therefore such a dismissal is indeed nothing short of unfair labour 
practice and the driver seems to have been dismissed without any reason 
whatsoever. So in law and equity, this order of dimissal is illegal and 
the driver must be reinstated. The back wages, if any, will be paid by

nr ً یججہعسسٍ‎ 


the Company, who will 8190 reinstate the driver in his former job within 
a month of the publication of this award. 


This is my award.

dated 25th April 1957. (Case No. ۷۱۱۱۰۲١۰ 30/57.) 


BEFORE THE FIRST LABOUR COURT, WEST BENGAL. 


PRESENT: 
Sunt N. C. CHATTERIJER, Judge, First Labour Court. 


Appearances : 
For the Union; Shri Madan Saha, Counsel. 


For the Company: Shri 8. K. Dhar, Adovate. 


The Government of West Bengal, in the Department of Labour, by 
order No. 1821-I.R./IR/111,-88/57, dated. 26th April 1957, referred under 
sections 7 and 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947 , the 
industrial dispute between Messrs. Tulsi Charan Das, 50 Battala treet, 
Caleutta-20, and one of their workmen, Shri Rajani Kanta Kayal, 
represented by the Calcutta Goldsmithy and Jewellery Workers’ Union, 
16/17 College Street (Room No. 49), Caleuttu-12, regarding ۵ءء‎ 
specified in the second schedule of the Act, to this Court for adjudication. 


Schedule. 


Is the discharge of Shri Rajani Kanta Kayal justified? To what relief 
18 he entitled? 


AWARD 


The case of the Union is ns follows; 


This workman was employed for about 8 yeara wnder the Company 
Messrs. Tulsi Charan Das, but was dismissed on 6th June 1953 without 
assigning any reason. This workman along with others formed a Tnion 
which enraged the Company and they were dismissed for their Trade 
Union activities without uny justification or reason whatsoever. The 
Union contends that the dismissal of the workman is unjustified, illegal, 
mala fide and an unfair labour practice. The Union therefore secks his 
reinstatement with back wages. 


The Company contends that this is an individual dispute as his 0086 
was not espoused by any. workers or the Union, that the’ allegations in the 


2781 


শা =‏ ہے 


Prat |] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 1, 1957 


written statement of the Union are false. [n fact this workman worked 
only for 2 years and took his arrears of wages on the 19th Juistha, 1363 B.S. 
and gave up his job voluntarily as he started a grocery at his native village. 
The workman is not entitled to reinstatement or any other relief. 


DECISION. 


The Company runs a jewellery business in the premises No. 50, 1 8 
Street, Calcutta-20. It is common ground that this workman Rajan 
Kayal was employed under this Company for some time. The parties are, 
however,.1n dispute as to the actual وا‎ of service of this workman 
under the Company. It is the case of the Company that this workman 
was employed under it roughly for 2 years from Balsakh, 18061 B. দি. up 
to ee 1363 B. 9. and even during this period he was absent for 
5 months and odd and that his wages were Rg. 2 per diem. On the clber 
band, it is urged on behalf of the workman that he had put im about 8 
years’ service and that at a monthly pay of Rs. 90 all told. 001) the 
disputed points, namely, (1) length of service aud (2) bis monthly wages, 
I shall state my findings later on. 


The main point for consideration is whether the discharge of this 
workman js justified. On this head the case of the Company is 11101 the 
workman voluntarily gave up his job as he started a grocery at his native 
village and that he intimated his desire to this effect to the Proprietor 
0). 1১. W. 1. This plea of the Company does not, however, stand scrutiny. 
Assuming that the workman voluntarily left the job it is difficult to believe 
that he would again raise a controversy over it and take up the matter even 
with the Labour Commissioner. [1 he had given up the job voluntarily 
the ordinary course of conduct for him coi be that he would not agitote 
this matter and rest contented with his grocery at home. It is also 
significant in this connection to notice that the Union addressed 0 letter 
Ext. 1 to the Labour Commissioner on 12th July 1956 complaining — that 
the workman was not given any work on and from 6th June 1956 and this 
discharge was stigmatised as motivated, unjustified and illegal and in that 
letter there was also a demand for compensation for the period of his 
forced unemployment. The Company did not reply to this letter 10 the 
T.abour Commissioner. Virtually, the Company accepted this position and 
did not raise any voice of protest against the case of the Union. If the 
allegations in this letter were not true we would expect that the Company 
would have certainly protested against these allegations and come forward 
with the plea now set up that the workman voluntarily gave up his job 
for his grocery at his native village. I am therefore unable to accept the 

len of voluntary resignation of the workman from this job and my finding 

ig that as the workman admittedly ahbsented bimself from his duty 10: 
about 5 or 6 months during the periud from 1361 to 1363 B.S., he obviously 
incurred the displeasure of the Company which therefore discharged him. 
And there is another cause for his discharge which is his enlistment ns 8 
member of the Caleutta Goldsmithy Jewellery Workers’ Union. The 
Company further raised a point that this is an individual dispute as the 
workman enlisted himself as a member of the Union subsequent 10 his 
discharge. P. W. 2, Hem Ranjan Das, the General Secretary of the 
Union, deposed in favour of the workman and his evidence goes unchalleng- 
ed. Therefore the point that this is on individual dispute is not 
substantiated by the Company and fails, As regards this dischurge, my 
finding is that the discharge of this workman is without any justification 
or reason whatsoever. 


The next question is what should be the workman’s relief, The 
workman himself has stated before the Court that he does not seek 


2782 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 1, 1957 [Pant | 


reinstatement. All that he insists on is his back wages for the 5 months 
since his discharge. 


Now | come to the question of monthly wages. The (Company states 
that he used to he paid at the rate of Rs. 2 per diem, and the payment was 
made weekly and that he served only for 2 years. The version of the 
workman, however, 18 different. His case is that he worked for about 8 
years, and hia pay was Rs. 90 per month. The Company _ prostuced 
Khatas (Fxts. Al-3) from 1361 B.S. and has not produced Khatas for uny 

eriod prior to 1361 B.8. The Union urges that if he would have produced 

hatas for years prior to 1361 B.S., they would have revealed his name ۶ 
one of the employees, and the case of the workman proved. I am con- 
vinced that the Company did not produce the Khatas for the previous 
period just to suppress the actual year of the commencement of his service, 
and if they were produced* they would have supported the case of the 
workman. 49 stated in Ext. A, T find that the workman was not 210 
any work on and from 6th June 1966. 


As regards his wages, ‘the statement on behalf of the Company that 
his pay was Rs. 2 per diem does not deserve credence. T accept the state- 
ment of the workman that his pay was Rs. 90 per month up to Kartic, 
1362 33.8. as stated in Ext. 1. The Company, ene has shown thnt on 
one occasion Ra. 27-12 was paid to the workman on 2nd June 1956 
including his overtime wages. This seems to be nothing short of a device 
on the part of the Company to show that this workman used to be paid 
weekly and for this his long absence for 6 months from his duty is 1es- 
ponsible. The Company cannot obviously like a man who chooses to he 
absent from duty for so long a time. Be that as it may, the workman is 
certainly entitled to some compensation for this unjustified discharge of 
his service. It would not be correct to say that this is a case of retrench- 
ment as defined in section 2(o0) of the Industrial Disputes Act. It would he 
retrenchment under the Act only if a workman who was surplus was dir- 
charged but there is no such case here. The worker ennnot therefore 
claim any retrenchment compensation under section 25F of the Industrial 
Disputes Act as laid down in the recent Barsi Light Railwav Co., Ltd., ox. 
K. N. Joglekar and others, reported in 1957 Supreme Court Appeals, 
page 57. The workman is still entitled to payment of compensation as 
equitable relief and that, in my opinion, would be equivalent to his 2 
montha’ pay, i.e., Rs, 180. In the cireumatances my finding is that the 
discharge of the workman is unjustified, and the workman is entitled to an 
equitable relief equivalent to 2 months’ pay, i.e., Rs. 90 plus 90, tatal 
Rs. 180 and not to reinstatement. The Company must pay this amount

ANNEXURE 


in the matter of an industrial dispute existing between Messrs. Bengal 
Corporation Limited, 14 Netaji Subhas Road, Calcutta-1, and their 
employee Shri Samar Chatterjee, 10 Becharam Chatterjee Road, 
Behala, Calcutta-34. (Case No. ۷۱۱۱۰223 of 1955.) 


BEFORE THE SIXTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAT. 


PRESENT: 
5৮৪] SAILESH SENGUPTA, Judge, Sizth Industrial Tribunal 


Appearances: 
For the Company: Shri P. R. Mookherjee, M.A., 17523. 
For the employee: None. 


This reference was made by Government order No. 3886Dis./D! 
11L-255/55, dated Calcutta, the 26th July 1955, for adjudication of the 
issue which is in the following terms in the order of reference :— 


Is the Company justified in debarring Shri Samar Chatterjee from 
attending his duty with effect from 7th February 1955? To what 
relief is he entitled? 


The case made out by Shri Samar Chatterjee, who, I may mention, was 
carrying on a fight against the employer unaided by any other member of 
the establishment or by any Trade Union, is that he had fallen ill on the 
20th of January 1955. On the day following he applied for leave 
through post for a fortnight. He reported for duty on the 5th of February 
and produced a medical certificate. At the time of payment of wages, he 
was offered his salury minus the proportionate amount for the period of 
his absence. He refused to accept the salary as offered and was then 
informed that his services were digpensed with from the 7th of February 
1955. Having failed to induce the Management to change its decision 
Shri Samar Chatterjee sought redress through the machinery of the law 
provided by the Industrial Disputes Act. 


The Company’s case is that Shri Samar Chatterjee was not a workman 
within the meaning of the Industrial Disputes Act, as he had not 
erform any manual or clerical work. On the merits the Company's case 
18 that he had absented himself from office from the 17th of January and 


2754 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 1, 19871 [Part 


pe oer a SR a عسعسسسّعععسمیمیس سسڈٔگپ ھی‎ A ST TY 


on the 21st he had sent a post-curd applving for 14 days’ leave on the 


ground of illness. Since then, he did not report for duty and had 
relinquished the post of his own accord. 


A question of law arose in consequence of which an additional issue 
was framed in the following terms :—- 


Issue No. 2; Is this an industrial dispute? 


issue No. 2: Taking up issue No, 2 for decision, ] came to the finding 
on the authority of two decisions of the Calcutta High Court 
reported in 5) C,.W.N., page 256 und 51 C.W.N., page 169, and a decision 
of the Supreme Court reported in 1953, 1, L.L.J., page 195, that an 
individual dispute is not an industrial dispute but it may be converted 
into an industrial dispute, if it is taken up by his fellow workers or by 
any Trade Union of which hg is a member. As in the present case the 
employee did not secure the assistance of his co-workers and did not also 
find any support from any Trade Union, >8 Tribunal held that the 
individual dispute was not transmuted into an industrial dispute. Hence 
the Tribunal had no juriadietion to adjudicate on the point referred. I 
had also referred to the case reported in 1956, 2, 15150 2 page 41 in 
which an Appellate Tribunal made it clear that the Full Bench decision 
in the Swadesh: Mills Case that an individual dispute ia an industrial 
diapute being covered by the language used in section 2(k) of the Act, was 
not applicable to the case of a discharged or dismissed employee w lose 
enuse has not been espoused by other employees or any Trade Union. 
The award made by me was set aside on appeal. Their Lordships of the 
Appellate Tribunal held that the Supreme Court did not make s 
‘declaration of the law in such clear terms as can lead to a definite 
conclusion either way’’. Their Lordships preferred to follow the Full 
Bench decision in Swadeshi Mills case and sent back the case on remand 
for disposal according to law on the merits after considering other legal 
objections raised in the pleading. Opportunity was to be given to the 
parties to adduce documentary and oral evidences, if any. 


The case being taken up the employee wus found absent. The lawyer 
representing him also did not jappear. The Tribunal heard the lawyer 
for the Company. 


The situation has been complicated by reason of a recent decision of 
the Calcutta High Court to which the attention of their Lordships of the 
Appellate Tribunal was not directed. In the case of Bengal Club 
Limited versus Santi Ranjan Samaddar reported in 60 C.W.N., page 856, 
his Lordship Sinha J. has held, after an exhaustive review of all the 
reported cases, that where an individual workman 1s dismissed and the 
dismissal is not objected to by any Union of workmen or a majority of 
hia fellow workers, that is an individual dispute between the employer 
and an individual workman and is not an industria] dispute. As ad 
pointed out Shri Samar Chatterjee is’ fighting his own battle on his own 
resources. Neither any Union nor other workmen of the Company have 
rallied to his support. The law laid down by his Lordship, Sinha 
applies squarely to the facts of this case. In the case reported in 1955, 
» ].[..1.., page 202, his Lordship the Chief Justice of the Bombay High 
Court made the followiug observation : 


“Kvery Tribunal in any State is subject to the judicial supervision 
of the State High Court. If ony Labour Legislation comes up 
for interpretation before the High Court of the State, that 
interpretation must be accepted by the Tribunal as the correct 
interpretation’. 


Their Lordships of the Appellate Tribunal did not make any pronounce- 
ment as to whether this observation is binding or not. If it is, this 
Tribunal must accept the interpretation of section 2(k) of the Tudustrial 
Disputes Act, made in the recent decision of the Calcutta High Court, 
notwithstanding the view taken by the Appellate Tribunal which 10081 
necessarily be subordinated to the interpretation made by the State 
High Court. This Tribunal owes allegiance to the Appellate Tribunal 
and has )مجر‎ to carry out its directions. Between conflicting loyalties 
the Tribunal was on the horns of ao dilemma. Fortunately thére have 
since been two decisions of the Supreme Court on this identical point 
which give clear guidance. In the case reported in 1957, 1, L.L.J., 
page 29, their Lordships of the Supreme Court delivered judgment 
eushrinjog the view propounded سا‎ the earlier Supreme Court decision. 
It may be said that their Tordships in clear terma guarded themselves 
against making any final pronouncement. Even then, the view expressed 
varries considerable weight. There is next the case reported in ۰ 
F. J. R., Part VI, puge 129, in which their Lordships have laid down the 
law that a dispute touching the individual rights of a workman was not 
intended to be subject of an adjudication under the Act, when 
the same has not been taken up by the Union or a nomber of workmen. 
Their Lordships poimted out that where the appropriate Government had 
referred a dispute on the assumption that ai dispute exists between 
the “employer and his workmen’’, but the points of dispute 11) the 
reference comprised the wrongful termination of the service of only one 
workman, whose case was not taken up by any Union of the workera of 
the establishment in which he was employed, nor by any Union of 
workmen employed in similar or allied trades but by a Trade Union with 
which he had no connection whataoever, the reference was bad. An 
individual dispute accordingly cannot mature into an industrial “age 
even if o Trade Union with which the workman concerned had no 
connection takes up his cause. In the present case, there is no Union 
in the picture. In the Appellate award, it was observed that in view of 
the divergence of opinion, it was desirable that disposul of the appeal 
should be postponed till the point was set at rest by the Hon'ble Supreme 
Court hefure which this point had been raised. Their Lordshipa did 
not, however, postpone the hearing awaiting the decision of the Supreme 
Court. As thereafter the decision of the Supreme Court has been 
available this Tribunal is now free to dispose of the case in the light 
flashed by the Hon’ble Supreme Gourt. The view taken by their Lordships 
of the Supreme Court 1s that this sort of dispute does not attain the 
status of an industrial dispute. This interpretation is binding on alk 
Tribunals, primary and appellate. Hence, I come to the conclusion that 
I am free to decide according to the law as declared by their Lordships. 
I hold that this is an individual dispute to which the Industrial Disputes 
Act cannot be applied. This Tribunal has no jurisdiction to adjudicate 
on the issue referred by the Government 


Dictated and corrected by me.

DECISION 


issue No. 1: Messrs. lmperial Engineering Works, Ltd. (hereafter 
culled the Company) is one of the small engineering concerns having 
workshop at 122 Belilious Road, Howrah. It employa about 25 workmen. 
11001180811 Engineering Mazdoor Union (hereafter called the Union) on 
behalf of the workmen submitted a charter of demands making various 
demands. Most of them were considered by the Government to be 
unreugonable (0৮26 Annexure A to the written statement of the Company) 
and as there could be no settlement regarding the rest, these were referred 
to for adjudication, Under this head the Union claims that minimun 
wages of the workers of the unskilled, semi-skilled and skilled categories 
should be fixed according to the award of the Major Engineering Tribunal 
of 1948 and D.A. should be fixed for them nome, کا‎ (0 the award of the 
Major Engineering Tribunal of 1900. The Company resists the claims 
rome ed on the ground that it has no capacity to bear any additional 
urden. 


Under the award of the Major Engineering Tribunal of 1948 minimum 
wages of unskilled worker was fixed at Rs. 30 per month or Ra. 1-2-6 per 
duy; and of semi-skilled worker at Rs, 30 per month or Rs. 1-5-6 per day, 
in the case of daily-rated workers. No minimum basic pay was, however, 
fixed for the skilled workers. Regarding minimum basic wages there can 
be no dispute that the worker must have it irrespective of the capacity of 
the industry or of his employer to pay. ‘Phe capacity to pay is relevant only 
in respect of upper limit as also D.A. The principles of fixation of minimum 
wages have heen discussed and settled in Buckingham & Carnatick Mills 
Co., Ltd., vs. the Workers of the Company (vide 1952 7,.A.C., 490). It 
has been held that the floor level of wages of an industria] worker must be 
such as would enable hin to maintain 3 consumption units including him- 
self in a state of efficiency with provision for education, and medical expenses 
of children. This is the minimum which the worker must have irrespective 
of the capacity of the industry or of his employer to pay. The Major 
Engineering Tribunal fixed the minimum wages of the unskilled and semi- 
skilled worker having regard to those factors, and I find no reason why 
the said minimum wages should not be extended to this concern. The 
Major Engineering Tribunal comprised big engineering firms as well as 
amall both in the city of Calcutta and Howrah. The Adjudicators fixed 
the aforesaid minimums und with due consideration of all relevant factors. 
So, unleas a special case is made out the Company cannot be exempted from 
adopting the said minimums. The fact that the Company is smail, cannot 
be accepted as a ground for such exemption. No doubt it appears = that 
since the Government of India introduced uniform prices for all controlled 
categories of steel and pig iron at all rail head destinations in the country, 
these small engineering concerns of Howrah have been hard hit due to 
said policy of equalisation of price of pig iron and steel as alao due to 
acute scarcity of raw materials, but none-the-less in the matter of minimum 
basic wages the claim of the workmen must have priority and other 
considerations cannot come. Similarly, if other small concerns of Howrah 
pay wages beyond the minimum as fixed, this would afford no justification 
for not falling in line with the minimum basic wages fixed. The claim of 
the union for minimum basic wages for unskilled and semi-skilled worker 
according to the award of the Major Engineering Tribunal of 1948 must 
so prevail and I fix the minimum accordingly, 


As to the minimum basic wages of the skilled workers, it has already 
heen noted that this was not fixed under the award of the Major Engineering 
Tribuual and J also find no special *circumstances to do otherwise in hia 
case. Ext, B is a chart about the wages and J).A. which are being paid

than to follow it, and provide leave card in Form No, 15 enjoined therein. 
The said rule 87 has been made under the provisions of sections 83 and 112 
of the Factories Act. The Management so has no option than to follow 
the provisions of the rules. The Company is accordingly directed to
