ANNEXURE 
in the mattor of a complaint under séction 33A of the Industrial Disputes 

Act, 1947, as amended by the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) 
Act, 1950, filed by Noor Mahammed and 44 others, workmen of 
Messrs. Anna Art Press (Private), Ltd., 26 Dr. Suresh Sarkar Road, 
6800٥٥8٦14, represented by the Calcutta Press Employees’ Congress, 
12 Dedar Box Lane, Calcutta-16, in connexion with the case which 
was referred to this Tribunal under Government Order No. 857Dis/ 
D /13L-3/56, dated Caicutta, the Sth March 1956. (Case No. 160 of 

1956 under section 33A.) 


BEFORE THE SIXTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST RBENGAI, 


PRESENT : 
Suzi SAILESH SENGUPTA, Judge, Sixth Industrial Tribunal. 


Appearances. 
For the Company: Shri N. ظ‎ Mukherjee, Advocate. 
For the workmen : Shri Tanmoy Basy, Pleader. 


This.is an application ynder section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act 
by a group of workers employed in the Anna Art Press (Private), Limited. 
he grievance giving rise to the’ present complaint’ is that during the 
pendency of a reference proceeding the Management raised the weekly 
working hours from 421 to 48 hours. One of the conditions of service was 
thus altered without the leave of the Tribunal. 


In reply,. the employer advanced the case that work was being conducted 
previously in two shifts. The second shift had to be oldsed down. Due 
to the abolition of the second shift the Press had to get extra work done 
by the employees during the busy season in the months of October to 
December every year. ‘Notice was accordingly issued that the working 
hours would be 48 hours a week at ordinary rate of wages and for overtime 
in excess of 48 hours up to 54 hours wages at double rate would he paid. 
The workers refused to submit to this alteration and thus caused embarass- 
ment to the Management as it could not discharge its obligation to fulfil 
contracts within the periods fixed. According to the Management, ٥ 
change did not contravene section 33 of the Act and the complaint made by 
the employees is misconceived. 


DECISION 


According to the evidence. given by the P.W. 1 wages at 1} rates used 
to be paid previously for work done in excess of 42} hours. If anybody 
worked for an extra hour he used to get wages for 14 hours. But accord- 
ing to the notice Ext. A henceforth up to a maximum of 48 hours per week 
the workers were to get single rate. This amounted to a far-reaching 
alteration in one of the conditions of service. It may be اہ وو‎ at 
the outset that section 33 forbids alteration of conditions of sorvice to the 
prejudice of the workmen concerned in the dispute. The application made 
in this cuse is defective in so far as nothing has been alleged as 60 the 
change being prejudicial to the workmen. The bare statement appears in 
the application that the working hours have been raised from 42} to 48 


2704 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 1, 7 [Parr 1 


সপ | 


hours per week, That this alteration affects the workmen prejudicially 
in regard to their emoluments or otherwise has not been specifically pleaded. 
In his evidence ۱۰۳۰ 1 has explained how their intereats are jeopurdized. 
The Manager Mr, Hallen has admitted that previously anyone working 
bevond 42} hours in a wébk used to be paid at the rate of 14 hours’ wages 
for one hour’s work. ‘‘We used to 085? to quote his words ‘‘for one 
hour’s work wages for 14 hours if he worked beyond 42} hours in a week. 
If an employee worked in a single shift and if we wanted his services for 
extra work we used to pay for 1} hours for one hour’s work.’’ In cross- 
exuminution he stated that if a person worked for 48 hours he would have 
got 14 rates for the extra 91 hours. But according to the notice Ext. A 
up to 48 hours the wages would be paid at ordinary rate. This change 
did affect the workers prejudicially as the rate was reduced. The rate of 
wages is certainly one of the conditiona of service. The alteration is 
ex-facie in derogation of section 33. The employees are however doomed 
to suffer tantalisation as there is a legal obstacle. The notice was issued 
on the 24th of September 1956. The change was to he effective from the 
Ist of October 1956. The amendment of Industrial Disputes Act of 1947, 
as made by the Act of 1956, effected subatantial change in section 33. The 
new section came into force on the 18৮ of September #956. Sub-section 1 
of the new Act which is applicable here provides that no employer shall 
alter the condition of service to the prejudice of the workmen concerned in 
the dispute pending before a Conciliation Officer, a Board .or_ before a 
Labour Court or Tribunal or National Tribunal im regard to any matter 
connected with the dispute. From the record of the reference proceedings 
't appears that the points for adjudication were ৮ 


(1) Minimum “Wages und. scale of + 400 for different categories of 
workers, 


(2) Casual Leave. 
(3) Puja Bonus. 
(4) Retiring Beneftt. 
(6) Are the dismissals of the following workers justified? - What 
relief are they entitled to?— 
(a) Jane Alam. 
(b) Md. Hossain. 
(c) Md. Sarif. 


The question of working hours or rate of wages for extra work was not 
of the points in dispute. The point now agitated not being within the 
ambit of the dispute no ban can be held to have been imposed upon the 
powers of the পদ সপ to make alterations in regard to condition, 
which were not pending decision of the Tribunal. In this view I hold 
that the present complaint is not maintainable and must fail. ھھ‎ thero 
is no case that these workers are protected persons, sub-section 3 of section 
38 need not be considered. The application is im these circumstances 
rejected. 


Dictated and corrected by me.

A COMPETITIVE examination will be held in Calcutta

The post is at সর sanctioned up to 28th February 
1958, but is likely to continue 61761795690, 


2. Pay.—The scale of pay is Rs. 150—5-—-240—10—300 
plub usual dearness and other allowances. 


3. Qualiftoations.— 
Essential 


(i) Citizenship of India as defined in Part II of the 
Conatitution of India. 


(ii) A degree of a recognised University. 


(iii) Sufficient command over English as well as over

from English into Nepali and vice-versa.

4. Concession in age.—(i) The upper age-limit is 
relaxable by 5 years for candidates belonging to Scheduled 
Castes and Scheduled Tribes and by 3 years for displaced 
persons from Pakistan. 


Note.—(a) A displaced person claiming age concession 
must furnish with his/her application satisfactory evidence 
that he/she is a bona fide displaced person from Pakistan, 
e.g., refugee registration card or o certificate from & 
gazetted officer or a Member of the Legislature in 
original (with an attested copy thereof).

Government servants in undivided Bengal, who had 
originally opted to serve in East Bengal and were working 
under the Government of East Bengal after partition but 
have since formally resigned their service under that

(iii) A candidate who before the 15th August 1947 was

his/her activities in connection with the country’s struggle 
for independence, not being convicted of an offence indicat- 
ing moral turpitude, shall be entitled to a concession in 
respect of the maximum age-limit. The concession granted 
will be equal to the exact period of detention, imprison- 
ment, internment or extornment suffered up to a maximum 
of four years. A candidate who claims the concession for 
relaxation of the age-limit should submit along with his/ 
her application a certificate in original (with an attested

sible person, testifying to the period of detention, etc., 
suffered by the candidate.

nagore who have received their education in Chandernagore 
through the medium of French is relaxable by 3 years.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 


The object of this Bill is to impose an annual tax cn the net weath of 
individuals, Hindu undivided families and companies, The proposed tax 
is an important constituent of an integrated tax structure which QGovern- 
ment have been aiming at for some time. With Income-tax, Estate Duty 
and a tax on Capital gains already in existence and with the addition of 
the Wealth-tax und a tux on large personal expenditures (separately being 
proposed) the direct taxes will form a composite system made up of com- 
plementary elements. Apart from the fact that a composite tax system of 
this type ھ7‎ to sutisfy the criterion of the ability to pay, it is consistent, 
with the avowed goal of the attainment of o socialistic pattern of soviety. 


New JEL; 


The 15th May, 1987. 
T. T. KRISHNAMACHARI 


FINANCIAL MEMORANDUM 


This Bill proposes 0 levy of tax with effect from Ist April, 1947 on the 
net wealth of individuals, Hindu undivided families and companies. This 
is a new tax but the procedure for assessment and collection of this new tax 
is very much allied to that of taxes on income. It 18) therefore, proposed 
that for the time being wealth-tax be administered by the TIncome-tax 
Department and that no separate administrative machinery should be set up. 
The existing pressure of work on the Income-tax Department is, huwever, 
alrendy quite heavy. This pressure is likely to increase further un account 
of the proposed lowering of the minimum taxuble limits. It will, therefore, 
be necessary to expand adequately the staff at various levels of the depart- 
mental cadres.

No. 5070/ M.LC-73 /57.—dl at Tuly 1957.—Where- 
na the Corporation of Calcutta hus recommended 
by a resolution passed in conformity with the 
১10৮1816১18 of clause (xxi) of section 526 of the 
0ا‎ Municipal Act, 1951 (West Bengal Act 
১111 of Wo), at its meeting beld on the 10th 
May 1997, that a grant of Rs, 1,000 towards the 
اھ‎ of orwanising a Seminar on Slum Clearance 
to be held in Bombay in May 1997, under the 
uuspices ١۶ the Indian Conference of Social 
Workers, be sanctioned ; 


And whereas the Governor is of the opinion 
that the payment of the said grant is likely to 


০০০ ڈ5‎ সিসি তি EIEIO hs th “উহা সস ০০০, 


OT জা শাল م۔ ہس‎ ety یہ‎ 


promote the public health and convenicnee of the

ferred by clause (xxi) of section 526 of — the

Burdwan.—No. P.H./8623/W-55/56.—2nd August 1957.—In pursuance 
of rule 8 of the rules for the preparation, publication and execution of 
projects for water supply, drainage or sewerage by municipal authoritiea, 
it is hereby notified for general information that the Water Supply Re- 
modelling Scheme of the Burdwan Municipality in the distriet of Burdwan 
ae been approved by Government and the particulars of the scheme are as 
ollows :— 


1. (a) General description of the scheme.—The present scheme has 
been drawn up in the lines of sketch project prepared in the year 1948 to 
eater for an ultimate population of 120,000 and the total supply has been 
estimated as 2,140,000 g.p.d. for the present which can be raised to 3,210,000 
g.p.d. by increasing the pumping hours from 12 to 18 hours a day and 
thereby the average supply can improved from 21.4 g.p.e.d. for lac 
population to 27 g.p.cd. for the ultimate population of 120,000 
in the sketch project. It was contemplated to supply at 20 g.p.c.d. to an 
ultimate population of 90,000 for the central conjested part of the town 
whereas for the rest 30,000 persons, 1 was proposed to supply at an average 
rate of 10 g.p.ce.d. But in the detailed project, however, considering 
importance of the town and more 90 after the present electrification of 
Railways up to Burdwan it is expected that Burdwan town will grow iu al) 
directions and sewerage will be an absolute necessity for the safe disposal 
of town waste. Consequently the detailed project hus contemplated to supply 
at an average rate of 21.4 g.p.c.d. for the present population of the town. 


The whole municipal town has been subdivided into four convenient zones 
for equitahle water supply in each part of town of which Zones I, TI, and 
III are being supplied from tube-wells whereas Zone TV will be supplied 
from the existing waterworks through the existing elevated Reservoir.

OFFICE OF THE ACCOUNTANT-GENERAL, WEST BENGAL 


NOTIFICATION. 


Subject: Travelling Allowance 


No. TM /627.—27th July 1957.—All Controlling Officers of the State 
Government may please refer to Government of West Bengal, Finance 
Department (Audit Branch), Memo. No. 805-F/F2A-152/56, dated 20th 
March 1957 (copy raproduced below) and ensure that claims of road mileage 
in terms of proviso to rule 49 of the West Bengal Service Rules, Part ,ال‎ 
ure invariably supported by necessary certificates to be furnished 
separately by them in terms of the second sub-paragraph of paragraph 1 of 
Finance Department’s Memo. referred to above. 


[Copy of Government of West Bengal, Finance Department (Audit 
Branch), Memo. No, 805-F/F2A-152/56, dated tho 20th March 1957.] 


In cases where the journey is made by a service open to the public on 
hire, the mileage allowancé is restricted to twice the actual fare paid for 
the journey. It is, therefore, necessary that the actual fare charged should 
be shown in the bills otherwise audit hos no means of satisfying itself 
that the road mileage claimed has not exceeded twice the actual fare 
charged and paid for the journey. As the information 1s not generally 
furnished by the Drawing Officers, Government are pleused to issue tire 
following instructions for guidance :— 

(1) When road journey is performed by a service open to the public | 
on hire, the mode of conveyance used should be indicated in the 
Travelling Allowance Bill within brackets under the word 
“road’’, e.g., ‘‘road (bus)’’ and the actual fare charged should 
be indicated in remarks column; 


(2) When road journey is actually performed in a private or hired 
conveyance and the road mileage is proposed to be allowed in 
terms of the proviso to rule 49 of West Bengal Service Rules, 
Part II, a certificate should invariably be furnished by 08 
8 Officers on the lines indicated in Note 1 below that 
rule. 


P. 0. HALDAR, 
Dy. Accountant-General (Admn.).

Questions 


(1) Whether all the workmen of the Jute Textile Industry other than

month in terms of the aforesaid award.

to increase in basic wages by Rs. 8 per month in terms of the said award.

was modified in part.

The parties who appeared and suggested answers to the questions referred

Question No. 1: The award of the Third Jute Textile Tribunal on the 
devision fixing the basic wages of the manual workers that has given rise 
to the question at issue is as follows: ‘‘We, therefore, decide and award that 
for 0 48-hour week, the lowest paid worker shall get a basic wage of Rs. 34.67 
or Rs. 84-10-9 and a dearness allowance of Rs. 32.50 or Rs. 32-8 per month. 
The total wage for the lowest paid worker will, therefore, be Rs. 67.17 or 
Rs. 67-2-9 per month. The result 16 that there will be an increase of 
Rs. 3.80 or about Rs. 3-12-9 per month for all categories of manual workers all 
along the scale. Consequent on the fixation of 2 basic wage of the lowest 
paid worker at Rs. 34-10-9 per month, every worker in the industry except 
the clerks, mistries and durwans will have his basic wage raised by Rs. 8.67 
or Rs. 8-10-9 per month (0 maintain the existing differentials. The dearness 
allowance shall be the same, 1.e., Rs. 32.50 or Rs. 32-8 per month for all 
categories of workers including the clerks, mistries and durwans. As a 
consequence, the standardised wages mentioned in Appendix VI of the First 
Award will undergo a change. The new standardised wages will appear 
in Appeidix VIIT of this award. The figures in Appendix VIIJ have been 
arrived at in the same way as detailed in paragraph 6(2) of the First 
Award, 1.e., by adding Rs. 8.67 to the old basic wage in Appendix VI of 
the First Award and then by pursuing a process of rounding off, so as to 
make each figures correspond to a rate expressed in annas and whole pies 
per hour. We have arrived at figures of rupees with decimal fractions 
which may be converted into rupees, annas and pies. We award that subject 
to the directions in regard to basic wages of the manual workers in the 
Prabartak Jute Malls and some other minor mills mentioned hereafter, the 
scheme of basic wages mentioned in Appendix VIII shall be applieable to

ہے گی 


all workers concerned in all other Jute Mills involved in this reference except 
the clerks, mistries and durwans.’’ (pages 54-55) ° * * “Consequent 
on a revision of the standardised wages as mentioned in Appendix VIIT of 
this uward, w revision of the piece-rates mentioned in Appendix V of the 
First Award has also become necessary’’ page 21) > ক جج‎ The 
standardised wages mentioned in Appendix VIII for these piece-rated 
workers mean that the piece-rated workers working with diligence and 
efficiency and maintaining the average standard of production does earn not 
Jess than the standard of basic wages which we have indicated in the

indicated in Appendix VIII. The new standardised piece-rates will appear

On the above statement of the Tribunal, the contentions of the Unions 
are as followa:— 


The Bengal Chatka] Mazdoor Union states that the employer refused to

present award, is not justified on a reading of the award. <A similar

The answer to the question is that all the workmen of the Jute Textile

The Third Jute Award follows the general plan of the previous two 
awards. At page 86, the Third Award states as follows :— 


“This is the, third of the Major Jute Textile Industry Tribunals 
appointed by the Government of West Bengal to adjudicate on the 
wage structure and other terms of employment and conditions of 
service in the Jute Textile Industry in West Bengal since August 
1947. We have found it proper to accept the basic structure of 
the two previous awards, and have advanced a step further in the 
progress of the wage towards a living wage. The three awards 
make a consistent whole and present a complete picture of the 
terms of employment and conditions of service in the Jute Textile 
Industry in West Bengal.’ 


This award follows the general pattern of the First and the Second Awards. 
The Third Award is silent as to how the wages that are above the standar«is- 
ed wages formulated in Appendix VIII are to be dealt with. The First 
Award at page 28 states on the point as follows سے‎ 


‘We agree generally with the principle enunciated in these observa- 
tions, and we have derided that no reduction in respect of the 
existing scales of wages should be allowed to take place by virtue 
of the scheme of standardisation which we have set forth in 
Appendix VI under the present iasue.”’ 


The clear direction was that the existing wages which were above the 
standardised rates shall not be reduced. As all the three awards follow the 
same general basic structure and together present a complete picture of the 
terms of employment and conditions of service in the Jute Textile Industry 
in West Bengal, it should he understood that the intention of the award is 
that no reduction in the existing scales of wages should take place by virtue 
of the scheme of standardisation as set forth in Appendix VIII of the award. 
This decision of the First Tribunal helps to clear the question as to how the 
existing wages above the newly constructed standardised rates should be 
dealt with und clarifies such disputes raised in regard to all the three questions 
dealt with this decision.

clearly show that the new standardised basic wages for the mistries have 
been mentioned in Appendix X of this Award and the mistries can claim 
the increase if they claim the basic wages prescribed in Appendix X of the 
award and not otherwise. Question No. 2 is, therefore, answered

These words appear to have given rise to a good deal of controversies.

and ward staff have not given any increment. The workers have

The flat increment of Rs. 8 to the wages of the jamadars, havildars and

awarded, the directions of a flat increment of Ks. 8.67 shall not apply. 
The learned spokesman for the Jute Workers’ Federation stated that this 
observation of the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal shows that the flat

the awarded wage and not where it was slightly lower than the awarded 
wage, but higher than the wage as prescribed by the Second Award. This 
contention is not supported by the statement of the Hon’hle Labour Appel- 
late Tribunal as mentioned above. It is clearly stated that the Tribunal 
clearly intended to retain in full conditions laid down in the Second Award 
and the said conditions are consistent with equity, justice and good con- 
science. There should not be any compulsion on the goodness and 
generosity of the employers to be more yenerous. To remove the confusion, 
the conditions as stated above were incorporated in the decision. 


The answer to the question is that all durwans in the Jute Textile Industry 
are entitled to an increase of Rs. 8.67, as allowed by the Hon’ble Labour 
Appellate Tribunal of India so as to reach the standardised wages of 
Rs. 73.67 for jamadars, Rs. 58.67 for havildars und Rs. 44.67 for 8۰

AWARD 


In the present case the workmen are represented hy two Unions, viz., 
Paharpur Works Employees’ Union (hereinafter called the Employees’ 
Union) and G.E.C. Staff & Workers’ Union (hereinafter called Workers’ 
Union). Regarding Issue No. 1 which is in respect of dismissal of nine 
workers, the G.E.C. Staff & Workers’ Union refrained from making any 
comment. But the Paharpur Works Employees’ Union took up the cause 
of those nine workmen. This Union contends inter alia that the dismissal 
of these nine workmen was illegul, improper, and mala fide and carried with 
ulterior motive. Five of them are members of the 14060000158 Committee of 
the Union or Executive Committee and the remaining four are active 
members of the Union. The Employees’ Union claims that they should be 
reinstated with compensation. Regarding the Issues Nos. 2, 3, 4 and 5 the 
demands of both the Unions are one and the same. The Unions contend 
that the workmen of the Company had all along been enjoying annual 
customary bonus at the rate of one month’s basic wages দি in the month 
of July-August every yeur irrespective of profit and lous. The workers got

such bonus till the year 1953 but the Company arbitrarily stopped payment 
of this bonus. Besides this annual customary bonus, the workmen are 
entitled to get profit bonus as the Company is earniug considerable profits 
every year. So the Unions have claimed both customary bonus and profit- 
sharing bonus for the year 1904-53. for the workinen of this Compuny. 
The Unions further contend that in this Company there are many workers 
who hail from up-country and the short holidays available from time to time 
cannot be properly utilised by them as they cunnot go to their native villages 
during these holidays. So they require ae with pay for a month or so 
in a year for the purpose of going to their villages in cases of emeryency. 
The Unions therefore demand that in cases of emergency up-country work- 
men shall be allowed such leave. Then again, the workmen in this Company 
have been enjoying the benefit of block closure of 10 days with pay during 
the Pujas without any condition attached thereto in respect of attendance. 
But in 1954 all on a sudden and without any notice whatsoever the Company 
refused to grant this henefit to the workers. The Unions claim that this 
benefit of block closure of 10 days with pay at the time of Puja is a right 
and condition of service and as such should be restored. The Unions urge 
that though the rates of basic wages and dearness allowance now existing 
in this Company are in accordance with the Major Engineering Tribunal 
Awards, they require revision as there has been a material change in the 
circumstances. It is high time that the rates of wages of different 
categories should be improved. The Unions further contend that this 
Company has a scheme of granting annual increment to workmen but it is

during the year 1954-55, the Company did not and could not make any 
€2z-gratia payment, The trading results of the Company for the vear 
1954-55 do not justify the claim of the workmen for any share as bouus. 
After meeting all the prior charges there is no available surplus to distribute 
among the workers. The Company in consideration of the interests of 
industry is compelled to discourage long Jeave without wages to its work- 
men as it affects the proper working of the factory and hampered production. 
Still it grants leave without pay to its workmen in emergency cases. Such 
emergency cuses depend upon several facts and circumstances and should he 
left to the discretion of the Management. The Company nays that the benefit 
of block closure is stil] being continued. So the question of restoration does 
not arise. Regarding the existing rates of wages and dearness allowance, 
the Company contends that it was a party to two Major Engineenng 
Tribunal Awards of 1948 and 1950 and the Company has fully implemented 
directions of the said two awards. In matter of wages and denrness 
allowance, the Company tollows the said two awards. So there 1s no scope

In upproaching the question as to whether the dismissal of these nine 
workmen was justified or not we have io keep in view the principles laid 
down in the Buckingham & Carnatic case (1942, J.A.C., page 490); that 
is to say, that an Industrial Tribunal should not sit in appeal over the 
decision of the Management in the matter of termination of service of 
employees unless— 


(a) there was want of bona fides on the part of the Management; or 


(b) that there wus victimisation or unfair labour practice or violation 
of the principles of natural justice; or 


(c) there was basic error on the facts; or 


(d) there was perverse finding on the materials available to the 
Management. 


Undue interference by a Tribunal with the administration and Management 
is not encouraged. It is of course open to the Tribunal to examine the 
findings of the Management on the allegation of misconduct to assure itself 
that there is evidence to support the finding and that the decision of the 
Management is possible in view of the facts before it. In such cases the 
Tribunal should refrain from substituting its own judgment for the 
judgment of the Management, as in auch matters the Tribunal does not act 
like a court of appeal but rather as a supervisory body.

I shall take up the question of profit bonus first. The claim for such 
bonus arises on the general principle that Jabour and capital should share 
the surplus left after meeting necessary and prior charges. All the 
Tribunals now follow in this respect the well-established principles laid 
down by the Labour Appellate Tribunal in its Full Bench decision in the 
case of Mill Owners’ Association, Bombay, versus Rashtriya Mill Mazdoor 
Sangha, Bombay (1950), 2 F.J.R. (107), It has been clearly laid down in 
the above case that the claim for bonus is to arise if there 18 any surplus 
profit left after making provision for prior charges and fair return on paid 
up capitul and on reserve employed as working capital. The financial year 
of this Company is from April to March. In the present case the claim for 
bonus is for the year 1954-55. That being so, we are to consider the financial 


Pant 1] THE CALMAUTTA GAZLTTE, AUGUST 8, 1947 2853 


position of this Company for the year ending 3lst March 1950. The 
Company has produced the audited balance sheet and profit and loss account for 
the year ending ا915‎ March 1955, The Company claimed that the said docu- 
اد‎ should be dealt with as confidential under section 21 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, 1947. Hence I cannot include in this award figures that can 
be got from the anid document. But it is patent thereform that this 
Company suffered loss over 3 lakhs during the year 1954-55. O.P.W. 8 
Shri A. K. Bose, Accountant of the Company, haa also stated so in bia 
evidence. The balunce sheet produced by the Company must be presiriued 
to be correct unless the contrary is shown by definite evidence. سا‎ the 
present case the Unions could not show anything that the balance sheet was 
not correct. Thus it is crystal clear that for the year 1954-5) there remuined 
no available surplus but on the contrary the Company suffered huge loss in 
its business in that year. Hence the claim of the Unions for profit bonus 
for এক 1954-55 1s untenable and cannot be sustained. It is accordingly 
rejected. 


Now I would take up the claim of customary bonus as put forward by 
the Unions. The leading case in this respect is Mahalaxmi Cotton Mill's 
case (1952-93, I.J.R., 248) and this is a চিক of the Lubour Appellate 
Tribunal of India. It is the contention of the Unions that the employees 
of this Company have been paid bonus equivalent to one month’s ۵ 
wages for good many years irrespective of profit and loss and that this 
leads to an inference of an implied grant as a term of employment and 
definitely excludes the hypothesis that payments have been made out of 
bounty. The Unions contend further that such payments made for a 
number of years had acquired the status of customary bonus. The Wnions 
took their stand on the authority of the Mahalaxmi Cotton Mill’s case and 
the entire claim is based, what the Tribunal finds, on the observation as 
made by their |ordships in the aforesaid case. 


The case of the Company, us I understood it is that these payments were 
mude ex-gratia, and only as a gesture of goodwill and that these payments 
were not mude out of an implied agreement nor did they acquire the status 
of 0 customary bonus. The learned representative of the Company has 
argued that no claim for «a customary bonus could be founded in a or 
equity and no claim of bonus could be made except on the basis of 
prosperity of tho concern. In support of this several decisions including 
the decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India in the Muir Mill’s case 
(1955 1..A.C., page 1) were cited. But it is to he remembered that in case 
of customary bonus the liability depends exclusively on the express or the 
implied contract under which a cluim thereto arises. It was pointed out in 
the case of Muhalaxmi Cotton 0111] that the mght to Puja bonus is not 
based on the general principle that Labour and capital should share the 
surplus left over after meeting the necessary and proper charges but, on 
the other hand, it rests on agreement which may he either express or implied. 
In the Mahaluami Cotton Mill’s case their Lordships further observe ‘‘where 
such agreement is not express, past practice may lead to an inference of 
on were agreement. But for implying an agreement the practice must he 
unbroken and for a sufficiently long period to exclude the hypothesis that 
payments had been made out of bounty. The fact that the payments had 
been made even in a year of loss would be an important factor on the 
question as to whether the payments were mere acts of bounty or an 
obligation on the part of the employers’’. 


Now let me consider the evidence on record. O.P.W. 5 Shri Arun 
Kumar Bose is the Accountant of this concern. He has been in service since 
1944 and took charge of the Accounts Department of this concern in 1948.

ee طحجحجصح٢صحصحصحصحصس‌کص سس‎ 


He was constrained to admit in his cross-exumination that bonus was paid 
to the workers since 1944, It however appears from his evidence ¢vide 
exuminstion-in-chief) that since 1948-49 this concern has been paying to its 
workers bonus equivalent to one month’s hasic pay. He deposed that 
{hough 1950-51 wae a year of loss to the Company yet it paid bonus at that 
rate to the workers in order to maintain good labour relation. It has further 
come out from his evidence that in the financial year 1953-54 there was ulso 
loss of this cuncern but still the Company on the basia of an agreement made 
with the workers paid bonus equivalent to 21 days’ basic wages. But he 
wanted to say that such payments were all made ex-gratin. In this 
connexion 1 um constrained to say that save and except the payment that 
wits mude for the financial year 1953-54 on the basia of an agreement (in 
respect of which I shall say presently) no positive evidence is forthcoming 
from the side of the Company that payments for all these years were made 
ex-gratiu and accepted as such by the employees. The Compuny could have 
produced cogent documentary evidence to show this. But the stubborn fact 
remains that the Company could not and did not produce such evidence. 
In the circumstances it can very well be presumed that the payments were 
not made ex-gratiu as alleged. The payment for the financial year 1953-54 
was no doubt made on the basis of an agreement. Exhibit T(1) is the copy 
of that agreement which is deseribed as memorandum of settlement. ۸ 
uppears from this document that Paharpur Engineering Employees’ Union 
raised a demand cluiming one month’s basic wage as annual customary bonus 
for the year 1953-54 from the Company and sought intervention of the Labour 
Directorate. The parties attended joint conference in the J.abour Directorate 
and the dispute سے‎ to the claim for bonus payable in the year 1953-44 
was settled on the terms that each workman would get a gratuitous sum 
equivalent to 21 days’ basic wages in respect of the fact that the Company 
had suffered heavy loss. It was also agreed that payment of bonus by the 
Company even in a year of loss should not be taken as precedent of future 
years, or in other words it would not confer on the workmen a right that 
honus thus paid was a customary bonus. The Company took its stand on 
this document and wanted to defeat the claim of the workera for customary 
bonus, But آ‎ may say straightway that this agreement cannot stand in 
the way. This agreement was made by the Company and a_ section of 
workers represented by Paharpore Engineering Employees’ Union. But 
other workers who are members of the other Union, that is, G.E.C. Staff & 
Workers’ Union were not parties to that agreement. An agreement by & 
section of workers only, when it 1s known that others were not parties to 
it, would not bind the workers [vide 1962 (1), L.L.J., page 493]. An 
agreement should not be the basis of an award when it is known that other 
workmen are not parties to this. So the agreement Ext. T(1) is of no help 
or assistance to the Company. The Unions, on the other hand, have 
produced a very important document. It ts Ext. 16. It is a notice dated 
29th September 1953, issued by the Company. Paragraph 2 of this notice 
is relevant for our purpose. It is clearly stated there that the customary 
annual bonus of one month’s basic pay has already been paid in July of 
that yeur. This notice was issued by no less person than the General 
Manager who is indeed a very responsible officer of the Company. There 
is no ambiguity or vagueness in the recital. Mention is made of customary 
annual bonus equivalent to one month’s basic pay in this notice in clear 
and unequivocal terms. It 1s an admission coming from the side of the 
Company that customary annual bonus equivalent to one month’s basic pay 
was being paid to the workers. I must say that this admission is fatal to 
the Company. 


The payment of bonus for an unbroken period of 10 years from 1944 
even in years of loss coupled with the admission of the Company as stated 


[98711] THE (কানা ক GAZETTE, AUGUST 8, 1957 2805 


above leads to the inference of an implied agreement of a customary bonus 
equivalent to one month’s basic wage or pay payable to the workers of this 
concern in the month of July-August every year. Finally, the learned 
representative of the Company has argued that a period of 10 years is not 
long enough for pronouncing an opinion that the practice to pay bonus has 
been for a reasonably long period. I am fully aware that in common law 
according to the maxima of jurisprudence a custom has to be ancient and 
invanable before it can be said to acquire the force of Jaw, I am afraid 
we cannot import rigidly those maxims of common law regarding antiquity 
into industnal law which is yet im the formative stage. The separate 
existence of this Company dates from 1948 or so and before this it was a 
part of the G.E.C. (India) Ltd. But still we have got from the evidence 
of the Accountant (O.P.W. 6) that such bonus was paid to the workers from 
1944. It would be absurd for us to insist that the custom of paying bonus 
in this concern should he ancient or even older than 1944. 1 feel inclined 
to the view that in industrial matters a custom need not be insisted upon 
to be uncient, and need only be sufficiently old according to the circumstances 
of the case. Their Lordships of the Labour Appellate Tribunal of India in 
the case of Mahalaxmi Cotton Mill observed also that it was not possible 
fo suy, in general terms, what should be the length of the period. In the 
present case the employer concerned started giving bonus and continued it 
from 1944 right up to 1953-54, even though in some years the Company 
suftered loss. During aj] this period the employees could well have been 
led to believe by regular payments of bonus that payment of annual bonus 
in this concern was customary. For the reasons stated above J hold that 
the workers of this concern are entitled to claim bonus as a customary right. 
Accordingly, I award customary bonus equivalent to one month's basic wage 
or pay for the year 1954-44 to the workers of this Company. Such payment 
must be made within a month from the date of publication of the award in 
the Calcutta Gazett®. The workmen shall get no other bonus for the year 
in question. This issue T decide thus. 


issue No. 3 


This issue is divided into two parts. Regarding the point whether in 
cases of emergency the up-country workmen should get leave without

to the up-country workmen. Granting of such leave is discretionary on the 
part of the Management. Certainly it should be left to the discretion of 
the Management. It is not possible nor is it desirable to make hard and fast 
rule. It tag purely management function, the Management shall decide 
the question of emergency as well as the period of leave for the yeur for 
the up-country workmen in cases of emergency. Exhibit X(1) series are 
few applications for leave without pay made by several up-country workmen. 
They go to show that the Management duly considered those applications 
and allowed such leave to the workers as was considered reasonable and 
proper in the circumstances. It cannot be said that the Management 
exercised their discretion in this respect arbitrarily or capriciously. 
would rather say that the Management showed রা and reasonable 
attitude in the matter of dealing with those leave applications. Hence the 
Tribunal is not disposed either to fix the period of such leave for the up- 
country workmen or to say anything regarding the emergency of such leave. 
It is left to the discretion of the Management.

Schedule 


Whether the termination of services of (a) Jaymangal, (b) Munshilal, 
and (c) Krishna Bahadur is justified? To what delief are they entitled ? 


AWARD 


The case of the Union is that the Company Messrs. Pravati Textile Mills 
is &, silk manufacturing concern under which these 3 dismissed workmen were 
working as Darwans. One of the dismissed darwans Jaymangal was granted 
leave for 90 days with effect from 10th May 1956 but دہ‎ his return on 
911) August 1956 he was not permitted to resume his duty. Two other work- 
men, namely, Munshilal and Krishna Bahadur, were not allowed to work 
since 11th August 1956 as the key was taken away from them. These 3 
workmen have thus been wrongfully dismissed without assigning any 
reason or justification. The Union therefore seeks their reinstatement with 
hack wages. 


In this case the Company did pot put in any written statement on the 
fixed date 5th June 1957, nor on any subsequent dates 1161) June 1957, 
18th June 1957, 25th June 1957 and 3rd July 1967. So on 8rd July 1957 
by its orders the Court fixed 12th July 1957 for hearing. Therefore the 
Company did neither put in any written statement, nor turn up at the time 
of hearing to contest this reference. 


DECISION 


The only point for consideration is whether the services of these work- 
men were wrongfully terminated. 


The Union has examined these 3 workmen. Their evidence establishes 
their case in the written statement. V’rima facie there is absolutely no 


2860 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 3, 1957 (1১৬1 1 
লা 


reason or justification for terminating their services. These 5 ৮05 ৯1011 have 
deposed uniformly that they were asked to sign application forms tor tresh 
admission into service which they refused to do because they were old 
servants und if they did so they would have been denied the benefits of their 
past services. Obviously for this attatude which cannot be decribed as un- 
reasonable or দশা | the Company did not allow them to work further 
and thus virtually discharged them from their services. It is evident that 
Jaymanyal put in about 9 years’ service, Munshilal and Krishna Bahadur 
put in about 14 years’ and 6 years’ service respectively. There i» nothing 
to show that these workmen committed any misconduct or offence to merit 
the dismissal. In the circumstances, i:cinstatement is the normal = relief 
which cannot justly be denied tu them. I therefore find that this is a very 
fit cuse for re1ustatement, 


As regards their claim for back wages, I consider it fit and proper to 
allow three months’ back wages to Munshilal who has put in a longer period 
of service aud one month’s back wages to the other 2 workmen. Munshilal 
will therefore get three months’ pay, i.e., Rs. 150, and Jaymangal and 
Krishna will each get one month’s pay, i.e., Rs. 44 and 50 respectively. The 
Company will reinstate them within a month of the publication of this 
award and also pay up the aforesaid amounts to them within the same period.

FINDINGS 


Issue Nos. 1 and 2: Issue Nos. ا1‎ and 2 are taken up together. The 
Union’sa case is that due to the change in circumstances, since the last 
settlement, dated 10th June 1949, the minimum wages and dearness allow- 
ance should be revised. The minimuin scale of pay for unskilled workers 
shall be Rs. 40 to Rs, 70 per month with annual inerement at Re. 4, 
Dearness allowance shall be at the flat rate of Rs. 80 per month. The 
Company resists these demands on the ground that both the existing wages 
and dearness allowance were udequate and = that there was no change in 
cirewnstances justifying their claim within such a short time, and that 
the financial condition does not permit any upward revision at the moment. 
Tt also pleaded that since the settlement, dated 10th June 1949, was not 
terminated by a notice under section 19(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
the issue should not be adjudicated. 


Both parties did not adduce any oral evidence. Shri N. M. Das (tupta, 
Advocate for the Company, relied upon the Ext. A, the settlement in ques- 
tion and Exts, B and Bl, Income ‘lux Assessment Order for two years and 
Pay Register (Ext. C) and contended that the issues should not be reopeved 
for fresh adjudication till the agreement, which is binding on the parties, 
was not lawfully terminated by ৮ valid notice under section 19(2) of the 
Industrial Disputes Act. The agreement, dated 10th June 1949, was made 
in the presence of the Conciliation Officer. It appears from paragraph 16 
that the terms of this agreement was binding on both parties for one year 
only, t.e., from the date (8lst May 1949) of its execution, The agreement, 
therefore, was meant to be binding on the parties till 9156 May 190).

According to section 19(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, such settlement 
was binding only up to that date, i.e., for such periud as was agreed upon 
by the parties. The question of its continuation beyond a period 01. Kix 
months, therefore, would not arise in this cnse. Neither it 1s required to 
be terminated by a notice under section 19(2) which is applicable in a case 
where no روکس‎ was specially mentioned in the agreement. Therefore, 
that objection 19118. 


That there has been change in the circumstances is apparent from the 
record. It is common knowledge that cost of living has gone up since the 
date of the last settlement. It is more so in the last few months. The 
cost of living index in April 1949 and April of this year is shown helow: 


1949 Working class 362.5 
1957 Working class 383.1. 


A glance at this figure shows that there has been an overall increase of at 
least 20 points over that of 1949, and that 7 years cannot be said to be a 
short time for considering w case for revision. Apparently, the basic needs 
of a worker are now more than what they were in 1949 and which could 
not be fully met out of the existing pay and deurness allowance. Shri 
Panchanan Bhattacherjee, for the Union, contended that the demands on 
the incoine of a worker are more than what the said index figures suppose 
to indicate and that it is high time for both the basic minimum wages 
which ure, undoubtedly, less than those prevailing in comparable industries 
and the dearness allowance which is equally inadequate should be raised to 
Rs. 40 and Its. 00 per month as in the demand. Shri N, M. Das Gupta 
wanted to make an additional point at the time of argument when he said 
that the workers are paid more than Rs. 29+ Rs. 2=Rs. 31 per month as 
stated in the written statement. In fact, they were paid initially 
Rs. 81+ Rs. 10= Rs. 41 per month. This was entirely a new case which 
was not stated in the written statement. I am unable to accept this conten- 
tion not only on this ground but also on the ground that there is hardly 
any acceptable evidence to establish that fact. Shri Das Gupta also pleaded 
that the Company is a proprietory concern in which the proprietor himself 
works as any other employee and earns very little profit as would ke 
evident from the Income Tax Assessment Order for the two years 1955-56 
and 1956-57 (Exts. B and Bl). The pay register (Ext. C) is not of much 
help on this point. It appears from Exts. B and B1 that the Company 
টির its account books, with profit and loss accounts, before the 
ncome Tax Officer, and that the net profit in 1956-57 was more than double 
of the previous year. It further shows that the Income Tax Officer did 
not completely rely upon the accounts shown to him. In any case, in the 
last two yeurs, the Company made profits out of the business, and there was 
nothing to show that it was unable to pay any increase on account of 
minimum wages and dearness allowance. That contention, therefore, fails. 


Shri N. M. Das Gupta contended that this reference concerned five 
employees only, who were employed in the Company’s shop at 128 
Khengrapatty Street, Caloutta, and it did not concern the employees who 
were employed in the Company's workshop situated at a different place. 
The workshop, where the five other employees were employed, is at 140 
Old China Bazar Street, within the same locality. Shri Das Gupta’s 
contention was that since the reference has omitted to mention the addreas 
of the workshop, it should be taken to concern those employees who were 
employed in the shop at 123 Khengrapatty Street. Shri Panchanan 
Bhattacherjee, however, contended that the reference was not limited to 
cases of employees who were employed in the shop only, but also to the 
employees who were employed in the workshop. At his request, I consulted 


Part ]1[ THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 8, 1957 2863 
পল্লি হা 
the Lahour Commissioner's file. There is nothing found either iu that file 
or in the charter of demands (Ext. 1) or in the order of reference itself, 
by which ا(‎ can be reasonably construed that the reference was meant for 
cases of employees of the shop, and not for those who were employed in 
the workshop. There is no word of limitation used in the order of reference, 
and the dispute is between the Company and its workmen represented by 
the present Union. I think the dispute relates to cases of all the employees 
of this Company. 


The minimum basic wages now paid to the employees compare favour- 
ably with the wages paid in such other big industries as teatile and 
engineering industries in the locality. However, no case had been 1,008 
out for increasing the suid wages to Rs. 40 as in the demand. A rise in 
the cost of living furnishes a good case for considering upward revision 
of dearness allowance. In the present case, u rise in the cost of living 
index to the extent of about 20 points since the last settlement has heen 
shown by the Union. A total neutralisation cannot be allowed. I think 
an increase in the dearness allowance at the flat rate of Rs. 5 per month 
will meet the ends of justice at present. The additional cost on this score 
is likely not to exceed six hundred rupees a year. The Company, although 
it is a small proprietory concern, will be in a position to bear this addi- 
tional financial burden. The incrensed dearness allowance at the rate of 
یا‎ Rs. 5=Rs. 25 per month should be puid with effect trom April 
1957. * 


I am told that at present there is no employee in the service of this 
Company who is paid on piece-rate, if any, basis. Nevertheless, the afore- 
suid increase in the dearness allowance shall be available to the piece-raters 
to the extent of Rs. 5 per mouth under the award. The issues are accord- 
ingly answered. 


Issue No. 3: At present all the employees are permanent. So, directly, 
no question of permanency arises just now. But both parties agreed that 
a provision to the following effect should be made for future guidance. 
“Probationers should be made permanent on completion of six months’ 
approved service; all temporary workers should be made permanent on 
completion of one year's approved service.’’ I answer this issue 
accordingly. 


issue No. 4: The Union demanded 14 days’ festival holidays in the 
written statement. This was reduced to 10 days at the time of hearing. 
The Company did not concede any portion of this demand alleging that it 
allows 45 days’ paid holidays to each worker in a year (30 days’ privilege 
leave and 15 days’ casual leave which included festival holidays). 
Accordingly, I do not see any reason why the employees in such a small 
concern should be allowed an additional 10 festival holidays mm a year. 
This demand is refused. 


This is my award. 
M. N. GAN,

ANNEXURE 
in the matter of an application under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes 
Act, as amended by the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 
filed by Shri Hiralal Yadab, a workman of Messrs. National Carbon Co. 
(india), Ltd., 5 Rustomji Parsi Raad, Calcutta-2, represented by 
National Carbon Mazdur Union, 1 Joy Bhattacharya Lano, Calcutta-3, 
against the aforesaid Company in connection with the caso which was 
referred to this Tribunal under C. 0. No. 1691Dis. /D/10L-42(A) /56, 
dated Calcutta, the 25th April 1956. (Case No. 154 of 1956, under 

Section 33A.) 


BEFORE THE SIXTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL 


PRESENT : 
9171 SAILESH SENGUPTA, Judge, Surth Industrial Trifunal 


Appearances : 
For the Company: Mr. J. K. Shafer. 
For the workman: Shri Hiralal Yadav. 


This is an application under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act 
by Hiralal Yadav, an employee of Messrs. National Carbon Co. (India), 
Lid., who was placed under suspension on 18th July 1956 pending enquiry 
into his conduct and permission of the Tribunal to mete out punishment by 
dismissal. As a reference proceeding was pending at the time the applicant 
moved this application alleging contravention of section 33. He has not 
heen paid his wages since the date of suspension. There is a further, griev- 
ance that he has not been paid advance bonus which the Company has paid 
to other workers. 


The Company opposed the application on the ground that the worker 
hed refused to carry out legitimate orders of the Company and all persuasions 
to induce him to take up a reasonable attitude having failed he was 
suspended on Idth July 1956 pending enquiry and final decision. As a 
reference proceeding was then pending the Company coutemplated applying 
for permission of that Tribunal to award him punishment. Pending the 
enquiry and permission of the Tribunal he was suspended and was not to 
draw any wages for the period. The action taken was not punishment within 
the purview of section 33 and hence the application is untenable. The Com- 
pany denied payment of advance bonus. 7 submitted that the question of 
bonus was under adjudication. There was only an advance made which was 
ما‎ be adjusted against the dues of the workers. Th: applicant having been 
suspended before this udvance was paid there was no ground for making 
payment to him. 


The short point on which decision of this case hinges is whether suspen- 
sion as ordered can be characterized as punishment. The law reports abound 
in decisions by Appellate Tribunals and also by the Hon’ble Supreme Court 
that suspension without pay even for an indefinite period pending enquiry 
jr pending permission of the appropriate Tribunal to dismiss a workman 


2870 THE CAIGUTTA GAZETTK, AUGUST 8, 1957 [Pant 1 


টি রত রা রা লারা 
th not puntahment (mde 1954, 2, J..J..J. page 328, 1965, 2, 115৭: page 693 
and 1967, 1, [.11.1. page 17). There i nothing to take this 0589 out of the: 
operation of the decisions referred to above. Since section 33 has not beer 


nfringed the application iy not maintainable and this Tribunal has no juris 
liction to grant any relief. 


The appheation m accordingly rejected, 
Dicteted and corrected by me 
S. SENGUPTA, 
Judge.

THE COMMISSIONERS FOR THE PORT OF CALCUTTA 


THE following By-law having been confirmed by the 
Government of India, Ministry of Transport and Com- 
munications, has been incorporated by the Commissioners 
in the By-laws for the Port of Calcutta in accordance 
with the provisions of section 126 of the Calcutta Port 
Act, 1890 (Bengal Act III of 1890):— 


New By-law No. 4A 


_ (i) The Commissioners shall, from year to year, issue 
licences to certain firms and individuals approved by the 
Commissioners granting such firms and individuals per- 
mission to perform the work of stevedoring vessels in the 
Port and no Stevedore shall be allowed to work on board 
any vessel in the Port without holding such a licence. 
The Commissioners may without assigning any reasons 
revoke, cancel, suspend any such licence st any time they 
think fit and proper or refuse to renew any such licence. 


(ii) اج‎ er led for issue of stevedoring licences have to 
satisfy the Commissioners on the following points and 
furnish the following proofs before their applications are 
entertained by the Commissioners:— 


(a) That the staff proposed to be employed by the 
applicants direct, is sufficient in number, fully 
trained and qualified, and the staff booked hy the 
applicants: through the Dock Labour Board are 
sufficient in number. 


(b) Production of a certificate, from an authority 
considered by the Commissioners to be competent, 
to the effect that the applicants possess proper 
gear for the due performance of their works. 


(c) Production of documentary evidence that a Steam- 
ship Company is prepared to enter into a contract 
with the applicants for stevedoring of its vensels. 


(d) Financial ability to meet obligations to labour 
employed, on account of wages, and levy under 
the Dock Workers’ (Regulation of Em »loyment) 
Scheme, 1956, and compensation payable under 
the Workmen's Compensation Act, 


(iii) A charge of Rs. 10 per licence shall be levied for 
the issue of a licence in the first instance which will be 
valid for one year only from the date of issue. The said 
fee will not be refundablo under any circumstances. 


(iv) A licence shall be renewed every year, the renewal 
fee in the first instance boing Rs. 5 per licence which is 
also not refundable. Applications in writing for renewal 
shall be submitted at least one month before the ex iry 
of the licence. Applications received Inte shall be liable 


to a penalty of Rs. 5 per licence at the discretion of the 
Chairman. 


(৮) The fees for the issue of a licence and for renewal 
thereof imay be revised by the Chuirman from time to 
time. 


P. C. MITTER, 
Secretary.

On 1061) June 1955 Shri Salip Ram Singh, Token No. 2.376, a workman 
of Messrs. Bengal Jute Mills Co., Ltd., applied under section 338A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, complaining against his dismissal on various 
grounds. The petitioner prays that he may be reinstated with other conse- 
quential reliefs. The Company opposed the claims on various grounds. 


The case was fixed for hearing on 6th July 1957, on which date the 
workman did not appear. Sm. P. Mitra, Lahour Officer of the I.J.M.A., 
however, appeared for the employers and filed documents, Exts..A and B. 
Exhibit A is 0 certified copy of the employer’s application under section 8 
of the Act, praying for permission to dismiss the workman during the 
pendency of the proceedings in the main case, and Ext. 1) is a certified copy 
of the Tribunal’s order No. 4, dated Gth November 1955, ‘striking off the 
application on the ground that it had lost jurisdiction to adjudicate »n it, 
as the pendency of the proceedings in the main adjudication had terminated. 
The present case is dismissed for default of the applicant. It is also not main- 
tainable in law (vide 1955 L.A.C., 221), and it is awarded accordingly.

DECLARATION 


Burdwan.—No. 15032L.A.—l14th August ۰ 
—Whereas the functions of the Central Govern- 
ment under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, (I 
of 1894), and the Land Acquisition (Mines) Act, 
1885 (XVIII of 1885), in relation to the acqui- 
sition of land for the purposes of the Union have 
been entrusted to the State Government by noti- 
fications No. 20/1/55-Judl.(I), dated the 14th 
May. and No. 20/9/54-Judl., dated 16th February 
1955, respectively, issued by the Government of 
India in the Ministry of Home Affairs under 
77 (1) of article 258 of the Constitution of 
ndia; 


And whereas the Governor is satisfied that land 
18 needed for a public purpose, being 8 purpose 
of the Union, namely, for the Township in connec- 
tion with the Durgapur Steel Project, in the 
village of Chakgopaldebpur, jurisdiction list No. 
45, thana Faridpur, pargana Shergarh, district 
Burdwan, it is hereby declared that pieces of 
Land in Block A/1, comprising cadastral survey 
lot Nos, 16, 45 and 46 and measuring, more or 
ess, 11.06 acres, are needed for the aforesaid 
public purpose at the public expense within the 
aforesaid village of Chakgopaldebpur. 


Mines of coal, iron-stone, slate or other 
minerals lying under the land or any particular 
portion of the land, except a such parts of the 
mines and minerals as it may be necessary to dig 
Or curry away, or use in the construction of the 
work for the purpose of which the land is being 
acquired, are not needed. 


This declaration is made, under the provisions 
of section 6 of Act I of 1894, and section 3, sub- 
section (1), Act XVITI of 1885, read with the said 
notifications, to all whom it may concern. 


A plan of the land may be inspected in the office 
of the Special Land Acquisition Officer, Burdwan, 
as well as in that of the Deputy General Manager, 
Durgapur Steel Project, Durgapur, Burdwan. 


By order of the Governor,

Cooch Behar, the Sth August 1957. 


Whereas it appears to me that commadities 
er-ential’ to the lite of the community, viz., rice 
and paddy, sre being smuggled out of the district 
into Hust Pakistan and it ts necessary for main- 
taining supplies of the aforesuid essential com- 
modities to impose certain restrictions on the 
movement and sale thereof in any market or place 
of sule lying within a belt of five miles from the 
Indo-Pakistan berder (heremafter called us the 
noid restricted area); 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers con- 
ferred by section 20 of the West Bengal Security 
Act, 1990 (Act XIX of 1950), as delegated to me 
by the State Government under section 3% of the 
sail Act by notification No. 2170P/40-9/50, dated 
Lith April 1950, from the Home (Political) 
Department, Government of West Bengal, با‎ 
K. 1১, Sen, T.A.8., District Magistrate and Deputy 
Commissioner, Cooch Behar, do Neely order that— 


(1) All transactions in the hats and markets 
lying within a belt of five miles from the 
Indo-Pukistan border shall be closed down 
before dusk. 


(2) Sale of rice and paddy exceeding five seers 
to any single buyer ut a time in the said 
restricted area, und also movement of 
such commodities in u quantity above 
five seers by any means of transport or as 
hend-load within the said restrieted aren 
without permit issued by a competent 
authority, is hereby prohibited. 


(3) The dealers having their place of business 
within the suid restricted area may bring 
in stock for sale under movement permits 
issued either by the  Subdivisional 
Contruller of Food and Supplies or by the 
Subdivisionul Officers. In case of 110101- 
bari puhce-station the Circle Officer, 
Huldibari, shall be the authority 
competent to issue such permits, 


(4) The aforesaid order shall remain in force 
for three munths, with effect from the 6th 
August 1957. Any person contravening 
the said order shall be punishable 
according to the provisions of law.

REGULATIONS PROVIDING FOR THE INSTITUTION AND

FOR THE EMPLOYEES OF THE BOARD OF SECONDARY

Scope of the Scheme. 


1. The following classes of whole-time employees of the Board shall 
subscribe to the Contributory Provident Fund maintained by the Board for 
the benefit of its employees hereinafter referred to as the said Fund :—~ 


(i) Permanent officers of the Board; 
(ii) Permanent members of the ministerial staff; 
(1) A person holding lien on a pensionable post under Government 


appointed permanently in the service of the Board, when he ceases 
to hold such a lien; 


(1v) A Government pensioner appointed to the service of the Board on 
a year to year basis, provided thut his pension remains suspended 
during the period of employment under the Board. 


2. The scheme may also he.extended by the Board to Peons, Durwans 
and similar other Lower Subordinate staff holding permanent appointments 
under the Board, 


3. If an employee, on probation, is subsequently confirmed, he may, if 
the 80 desires, join the Fund on such confirmation, with retrospective effect 
from the date of his substantive appointment, on payment of the presoribed 
amount as ‘his contribution and the Board shall make the prescribed share 
of its contribution. 


4. The payment by an employee of the Board of premium دہ‎ 5 Life 
Insurance Policy held by him, at a rate not leas than the rate of subscrip- 
tion to the Fund payable by him, may, ot his option, be substituted for his 
subscription to the Fund, and thereupon he shall be entitled to the contri 
bution of the Board to the Fund, provided the Life Insurance Policy is on 
the employee’d own life and js in the assignable form and is hypotheceted to 
the Board for safe euatody,

16, (1) An advance shall he recovered from the subscriber in’ such 
number of equal monthly instalments as the sanctioning authority may 
direct; but such number shall not be less than twelve sen the subscriber 
so elects, or in any case more than twenty-four. <A subscriber may, at his 
option, repay more than one instalment in a month. Each instalment shall 
be a number of whole rupees, the amount of the advance being raised or 
reduced, if necessary, to admit of the fixation of such instalments. 


(2) Recoveries shall be made monthly by compulsory deduction from 
salary, commencing from the first payment of a full month’s salary after 
the advance is granted. Recoveries shall not be made, except with the 
wubscriber’s consent, while he is on leave (other than casual leave), or in 
receipt of subsistence grant. Recoveries of advance made shall be in 
addition to the usual subscription. 


16. When the advance is repayable in twelve or Jess instalments, an 
additional instalment representing interest and equivalent to 4 per oent. of 
the amount of the advance shall be paid in the month following that im which 
the last instalment is paid. Similarly, two additional instalments represent-. 
ing interest each equivalent to 4 per cent. of the total amount of the advance 
shall be paid when the advance is repayable in more than twelve instal- 
ments. Interest shall be credited to the account of the subscriber from 
whom it is realised. |

The Government of West Bengal, in the Department of Labour, by

Shri K. 0, Dutta, Shri N. N. Roy and Shri D. K. Roy, all of 92 Maty 
Garage, Bongaon, 24-Parganas, and one of their workmen, Shri Narendra 
Nath Ghosh, represented by the Bus Workers’ Union, 249 Bowbazar Street, 
Calcutta-12, regarding matters specified in the second schedule of the Act to 
this Court .for adjudication. 


Schedule 


Is the dismissal of Shri Narendra Nath Ghosh justified? To what relief 
is he entitled? 


2914 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 15, 1957 [Pant I 


সো I A TE TR ATR TNT te ےت شس‎ 


AWARD 
The case of the Union is in short as follows: 


The workman Shri Narendra Nath Ghosh on Ist December 1953 entered 
into the service of the employers Messrs, Shri P. K. Roy, Shri ٠. K. 
Mukherjee, Shri K. L. Dutta, Shri N. N. Roy and Shri D. .کا‎ Roy, joint 
proprietors of Bus No. WBR 1033, plying on Route No. 92 in the ٥۱+ 
urea. The conditions of work in the Company were very harsh and some- 
times non-licensed conductors on petty salary of Rs, 30 a month used 
to be employed. This workman took up the cause of the aggrieved workmen 
and pressed before the Company their demands for wage increase. This 
enraged the Company which therefore summarily terminated the service 
of the workman on July 1955. No charge-sheet was given, nor any 
enquiry held. The Union therefore contends that this termination of the 
service of this workman is thoroughly unjustified and is a case of victimisa- 
tion and an unfair labour practice. The Union therefore claims that the 
workman should be reinstated with compensation for the period of his, forced 
unemployment. 


The Company in their written statement generally retutes the allegations 
in the written statement of the Union and contends, infer alia, that for acts 
of misconduct this workman and the entire staff were suspended ‘from their 
services with effect from 2181 June 1956 as a securify measure on the basis 
of a proper charge-sheet and after due enquiry. The bus plies between 
Bongaon and Boyra and starters are maintained at Bagda and not at Boyra 
und the hour for arrival of buses at Bagda from Boyra is fixed. On 8 
June 1956 the driver and the entire stuff were engaged in idle gossips and 
did not atart in time. In the result the passengers in the bus, vere murmur- 
ing and the bus arrived at Bagda long after the scheduled hour. The staff, 
however, set up a plea of “‘breakdown’’ journey and o fine of Rs. 10 was 
imposed on the bus by the starter of Bagda. The plea of breakdown journey 
was absolutely false. The bus was in perfect running order and this false 
plea was resorted to with a view to evading the imposition of heavy fine. In 
consequence the up and down trips of the bus were lost to the Company 
Involving it in a loss of Rs. 60 plus a fine of Rs. 10 and the pnssengers were 
also greatly inconvenienced. Charges were framed against this workman 
and the stoff and a proper enquiry was held and they were found, guilty of 
grave misconduct and so this workman was dismissed. 11) short, the 
Company justifies the termination of the services of the workman for grave 
misconduct after proper charge-sheet. The Company therefore contends 
that the workman ia entitled to no relief. 


DECISION 


The main point for determination in this case is whether the dismissal 
of Shri Narendra Nath Ghosh who wos a driver under the Company 18 
justified or not. As already stated the case of the Company is that on 21st 
June 1956 the dismissed driver and the entire staff including 3 others, 
namely, Prafulla Paul, Biswanath and Sukumar were engnged in idle 
۱۹۱8ی‎ at Boyra and suddenly it dawned on them that the bus should have 
left Boyra onrlier and it had already heen 20 minutes too late. Apprehend- 
ing trouble, the driver and the staff set up a false plea of “‘breakdown’”’ as 
an excuse for the delay. The truth came to light and the Company drew 
up a charge-sheet against thie workman and the aforesaid 3} others as per 
Ext. B. The workman submitted an explanation Ext. ১ so an 7 
was held and they were found guilty and were dismissed all at a time. 
For the workman, it is stated that the charges levelled against him are falae 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 15, 1957 2915 
ST Tce a A SE SE LE ہت جج‎ an aro 


and baseless, in tact, he was dismissed for his Trade Unign activities. In 
this case the Company has caamined QO. P. ٢ 1 Shri Sudhir) Kumar 
Mukherjee, a proprietor, U.P.W. × Shri Hari Mohon Mukherjee, a passenger 
of the same bus on the relevant date and O.P.W. 3 a dismissed conductor tor 
the journey concerned. On the other hand, the Union examined the 
dismissed workman |’. W. | Shri Nurendra Nath Ghosh and P. W. এ 
another proprietor of the Compauy. 


Let us now turn to the evidence adduced in this case. Before referring 
to the oral evidence it will be useful to briefly refer to the charge-sheet 
Ext. B, dated 21+) June 1956, wherein these 4 workmen were called upon to 
expluin the delay in starting the bus from Boyra and for submitting a 
8 explanation of breakdowu and why they should not be dismissed. 
Seven days’ time was given to them tor submitting their reply. On 26th 
June 1956 the Bonagram Bus Workers’ Union addressed a letter, Ext. C, to 
the Company admitting that these workmen have committed the offence 
but prayed tor their reinstatement, considering that they are all refugees 
from Hastern Pakistan faced with critical conditions in these hard days. 
The Company as per Ext. 1) served a notive on these workmen intimating 
that an enquity would be held on 2nd July 1906 at 4 p.m. in the office of the 
Bongaon Bus Syndicate. This enquiry was attended by these workmen and 
certain other passengers including Harn Mohon O.P.W. 2 and they were 
found guilty and tor this they were dismissed with effect from 218+ June 
1956 as per orders Ext. G, dated 3rd July 956. It is worth mention in 
this connexion that some passengers made ao statement in writing Ext. E 
setting torth the offence committed by the workmen. This statement lends 
further support to the contention uf the Company that the staff of the bus 
requested the passengers not to disclose this to the proprietors and for this 
undue request these passengers were exempted from paying any fares for 
the journey between Boyra and Bagda. The oral evidence adduced in this 
case by S. K. Mukherjee, 0.P.W. 1 (a proprietor), 0.P.W. 2 Hari Mohon 
Mukherjee (a passenger) and 0.P.W. 3 (one of the conductors) coupled with 
the documentary evidence on record leaves absolutely no room for doubt 
that this workman with 3 others dismissed for the same offence really com- 
mitted an offene by not starting the bus in time from Boyra on 21st June 
1956 وہ‎ they indulged in idle gossips without caring for the financial loss 
of the Company, convenience or inconvenience of the passengers, ete. ‘The 
Company has also offered an explanation as to why these workmen resorted 
to falnehood in setting up a plea of breakdown and the explanation is that 
one minute’s delay entails a fine of Rs. 2, so the usual fine for 20 minutes 
would have come up to Rs. 40, whereas the fine for breakdown 1s only Ra. 10 
and so the underlying motive was to avoid a payment of a larger fine. In 
the first place these workmen committed an offence the seriousness of which 
was aggravated by their adding a lie to it. The offence has heen proved 
to the hilt. Then again, the Union contended that this workman was sacked 
for his Trade Union activities, but strangely enough the workman has not 
made a single atatement about his Trade Union activities. Therefore the 
plea that he was dismissed for his Trade Union activities is a myth, pure and 
sianple. 


Tn this connexion T feel cajled upon to add a word about the testimony 
of the P. W. 2, one of the proprietors of the bus whose sympathy was 
evidently enlisted by the worker. This proprietor was previously a conductor 
under the Company and the suggestion is that his services were terminated 
for defaleation which, however, he has denied but he has been candid 
enough to admit that he was a party to a resolution Ext. I of the meeting 
of the proprietors held on 19th June 1956, wherein the decision reached ٥۹ 


2916 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 15, 1957 [Purr I 
০ acne Sr ৯৯৯ 


that the service of these workmen should be terminated. Therefure being once 
a party to the aforesaid resolution it ill-behoved this proprietor, ۶.۱۴۰. 2 now 
to come forward and blow hot and cold at the same breath. I am unable 
to place the reliance on the evidence of this proprietor which it otherwise 
deserved. It may also be pointed out that the oral evidence of the witness 
for the Company goes unchallenged. Thus, having regard to the entire 
evidence on record, I must find that this workman was duly charge-sheeted 
and an enquiry was held with due notice to the workmen and they were 
tightly found guilty and their services were justly terminated. 


As regards the punishment, it has been urged on behalf of the Company 
that the punishment, having regard to the offence committed, has been too 
pevere. This driver, it 18 evident, had not a clean record of service. He 
wan (dismissed on & previous occasion and on his prayer as per Ext. H, dated 
3061) April 1956, he wus reinstated. So having regard to his past record the 
punishment cannot be argued to be a severe one. Furthermore, as laid 
in several reported cases and the recent one would be found in the case of 
Radha Raman Bajpai and others and J.abour Appellate Tribunal of India 
and others reported in 1957 1.J..3., Vol. II, page 16, “‘the question of 
punishment must be held to be within the discretion of the employer and 
exercise of that discretion by the employer could not be interfered with by 
the Industrial Tribunal on the ground that the punishment is excessive in 
its view, and when the punishment could not be regarded as arbitrary or 
unauthorised, it could not be interfered with by the Industrial Tribunal’. 
Benring in mind this principle of law I refuse to interfere with the punish- 
ment inflicted upon this workman since this Court, on a consideration of 
the three main questions, namely, (1) whether the workman was found 
guilty of misconduct by the employer, (2) whether the correct procedure 
was followed in arriving at the finding, and (3) whether the misconduct 
should be visited with سوا‎ es finds that the charge of misconduct has 
been duly proved on a proper enquiry attended by the workmen. 


Before parting, I would point out that the Company wrongly dismissed 
this workman with effect from 2lst June 1996 by an order, dated 3rd July 
1966. This is clearly incorrect. Tho order of suspension cannot be made 
retrospectively, Correctly he should have been dismissed with effect from 
ord July 1956 (i.e., the date of the order of dismissal). The workman may 
be entitled to some back wages for correcting the date of dismissal as 3rd 
July 1956. The Company will be good enough to pay the arrears of wages 
due to the workman on this account within a month of the publication of this 
award. Hesides this, he is entitled to no other relief. 


This is my award. 
Typed to my dictation and corrected by me.

Act, 1947, arising out of the original reference, which was made by the 
Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, under its order No. 5018-

AWARD 


The petitioner’s case is that during the pendency of the original 
reference, his services were terminated by the Company by a letter, dated 
27th November 1956, without taking permission from the Tribunal. So, 
the petitioner claimed reinstatement with back wages for the period of forced 
unemployment. 


The Company filed written statement and contested the application. 
The Company wanted to say that the application under section 33A waa

not maintainable, inasmuch as there was no contravention of section 33 
of the Act. It further contended that as the applicant’s continued 111 
health precluded him from doing his normal duties in the main for which 
he was appointed, his services were terminated. 


On the date fixed for hearing, the parties filed a joint petition of
