This industrial dispute between Messrs. Prabashi Press (heremafter 
called the Press), 120-2 Upper Circular Road, Calcutta, und their vorkmen 
represented by the Press Employees’ ۸۸30۰11٤107, 249-B Howbazar Street, 
Calcutta-12, regarding the following issue, was referred to this Tribunal for 
adjudication by the Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, 
order No, 146-1.R./D/15L-43/56, dated the 1010) January 1967, 


Both parties filed written statements, adduced evidence, oral and doru- 
mentary, and advanced arguments. 


Issue 


Whether the workers whose names sre given below are entitled to any 
relief for the transfer of their service from the Prabashi management to a 
contractor ?— 


(i) Shri Matiar Rahaman, (1) Shri Mahadev Kurmi, (iii) Shri Satya 
Bhattacharjee, (iv) Shri Anil Dam. 


AWARD 


issue No. 48 The four employees mentioned in the sachedule were iu 
permanent service of the Press. It appears from the evidence of Shri K. N. 
Chatterjee, one of the two proprietors of the Press and Chairman of the 
Board of Directors, that between August 1946 and 1954 the work of the 
binding department was in a hopeless condition due to frequent absence of 
employees of the department, on whom was entrusted the work of regular 
despateh and supply of monthly journals to all agents and subscribers. 
Naturally, Shri Chatterjee thought of either abolishing the binding depart- 
ment and getting the binding work done, as in cases of other monthly 
journals, by outside agency, or reorganising it with the help of more active 
employeer or a contractor. After consultation with the Manager, who in 
turn also consulted the employees of the binding department, Shri 
Chatterjee decided to run the department through a contractor and entered 
into an agreement, as per Ext. B, with a former employee, Abdul Rashid, 
naa contractor and transferred the services of the aforesaid employees of the 
said department, presumably, with their consent, under the said contractor 
Abdul Rashid with effect from February 1965. Shri Chatterjee himself paid 
half of the wages and drearness allowance to the employees directly from his 
office and the remaining half of the wages was paid through the contractor. 
The four employeea examined themselves in this case. They admitted this 
transfer, but said that it was done without their knowledge and consent. 
At the same time they admitted that there was no protest for several months, 
1.٥. till June 1955 and that they received the same wages and dearness 
allowance aos before. They also enjoyed other benefits, e.g., leave and 
holidays, etc., along with other employees of the Press. Jt was only in 
June of that year that certain discriminatory treatments were meted out to 
them, when they were not paid the increased dearness allowance of Rs. 28 
in place of Rs. 22 per month, and their names were removed from the 
office Attendance Register. They said that they approached the Manage- 
ment hut failed to obtain redress of their grievences. Thereafter, they 
complained to their Aasociation about this matter (Ext. D) and also to the 
Labour Commissioner as per Ext. E. The written statement filed on behalf 
of these employees is in some places incorrect and, on the whole, confusing. 
The only grievance of the employees, as far us ] have gathered, is that 
they were denied the inrreased rate of dearness allowance since June 1995. 
Shri Chatterje says that this fact was not brought to his knowledge by the 
employees. Here he contradicted the evidence of the employees. He 
further said that he would certainly look into the matter now. 


Part l] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 15, 1957 20923 


سے eee‏ ےے۔ دکسے۔ ووسعد _ _ سے আজ পাদ ৪৮৮০ পর ee‏ - إ؛+ سے مد ھے আত‏ 


The admitted position is that due to many reasons, the binding depuart- 
ment which waa responsible tur regular despatch and gupply of journals to 
agents and subscribers, was not functioning properly with the consequential 
loss to the Press, and damage to its good will. So to obviate all possible 
delay in despatch as also to put & restraint upon the loss, a reorgunisution of 
the department was necessary. This was never disputed in any stage of 
the case. The Management is within its right to reorgunise the work of the 
department 80 as to put it on the right track. There is nothing initially 
wrong in the arrangement, which exista even row. The conduct of the 
employees shows that they had full know!edge of this arrangement and they 
consented to it, otherwise there could not be any trausfer of service without 
objection for several months. Such transfers could only be effected with the 
consent of the employees concerned, and we can reasonably presume such 
consent in this case. The existing conditions of service remained ژ۷‎ 
since the beginning of 1956, and the employees were getting the same wages 
ond dearness allowance as before. Shri K. N. Chatterjee, true to the tradi- 
tion of his illustrious father, 18৮6 Ramananda Chatterjee, the founder of the 
Press, did not like the idea of throwing any of the employees of the Press 
out of employment, and he did not do that. It is his evidence that these 
employees are now emploved under the contractor in the Prabasi Press and, 
therefore, there cannot be any justification for a Jong-drawn proceeding 
based on alleged half truths and inaccurate statements. 


The only grievance of the employees, as stuted above, is that they are not 
heing paid the same rate of dearness allowance as given to the rest of the 
employees of the Press. They are getting at the old rate whereas other 
employees are getting at the increased rate of Rs. 28 per month. That 
dearness allowance was increased at Its. 28 is not disputed in this case. It 
is the common case of the parties that the services of these four men were 
not terminated by the Press. Their services were transferred or, to put 
it more correctly, were placed under a contractor engaged to run the 
department efficiently. Accordingly, the employees continued to be in the 
service of the Press and, as such, are entitled to all the benefits in the same 
way as enjoyed by all other employees. So it is meet and proper that 
these four employees should get the increased rate of dearness allowance 
while being employed under the contractor, Shri J. C. Bose, learned 
representative of the Press, accepted the position that the increased rate of 
dearness allowance should be paid to these employees. I, therefore, find 
that these employees are entitled to get increased dearness allowance of 
Ra. 28 per month along with other employees of the Press. The increased 
dearness allowance should be paid with effect from the date of this reference, 
1.6.) the 10th January 1957. The employees are not entitled to any other 
relief in this case. 


This is my award. 
M. N. GAN, 


Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal.

For the Company: Shri 8. C. Sen, Advocate.

By order No, 4323Dis. /D/8L-32/55, dated Calcutta, the 27th September 
1956, the Government of Weat Bengal has referred for adjudication the 
following points connected with a dispute between Messrs. Shree Radha 
Krishna Cotton Mills, Ltd. and their employees named in the order of 
reference. 


Schedule 


(1) Is the discharge of Shri P. B. Mukherjee, Shri Nitai Charan Adak, 
Shri D. Roy and Shri Nahar Singh justified? 


(2) To what relief are they entitled ? 


AWARD 


The four employees named in the schedule of the order of reference 
used to work in the Head Office of Shree Radha Krishna Cotton Mills, Ltd. 
From 19৮ November 1955 their services were terminated professedly on the 
ground of lock-out. The employees moved the Labour Department and 
finally secured the help of the Union to fight their cause. Their case 1s that 
termination of their services was unwarranted and they should be reinstated 
with full compensution. At the time of hearing, case of Nahar Singh was 
dropped by the Union as he had made up his differences with the Company 
and obtained full satisfaction of bis dues. 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 15, 1957 2995 


The Company raised an objection that this waa not an _ industrial 
dispute but an individual dispute which was not cognizable by this 
Tribunal. On the merits the Company’s case is that owing to financial 
difficulties the Company had to close down the business and the services 
of et people were not required. They can claim no relief as the business 
is dead. 


Admittedly the discharged employees had approached the Government 
directly and laid their grievances before the Jahour Department. The 
Assistant Labour Commissioner suggested that they should come through 
oa registered Trade Union. Thereafter they enrolled themselves as members 
of the Radha Krishna Cotton Mill Mazdoor Union and solicited the help 
of the Union. The Union rallied to their support and represented them 
before the Government. In the order of reference the workers ure 
described as represented by the President, Radha Krishna Cotton Mill 
Mazdoor Union. The learned Advocate for the Company Shrijut Sen 
waxed indignant over the conduct of the Assistant Labour Commissioner 
in tendering advice that the matter should be represented through a Union. 
Shrijut Sen castigated the Assistant Labour Comimisisoner in acid terme 
aud expressed the view that it was not the Government's business to 
suggest how an individual dispute should be converted into an industrial 
dispute. I am afraid the criticism is misdirected. The highest Tribunal 
in India—the Supreme Court—hus made the pronouncement that an 
individual dispute may be turned into an industrial dispute if it is taken 
up by a Trade Union or a substantial section of the co-workers. What 
was an individual dispute at the inception may mature into an industrial 
dispute. ‘here was nothing wrong in the Assistant Labour Commussioner 
telling the aggrieved persons that their case could not be taken up _ for 
pata Sor unless it appeared in the form of an industrial dispute and to 
have that character impressed upon it, the dispute must have the champion- 
ship of a Trade Union. The Assistant Labour Commissioner did nothing 
unseemly or improper in apprising the employees of the correct legal 
position. 


According to Shrijut Sen, the President of the Union was simply 
representing the workers on the authority granted by them in accordance 
with section 36(1)(c). This was not equivalent to espousal of their cause 
by the Union. The case reported in 1954, 2, ...ہا‎ page 477 was 
referred to. The employees were, according to Shrijut Sen, being helped 
by the President. The evidence of P.W. 1 is to the effect that the 
Assistant Labour Commissioner having suggested that they should be 
represented through a Union the Union had taken up their cause on request. 
It is not a case of mere representation in the Tribunal or helping the 
employees to fight for their rights. On the facts and evidence of P.W. 4, 
I hold that the Union had in fact taken up the cause of the employees aud 
hence the individual dispute was transformed into an industrial dispute. 
The Tribunal is quite competent to deal with this matter. 


The Company had two mills. Mil No. 1 was admittedly closed in 
1946. There were labour troubles in Mill No. 2 which resulted in a 
lock-out with effect from 23rd August 1955. This lock-out was considered 
by this ‘l'ribunal on another reference and was held to be justified. The 
award made on that reference has been published in the Calcutta 
Gazette, dated the 4th July 1957. Notice Ext. 2 was served on Shri P. B 
Mukherjee on 30th September 1955, terminating his services with effect 
from Ist November 1955. Similar notice was served on the others. In 
this notice it was stated that as the mills were closed since 23rd August 
1955 due to an illegal strike started hy the workmen and as there was very 
megre chance of restarting the mill in the near future the management 


2926 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 15. 1957 [Parr I 


rt পপ ۔ سو ہمہ‎  - ee 


কব ৮৮ ee ساس‎ ee ee ہے‎ 


.ےت بات سر ہہ ہے ھت ات اوس 


had to dispeuse with his services. It is in evidence that the mill did not 
reopen since the date of lock-out. The Management found that it could 
not curry on the business and took the decision to dispose of the machineries 
and 19005 on which the mills stood. Negotiations for sale were started in 
October and agreement was concluded on the 16th of November 19595. 
The contention advanred on behalf of the workers is that there was lock-out 
and not closure on the date the notice of discharge was served, and the 
workers were entitled to compensation on termination of their services on 
the ground of lock-out. Strictly speaking what was lock-out at the start 
developed into a closure in the long run. At the date of the notice the 
Management had made up its mind to close the business and dispose of 
the machineries, plants and the land. Termination of service was therefore 
in anticipation of closure. There are decisions by the Supreme Court that 
Industrial Disputes Act can be applied only in the case of an_ existing 
industry. Discharge on account of closure is not retrenchment aud no 
retrenchment relief can be claimed. 45 in this case the business was 
ultimately closed and at the date of the notice closure was in contemplation 
the position appears to me to be the same, Cases reported in 1956, 2, 
l..L.J., page 4, page 238 and 1957, 1, L.L.J., page 235 may be referred to. 
I think the principles enunciated in these cases would apply though the 
closure was not un accomplished fact at the date of the notice: The mill 
was not working und at the date of the notice the authorities were satisfied 
that they could not be reopened. These are sufficient for the irference 
that closure had been decided upon and the termination of services of the 
employees was the proximate result of the decision. In this state of things 
the discharge cannot be turned retrenchment since this action had been 
tuken in relation to closure of the business. The employees are not entitled 
to any 26191, 


The employees may recover from the Company the wages admittedly 
due for the month of October 1955 and Provident Fund money.

in the matter of an industrial dispute existing between Messrs. Harrison 
Saw Mills, E-3 Clive Buildings, Caloutta-1, and their workman, Shri 
Bechulal Chandra, represented by Motor Transport Workers’ Union, 
249 Bowhbazar Street, Caloutta-12. (Case No. ۷۱۱۱۰277 of 1956.5 


BEFORE THE SIXTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGALI 


PRESENT : 
ذٌ‎ ۶۲٢ SAILESH SENGUPTA, Judge, Sizth Industrial Tribunal. 


Appearances: 
For the Company: Shri ۸. A. Q. Parry, Labour Adviser. 
For the Union: Shri Patit Paban Pathak. 


The points referred for adjudication by Government order No. 4330 Dts. / 
D/111.-267 /56, dated Calcutta, the 27th September 1956, are as followa: — 


(1) Is the discharge of Shri Bechulal Chandra justified P 
(2) To what relief is he entitled ? 


AWARD 


Shri Bechulal Chandra was a motor driver in the employ of Messrs. 
Harrison Saw Mills. His case is that a notice of discharge was served on 
him on 30th December 1954 terminating his services with effect from Ist 
of January 1956, without any reasons being assigned. He failed to 
persuade the Management to revoke this arbitrary order of discharge. 
Ultimately the matter was referred by Government for adjudication by this 
Tribunal, 


The Company’s case is that Bechulal Chandra was concerned 17 the 
theft of some part of a circular saw on 27th December 1995. Bein 
detected he absented himself from duty from the day following withou 
leave or notice. Though for 0 misconduct of this description the Company 
was entitled to order dismissal, he was dealt with leniently, his services 
being terminated in accordance with rule 12(a) of the Standing Orders by 
service of notice. 


Pare I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST ہ13‎ 7 2931 
তল 


In the foretront of the arguments udvanced on behalf of the Company 
was the puint that this dispute is un individual dispute and not an 
industrial کک‎ There is nu Union of the workers serving in this 
Company. The case of Bechulal Chandra was being represented by Motor 
Transport Workers’ Union. According to the Company’s representative, 
representation by on alien Union cannot have the effect of converting the 
individual dispute into an industrial dispute. Reference was made in 
ive gat of the argument to a decision of the Supreme Court reported in 
1907, 2, اط‎ page 1. It Appears from the report at page 2 that the case 
of the aggrieved worker was not taken up by any Union of workers of the 
Company nor by any of the Unions of workmen employed in similar or 
allied trades but by a Union with which the workman had no connexion 
whatsoever. It ts already been stated that there is no Union of workmen 
employed by this Company. The Union which has espoused the cause ot 
this employee is composed of motor transport workers. The Company 
does not carry on business in motor transport. It is a Company working 
saw mills. The Motor Transport Workers’ Union is not a Union of work- 
men employed in a similar or allied trade. Espousal of the cause by a 
Union of workers employed in an entirely different undertaking does not 
accordingly turn the dispute into an industrial dispute as it cannot be said 
to be a dispute between the Company and its workmen. The preliminary 
01019038101) raised on behalf of the Company succeeds on the authority of the 
decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court. 


Though it is unnecessary for me in the view I have taken with regard 
to the preliminary objection to enter into the merits, I may observe in 
passing that the Company’s contention that it is entitled under rule 12(1) 
of the Standing Orders to terminate the services of an employee without 
Assigning wny reasons is not at all sound. Rule 12(1) of the Standing 
Orders has been quoted verbatim in paragraph 8 of the written statement. 
It only lays down the procedure to be followed for terminating the 
employment of a permanent workman. It is not provided that the 
Company has the inherent right to throw out of গা a worker 
according to its whims without there being any ground for termination of 
service. The procedure laid down ia to be followed when there is sufficient 
grounds for dispensing with the services of a workman. Had this been an 
industrial dispute the Tribunal would have come to the conclusion that 
there was no ground for termination of service of thia employee, as the only 
argument pressed that the Company had the right to discharge the employee 
on service of one month’s notice could not be upheld. The Company did 
not bring any evidence to prove that this worker had committed theft of 
its property. As, however, the dispute happens to be an individual 
dispute no relief can be granted by the Tribunal.

This is an application under section 338A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
1947, arising out of the original reference, which was made by the Govern- 
ment of West Bengal, Labour Department, to this Tribunal under its

AWARD 


The petitioner’s case is that during the pendency of the original 
reference, on 7th August 1956 he had gone out of the factory for tea with 
a gate-pass but he was charge-sheeted for using a forged gate-pass. He 
duly submitted his explanation. But from 8th August 1956 he was not 
allowed to join his work in the factory ond since then he has been without 
employment. 


The Company filed written statement and contested the application. 
The Company wanted to say that the application under section 33A was 


Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTH, AUGUST 15, 1957 2933 


کجمٌر — 


not maintainable, inasmuch as there was no contravention of. section 33 of 
the Act. The petitioner has examined himself and a :witness while on 
behalf of the Company, one of the Directors and a darwan deposed. 
Documentary evidence was also produced by both sides. I am not prepared 
to believe the version of the petitioner or his witness. Both of them did 
not commend themselves to me to be truthful witnesses. Accordingly, 
I am unable to hold that the petitioner after the incident of 7th August 
1956 was not allowed to join. I am prepared to believe the evidence as 
adduced by the Company. From the evidence of one of the Directors and 
darwan, I om satisfied that the petitioner for the alleged offence in respect 
of which he was charge-sheeted did not himself attend factory for any day 
aince 8th August 1956.

mise oe আরম ما‎

From the materials placed before the Tribunal, the Tribunal is of the 
view that there was no contravention of section 33 of the Act. The peti- 
tioner has not yet been dismissed. He was charge-sheeted and an enquiry 
was held by the Management. As a result of this enquiry the Management 
has decided to dismiss him after taking permission from the Tnbunal. 
That permission has not yet been taken or granted by the Tribunal. As 
the things stand at present, it cannot be said that section 33 of the Act has 
been contravened. It is decided hence that the present application is not 
maintainable. It is accordingly rejected.

——— EE ee 
The Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, by its order 


No, 1944Dis./D/111.-126/56, dated 11th May 1956, referred the above 
dispute to this Tribunal, for adjudication. 


The issues contuined in the said order of reference stand as follows:— 
(1) Pay and scales of pay. 

(2) Dearness allowance. 

(3) Leave. 

(4) Holidays. 

(5) Overtime. 

(6) Working hours. 

(7) Bonus for the years 1952, 1953, 1954 and 1955. 


(8) Reinstatement of Shri Debi Prosad Mukherjee, Kamala Hazam, 
Shri Monmohan Banerjee and Shri Santosh Kumar Mukherjee. 


(9) Whether the retrenchment of Shri Ramesh Chandra Mukherjee 
is juatified. What relief is he entitled to? 


(10) ‘Tiffin allowance. 
AWARD 


It is the Union’s case that the Howrah Motor Accessories Agency, Ltd. 
(hereinafter to be called the Company), carries on business in automobile 
parts and accessories as 0 premier concern in this respect. The said 
Company has got Branches at Howrah and Bbhowanipore besides the 
Head Office at 3/1 Mangoe Lane, Calcutta. The Company is financially 
sound and prosperous and earns good profita year to year. But there is 
no terms and conditions of service in this Company. The employees have 
to depend always on the whims and discretion of the Company. The 
security of service is absolutely nil. The rate of salary is much below 
the starvation level, and the dearness allowance is absoultely inadequate. 
The employees tried their best to improve their service conditions, but 
all their efforts in this respect failed. So, they decided for collective 
action through the Trade Union known as ‘‘West Bengal Motor Dealers 
Employees’ Union” for agitating their grievances. This Union placed 
8 ا‎ of demands in 1954 before the Company. But the Company 
was not happy on the formation of the Union, and as a retaliation carried 
on persistent attack on the employees in general and the leaders of the 
Union in particular. The minimum earnings of a clerk and a 
subordinate staff are Rs. 40 and Rs. 25, respectively per month. The rate 
of dearness allowance is Rs. 10 in the minimum and Rs. 50 im the 
maximum. The rate of annual increment for clerks and subordinate 
stiff is also very unsatisfactory. The Company has capacity to pay 
higher pay and wages and also dearness allowance. There is also no 
leave rules in this Company. Holidays under the Negotiable Instruments 
Act are not granted to the employees, and for extra hours of work, no 
overtime is paid to them. The employees are to work for longer hours 
in this Company. In the yeurs 1952, 1953, 1954 and 1955, the Company 
had earned substantial profits, but the employees have not been paid 
adequate bonus for those years, although the Managing Director of the 
Company gave on assurance to pay due bonus on profits for those years 
within November 1955. Shri Debi Prosad Mukherjee, Kamala Hazam, 
Shri Monmohan Banerjee and Shri Santosh Kumar Mukherjee were 
arbitrarily dismissed by the Company because of their Union activities, 
and Shri Ramesh Chandra Mukherjee was retrenched for no justifiable 
ground. The tiffin allowance that is being paid to the employees of this 


Parr I] THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 14, 1957 2041 

© ANSE ات سمس۔پممسسے پموسممااہ۔-وےچےوجومج وت خہملےڈ سے‎ 
Company is very meagre and inadequate. Hence, the Union has claimed 
that the salary and wage of every employee should be increased from 
Ist January 1955, on the principle of point-to-point adjustment, and that 
dearness allowance as per scheme of the Bengal Chamber of Commerce 
should be given. The Union has further demanded that the employees 
named above should be reinstated with back pay and other allowances 
for the period of forced unemployment. The Union has further demanded 
that tiffin allowance at the rate of annas 12 per day should be given to 
all employees, and that overtime should be paid at double the rate of 
salary. Regarding bonus for the years in question, the claim of the 
Union is that the Company should pay bonus equivalent to one month’s 
pay with dearness allowance as Puja bonus and one-sixth of the total 
earning of the employees as profit bonus. The Union also contended that 


the privilege leave should be raised’ to one month besides usual casual leave 
and sick leave. 


The Company in reply denied most of the allegations as made by the 
Union in its written statement. It submits that it is not a manufacturing 
concern, but is mainly an importer of motor spare parts and has sale 
agency for Ford genuine parts, Ferrodo brake lining and clutch facings. 
There are about 400 motor parts dealers in Calcutta. The present 
position of such business, particularly of importers, is very disquieting.

Now let me consider whether the employees of this Company are

entertained. 1118 line of argument was that such claim was not only a 
belated one, but also made at a time when the accounts of this 
Company for those years were finally closed and odjusted. The financial 
yeur of this Company is from January to December. This claim for 
additional bonus was made for the first time by the Union at the end of 
the year 1954, in its charter of demands, and also later on when 
conciliation proceedings were pending in the Labour Directorate. As 
stated already, it has transpired from the evidence of the General 
Manager, who is 0.P.W. 1, that the employees of this Company accepted 
bonus for the years 1952, 1958 and 1954 without any protest and demur. 
That evidence also stands unchallenged and uncontradicted. In the case 
of Associated Electrical Industries (India), Ltd. Employees’ Welfare 
Association vs. Associated Electrical Industries, Ltd., and Others reported 
in 1954, 1.1... (1), page 709, it has been held by their Lordships of 
‘the Labour Appellate Tribunal that where the Company paid one 
month’s basie earning as bonus to their workmen in September 1950, for 
the year 1949, and it was accepted by the workmen without gee the 
demand made by the workmen in March 1951, for additional bonus for 
the year 1949, must be deemed to be belated, and as such it should be 
rejected. Their Lordships further observed that as the bonus for the 
year in question was accepted without any protest, it was not open to the 
workmen to reagitate the same after such a lapse of time. In my view 
the claim for additional bonus for the years 1952, 19683 and 1954, should 
be rejected being belated. It has also been held by the High Court of 
Madras in a case reported in 1957, L...J. (1), at puge 282, that the 
principle is now well established by a series of decisions by the Tabour 
পা aed Tribunals that if the claim for bonus is made long after the 
year for which bonus is claimed has ended, and accounts have been 
closed, the Tribunals would be justified in rejecting such a belated claim. 
The Hon’ble Supreme Court of India, in the case of Muir Mills Company 


2948 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 15. 1957 [Pant I 


vs. Suti Mills Mazdoor Union (1955, L.U.J., page 5) has laid down— 
“On the accounts of earh year being made up and_ the profits of the 
industrial concern being ascertained, the workers during the particular 
yeur have their demand for bonus fully satisfied out of surplus profits, 
and the balance of the profits is allorated and carried over in the accounts. 
No further claim for payment of bonus out of these reserves or 
undistributed profits can, therefore, survive’, In view of the principles 
‘enunciated above, I am definitely of the opinion that the 6۵ 
claim for additional bonus for the years 1952, 1953 and 1954 is not 
tenable. At least, it is crystal clear that the claim for such additional 
bonus, particularly for the years 1952 and 1953, is barred, because the 
demand for such additional bonus was made at a time when the accounts 
for those years had been closed and adjusted, and the workers during those 
particular years had their demand for bonus fully satisfied out of surplus 
profits. The balance of profits in respect of those years was allocated 
and carried over in the accounts. That being s0, the claim for additional 
bonus for those years could not survive. Such a belated claim for 
bonus should not be investigated. This principle has also received the 
gr of the Supreme Court. In the case of Muir Mills as mentioned 
above, their Lordships pointed out that no further claim for payment 
of bonus out of reserves and undistributed profits, after the accounts of 
each year were made up, did survive. I may say incidentally here that 
from the balance-sheets which have been fled by the Company 
confidentially it appears that piggies and finalising of balance-sheets 
for the years 1952 and 1953 were completed by the chartered accountant 
on 2nd March 1958 and 18th June 1954, respectively, that is long before 
the claim for bonus for the years 1952 and 1953 was made, I have 
observed no doubt that the calim for additional bonus for the year 1954 
19 2180 a belated one. But it apears from the balance-sheet for the year 
1954 that the auditing and finalising of the balance-sheet for that year 
was made by the chartered accountant on 14th June 1955, that 18 after 
the demand for additional bonus for that year was made by the Union on 
behalf of the employees. The employees come to know of the financial 
position of the Company only when they get a copy of the 
audited accounts. So, the bonus claim can very well be made on behalf 
of the employees even after the closing of the accounts, if the claim for 
bonus has not been fully satisfied out of the undistributed profits of the 
yeur. The employees, admittedly, got bonus for the year 1954, equivalent 
to one month’s basic wage with dearness allowance. From Ext. M(1) 
which is a statement of account prepared by the Company from the 
balance-sheet for the year 1954, it appears that the Company had 
Rs. 1,05,358-11-12 as profit. The present theory regarding profit bonus 
according to the Full Bench Formula is that bonus can only be paid, 
should there be a residue or surplus after deducting prior charges and 
also after making provisions for the return on paid-up capital as well 
as on working capital, and if there be no substantial profits or available 
surplus after such deductions, the claim for bonus on the basis of profit 
cannot be sustained. From Ext. M(1) which is a statement of account 

repared by the Company from the balance-sheet on the basis of the Full 

ench Formula, it appears that the income-tax demand for the year in 
question was Rs. 50,965-13, return on paid-up capital at the rate of 
6 per cent. was Rs. 24,000 and dividend calculated at the rate of 6 per cent. 
was ulso Rs. 24,000, that is Re. 98,965-13 in all. Nothing has been 
claimed on reserves employed as working capital. In my view, the 
Company is entitled to get legitimate deductions of the items mentioned 
above from the gross profit. So, after deducting the amounts in respect 
of those items, it appears that the surplus available for the year 
1954 was Rs. 6,392-14-2. It is evident from Ext. J, that the wage 


Pant 11 ‘ME CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 15, 1957 2949 


bill of al] employees in this concern for the month of December 1954, was 
Rs. 11,286. That being 50, it is manifestly clear that the available 
surplus was insufficient and the employees of this concern were not 
entitled to get bonus even for 15 days out of this surplus available for 
that year. So, in any view of the matter, the Union’s claim for additional 
bonus for the year 1954 is not tenable. Therefore, it is decided that 
the employees of this concern are not entitled to get any additional bonua 
for the year 1954. Now remains for consideration, the Union’s claim 
for profit bonus for the year 1955. Admittedly, the Company had already 
paid two months’ basic salary as bonus to the employees for the year 
1955. It is contended on behaff of the Union that over and above the 
said payment, the employees are entitled to get bonus for that year as 
profit bonus. It appears from Ext. M, which is a statement of account

per Full Bench Formula, that after making allowance for prior charges 
and also after making provisions for income-tax, fair return on the paid- 
up capital and dividend, and transferring certain amount to general 
reserve, there remained available surplus to the extent of Rs. 2,960-12-10 
only, although the gross profit for that year was Re. 1,40,943-10-10. 
It has transpired from Ext. J, that the total wage bill for the employees 
of this concern in December 1955 came up to Rs. 11,0380. This bemg 
the position, the Union’s claim for any further bonus for the year 195d 
cannot be sustained, as the available surplus was insignificant. It is 
accordingly held that the claim of the Union for additional bonus for the 
year 1955 must also fail. 


I may say in this connection that I have perused the baalnce-sheets 
for the years 1954 and 1955, which were produced confidentially before 
the Tribunal. It appears from the halance-sheets that the items of 
deductions as made by the Company in their statementa as per Full 
Bench Formula are quite legitimate, inasmuch as the balance-sheets 
support the same. The balance-sheets should be deemed to be correct, 
unless the contrary is shown by evidence. In the present case, the Union 
did not and could not adduce any evidence to show that the balance- 
sheets were not correct. Even, no endeavour has been made in this 
respect. I am fully alive to the fact that this Company is not a 
manufacturing concern. But that does not stand in the way of applying 
Full Bench Formula in the matter of calculating profit bonus in the 
present case. I am of the view that the Company is certainly entitled to 
get the henefit of that formula, so far as the deductions as shown in the 
statements of account prepared by them are concerned, inasmuch as they 
are legitimate deductions, In result, it is decided by the Tribunal 
that the employees are not entitled to get any further bonus for the years 
1952, 1953, 1954 and 1955. This issue is answered accordingly. 


issue No. 8: This issue relates to reinstatement of 4 workers— 
Shri Debi Prosad Mukherjee, Kamala Hazam, Shri Monmohan Baneriee 
and Shri Santosh Kumar Mukherjee. At the very outset, 1 may say 
that Shri Debi Prosad Mukherjee did not come to depose before the 
Tribunal or to defend himself. He was the Assistant Secretary of the 
Union. The contention of the Union is that he was dismissed on 3rd 
February 1956, and that his dismissal was unjustified and mala fide. 
Tt has also been contended on behalf of the Union that he was sacked 
simply because of his Union activities, as he was the prime mover of the 
Union being the Assistant Secretary. As stated already, Shri Debi 
Prosad Mukherjee has not deposed in this case. O.P.W. 1, the General 
Manager, has stated in his evidence why and under what circumstances 
Shri Mukherjee was charge-shected. From the evidence of the General

by 0.P.W. 1, General Manager. He has stated that Shri Debi Prosad

to go on a pen-down strike on that date, and as a result thereof, there

the Tribunal, and they are 10568, C(1) and C(2). It appears that Shri Debi

What he did, was indeed reprehensible. He adopted an attitude 
unbecoming an employee of the Company. No Company in the interest 
of discipline and good administration can afford to tolerate such acts of 
mirconduct on the part of 0 worker. Such insubordination and grave 
misconduct undermine discipline, and the gravity of such action and 
conduct cannot be underrated. In my view, the punishment was 
commensurate with the offence. Though Shri Mukherjee happened to 
occupy what he considered to be the august position of the Assistant 
Secretary of the Union, he did not cease to be an employee of the 
Company. He should have remembered that he was first and foremost an 
employee of the Company and owed allegiance to it. So, the dismissal of 
Shri Debi Prosad Mukherjee was justified, and he is not entitled to 
reinstatement or any relief whataoever.

issue No. 9: This issue relates to retrenchment of Shri Ramesh 
Chandra Mukherjee. According to the Union, he was appointed hy the 
Company as a clerk 10 the Mofussil Department, ond had served the 
Company for about 9 years with credit. Fle was the Treasurer of the 
Union, and as such he was in the black book of the Nompany. So, all 
on a sudden, he was retrenched by a notice, dated 5th December 1955, on 
the alleged ground of “‘trade depression’. It is contended by the Union 
that his retrenchment was unjustified and mala fide. His retrenchment 
was rather a device to get rid of him, because he was considered 
undesirable for his Union activities. The Company in its written 
atatement justified the retrenchment of Shri Ramesh Chandra Mukherjee. 
The version of the Company is that Shri Mukherjee was 0, clerk in the 
Packing Section of the Mofussil Department. But as there was gradual 
fall in the work of this section, and as the financial prospect 
of the Company became gloomy, Shri Mukherjee had to be retrenched 
by a notice, dated Sth December 1955. The Company further says that 
Shri Mukherjee was the juniormost in the particular section of the 
Mofussil Department. Now let me consider the evidence. Exhibit 16 
is the letter of retrenchment that was served on Shri Mukherjee, and it is 
dated 5th December 1955. The said letter runs thus: — 


‘Due to present trade position and gloomy financial outlook, the 
Company is faced with a situation which calls for reduction of 
staff in the interests of economy. The Management has decided 
to effect retrenchment gradually. Therefore, your services are 
being terminated with immediate effect.”’ 


O.P.W. 1, the General Manager, has stated 10 his evidence that 
Shri Ramesh Chandra Mukherjee worked in the Packing Section of the 
Mofussil Department, and the work in the Packing Section at the 
relevnt time decreased. He has further stated that at that time, there 
were 3 clerks in that secion including Shri Ramesh Chandra Mukherjee, 
who happened to be the juniormost in that section. It has further 
transpired from his evidence that since the retrenchment of Shri Mukherjee, 
no other clerks were taken in the Packing Section, though the 
work in that section remained the same. Shri Ramesh Chandra Mukherjee 
has deposed in this case, and he is P.W. 4. His evidence is that he did 
not work in the Packing Section, but he used to work صا‎ the 
Mofussil Department of the Head Office as a clerk. He has stated on 
oath that there was no decrease in the volume of work in this department. 
He haa further stated that the ground ag stated by the Company 
for his retrenchment in the letter marked Ext. 16 is not correct. It has 
also transpired from his evidence that since his retrenchment clerks 
were taken, and that there are still in service of the Company clerks 
who are junior to him. The Company could _ not establish by -uny 
satisfactory evidence that there was any Packing Section in the Mofussil 
Department of this Company. Shri Ramesh Chandra Mukherjee was & 
clerk attached to the Head Office of this Company, and he was workin 
at the relevant time in the Mofussil Department as clerk. He has prove 
a list (Ext. 17), which goes to show that after his retrenchment the 
clerks as mentioned in that list were appointed by the Company, and one 
of them was taken in the Mofussil Department in his place. The 
Company could not prove by any cogent and satisfactory evidence that 
what was stated in that list (Ext. 17), was not correct. That the Company 


2964 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 15. Wot [Perr 1 


had retained in their service several clerks junior to Shri Ramesh 
Chandra Mukherjee is evident from Ext. F, which is a statement filed 
by the Company itself. So, it cannot be believed that Shri Mukherjee 
had to he retrenched, as he was the juniormost clerk at that time. 
Thus, it is clear that the principle of “‘last come, first go’’ was not 
followed, while Shri Mukherjee was retrenched. Shri Mukherjee was 
appointed as aclerk, and at the relevant time was working in the 
Mofussil Department. So, his case should be taken in the same pool 
with other clerks. He should have heen considered as a member of the 
clerical staff, and did not constitute a different category by himeelf, 
hecause he was working at the relevant time in the Mofusail Department. 
Therefore, he cannot be hit by the principle of ‘‘last come, first go’, if 
he is taken in the same pool with other 002 there being several junior 
clerks to him in the service of the Company at the time of bis retrench- 
ment. He should not, therefore, have been retrenched. Then again, 
on a consyleration of the evidence and the materials placed before it, 
the Tribunal comes to the conclusion that the Management has not made 
out a case for retrenchment of Shri Ramesh Chandra Mukherjee. Nor 
enn it he said that the Management acted bona fide in this respect. 
The Tribunal has every reason to believe that the Gompany in effecting 
retrenchment of Shri Ramesh Chandra Mukherjee was actuated by 
improper motives, and acted on extraneous considerations. The reason 
as given in the letter of retrenchment, which is dated Sth December 1955 
(Ext. 16), cannot be accepted. At that time, neither the trade position 
of this Company, nor the financial outlook of its business was bad or 
gloomy in any way, as the balance-sheet for the year ending 1955, shows 
that the Company earned considerable profits in that year. In the letter 
of retrenchment txt. 16), it is mentioned that the Management decided 
to effect retrenchment gradually. But it is very interesting to note that 
save and except Shri Ramesh Chandra Mukherjee, the services of no 
other employee had been terminated by the Company till now by way of 
retrenchment. Therefore, it is decided that the retrenchment of 
Shri Ramesh Chandra Mukherjee is unjustified. Accordingly, it 18 ordered 
thnt he be reinstated. He will report himself for duty to this Company 
within 15 days from the date of publication of this اش‎ in 
the Calcutta Gazette. He will get full pay and dearness allowance for 
the period from the date of his retrenchment till reinstatement. The 
payment as directed above, should also be made within a month when 
this award becomes operative. Be it further noted that the period of 
this forced unemployment of Shri Ramesh Chandra Mukherjee should not 
be regarded as a break in his service for the purpose of benefits, to which 
he may be entitled as an employee of the Company. This issue 18 decided 
accordingly,

issue No, 1. 


Messrs, Jewel of India Perfume Company is a proprietary concern 
manufacturing mainly hair oils. Proprietor lives at 930 Diamond Harhour 
Road, Cocola House, Pehala, Calcutta-34. In the said premises the ilead 
Office of the concern is also situated wherein the workman P.W. 3 Ramdeo 
Jaiswal was employed as a cleaner of vans. Thé concern had only one 
factory ut Simultala, Behala. P.W. 2 Shri Luxman Chandra Khamaru and 
Shri Amritalal Mondal were employed there, of whom P.W. 2 was 
dismissed on 26th April 1955 and P.W. 4 was alleged to have been refused 
employment from 9186 October 1955. Besides it employed 31 workmen as 
shown in the list attached to the order of reference in addition to two 
durwans at the relevant time (7th December 1955), The said factory was 
closed with effect from 7th December 1955 by a notice, dated 6th December 
1956 and as & result 31 workmen named in the list were discharged from 
19) December 1965. Before such closure the Company had started another 


factory with new hands on 8th August 1955 in the premises at 330 Diamond 
Harbour Road. 


For betterment of their conditions the workmen employed at the factory 
at Simultala formed the Union (Jewel of India Perfume Workers’ Union) 
on 9001, April 1965. The Union was duly registered on 15th July 1965. 
It submitted a charter of demands on 9th August 1955 (Ext. 1). 


Following dismissal on 25th April 1955, P.W. 2 Shri Juuxman Chandra 
Khamaru moved the Labour Directorate on 27th April 1955, whereupon 
conciliation started. Then after submission of charter of demands separate

eections 7 and 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the

Bus Service, 138A Nirode Rehari Mullick Road, Calcutta-6, and their work- 
map Shrt Joydev Paul, represented by the Bus Workers’ Union, 249 Bow- 


bazar Street, Calcutta-12, regarding matters specified in the second schedule 
of the Act, to this Court for adjudication. 


Schedule 


Whether the dismissal of Shri Jovydev Paul is justified? To what relief 
including reinstatement is he entitled ? 


AWARD 
The case of the Union may be thus stated in a nutshell— 


The workman Shri Joydev Paul entered the services of the Company 18 
a driver in April 1955 at a monthly salary of Rs. 150. Joydev Paul took 
on active part طط‎ Trade Union activities of the workmen of the Union and 
took up the terms and conditions with the Company with a view to ameliorate 
them, The Company did not take the Trade Union activities of the work- 
man In good grace and advised the workman to dissociate himself from 
the Trade Union but to no effect. The Company drew up a charge-sheet 
on certain allegations which he denied and refuted as baseless and false. 
Thereupon the Company dismissed him summarily without any further 
enquiry. The Union therefore contends that the discharge of the workman 
is unjustified, illegal, mala fide and a case of victimisation and an unfair 
labour practice. The Tnion therefore seeks the reinstatement of the workman 
tovether with his full back wages and compensation for the period of forced 
unemployment. 


The Company 8180 put in a written statement denying the material 
nilegations in the written statement of the Union and contends, inter alia, 
that ‘the workman was engaped purely on temporary basis; that this driver 
drove fhe bus so rashly and negligently on 2nd October 1956 that the 
universal joint of the bus was broken for which the bus needed to he 
repaired resulting in financial 1089 to the Company; that on 5th October 1968 
he was sd reckless in driving that the valve of the bus was burnt; that even 
after his suspension from work he forcibly took out the hus from the garage 
and drové it on 8th October 1956 in the evening and 9th October 1956 in 
the morning without the permission of the Company; that the driver is 
guilty of insuhordination and misconduct and against him the Company 
received ‘several complaints; that the driver was duly charge-sheeted and 
wns dismissed after proper enquiry. The Company therefore urges that the 
worknan is entitled to no relief. 


DECISION 


The point for determination in this case 1s whether the dismissal of this 
driver Shri Joydev Paul is justified or not. The Company drew up a 
charge-sheet against this workman as per Ext. A on 10th October 1956. 
The charges framed may he briefly stated as follows: (1) that on 2nd 
October 1956 he drove the bus No. WBS 482 so rashly and negligently that 
its universal joint was broken for which the bus needed repairs and loss was 
(1861 to the Company, (2) bv reason of his rough handling of the bus on 
hth Octoher 1056 at about 1-80 p.m., the valve was burnt similarly causing 
financial loss to the Company. On the basis of the two charges, the work- 
man was called upon to show cause within 7 days why he should not be 
discharged for ‘his gross negligence of duty. He was also suspended from 
duty with effect from 10th’ October 1956. The driver showed cause as per 


2064 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 15, 1957 = [Paur ا‎ 


Annexure B, dated 16th October 1956, Ext. 1. Herein the driver has affirmed 
that there wis no sueh happening on 2nd Octoher 1956 and that the 
universal joint was all right up to 8th Uctober 1956 until he was suspended 
frum duty aud that the bus ran without any break up to Sth October 1956 
when it remained invalid for a few hours only for repairs to the universal 
joint, As regards the second charge, his reply is thai the bus remained 
idle up te 4 p.m. at the stand as the misiry was reneiring 1۲ and so the 
allegntion of causing damage to the valve at about 1-40 p.m. 1s not true. 
The driver, therefore, in a word, stuted that both jis charges are unfounded. 
Thus there was the charge and the reply thereto. After this there is nothing 
on record to show that the Company held any sort of enquiry but the driver 
was abruptly told that he was dismissed. In the meantime we find that 
there was a conciliation proceeding by a Labour Officer of Government of 
Weat Bengal but the dispute was not satisfactorily solved. In this case ا‎ 
is quite clear that no enquiry waa held before terminating the service of this 
driver, nor was he given any opportunity whatasever to explain his viewpoint 
to the Company. The Company appears to have adopted a high-handed 
policy casting to the wind the principles of natural justice and the action 
of the Company cannot therefore be supported. The Company’s action was 
simply capricious, arbitrary and unjustified. Tet alone the truth or 
otherwise of the charges framed which [ shall discuss presently. 


As already stated the charge of the Company against this workinan is that 
the universa! joint of the bus was broken on 2nd October 1956 due to rash 
driving by this workman and that on 5th October 19660 due to his rash 
driving the valve got charred. Though Shri Sudhukhan, 0. P. W. 1, has 
stated that the universal joint was temporarily repaired on 220 October 
1956 by a mistry the absence of the mistry from the witness box is simply 
inexplicable. In this case the mistry who repaired the universal joint and 
valve would have been the most important witness, but he is conspicuous 
by his absence. Another important thing is that Sadhukhan states that 
Company was put to heavy expenditure to the tune of Rs. 500 for repairs 
and for suspension of the running of the buns but no account of the cost for 
repairs 1s produced to convince the Court that the bus really needed repairs. 
In this connexion 11 may be very useful to mention that the Union has shown 
with reference to their way-bill (Ext. F) that the bus did not at all run 
from 12-11 to 3-30 p.m. on 5th October 1956 and this obviously negatives the 
allegation of the Company that the value of the bus gat charred at about 
1-30 p.m. while being driven nearabout Howrah Station. 


Beyond dispute the universal joint is a long iron road placed beneath 
the body of the bus and this bus was udmittedly purchased in 1949 and we 
would expect that the bus naturally underwent normal wear and tear during 
these years. This bus used to he driven not only by this workman but also 
by another, 80 the Company bas failed in fixing the guilt of breaking the 
universal joint on this driver alone, if the universal joint did at all break. 
A suspicion that the other drivers:might also have contributed to the breach 
of the universal joint is thus not altogether excluded, On a consideration 
of the facts and circumatances of this ense and due regard being had to the 
evidence of Shri Sadhukhan, the Court cannot find that the charges have 
heen established. Rather the Court finds that there is no truth in the 
charges themselves. In such cases as laid down in the recent case of Bazpai 
and others vs. Labour Appellate Tribunal, reported in 1957, Vol. II, page 
16, the Court is to consider three questions (1) whether the workman was 
found guilty by the Company, (2) whether the correct procedure was 
followed by the Company, and (3) whether the misconduct could be visited 
with the dismissal. In this case it is quite clear that no procedure wag at 
al} followed by the Company because no enquiry was held, nor was any 
opportunity given to the workman to explain his conduct. That being so, 


Parr }] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST. 16, 1957 2965 
তত 


the Company not having followed the correct procedure, the workman should 
not have been visited with this punishment. [may add that the Company 
pul in an uncertified copy (3:51. 13) of a G. D. ‘entry with the avowed ob,ect 
of supporting the dismissal of the workwan which was apparently 
unjustified. 


0 the other hand, it is-quite clear that this workman was victimised 
as he took up the cause of the other aggrieved workmen under the Company 
and 19010 part in the Trade Union activities which the Company did 10001 
obviously like. This is a clear case of victimisation and un unfair labour 
practice, Therefore the discharge of this workman is found to be unjustified, 
mala fide and an unfair Jabour practice. 


This workman is therefore entitled to relief. Of course, the normal 
relief in such cases is reinstatement but in view of the complaints about his 
rash driving and insolent and objectionable behavior with other colleagues 
as evidenced by the complaints Exts. C, D, EB, I find that it will not be 
conducive to the interests of peace and harmony in the Company to give him 
the desired relief of reinstatement. This workman admittedly put in service 
for about 2 years and so in law and equity he is entitled to a month’s pay 
in lieu of notice and another month’s pay as compensation. This entitles him 
to recover Rs. 300 from the Company. The Company must pay the sum ef 
Rs. 800 to the workman within a month of the publication of this award. 


This 1s my award.

Road, South, Calcutta-33. (Case No. ۷۱۱۱۰7۶2 of 1956.) 


BEFORE THE SIXTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL, 
NEW SECRETARIAT BUILDINGS, CALCUTTA 


PRESENT: 
Sur1 SAILESH SENGUPTA, Judye, Sixth Industrial Tribunal. 


Appearances: 


For the Association: Shri Pasupati Chattopadhyay, President, Shri 
Bhupendra Nath Ghosh, Secretary, and Shri R. R. Sinde. 


For the New Theatres, Ltd.: Shri P. R. Mukherjee, M.A., LL.B. 


For the Receiver: Shri N. K. Mukherjee, Advocate, and Shri Subodh 
Chandra Mukherjee. 


This reference made by Government order No. 4205Dis. /D/111-125/56, 
dated Calcutta, the 19th September 1956, is concerned with the question 
of arrears of salaries due to eight employees of the New Theatres Limited. 


The points for adjudication are in the followimg terms :— 


(1) Whether the following eight employees are entitled to get any 
relief for the termination of their services :— 
(i) Shri R. N. Dhar, (ii) Shri R. R. Shinde, (i) Shri N. D, 
Majumdar, (iv) Shri Arabindu Mukherjee, (v) Shri Prabhakar 
Haldar, (vi) Shri Dinesh Das, (vii) Shri Naresh Lose and 
(viii) Shri Charu Ch. Ghosh. 


(2) The arrear salaries of these eight employees. 
The employees confined their claim to recovory of arrears of pay. 


The Company raised various legal objections, viz., this was not an 
industrial dispute, that the proper forum was the Tribunal set up under 
the Payment of Wages Act. Regarding the claim the Company submitted 
that it was exaggerated and none of the workers presented themselves to 
recelve payment. 


During the pendency of the proceeding The New Theatres Limited 
informed the Tribunal that a receiver had been appointed by the Hon’ble 
High Court who had tuken possession of the assets. An application was 
made by the Cine Technicians’ Association to issue notice to the receiver. 
Notice was issued and the receiver appeared and filed written statement 
objecting to his rejoinder as a party. 


At the time of hearing it was pointed out that two of the workers 
Charu Chandra Ghosh and Provakar Halder had withdrawn their case and 
Naresh Bose wus dead. 


-Having heard the learned Advocate for the receiver and read the order 
made by the Ifon*ble High Court I om satisfed- thatthe receiver cannot 


Part 2] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 15, 1957 2967 


eee es et এর ges জাল ৮. ہے‎ 


be treated as a party. He was appointed receiver in a mortgage auit filed 
ugainst The New Theatres Limited. The learned Advocate read out the 
order of appointment and a plain copy thereof has been filed before the 
Tribunal. It appears that the receiver was given authority for the specific 
purpose of making collections of outstanding debis, ete., and certain other 
ancillary purpose. He was not directed to manage the business. He was 
not charged with the duty of meeting liabilities. On the terms of the 
order no duty was cast upon him to discharge habilities. No award can 
be made against him by this Tribunal in respect of the salaries claimed. 
Further the receiver cannot be made a party with the leave of the Hon’ble 
High Court. For these reasons the Tribunal finds that the receiver has 
been unnecessarily summoned. 


On behalf of The New Theatres Limited an objection was taken that 
this is not an industrial dispute. Section 2(k) of the Industrial Disputes 
Act defines industrial dispute which means any dispute or difference between 
employer and employer or between employer and workmen, or _ between 
workmen and workmen which is connected with the employment or  non- 
employment or the terms of employment or with the condition of labour of 
any’ pérson. Non-payment of salary cannot be fitted in with any of the 
clauses in the definition. No industrial dispute can therefore arise on the 
ground of wages being in arrears. ‘The argument pressed 01) bebalf of 
The New Theatres Limited on this point accordingly succeeds. 


Allied to the above is the point that the Industrial Tribunal is not the 
proper forum for an action to recover arrears of wages. The Payment of 
Wages Act (Act IV of 1936) provides the forum. Section 22, clause (qd), 
lays down that no Court shall entertain any suit for the recovery of wages 
or of any deduction from wages in so far as the sum so claimed could have 
been recovered by an application under section 15. The workers could 
have their relief by an application made before the Authority under the 
Payment of Wages Act. No other Tribunal can exercise jurisdiction in 
this regard. The workers in this case, as already pointed out, claim nothing 
other than arrears of wages. Their remedy therefore was available in the 
Tribunal set under by the Payment of Wages Act. 


The learned lawyer for the New Theatres Limited challenged the 
reference itself on the ground that the New Theatres Limited was not in 
existence on the date of the reference. I am not impressed with this 
argument. ‘I'he New Theatres Limited has not gone into liquidation. A 
receiver was appointed by the Hon’ble High Court on the 7th of August 
1956 only for some specific purposes in connexion with a mortgage suit. 
The New Theatres Limited still exists as an independent entity. There is 
nothing wrong therefore in the order of reference in which The New 
Theatres Limited has been named as a party. 


Another point was pressed that the studio having been closed entirely 
the employees are not entitled to any relief on the principle that the 
Industrial Disputes Act can be applied only when any industry is still in 
existence. This point also is void of substance as the arrears fell due 
before the closure. I need not however dilate upon this point as on two 
other points of vital importance, the Tribunal finds in favour of The New 
Theatres Limited. The employees cannot recover arrears of wages by a 


2968 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 15, 1957> [Parr I 


Se een 


proceeding before this Tribunal. They are not therefore entitled to get 
the relief claimed.

This reference made by the Government of West Bengal, Labour 
ee under order No. 5۰ 2 /11L-315/56, dated the 22nd 
October 1956, relates to the discharge of the employee Shri J. K. Purecha 
by Messrs. 8. I). Sethia & Co. (Private), Ltd. 

The issue framed in the order of reference is as follows :— 

What relief is Shri J. K. Purecha entitled to for his loss of service? 


Pant I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 16, 1967 2960 


পেস UT LR ৯ পাপ 


AWARD 


It 18 stated by the Union which has espoused the cause of Shri J. .ا‎ 
Purecha that he entered service under this Company and had put in two 
ears’ service. But all on a sudden, he was discharged on 29th July 1955. 
‘he employee wanted relief by way of reinstutement ond wages for the 
period he had to sit idle. Bonus eytivalent to what had been paid to other 
employees was 8180 claimed. 


The Company submitted written statement, and stated that this 
employee was employed for maintaining the accounts in the Head Office, 
but he was found to be inefficient and incompetent for which he got several 
warnings. He himself admitted in writing that he had committed many 
ministakes for which he begged to be excused, and gave an undertaking also 
not to commit such mistakes in future. But despite this, he went on 
committing mistakes as before in his work. So, at last on 29th July 1955 
his services were dispensed with. He was, however, given one monath’s 
salary in 1150 of notice, and he voluntarily signed a formal receipt in full 
and final settlement of his dues. For his persistent negligence of duty 
and inefficiency, he is not entitled to reinstatement. Nor he should 109 
granted any compensation or bonus. 


Findings 


The employee concerned has deposed before the ‘Tribunal. Scveral 
documents have also been proved by him, und they are Exts. 1 to 5. The 
Company adduced no evidence—either oral or documentary. It remained 
content by cross-examining only the employee. Admittedly, this employee 
was in the service of this Company for two years, but his services were 
dispensed with on 29th July 1955. Before his discharge, he got no notice, 
nor was he charge-sheeted. He was not given any opportunity even to 
explain. He was, however, paid his salary for the entire month of July 
1955 plus one month’s salary in lieu of notice, on the date on which his 
services were terminated. The employee has admitted no doubt in his 
cross-examination that he committed mistake once while in the service of 
this Company, and that for this he gave an undertaking to he careful in 
future. But this did not necessarily mean that he was to be kicked out 
from his service at any time at the sweet will and pleasure of the Manage- 
ment. Nor did such undertaking clothes the Management with power to 
dispense with his services in an arbitrary fashion—even without following 
the principles of natural justice. Modern concepts of social justice would 
be outraged if the employer is given such a long rope. Such concepts do 
require that an employee should be protected from capricious or vindictive 
action on the part of the employer, whatever be the nature of his lapse, 
or whatever be the cause of such lapse. Having regard to the conditions 
of labour relation as is now prevalent in this country, it would not he 
conducive to industrial peace, if an employer is given such an unfettered 
right to dismiss an employee in this fashion. An employee should he 
protected against the vindictive or capricious action on the part of 909 
Management, which may affect the security of his service. earned 
representative on behalf of the Company who cross-examined the employee 
and also argued the case before the Tribunal, wanted to say that the 
employee concerned was thoroughly inefficient und mcompetent, and ۹۷ 
the previous warnings had no effect on him. But it is interesting to note 
that the Company adduced no evidence whatsoever in support of this. 
So, the alleged charge of inefficiency and incompetency as made against 
this employee stands absolutely not proved. The employee concerned was 
employed for maintaining the accounts in the Head Office of the Company. 
After all, he is a human being. So, he waa likely to commit mistake on 


2970 THE CAILUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 16, 1957 [Panr I 
উহু 8 A te a a eo 


wome occasion, and such mistake cannot possibly be altogether avoided, 
specially in accounting work. In my view, his admission that in course 
of employment he committed mistuke once for which he begged to be 
excused and gavé an undertaking to be careful in future, cannot possibly 
be used as a weapon by the Company against the employee conecrned for 
all time to come. The work of the ‘employee wus important, und the 
interests of the Company demanded and required that it should be done as 
carefully as possible. But human nature being what it is, we are likely 
to commit mistakes now and then, and this inight be one such instance of 
mistake in course of work. For the foregoing reasons, the findings of the 
Tribunal must necessarily be that the order of discharge of Shm J. .ا‎ 
Purecha was not justified and proper. 


2, Urdinarily, the proper relief shonld have been reinstatement. But 
Shri J. K. Purecha in his evidence hus stated that he does not want 
reinstatement, as he had been employed elsewhere. 


This employee had put in two years’ continuous service in the Company. 
it appears that he used to get Rs. 160 as his emoluments including dearness 
allowance, when his services were dispensed with. So, one month’s 
compensation at that rate should be sufficient recompense. The question 
of his getting one month’s pay in lieu of notice does not arise any longer, 
as he has already got the same. He has also received salary for the entire 
month of July 1955. He has claimed bonus also. It appears trom Ext. 
2 that one month’s bonus was sanctioned to him for the year 1954-95. , He 
has not received the amount of that bonus as yet. So, he is entitled to 
get the same from the Company. He has further claimed wages for the 
earned leave due to him, but not availed of. But nothing has been proved 
by him in this respect. So, the Tribunal is unable to give him anything 
on this account. ‘To be more precise, this employee is entitled to get trom 
the Company one month’s pay aa compensation and also one month’s bonus 
as sanctioned to him by the Company for the vear 1954-55. Payment as 
directed above should be made within a week from the date of publication 
of this award in the Calcutta Gazette. 


‘This is my award in the present case,

PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION, WEST BENGAL 


General instructions to candidates applying In response to 
advertisements issued by the Commission for recrult- 
ment te posts by ‘‘Selection’’. 


(1) Instructions regarding submission of appiication.— 
Applications are to be made on the prescribed form which 
will be available from fhe office of the Public Service 
Commission, West Bengal, Anderson House round 
floor), Alipore, Caleutta-27, personally or on sending a 
large selt-addressed envelope with etamps sufficient to 
eover the postage affixed to 1t. Candidatos who are unable 
to obtain 2 of the prescribed form may apply on any 
similar typed (not handwritten) form showing exactly the 
wording and spucing of the sample form published in the 
“Calcutta Gazette’? of the Ist September 1955, provided 
the blanks ure filled up in the candidates’ own handwriting. 


(2) Partloulars and certificates required.—Candidates 
should furnish evidence of their age, qualifications and 
previous experience together with certificates written not 
mare than one year prior to the date of their applications, 
from responsible persons, testifying to their private 
character. 


(3) Fee.—Candidates must enclose with their applica- 
tions a fee of Rs. 5 (for each category of posts) in the 
form of a reeoknted chalan from a Government Treasury 
or the Reserve Bank of India under the head “XXXVI— 
Miscellaneous—Recoeipts of the Public Service Commission 
West Bengal’. Money orders, cheques, vtc., in lieu o 
treasury chalans are not accepted. Postal orders 
however, may be accepted from candidates. They should 
be crossed and made payable to “The Secretary, ٥۹ 
service Commission, West Bengal’’. No application will 
be considered unless accompanied with the requisite 
application fee. 


Candidates in Government service should make sure 
hefore depositing fee that their applications will be 
forwarded by their superior officers. In no case will the 
fee paid with the application be refunded. 


_ The Commission may remit fee in case of genuinely 
indigent and bona fide displaced persons from Pakistan. 


Note.—‘'(i) A displaced person claiming age concession 
must furnish with his application satisfactory evidence 
that he is a bona fide displaced person from Pakistan, 
©.g., refugee registration card or a@ certificate from ৬৬ 
تع مگ‎ officer or a Member of Parliament or State 

gislature, in original. 


(ii) A member of the Scheduled Caste or Scheduled 
Tribe claiming age concession must furnish with his 
application a certificate in original from a gazetted officer 
or a Member of Porliament or State Legislature belonging 
to the Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe, specifying the 
particular caste or tribe to which he claims to belong. 

(iii) A displaced person seeking remission of the 
application fee muat furnish besides the evidence required 
under Note (i) above, a certificate (in original) from a 
District Officer or a garetted officer or a Member of 
Parliament or State Legislature to show that he is not in 
a@ position to pay the prescribed fee.’’ 


(4) Address.—Candidates should give their present 
address and should communicate at once any subsequent 
change of address. 


(5) Canvassing.—Any attempt on the part of candidates 
to enlist support of their applications through persons of 
influence or officials of Government will disqualify them 
for appointment. Spontaneous recommendation from 
persons interested in tho candidates or otherwise known 
to them will be disregarded. 


(6) Applications from candidates who are in permanent 
or temporary employment under any Government, a local 
or Statutory Body (e.z., Damodar Valley Corporation), in 
India will be rejected unless they are submitted through 
the appointing authority of their posta or service, 


Candidates شا‎ under Government or a local or 
statutory body should submit an advance copy in the 
peas form, The application fees should in such cases 
5 attached to the advance copy and not to the original. 
The candidature of such applicants may not however be 
considered if the original applications do not reach the 
Commission's office within a ‘fortnight from the closing 
dete, Unless applications in omginal or advance copies 
with application fees are received within the clesing date, 
lute applications may be rejected.

CORPORATION OF CALCUTTA 
710110 
Calcutta, the 8th August 1957. 


The oy om, Finance Committee of the oo by ite Hesolution, 
dated the 27th July’ 1957, adopted finally the following rules framed under 
section 173 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1961 سے‎ ۰ 


1. For the purpose of valuing the land contained 16) a bustee and 
the huts standing on ار‎ separately, as provided in section 173 
of the Act, the following principles shall apply— 


(a) the annual value of the land contained within a bustee shall 
be deemed to be the gross annual rent at which such land 
might at the time of assessment be expected to let from year 
to year: 


Provided that vacant land within a bustee shall be valued at half 
the rate of rent taken for such land if actually let out: 


(b) the annual value of 8 hut standing in a bustee shall be deemed 
to be the groas annual rent at which the hut might at the 
time of assessmertt he reasonably expected tq let from fear to 
year after deducting therefrom the gross annual rent of the 
land appertaining thercto and an allowance of t6n per eent., 
for the Sost of repairs and for all expenses necessary to 
maintain such hut in a state (0 command such gross-rent. 


2. The total value of a hut including the land appertaining ‘thereto 
shall be deemed to be the sum obtained by adding fhe annual 
value of the land appertaining thereto to the annual value of tha 
hut as determined under rule 1(b). 


B. GHOSH, Secretary.

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 
DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH 
Public Health 
NOTIFICATION 


No. P,H.3867 /2R /68/57.—20th August 1957.—Whereas the Governor 
is satisfied that the district of 24-Parganas is threatened with an outbreak 
of cholera; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the power conferred by section 2 of the 
Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 (III of 1897), the Governor is pleased to 
prescribe the following temporary regulations for the prevention and control 
of cholera, and for the medical inspection, isolation, observation and 
surveillance of persons suffering from, or suspected of being infected with, 
cholera in the said districts for a period of s1x months : 


TEMPORARY RECULATIONS FOR THE PREVENTION AND 
CONTROL OF CHOLERA. 


1. In these regulations, unless there is anything repugnant in the 
subject or context— 


(a) ‘‘District Health Officer’? means the Health Officer of the district 
appointed by the district board under sub-section () of section 91 
of the Bengal Local Self-Government Act of 1885 (Bengal Act III 
of 1885); 


(b) “Sanitary Inspector’? means a Sanitary Inspector appointed by the 
district board under sub-section (8) of section 91 of the Bengal 
Local Self-Government Act of 1886; 


(c) ‘Board’? means a district board constituted under the Bengal Local 
Self-Government Act of 1885;

and diarrhoea; 


(f) “Patient” means a person suffering from or suspected 10 be suffering

(9) ‘Medical practitioner” means any person practising the medical

2. Whenever any land is held jointly by two or more persons, whether 
as owners or occupiers of that land, such persons shall be held jointly and 
severally liable for carrying out any measure ordered in ৪. notice under 
these regulations, and the names of any one or more of such joint-hotders 
may be entered upon such notice at the discretion of the District Health 
Officer and the District Health Officer shall not be bound to enter the names 
of all the joint-holders in the notice, 


Notices. 


3. If in any case the District Health Officer considers that the issue of 
a notice under these regulations is likely to lead to such an amount of delay 
nx might facilitate the spread of cholera he may forthwith take such step as 
he may think fit tor carrying out the work, and shall thereafter, as soon as 
possible, issue a notice on the person concerned stating the reason why such 
work has been carried out.

oid by that person:

(2) The board may recover all expenses incurred by the District Health 
(10809: in carrying out the measure under regulation 4 from the person or

Provided that no person shall receive any compensation for anything 
done, or suffered under these regulations, if he has foiled to carry out an 
order issued under these regulations within the time specified in the order 
and to the satisfaction of the District Health Officer.

Isolation of patients 


10. When the District Health Officer or a Sanitary Inspector considers

of the neighbouring population, he shall order the patient to observe

specified in the order,

Sanitary Inspector. 
14. When a patient has heen removed froma house for isolation under 


regulation 10, the board shall provide for him free of charge a suitable 
place, with necessary attendants, diet, etc.

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 
HOME DEPARTMENT 
General Administration 


RESOLUTION 


No. 2564G.A.—l17th August 1957.—Government have received with 
decp regret the news of the untimely death of Shri Kshetradas Banarji, 
লা District and Sessions Judge, Burdwan, on the night of the 11th 
July 1957. 


2. Shri Banarji joined the Bengal Civil Service (Judicial) in August, 
1936. He served in various districts in Bengal and Assam and ufter Parti- 
tion, he continued to serve in West Bengal. At first, he served as a Munsif 
and, later, as a Subordinate and Assistant Sessions Judge. He was pro- 
moted to officiate in the West Bengal Higher Judicial Service in May, 
eae and was appointed as the Additional District and Sessions Judge, 
Burdwan. 


4. Throughout his service, Shri Banarji upheld the highest traditions 
of integrity and devotion to duty of the Judicial Service. His sense of 
fairness earned him the esteem and affection of all those who came in 
contact with him. 


4. The Government of West Bengal desire to record their profound 
regret at the untimely loss of an experienced officer and“wish to convey to 
his family the sincere expression of their sympathy. 


By order of the Governor, 
S. N. RAY, Chief Secretary.

Qualifications

and above 6() years.

(e) He must he a man of known integrity.

service or be a practising Inwyer.

OFFICE OF THE DISTRICT MACISTRATE, 
COOCH BEHAR 


ORDER 
Dated Cooch Behar, the 13th August 1957, 


In exercise of the powers conferred hy section 
20 of the Weat Bengal Security Act, 1950, as 
delegated to me under section 33 of the said Act 
by the Government of West Bengal, Home 
(Political) Department, notification No. 21701| 
30-9/50, dated llth April 1950, I do hereby 
order that movement of all sorts of cloths and 
yarns within two milea from Pakistan border of 
this district be prohibited. Indian citizens resid- 
ing within the aforesaid area may, however, 
obtain their supplies of the aforesaid com- 
modities for their own consumption only. 


The dealers having their places of business with- 
in two miles from the border may bring in eu 
for sale with a permit issued by either the Sub- 
divisional Controller of Food and Supplies or the 
Subdivisional Officer concerned and shall maintain 
accounts of cash sales to bona fide customers and 
will also mention names und addresses of such 
purchasers in the Cash memoa, issued مع‎ as 
to enable police officers or any other officers 
authorised in this behalf to verify the same at 
any time. 


The aforesaid order shall remain in force for 
three months with effect from 15th August 1967.

(1) Is the dismissal of Buaijnath justified; if not, what relief he is

(2) Ts the dispute an industrial dispute; if not, has the Tribunal juris-

155888 No. 2: The Company’s contention is that since on dispute over 
the dismissal gf a single workman cannot be an industrial dispute, this one 
is not an industrial dispute. Tt is an individual dispute and cannot 
become an industrial dispute, unless the dismissed workman’s cause is taken 
up by his colleagues or by a Union of which he is a member. The Company 
further contends that even the representation by Md. Ismail, Secretary, Bus 


3006 THE CAILUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 22, 1957 = [Part I
