Workers’ Union, is tmnproper and not in accordance with = the 
provisions of section 36 of the Industrial Disputes Act. The order of 
reference is to the following effect: ‘‘Whereas an industrial dispute exists 
between Messrs. Harnam Singh Co., 116/1 Hazra Road, Calcutta, and 
their workmun Shri Baiyhath, represented by Bus Workers’ Union, 249 
Bowbazar Street, Caleutta, ete.’’ ‘he admitted evidence of Ext. A and 
Ext. I is that the Company received'a letter from the Secretary, Bus Workers’ 
Union, dated 10th May 1996, in which the Union complained of arbitrary 
disinissal from service of its member, Shri Baijmuth and held out threats 
that further action should be taken unless Shri Baijnath waa reinstated in 
service und paid his arrears of ‘wages. The details of the letter mentioned 
in Ext. A are not before us. Elaborate arguments were advanced on the 
assumption that Shri Baijnath’s case was not taken up by the Union but 
the Union only ‘‘represented’’ it before the Con¢iliation Officer and the 
Government, as it had done before fhe Tribunal. In fact, the Union took 
up bis case ‘‘Threating action’, long before the matter was referred to a 
Conciliation Officer and before the case was referred to this Tribunal. It 
ia idJe to speculate in the face of this evidence and absetice of details either 
side that 4% Union merely ‘‘represented’’ the case according to the 
dictionary meaning of the word, and did not take up the cause of this 
workman. A Trade Union means a body of workers who combine them- 
selves with a view to further their common interests. There is no scope for 
making any assumption in this case in the face of the order of reference and 
the evidence on record that the Bus Workers’ Union merely ‘‘represented’’ 
Shri Baijnath’s case in the sense of putting it before the রি or the 
Conciliation Officer and did not take it up in right earnest, as a corporate 
body of workmen to safeguard the interests of one of its members. The law 
is now clear on this point. The Supreme Court decision in the Newspaper 
Limited and Industrial Tribunal, U.P. and others, 1957-IT, L.L.d. T, settles 
once for all controversies on this point. A single dispute per se is not an 
industrial dispute, but it becomes one when such dispute is taken up by a 
body of workers, the colleagues of the aggrieved workman or by a Union 
of which he 1s a member. I am satisfied from the materials on record that 
the Union did take up the case of the aggrieved workman and the present 
dispute is un industria] dispute. As such, the Government has rightly 
referred it to this Tribunal and this Tribunal has jurisdiction to adjudicate 
it. The representation in this particular case, before this Tribunal, was 
made by Md. Ismail, the Secretary of the Bus Workers’ Union, who is 
competent to do so under section 36 of the Tudustrial Disputes Act. I 
answer this issue aguinat the Company. 


issue No. 1: The Union's case is that Shri Baijnath wha was in the 
service of this Company since March 1947 was summarily dismissed on the 
Ist March 1956 without notice. He was a cleaner on a pay of Rs, ,80 per 
month and was not paid his arrears of wages since December 1956. lence, 
he prayed for his reinstatement with arreara of wages, and wages for the 
period of unemployment. The Company’s case is that Shri Baijnath did 
not work since 1947 but worked only for two months in Jautury and 
February زا185‎ as a substitute in place of the permanent workman who went 
home on leave. 


Shri Baijnath examined himself in this case and spoke in support of his 
claims He said he was geiting monthly wages of Rs. 20 for cleaning o taxi 
and Ra. 60 for cleaning a bus belonging to Harnam Singh, who has other 
buses as well. The bus was not plying since December as>})issel engine was 
being fitted in it. He received wages for cleaning the taxi, but his wages 
for cleaning the Bus remained in arrears. The Company refused when he 
demanded the payment of the arreurs. At this the owner, Harnam Singh,

ANNEXURE 


in the matter of an industrial dispute existing between Messrs, M. A. M.

598 Chowringhee Road, Calcutta, referred under 0.0. No. 1131-1.R./! 
IR /11L-88 57, dated 11th April 1957. (0856 No. VIII-C8 57.) 


BEFORE THE FIRST LABOUR COURT, WEST BENGAL 


PRESENT: 
Suri ۲۰. 0. CHATTERJER, Judge, First Labour Court. 


Appearances: 
For the Union: Shri N. Barman. 


For the Company: Shri Haripada Ghosh, Accountant. 


The Government of West Bengal, in the Department of Labour, by order 
No. 1131-1... /IR/11L-88/57, dated 11101) April 1957, referred under sections 
7 and 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XLV of 1947), the industrial 
dispute between Messrs. M. A, M. Kashani & Sons, 17 Mangoe Lane, 
Calcutta, and their workman, Md. Hanif, represented by the Calcutta Lorry 
Transport Workers’ Union, 59B Chowringhee Road, Calcutta, regarding 
matters specified in the second schedule of the Act to this Court for 
adjudication : 


Schedule 


Whether the dismissal of Md. Hunif was justified; to what relief includ- 
‘Ing reinstatement is he entitled? 


AWARD 


This ig a case by a driver for abrupt termination of his services. The case 
of the Union is that this driver was in the service of the Company for about 
one year and 9 months. He had no fixed hours of duty. Sometimes he was 
kept on duty for hours together even up to late hours of the night. On 8th 
April 1956 at about 8 p.m. the driver was sent for by the proprietor of the 
Company through a servant. The driver was then engaged in preparing bis 
meals. So the driver asked the servant to inform the proprietor that he was 
not in a position to come immediately. To this the proprietor did not pay 
any heed. But the proprietor adhered to his orders demanding the 
immediate presence of the driver. The driver obviously could not carry out 
the orders and hence the termination of the service. 


The Company put in a written statement denying generally the allega- 
tions in the written statement of the Union, and uffirms that the driver was 
of late behaving improperly and on that particular night he did not carry 
out the erders of the proprietor. He was rightly dismissed. 


The point for determination is whether the dismissal of the driver is 
justified. What relief is he entitled to? 


The evidence in this case is one-sided. The proprietor did not appear to 
contest the case. On behalf of the Company Shri Haripada (thosh, an 
accountant of the Company, stated hefore this Court that his proprietor 
had asked him to tell the Court that he had nothing further to add to his 
written statement. The Company did not adduce any evidence. So the 


3010 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 22, 1957 [Paur I 
Sg tn জাতে 


atutement of the driver stands uncontradicted. The Court has no alternative 
but to believe the statement of the driver. ‘The Court therefore finds that 
the services of the driver were terminated without any reason or justification. 
No reasonable man can expect that a driver who had put in his day’s 
strenuous work would be again summoned at about 8 p.m. to drive the car 
for the proprietor’s family to have a ride in the Muidan and that while he 
was preparing his meals. What was recreation for the proprietor’s family 
was nothing short of oppression to 4 hungry driver. The fire of hunger was 
burning ablaze in his stomach, so it could not be expected that he would 
gladly carry out the orders without taking hie meals at that hour. What 
the proprietor should have done is that he should have granted the driver 
some reasonable time to finish his meal and then to call him for further 
duty. It was really nothing short of cruelty on the part of the proprietor 
to drive the driver to drive the car at that hour after his day’s hard work. 


I must, therefore, find that the action of the proprietor in summarily 
dismissing the driver is utterly unjustified and unreasonable, 


‘Next comes the question of relief. In the interest of both the driver 
and the proprietor I feel reluctant to drive the driver back to his old master, 
who thus behaved cruelly with him. If I do so I shall be really throwing 
the driver from frying pan into fire. Jn this view of the matter the prayer 
of reinstatement is refused. The driver must, of course, get his due 
ne grag The compensation in this case should be one month’s pay 
for his 21 months’ of services, and one month’s pay in lieu of notice. So 
in all the driver is found to be entitled to two months’ pay, i.e., Rs. 200 
from the proprietor, besides arrears of wages, if any. The Company must 
pay up the aforesaid dues of the driver within a month of the publication 
of this award. 


This is my award. 
Dictated and corrected by me. 


N. C, CHATTERJEE, N. C. CHATTERJEE, 
Judge. Judge, First Labour Court.

AWARD 


The Union claimed five months’ wages ag bonus out of profits for 1956, 
“over and above customary bonus’’. 


The Company did not concede this demand. It resisted the claim on 
merits as also on law. Among others, the contention of the Company is 
that the employees are estopped from raising the dispute over payment of 
bonus for 1956 by an agreement in writing arrived at hetween the Company 
and their workmen, and that the reference of this dispute is ultra vires, and 
this Tribunal is not competent to adjudicate it in the present proceedings. 


In an application filed on 4th July 1957, with a copy of it to the Union, 
the Company prayed for an order that the present order of reference ia 
ultra vires the Industrial Disputes Act, and this Tribunal has no jurisdiction 
to entertain, proceed or continue the present adjudication proceedings. In 
the alternative, it asked for stay of the present proceedings till the lsposal 
of the appeal now pending before the Hon'ble Supreme Court against the 
award of Second Industrial Tribunal, dated 9th November 1956, allowing 
the workmen bonus for 1955. The Union opposed this application. At the 
suggestion of hoth parties, the hearing of this application along with the 
88718 of jurisdiction was taken up on ے‎ day fixed for hearing and evidence 
of both sides was recorded and arguments were heard. 


Points for decision

dispute over payment of bonus for 1956 referred to it by order of the State 
Ltovernment ? 
(11) Whether the hearing of the dispute (۷ stayed till the disposal of the 
abovementioned appeal to the Hon’ble Supreme Court?

FINDINGS 


The dispute over payment of bonus for 1954 was heard by Shri G. P. 
Mokherjee, Second Industrial Tribunal, who allowed it in part, by his award, 
dated 9th November 1956. It appears from the evidence of Shri R. S. 
Sarma, the Finance Officer of this Company, that the Company had 
preferred an appeal to the Supreme Court against the said award and the 
appeal was admitted, The appeal is now peuding for hearing. The present 
dispute, as stated above, relates to a demand for payment of bonus for 1956, 
This has to be paid out of the profits of that year. Jt has 001 been shown 
before this Tribunal what common questions of law and fact will arise in 
the appeal before the Hon’ble Supreme Court and the proceedings before 
this Tribunal. On the contrary, it gppears that the claim in the present 
dispute relates to a different period, and bas no connection whatsoever with 
that in appeal before the Hon’ble Court. No endeavour was made by the 
‘Company to obtain an order of the Court for staying all further proceedings 
in the present dispute before this Tribunal. I see no good reason why the 
hearing of the present adjudication proceedings should be stayed till the 
disposal of the appeal before the Hon'ble Supreme Court. That question is 
decided against the Company. 


The questions now before this Tribunal are (1) whether the references 
made by the State Glovernment is ultra vires the Industrial Dispute Act; (ii) 
whether it is beyond the jurisdiction of this Tribunal to entertain, proceed 
or continue with the hearing of this reference, and (111) whether the present 
dispute is premature, and raised in breach of agreement to the contrary 
made between the Company and the workmen. 


The agreement, dated the 6th October 1956, between the Management 
of the Company and their workers’ representative of the Works Committee 
over payment of bonus for 1956 is admitted by both parties. The agreement 
Ext. A is appended to the Company’s written statement and to its application 
filed on 4th July (957. It is in evidence of P.W. ,ا‎ Shri 1৮, S. Sarma, the 
Finance Officer of the Company, that this agreement for payment of bonus 
for 1956 was made at a time when u case for bonus of the previous year 
(1950) was pending for disposal before Shri ہما‎ P. Mukherjee, Second 
Industrial Tribunal, as previously stated, the Company has preferred an 
appeal against the award of the said Tribunal, dated 9th November 1946. 
The second paragraph of this agreement Ext. ۸ 5 relevant and runs thus: 


‘As the question of payment of bonus for the year 1955 is under 
adjudication and the accounts for the year 1956 are nol yet ready 
und finalised, parties herein agree that the issue for the payment of 
bonus for the year 1956 should be ratsed and discussed only after 
the hearing for the 1955 bonus case is concluded and the account 
for the year 1996 are finalised and published.”’ 


The parties agreed that the issue for the payment of bonus for the year 1956 
should be raised and discussed only after the hearing of the case of bonus 
for 1955 is concluded and the accounts for the vear 1956 are finalised and 

ublished. The Company’s contention is that both these conditions have not 

een fulfilled in this case, 1.¢., hearing of the said case is not concluded, for 
an appeal is pending for disposal in the Hon’ble Supreme Court, and that 
the accounts for the year 1956 were audited long after this reference, and 
not yet adopted by the shareholders of this Company and not yet published 
according to the provisions of the Company’s Act. On the other hand, the 
Company has curried out the terms of this agreement by making an advance 
সাদ to their workmen which the workmen received in due time. The 

nion’s contention, on the other 11100) is that the hearing of the case was

concluded by an award of the Second Industrial Tribunal on 9th November 
1956. The agreement had nothing to do with the appeal now pending 
before the Hon'ble Supreme Court. Further, the accounts of the year 1956 
were closed on the 3lat December of that year and must be taken to be 
finnlised and published on that day. Besides, this agreement was not fully 
implemented by the Company for about 800 workmen out of a total of 3,190, 
as deposed to by Shri Sunil Kumar Das, Treasurer of the Workers’ Union, 
were not paid any advance in terms of the agreement. In my opinion, the 
agreement 155৮. A never contemplated a case of an appenl against the award 
of Second Industrial Tribunal for the case for payment of bonus of 1955 
was pending at the time of agreement before the Second Industrial Tribunal. 
The parties could never have intended that the hearing of the case would 
mean any possible appeal that may be filed against an award of the Tribunal 
disposing of the case. The words of the agreement do not warrant uny such 
interpretation. It is, no doubt, true that the accounts of this Company for 
1956 were closed on the 3170 December of that year. Their financial year is 
the same as u calendar year. But then, the parties did not intend that the 
disputes could be raised as soon as the accounts were closed on the dlat 
December 1966. Any intention to the contrary is excluded by the use of 
euch words as ‘‘Finalised and published”. If নী of accounts was really 
intended by the parties then there could not have been any objection to 

aay that in so many words in the text of the agreement. 


Now the question is when the accounts were finalised and published. 
Shri Sarma’s evidence is that the balance sheet for the year 1956 was now 
completed and would he placed before u meeting of the shareholders on 27th 
July 1957. Until the shareholders passed the accounts of that year in a 
general meeting, the accounts could not be said to be final. He further said 
that the udvance to the workers was paid in terms of the agreement. It 
appears from the Ext. B, copy of the balance sheet, that the balance sheet 
wan audited on the 14th June 1957 ond the present reference of the dispute 
was made by the Government on 23rd February 1957, 1.¢., long before the 
same were audited according to the provisions of the Company’s Act. 
Every Company maintaing its proper books of accounts under section 180 of 
the Company’s Act. According to section 131 of the said Act, the Company 
should prepare a balance sheet and profit and loss accounts and get them 
audited by the auditor of the Company before placing them to the share- 
holders at a general meeting. Under section 197 of the Act, no document 
purporting to be a report of the general meeting shall be circulated or 
advertised unless some other requirements were complied with. In any view 
of the matter, it must he held that the accounts for 1956 were not finalised 
and দাড়া before the dispute was referred to this Tribunal. It should 
also he held that the said accounts had not yet been finalised and published 
according 10 law. The agreement Ext. A prohibits the parties from raising 
this dispute over payment of honus for 1956 before the accounts for that year 
were finalised, and it seemed for good reasons. The dispute was settled by 
this agreement and admittedly advance was paid in terms of it to the work- 
men. It has heen said on behalf of the Union that 800 temporary workmen 
out of the total of 3,750 were not paid this advance. There is no evidence 
on the Company’s side to deny this allegations but that is not the whole 
point. 1৮ has been argued on behalf of the Company that the temporary 
workmen were not entitled to it in terms of the agreement. In the absence 
of details, [ am not making any endeavour to decide this point here and 
now, for I consider it irrelevant for our present purpose. The Union's con- 
tention was that the agreement should be held to be non-existent for it was 
not fully implemented. That view is on the fact of it totally unsound. 
Non-fulfilment, either in part or whole, of a contract does not extinguish it 


8014 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 22, 1957 (Pant 1 
سےح‎ ১ সাপ সিসি | 


and the parties are at liberty to enforce its performance in law. Another 
contention of the Union is that this agreement was made, not in course of 
conciliation proceedings, under the Industrial Disputes Act but privately, 
and, accordingly, it ia not binding on the parties. The learned representa- 
tive for the Union invites a reference to the provisions of section 18 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act before and after its lust amendment. His case is 
that since there was no such provision in law before the amendment of section 
18 at & time when the present reference was made the old section applies to 
the case and the amended section has no application. The amended section 
18 came into force on 10th March 1957 and the relevant date of the order of 
reference 18 23rd February 1957. So it may be said that on the day of 
reference the provision of the amended section 18(1) was not there. But 
it is settled Jaw that an act creating a new obligation has no retrospective 
effect, unless expressly or by necessary implication so made, and the same 
rule would apply when the burden of the obligation is only increased b 

such an Act. Here, the amended act does not do anything of that sort. It 


only the position of law regarding agreements entered into privately 
outside the conciliation proceedings. I, therefore, do not see any sound 
reason why section 18(]) will not any here. Question now 


is whether a settlement of a dispute arrived at by agreement between the 
employer and the workmen otherwise than in the course of conciliation 
proceedings as in this case, shall be binding on the parties. In my view, 
auch an agreement which settles the dispute is for more reasons than one 
to be taken as binding on the parties till] it is avoided in due course of law. 
The Industrial Disputes Act has nowhere laid down that settlement of dispute 
by agreement should be disregarded irrespective of its consequences. In 
fact, except in the matter of payment of lay-off and retrenchment compenaa- 
tion as provided in Chapter VA of the Industrial Disputes Act, the said Act 
has not expressly conferred any power on the Tribunal to disregard any 
such agreement, whether made, in the conciliation proceedings or otherwise. 
In my opinion, both are equally binding. Sections 18 and 19 have to a 
certain extent, extended their application. Whether in the matter of fixa- 
tion of wages, etc., a Tribunal set up under the Industrial Disputes Act, 
would in the larger interest of society and social justice mitigate some of 
the rigours of an existing contract is another matter. As a matter of fact, 
the amendment of section 18 makes it abundently clear now that an 
agreement settling a dispute, otherwise than in the conciliation 
roceedings, would be binding on the parties thereto. This view seems to 
ave received strong support from a decision of Mr. Justice Desai of 
Allahabad High Court in a case between Radha Raman Bajpai and others 
and Labour Appellate Tribunal and others reported in 1957 L.L.J. II, 
page 15. Therefore, in my opinion the aforesaid agreement Ext. A was as 
much binding on the workmen as it was on the Company both at the time of 
reference of this dispute to this Tribunal and at this day. The result is that 
the workmen are precluded by this agreement from raising and discussing 
this dispute not only before the reference but even now. That being so, the 
pretended dispute could not be supposed to be in existence in the eye of law, 
at the time of its reference, and the State Government had no jurisdiction 
under section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act to refer it to a Tribunal for 
ita adjudication. To hold otherwise would be to encourage reopening of 
issues lawfully settled privately between the parties and thereby disturb the 
industrial peace. In my opinion the agreement stands, It haa not been 
avoided in due course of law or otherwise terminated in accordance of the 
rovisions of this Act. The reference heing without jurisdiction this 

ribunal, which derives its jurisdiction from a valid reference under section 
10 of the Act is not competent to entertain, proceed with or continue the 


adjudication of this dispute. This dispute appears to be premature and

০০ a شسب_۔‎ 


illadvised. I, therefore, uphold the contention of the Company and decide 
the issue against the workmen. “The reference stands rejected.

demanded bonus for the years 1953, 1954 and 1946 at the rate of 3 months’ 
may with dearness allowance for each year. There is also a claim for 
intraduction of pay scale and overtime allowance for the drivers. 


The Company resists the said demand and claim. It alleged in the written 
atutement that its business is entirely confined to securing the freight

Though there has not ee any grade and scale of pay for the drivers, their 
atarting pay as well as their existing basic pay are fair and decent. Tnere- 
ments from time to time are granted to them. Regarding bonus, it ia the 
contention of the Compauy that in the pest it paid some moneys in inatal- 
ments in certain years, but the payments so made were purely er gratia and 
never as a condition of service. The Company denied that it paid one bonus 
to its drivers for the last 35 years or more. The said allegation was false. 
The drivers have no legal claim for bonus for any of the years under 
reference. The claim is also belated and should be rejected. The Com- 
pany has finally submitted that the drivers are normally not required to 
work in full, the hours per week that is scheduled for them under the law. 
[f any car 1s driven outside the normal office hours the same is done accord-

Issue No. 2: This issue relates to bonus. A perusal of the written state-

The issue as submitted for adjudication speaks of bonus in general terms. 
So having regard to the terms of the issue as framed the Tribunal is required 
to decide whether the workers concerned in the present dispute are entitled 
to get bonusa—both customary and profit, for the years under reference. 
shall deal with the profit bonus first. The financial year of this Company 
এল from January to December of that year. It is clear from Ext. B, which 
18 a letter addressed by the General Secretary of this Union to the Company, 
that the Union claimed bonus for the years 1953, 1954 and 1955 for the first

has contended that the claim for bonus 11) the present case is tainted with

delay and that in the circumstances such beleated claim cannot be entertained 
by the Tribunal. 1 have given my due consideration to this contention aud 
in my estimation, the contention cannot be said to be devoid of merit or 
substance so far as the claim for bonus for the years 1953 and 1954 is con- 
cerned. It has now been well established by 0 series of decisions of the 
Labour Appellate Tribunal of India that a claim for bonus for a particular 
year cannot be entertained after the accounts of that year have been closed 
and completed. This would mean only the reopening of the accounts which 
have been finalised. Recently there have heen two decisions of two different 
High Courts also on this point, and they are reported in 1956(1), L.L.J. at 
pages 272 and 370), respectively. The said decisions clearly support the con- 
tention rgised on behalf of the Company and certainly it is open to Indus- 
trial Tribunal to reject a claim for bonus for a particular year on the 
ground of belatedness. A demand for bonus must be made within o reason- 
able time from the date when the yenr under reference ends, otherwise 
such claim should be rejected. Jt cannot be argued that the Tribunal has 
no 8=6(power to reject oa claim for bonus on the’ ground 
of delay inasmuch 788 the Government, notwithstanding «such 
delny, deeded to refer the bonus matter for the years 
t95.4, 1954 and 1955 to the Tribunal for adjudication. There is nothing in 
pectiona 1001) and 12(5) of the Industrial Disputes Act which empowers the 
(tovernment to make a decision, affecting the merits of an industrial dispute. 
(dovernment is only concerned with deciding whether an industrial dispute 
etists and whether in the circumstances of the particular case it should be 
referred to an [Industrial Tribunal. Once the reference is made, it is for 
the Tribunal to consider the matter on merits. Therefore, the claim for 
profit bonus for the veara 19533 and 1954 is rejected on the ground on 
belated ness, 


Regarding cluim for such profit bonus for the year 1955, there is no 
10181617181 before the Tribunal to come to a finding whether there remained 
wuny available surplus out of the profit of 1955 for payment of any bonus to 
the workers. The Company has not produced = the  balance-sheet 01 
that year. The Company cannot be entirely blamed for this because the 
Tnion in its written statement demanded bonus only as a condition of 
service. Nowhere within the four corners of that written statement any 
eluim was laid for profit bonus. It was for the first time at the time of 
hearing that such claim for profit bonus was made by the Union. The Vice- 
President of the Union who gave evidence on behalf of the Union depored 
while the case was taken up, that besides the customary bonus, profit bonus 
was also claimed. The Union did not ask 5180 the Company to produce the 
balance-sheet. The workers were the persons to suy whether the Compan 
earned such profit as to give them profit bonus of 1955. But as stute 
already, none of them appeared before the Tribunal to depose. ‘he Vice- 
President of the Union is the only witness who has deposed in this case 
on behalf of the Union. But his evidence in this respect is not at all helpful 
and leads us nowhere. He has not said a word in his evidence regarding 
profit of the Company for the year 1955, or for any other year. He is not 
even a worker of this Company. His evidence indicates that he 198 
absolutely no knowledge regarding the financial position of the Company. 
۲۶۲۷۰ 1, one of the Directors of the Company who deposed on bebalf of the

It is, therefore, decided that the drivers are not entitled to get any profit 
bonus for the years under reference. In this connection I may observe that 
revard being had to the nature of this Company’s business which is entirely 
confined to securing freight contracts for shipment of commodities expurted 
from India and in view of the fact that such contract are obtained solely by 
the personal endeavours of the Directors and other senior Executive Officers 
of the Company, the drivers cannot legitimately demand any profit bonus 
from ‘the Company because they did not contribute anything whatsoever in 
the earning of the profit of this Company. A workman can claim bonus 
only when as result of his effort any profit has been earned. Here in the 
present case there is no evidence in this respect on behalf of the Union. On 
the other hand, there is positive testimony of O.P.W. 1, one of the Directors, 
that the drivers do not contribute anything in the earning of profit. Then 
again, it has transpired from the evidence that this Company was formerly 
a partnership business and was incorporated in 1953 as a private limited 
Company. This limited Company owes still a sum of Rs. 44 lakhs to the 
ex-partners for which no interest could be paid even. The Company has no 
reserve set apart to repay the outstanding loan due to the ex-partners. If 
the facts as stated above be considered dispassionately, no Tribunal can 
possibly direct such a Compauy to pay any profit bonus to its workers. 


ze: یی‎ 


Now I shall take the question of customary bonus. The Union pressed 
such bonus on the basis that payment of this bonus was u condition of ser- 
vice founded on implied agreement and acquired the statua of a customary 
bonus. According to the Union such bonus has heen paid on the eve of 
Puja every year for more than 35 years und as such the مس‎ was under 
an obligation to pay bouus by virtue of an implied agreement. So it has 
been urged on behalf of the Union on the authority of the Mahaluxmi Cotton 
Mill’s case (1952 L.A.C. at page 374) that this leads to an inference of an 
implied agreement as a term of employment and definitely excludes the 
hypothesis that payment had been. made out of bounty. The case of the 
Compnny, as I understood it, is that some payments were made from time 
to time to the workers since 1944 at variable rates and that those were made 
er gratia, Tt was urged on behalf of the Company that those paymenta had 
not attained the status of an obligation or a condition of service 1101 were 
they made out of implied agreement—even they did not acquire the status 
of a customary bonus. The Company has emphatically denied that one 
such payment was made for 35 years or so. This allegation has been stigmatia- 
ed to he false hy the Company. The Union could not furnish 
any evidence or material whatsoever to show that one bonus was paid to the 
workers on the even of Puja for the last 35 years or more. P.W. 1 who has 
deposed on hehalf of the Union has no personal knowledge about this. He 
frankly confessed that he was not in a position to say when and for how 
many vears one such bonus was paid to the workers. [Ie heard only from 
the workers that bonus was paid by the Company to the workers for good 
many years. But curiously enough, none of the workers has deposed in 
this case. The Wnion has not produced any paper showing previous pryment 
of such bonus. So the Tribunal is to depend on the evidence as adduced on 
hehalf of the Company because that evidence stands unchallenged and un- 
contradicted. The evidence as adduced on hehalf of the Company consists 
ouly of the testimony of 0.P.W. 1, Shri A. C. Mukherjee, one of the 
Directors of the Company. His evidence is that since 1944 this Company 
used to make some payments to its workers at varying rates, but these 
payments were always er gratia. He has further said that in 1958 the 
Company psid some honus to its workers including the drivers. In the 
instant case, barring the fact that bonus by way of er grateq payment was 
given for 9 venra (i.e., 1944-1953), but not at uniform rates, there is no 
other factor to suggest that payments were made in terms of an agreement,

express or implied, In similar circumstances, their Lordshipa of the 
Labour Appellate Tribunal held that bonus was not a condition of service 
nor was it customary bonus ০ 1952 (IT) L.L.d., 324}. In the present 
case there is no evidence to show that the Company made any payment by 
way of bonus to its workers before 1944. So there 1s no figure available 
before 1944. Beginning from the year 1944, it appears that some er gratia 
payments were made to the workers ٦ to 1953 at varying rates. It is 
Imposwble on such material alone to hold that bonus was a condition of 
service in this Company or had acquired the status of customary bonus. 
Even if it be assumed that a practice had grown up in terms of which one 
bonus was heing paid year এ year on the eve of the Puja, there 1s 
nothing to prevent the Company from setting a period to it and withdrawing 
that coneession. A practice of this nature cannot be treated as binding for 
ever or of perpetual effect. Even if the case be considered to be one of 
customary right, the law enjoins that in order to crystalise into a right a 
custom must . immemorial, reasonable and certain, and further the enjoy- 
ment must have been as of right. In the present case, there is the positive 
evidenee that payments were made er-gratia. So it is not possible to affirm 
that the workers had received one bonus each year ot the time of Puja 
during these 9 years as of right. No legal right therefore accrued to the 
workers to claim such bonus. Furthermore, a period of 9 years cannot ار٥‎ 
considered to be long enough for pronouncing an opinion that the practice 
to pay bonus has been immemorial or for reasonably long time. Therefore, 
the claim of the Union based on custom cannot be sustained. Considering 
the matter I am of the view that the claim of the Union to get bonus for 
the years under reference either as a condition of service or as one based on 
custom must fail. 


The result, therefore, is that the drivers concerned in the present 
reference are not entitled to any bonus either profit or customary or as 
condition of service for the years 1953, 1954 and 1955. This issue ts 
answered accordingly.

The two workmen concerned, P.W. 1 Shri Kalachand Dutt and ٣۶

In the case of Buckingham and Carnatic Co. rs. their workmen reported 
in 1962 L.A.C. 490, a Special Bench of the Appellate Tribunal laid down 
guiding principles about interference in different cases of termination of 
service by the Tribunals. It has been held therein: ‘There are 3 other 
accepted fundamental principles; namely,— 


(i) that the industrial worker must be placed in such a position that 
the security of his service may not depend upon the caprice or 
arbitrary will of the employer; 


(ii) that industrial peace should be maintained; and 


(211) that industry should be efficiently managed. 


fhese principles underlie the Industrial Employment (Standing Order) 
Act, 1940, Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and other Local Statutes of like 
nature. The former Act makes it obligatory on employers of large 
establishments employing 100 workers or more to have Standing Orders 
following the model pattern certified by the appropriate authority. They 
are to be regarded as conditions of service by which both emplovers and 
employees are to be governed. When the services of an industrial worker 
are terminated an industrial dispute can be raised under the Industrial 
Disputes Act, for it would be a question of ‘‘employment and non-employ- 
ment’’ and it would be competent for the Industrial Tribunal to determine 
whether the termination of service is justified. To determine whether 
termination of employment is unjustified, it is necessary to see whether 
it is in accordance with the Standing Orders.

The Standing Orders of a concern provide for 3 typea of cases in which 
the services of an employee can be terminated, namely,— 


(1) automatic’ termination for absence without leave; 


(ii) discharge without assigning any reason, on notice or payment in 
lieu of notice; and 


(itt) dismissal for misconduct. 


In cases where the ground ulleged by the employer is misconduct, rules 
of নার to be followed before the order of dismissal is passed,-are 0 
18161 down in the Standing Order. In all these types the requirement of 
lona fides is essential. The termination of service in colourable exercise 
of the power or as a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice or of 
caprice, should he prevented us otherwise some of the fundamental rights 
and principles which have been noticed would be violated. Arbitrary 
conduct or unnecessary harshness on the part of the employer judged by 
the normal standard of a reasonable man may be cogent evidence of 
victimisation or unfair lubour practice. 


In the first type of cases the Tribunal would be at liberty to examine 
the explanation offered by the employee for his absence and other circum- 
atances also for the purposes of seeing whether the employer acted with 
honest purpose, In the second type of 08464 even when the Standing Order 
authorises discharge on notice without assignment of reason the scope of 
the enquiry would be similar. If the termination of service in these two 
types of cases be held to he justified, no further question would arise 
though in exceptional cuses of the second type there may he scope for 
giving compensation, On examining the cases with this approach, if the 
Tribunal finda the termination to he unjustified, the question of relief— 
reinstatement and/or payment of compensation will arise and dealing with 
that question the considerations arising in case of wrongful dismissal 
would he applicable. In the third type, namely, dismissal for misconduct, 
if there is evidence to support the action of the Management the Tribunal 
will not substitute its own judgment for the judgment of the Management 
but the decision of the Management with regard to the charge of mius- 
conduct ugainst an employee will not prevail if— 


(1) there is want of bona fides; or 


(01) it is a case of victimisation or unfair labour practice or violation 
of the principles of natural justice; or 


(111) there is a basic error of facts; or 
(iv) there has been a perverse finding on the materials."’ 


Let us now consider the case of two workmen separately in the light 
of the principles enunciated os aforesnid. Before so doing it is better that 
the case of victimisation as pleaded by the Union being common to the 
workmen is gone into first. I may note at the very outset that on giving 
careful consideration to the evidence and circumstances, [ am unable to 
accept that there was want of bona fides or victimisation or unfair labour 
practice in the termination of employment of any of the two workmen 
PW. 1 and P.W. 2. According to the written statement and the 
evidence the present Union was forined in March 1956 and registered on 
2186 May 1956, while the two workmen were discharged long hefore on 
29th July 1955 on the hasia of the allegations followed by search on 4th 
March 1955. There is nothing satisfactory to show any Union activities 
on the part either of P.W. 1 or P.W. 2 prior to 4th March 1955. They 
inight have been ordinary members of the old Union which became defunot 
in 1950 but it 0068 not appear that after it became so defunct any of these

that he had taken the causes of Panna Lal Das and Bhoja in the Labour

their joining in the strike, even if true, is of no use as according to him 
the incident took place long ago in 1958-54. None of P.W. 1 and P.W. 2 
has been important office bearer of the present Union but was merely

actuated from a motive of victimisation.

_ This is a case of dismissal with oa prayer for reinstatement and other

In short the case of the Union is that Shri Arun Kanti Mukheryi 
(hereinafter referred ما‎ as Mukherji for the sake of brevity) hud been on 
employee under Messrs. Gladstone Lyall & Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred 
to as the Company), a top-ranking mercantile firm in Calcutta, since March 
1947. Due to the Company’s apathy towards the just demands of the 
employees the latter furmed a Union to represent their grievances to 
the Company collectively and Mukherji was the Secretary to the Union 
for زا‎ years from 1950-55. Feelings were quite cordial between the Union 
and the Company at the inception, but trouble started over the demand 
of bonus for the year 1994. The matter came up to the Tribunal which 
passed an award and = the trouble was smoothed over for the present. 
The Company did not take the Union’s activities of Mukherji in good 
grace und was awaiting an opportunity to sack him. On the complaint 
of a customer the Company i for an explanation from Mukherji on 
6th April 1957, which was gubmitted on 1111) April 1957, but the 
Company dismissed Mukherji on 22nd 40111 1957, summarily without 
holding an enquiry at all. The Union took up the matter and the 
Company agreed to reconsider it only if Mukherji tendered an unqualified 
apology, which was not offered though the Union agreed to withdraw 
the offending letter of Gth April 1957. No happy solution was reached 
and the Company persisted in their wrong arbitrary course. The Union 


therefore challenges this mala fide and unjustified action of the Company 
and seeks reinstatement, etc. 


The Company repudiates the allegations of the Union and contenda 
that Messrs. Surendra (Overseas), Private Ltd., a client of Lloyd's, 
complained against the conduct of Mukherji, a clerk in the Lloyd’s 
Insurance Department of the Company. Mukherji’s comments were 
called for on this compluint on 6th April 1957 and in his letter, dated 
llth April 1957, Mukherji challenged the genuineness of the complaint 
and attacked the integrity of the Company. The Company took serious 
exception to the tone and language of this letter and the insubordinate 
uttitude of Mukherji and terminated his services by their letter, dated 
22nd April 1957. The Union intervened and demanded withdrawal of 
this letter which the Company did not accede to, but the Union agreed to 
withdraw Mukherji’s letter, dated 11th April 1957. The Company, 
however, demanded that mere withdrawal of the letter would not suflice, 
but Mukherji should offer an apology. Mukherji did not agree to offer 
the apology und the Company treated negotiations for the amicable 
settlement us closed, which was communicated to the Union by their 
letter, dated 26th April 1957. The Union did not approach the Labour 
Commissioner, but on 6th May 1957, Mukherji resorted to the coercive 
tactics of o hunger-strike on the Company’s own premises which did 
much humiliate the Company. Then the Company informed Labour 
Commissioner of this critical impasse and_ the Police intervened and 
arrested Mukherji on 7th May 1957 at midnight. The Company therefore 
urges that the termination of Mukherji’s service is justified and Mukher)i 
is not entitled to reinstatement. 


DECISION 


here is no dispute that the Company is one of the top-ranking 
concerns in Calcutta and that the relation between the Company and the 
TWnion was quite cordial in the beginning. Then the tie o goodwill 
slnckened and recognition of the Union was withdrawn in March 1955. 
The first trouble started with the question of bonus for 1954. No 
amicable settlement was arrived at over this issue and the matter came 
up to the Tribunal which gave its award which is reported. The awards 


made by the Tribunals for the quarter ending June 1949, laid down 


Part ([ا‎ THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 22) 1957 3041 


সস 


Company's service conditions, the procedure to be adopted before 
imposing punishment, etc, The procedure is explicit an Jays down 
that a charge need be framed, its copy should be given to the delinquent 
clerk who will submit his explanation and an enquiry will be held and 
if the clerk is found guilty, 0 copy of the findings together with the 
punishment propused to be imposed should be furnished to the clerk and 
the clerk will show cause against the punishment only at this stage 
and will be heard too 20. his defence, otc., und there is also a provision 
for an apeal. In this case, it is admitted by the learned Advocate for 
the Company that no enquiry at all, nothing of the kind, was held. The 
Company therefore did not comply with the procedure laid down by the 
Tribunal in awarding the instant punishment on Mukherji. 


What the Company did? The Company took serious exception to the 
tone of Mukherji’s letter, dated 6th April 1957 (Ext. A). In this letter 
Mukherji complained of the shortness of time granted to him for a reply 
and he also described the procedure as irregular and opposed to i 
and practices ond said that at least a reasonable time up. to 11161) April 
1957, should be allowed to him. Then came his reply (Ext. A, 
Annexure B), dated 11th April 1957. In this letter, Mukherji stated that 
the charges are not specific and also complained that the present charge 
is one hike the fictitious charges previously levelled against him 
unsuccessfully and this is a mala fide und reprisal measure of victimisa- 
tion and that the complaint is a piece of pure imagination having no 
truth in it. He further asserts that, in fact, he refused to do overtime 
work as insisted by the Management, so this is a colourable device to 
enter an adverse remark in his service report to blight his prospects for 
further promotion. The Company took serious exception to this letter 
from their subordinate and issued the letter (Ext. B) on 22nd April 
1957, giving notice of termination of his service as he attacked the 
character of the Company and 28 his conduct undermines the discipline 
of the office. The Company in their letter also offered him notice-pay, 
his entire Provident Fund money and 15 days’ wages for each completed 
year of service. Then there were certain correspondences between the 
Company and the Union which need not be referred to in details. The 
Union produced two drafts of letter of a ۸۷ (Exts. 2 and 2A). 
Exhibit 2 is drafted by Maharaja of Mayurbhanj, one of the Directors, 
and Ext. 2A by Mr. Whithouse, an ex-Director. Kxhilnt 2 reads as 
follows: ‘‘I sincerely regret my‘ letter, dated llth April 1957, to which 
the Directors, I realise, have every reason to take exception. I ask to 
be forgiven’? and Ext. 2A is almost in the same vein in which there 1s 
the additional admission that the allegations made therein are 
completely unfounded and there is a prayer for reinstatement. Mukher}i 
did not, however, offer apology which, if tendered, would have poured 
oil on troubled waters. In not offering an apology, Mukherji, I must 
observe, was clearly ve much ill-advised. If he could not accept 
Company’s draft, a suitable draft offering on apology would have been 
acceptable to the Company. So the negotiation between the Company 
and the Union for × peaceful settlement failed and the letters, therefore, 
do not call for any specific mention. What followed next—Mukherj1 
served a letter (Ext. G) on the Company on 6th May 1957 intimating 
that he would launch a hunger-strike, ‘‘fast unto death’’ in the Company's 
premises. This hunger-strike was actually resorted to at about 10 on 
6th May 1957, in the Union’s own office, which, however, 18 situated in a 
corner of the first floor of the Company's office at 4 Fairlie Place. This 
was a most unenviable sight creating a sensation in the locality und the 
Company naturally felt very uncomfortable. Labour Commissioner was 
‘ntimated about it and Police informed and at about the midnight of 7th 


3042 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 22, 1957 [Parr I 
সস چپ‎ NAS eee ern anna regener] 
Muay 1957, the Police arrested Mukherji, who was subsequently released 


0 bail and this, 1 must observe, wasn a totally wrong step taken by the 
nion. 


In the above circumstances, my finding on the Company’s terminating 
the services of Mukherji is that the Company not having followed its 
own procedure for enquiry transgressed the rules laid down by the 
Tribunal, no opportunity was given to Mukherji and there can be no two 
opinions that the principles of natural justice were altogether violated. 
Fundamental pinciple of law is that no man _ should he condemned 
unheard. Of couse, Mukherji stigmatiged the allegation of Messrs. 
Surendra (Oversens) & Co., a8 a piece of imagination. Nonetheless 
Mukherji should have been given an opportunity to explain why he did 
ao. Of course, having regurd to the evidence of Mr. Cooper (O.P.W. 1) 
which I have no reason to disbelieve that Mukherji did not pay the 
attention which he (Cooper) deserved and rather he (Mukherji) left the 
office for a considerable length of time. This, of course, does not speak 
well of Mukherji as an nosistant. I must observe that the [0101 made a 
very futile attempt to show that the complaint of Messrs, Surendra & Co. 
was unfounded as the Company did not = issue any previous intimation 
to them that the survey report was ready and so on and so forth. May 
be in this case the usual formalities were not complied with, but the 
truth of the incident could not be shaken in the least. The fact remains 
that there was the complaint of unethical conduct and temporary absence 
from his seat from Messrs, Surendra & Co. and non-compliance with usual 
formalities of stereotyped nature is not material in this case. 


There might be other اہ ا‎ incidents hetween the Union and the 
Company in which Mukherji took a leading part, as for example, over the 
scarcity of drinking water in the office premises. Over the dismissal of 
a mad driver, etc. For the determination of the present issue these are 
not material and whatever might have been the bad past record of 
Mukherji, the Company for that reason cannot dispense with the 
enquiry in which he should have been given a reasonable opportunity to 
explain his conduct. ‘This is a right guaranteed to the workman by the 
Tribunal’s award like those to the civil servants by the Constitution of 
India and rightly laid down in the Tribunal’s award and I must find 
that the present punishment imposed by the Company stauds vitiated, as 
no opportunity was given to Mukherji to explain his conduct, nor was 
any opportunity given to him to show cause against the punishment 
proposed to he inflicted. The action of the Company in not affording the 
opportunities to Mukherji was arbitrary as the Company took the law 
into their own hands. The Management obviously got enraged and did 
not adopt a reasonable attitude in this behalf. In this connexion it must 
be pointed out that the Union’s plea that for Mukherji’s refusal to do 
overtime work, and for his Union activities, the Company mala fide 
victimised him, does not stand scrutiny. This plea was taken just to 
ive a colour of mala fides to the entire proceeding leading up to the 
dismissal of Mukherji. So the termination of services in the absence of 
an enquiry and in transgression of the principles of natural and social 
justice cannot be held to be justified, however, insolent, unbecoming the 
tone of his letter might be. There are numerous reported cases to support 
such a finding. At the same time, I must observe that the conduct of 
Mukherji in stigmatising the Company which he serves in the manner he 
did, is not praiseworthy. The Court in this case held an independent 
enquiry which. to put in short, does not also justify the drastic action 
taken summarily by the Company. 


Past 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 22, 1957 3043 


=e 


SS ল্লশ 
Next, I come to the question of relidf. The Union seeks reinstatement 
but the Court is not bound to reinstate an employee simply because there 
was a breach of the Standing Orders of the Company. The felief is 8 
matter of Court's discretion. The Labour Courts in the interesta of 
industrial peace and for eliminating sources of industrial strife have been 
vested with wider powers than merely giving effect to the 
contractual relation between the employer and the employees. The main 
round which deters me from granting the relief of reinstatement is 
ukherji’s resort to hunger-strike. He resorted to hunger-strike to coerce 
the Management to take him back in service. What an awful time the 
Company had for about 88 hours, when Mukherji was on hunger-strike. 
There was a sensation in the busiest office quarters, how small the 
Company looked before the people: This was an attitude wholly 
unbecoming of Mukherji. He is a graduate of the Calcutta University 
and he was intelligent enough to know that law has made ample provisions 
for redress against unjustified and wrongful dismissal. Instead of 
adopting lawful methods Mukherji resorted to hunger-strike which he 
calls ‘Gandhian method of Satyagraha”. Mahatma Gandhi if alive 
this day would have been shocked to see his sacred policy being thus 
profaned for selfish motives. So Mukherji does not deserve reinstatement. 
He forfeits reinstatement by his own conduct. I am also reluctant to 
grant reinstatement in the view that neither Mukherji would be happy 
to work in the Company, nor would the Company be happy to have 
29 to do with him. So in the interest of the peace and harmony 
of the Company, apart from Mukherji’s conduct which is subversive of 
all discipline in the Company, I find myself unable to grant reinstatement. 
If uny authority be needed reference may be made to the ruling reported 
in 1956, 1..L.J., Vol. I, page 192 (Vithal Shetty & Chokshy Silk Mills). 
In this case also a grave view was taken of the hunger-strike resorted to 
by the employee cof reinstatement was refused. In that view, I consider 
adequate damages would be proper remedy. The Company offered 
Mukherji notice-pay, his wages equivalent to 15 days’ pay for each 
completed year of service and his entire Provident Fund money. I 
think in the fitness of things, Mukherji, who is still below 30, should be 
awérded a month’s wages for each completed year of service and one 
month’s notice-pay and his entire Provident Fund money which I grant 
to him as compensation for his loss of service. 


The Company will pay tbe above sum to Mukherji within a month of 
the publication of the award. The prayer of reinstatement 18 refused. 


This is my award.

AWARD 


The case of the Union is us follows: 


The Company is a firm ,of importers and distributors of automotive 
parts of international repute and commands an extensive business extending

over different States of India. The terms and conditions of employees 
under the Company were far from-satisfactory, so the workmen formed a 
Union with a view to ameliorating their lot. Singe the formatiop of the 
Union the Company started victimising their employees on some pretext 
or other. One Chittaranjan Das, a member of the Union who was due 
for permanency, was retrenched on 3rd November 1956 without any reason 
whatsoever. Then again on 8th November 1956 another workman named 
Amarendra Nath Banerjee was kept under duress for the whole day and he 
was dismissed by a letter, dated 17th December 1956, after a sham enquiry. 
These two workmen were dismissed for their Trade Union activities without 
any justification whatsoever, So the Union prays for their reinstatement 
with back ٣ئ۵8۰‎ 


The Company in their written statement denies the material allegations 
in the plain and contends, unter alia, that Shr Chitiaranjan Das was 
appointed temporarily to pull up some arrear works and he was employed 
for 6 months only and his services were terminated as he proved a surplus. 
So far as Amarendra Nath Banerjee is concerned, the case of the Company 
is that he was originally employed as a booking clerk in charge of 
forwarding and booking of goods but as there was a fall in the 8 
the goods of the سا رٹ‎ Pee to be despatched through o forwarding ond 
clearing agency and the Management transferred Shri Amar Banerjee as 
a helping hand to other clerks if and when necessary. This workman, 
however, wasted his time in loitering about in the office and gossiping 
with other clerks who made a complaint to the Management. The 
Management therefore segregated him from other clerks and allotted him 
to a seat far off from other assistants. This enraged this workman and he 
vilified the Company. The Management therefore charge-sheeted him,

found him guilty of misconduct and dismissed سنا‎ from services. The 
dismissal is therefore fully justified and not mala fide, nor is it a result 
ران ا‎ victimisation. His praper for reinstatement should therefore he

DECISION 


The issues originally referred to the Court were whether the discharge 
of Shri Chittaranjan Das and Shri Amarendra Nath Banerjee, two workmen 
under the Company, was justified or not, and what relief, if any, they are 
entitled to. Before the trial commenced the case on behalf of Shri 
Chittaranjan Das was adandoned by the Union. So there remained only 
the case of Shri Amarendra Nath Banerjee (hereinafter called Amarendra 
for the sake of brevity). 


Admittedly this Amarendra had put in 6 years’ service under the 
Company in the Forwarding and Packing Department when there was no 
complaint against him. The trouble, however, startled when Amarendra 
was transferred from the Forwarding and Packing Department ہا‎ the 
Department of Clearing Agency which the Company newly started. 
Amarendra did not apparently like this transfer and he had very little work 
to do and according to the Company he used to loiter here and there inside 
the office and wasted time in idle gossips with other assiatants «and thus 
interfered with their work. So the Company on receipt of complaints 
against Amarendra segregated him to a different place in a secluded corner 
at a distance, so that he might not disturh others. Amarendra did not 
obviously like this change of his seat which is described as a dark, dingy 
corner near to a urinal where rejected goods are dumped. This seems to 
he the origin of the entire trouble hetween the Company and this workman. 
For the Compuny it is said that Amarendra did not carry out this order

Company and the proprietors and the Company should also show common

unduly harsh and incivil, the workmen have every right to gomplain of it. 
No workmen should pry into the prjvate character of a Director or

dealings towards them while acting in office so as to humiliate them before 
their co-workers or cause annoyance to them. By this, of course, J should 
not be interpreted to mean that the Company has no might to punish 
workmen for their misconduct or negligence in the discharge of their 
duties. That is Company’s own affair. The Company is within its right 
to a workmen for their faults and to recognize their good work vith 
rewards.

The Management accordingly dismissed him from service for the ahove 
mischnduct with effect from the date of suspension. No reasonable Enquiring 
Officer could reach such a perverse decision as the assistants examined testified 
to the diseourteous behaviour of Shri Arun Mukherjeé and this finding of 
guilty is perverse against the weight of evidence on record and must he 
interfered with. Then again, this enquiy is severely criticized before me 
on behalf of the Union and ] think rightly ao. In the first place the 


[০4৮  ا[‎ THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 22, 7 3049 


১১৯ tte, manana apna ‫ عپیپ‎ 


Director vilified (Shri A. K. Mukherjge) was n Judge amungat two other 
Directors who formed the Board of Enquiry. Thus if is clear that the 
prosecutor was himself a Judge and that apparently excluded the poasibi- 
lity of a fair and reasonable trial agd made the chance of the workman's 
obtaining justice at the hands of the Board of Enquiry all the more 
remote. In the circumstances in which the present enquiry was held 

cannot find that the enquiry was properly and fairly conducted. Obviously 
the workman was much prejudiced im his defence as he found the 
prosecutor in the position of an Mnquiring Officer. The present circum- 
stances were enough to create in the mind of a reasonable man a auspicion 
of the Enquiring Officer’s (A. K. Mukherjee) impartiality and there was 
violation of nic well-known principle of natural justice that justice 
should net only be done but should manifestly ond undoubtedly seem to be 
done. These principles appear to be clearly enunciated in the ruling 
reported in 1956 ھ۶‎ Vol. II, page 433 (Amalgamated Tea 8 
Company Ltd., and Kerala Union Plantation Workers’ Union). Having 
regard to the above principles regulating an enquiry, I must find that the 
জি enquiry was vitiated and the workman was much prejudiced in his 
efence. 


That_being so, the punishment of dismissal inflicted upon the workmun 
hased on the vitiated enquiry cannot stand. In this connection the 
learned Advocate for the Company contends that it was quite open to the 
Management to summarily dismiss the workman as he vilified « J)hrector 
which is a misconduct clearly subversive of all discipline in the (‘ompany 
and that the punishment 1s the sole discretion of the Company with whic 
this Court as a supervisory body und not as an Appellate Court should 
interfere. In support of this contention the Court has been referred to the 
well-known cases of Buckingham Carnatic Co., 140. (reported in 1982- 
5.۸.0. at page 497 and the cnse of Caltex Istd., reported in 11 F.J.R., 
page 287 and Laxmi Debi Mulls case at page 273 of the same volume). 


In the case of Buckingham Carnatic Co., Ltd., it was observed that ihe 
Tribunal should refrain from substituting its own judgment for the 
judgment of the Management, as in such matters the Tribunal does not 
act like a Court of Appeal but rather as ao supervisory body, exercising 
what would ordinarily be regarded as powers of revision for correction of 
basic errora’ which go to the root of the matter and of perverse findings. 
This, of course, does not preclude the Court from examining the findings 
of the Management on the charge of misconduct to assure itself that there 
is evidence to support the finding and that the decision of the Management 
is a possible view on the evidence before it. 


In the case of Caltex I.td., reported in 11 F.J.R., page 287, the enquiry 
held by the Management was found to be fair and no principles of natural 
justice were violated and the Company bona fide dismissed the workman 
and it was laid down that the Tribunal has no power to substitute another 
punishment for the one sought to be meted out by the employer. In _ the 
case of Laxmi Debi Sugar “Mille case (reported in 11 I'.J.R., page 273) 
it was held that the enquiry cannot be said to be unfair if the workmen in 
spite of opportunities given to them for defending themselves, did not 
avail themselves of them. 


But the facts in this case are quite distinguishable and these rulings 
have got no নিপা here. If there were a due charge-sheet, a proper 
enquiry held allowing reasonable opportunity to the workman and if the 
misconduct were proved, this Court would not have interfered with the 
punishment on the ground of its severity or hardness. The rules of 
natural justice have been violated in this case, so the Court has the right 


3050 THE CATLUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 22, 1967 [Parr I 


De সব 


to yo into the merits of the dismissal prder and see whether the action of 
the Management is justified or not (vide Bathgate Mmployees Unions’ 
case in 1953 [1.১ Vol. I, page 49%). | 


Furthermore, it may be pointed out, though this point was not taken 
at the bar, that the first charge as per Ext. A waa dropped during the trial 
and the second chnurge based on the penultimate paragraph of the 
workman's explanation, Ext. 1, dated 15th November 1956, where 11) 11 
was stated that “Shri Arun Mukherjee, one of the Directors, comea to the 
office in a drunken condition’’, was proceeded with in the manner already 
shown culminating in the order of his dismissal. The second charge muy 
thus be termed on offspring of the first parent charge which was abandoned. 
As the first charge was dropped this second offspring charge fell along 
with the parent charge. If a different view be taken a charge may lead 
to multiplicity of charges. As for example, during this very enquiry by the 
Company, severul other assistants also stated that Shri Arun Mukherjee 
comes to the office in drunken condition. Will the Company be justified 
in drawing up charges against these witnesses, namely, Shri Jitendra 
Chakravorty (1১, W. 3), Shri Palan Chandra Sarkar (P. W. 4) who, us 
ver Exts. F.—¥F.(2), testified to the drunken state in which Shri Arun. 

ukherjee attended office on some dates? The answer must he ۳ء‎ 
41071, ‘The witnesses stated the facts known to them and oannot be 
proceeded against for deposing to facts, however unsavoury their deposition 
may seem to the Company. 0 the Company was not justified in drawing 
up the second charge against the workman, مک‎ as it was on ٣ statement 
in his explanation which is said to have vilified the Director Arun 
Mukherjee. No second charge may be sustained on something stated in 
an explanation for the first charge. In this view of the matter also the 
enquiry leading to the dismissal of the workman cannot be upheld. 


Then again, the Union in this case has amply proved that the Company 
since the formation of the Workers’ Union started victimising some of the 
workmen, namely, Shri Abhimanyu Bhattacharjee, Shri  Debnarayan 
Banerjee and Shri Santosh Chandra Ghosh which gave rise to conciliation 
proceedings leading to the settlement of the disputes (wide Ext..5) and that 
even now one of the assistants 1s still under suspension and that the 
relation between the Company and the workmen has further deteriorated 
after the dismissal of Amar (vide Ext. 4, series of letters addrensed to 
the Company). The evidence of ٣. W. 2, Talit Mohon Biswas, a nephew 
of one of the Directors of the Company, J. N. Biswas and P. W. 8 Jitendra 
Chakravorty goes clearly to طمناطمادہ‎ that the relationship hetween the 
Company and workmen is very strained and far from satisfactory. Besides 
that, the Company subsequently started a parallel Union of the employers 
as against that of the workmen and launched as it were a campaign agninsi 
the workmen who protested against anything relating to the Company. 
It may also be pointed out that the Director Arun Babu brought a criminal 
case against this workman for the latter vilifying him. That case was, 
however, compromised (vide Ext, 6, order sheet of the Criminal Court), 
but still the hatchet was not buried. 


In the circumstances, I must find that the termination of the services of 
the workman was not justified, rather he was vindictively victimised and 
this is a case of an unfair labour practice. 


_The normal relief is reinstatement, but in view of the fact that the 
reinstatement, if granted, would seriously tell upon the industrial pence 
of the Company and be detrimental to the discipline in the rank and file 
of the Management, I do not grant reinstatement. In lieu of reinstatement

ANNEXURE 
BEFORE THE FIFTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL 


(Ref: Labour Department No. 679-1R /D /10L-69 /56, dated 4th 
March 1957.) 


This relates to certain points in the award relating to an industrial 
dispute between Messrs. F. & )'. Osler (India), Ltd., and thoir omployees 
referred to the Fifth Industrial Tribunal under Government order 
No. 6833Dis./D/11L-70/53, dated 26th February 1953. The award was 
signed and sent on 12th January 1954 to the Government. The present 


Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 22, 7 3059 


See সি টা তর সপ স্যার ee প্রহর এরা ےن‎ 


=— 


matter of clarification has been sent by the Labour Department, Govern- 
ment of West Bengal, under tts order No. 679-LR./D/10L-69/06, dated the 
4th March 1957, under rule 20۸ of the Industrial Disputes Act, ۷۴۰ 
After the amendment of 1956 this power of reference for clarification is 
specifically given to Government under section 386A of the Act. Uuder this 
section 36A, 1f there is any difficulty or doubt in the opinion of Government 
regarding the interpretation of any provision of any award or settlement, it 
101১8 refer the question to the Tribunal, and the said Tribunal shall, after 
giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, decide such question, and 
its decision shall be finally binding on all such parties. In pursuance of 
that, the parties were given notices, and they were heard on 20th July 1967. 


DECISION 
The Government have referred two questions for decision, viz.— 


(1) Whether Messrs. F. & C. Osler (India) Limited, 12 Old Court 
House Street, Calcutta, would be justified in deducting trom the 
compensation payable under the award of the 45th Industrial 
Tribunal to its retrenched employees, the amount earned from 
other sources in the period trom the lst January 1953 to the date 
on which reinstatement was uctually made or offered aud if so, 
whether the declaration already submitted by the employees 
concerned should be accepted? If any other form of declaration 
is required, in what form should it be made? 


(2) Whether the retrenched employees who declined reinstatement 
offered hy the Company are entitled to the retrenchment 
compensation payable under the award. 


It appears that the award of this Tribunal was taken up in appeal and jt 
was -confirmed with slight modification regarding two employees, viz., 
Shri Bhutnath Bhattacharjee and Shri Mohan Chura Das. Regarding relief 
to these retrenched men, the observation of the Tribunal in the original 
awiurd runs thus: 


“T must award that they would get the salury including dearness 
allowance for the period of this foreed unemployment, i.e., trom 
the Ist January 1953 up to the date of their reinstatement, less 
any amount drawn meanwhile either by way of re-employment, 
or by way of notice pernod pay. The reinstatement and 
compensation must be given effect to within one month of the 
award coming into operation.’’ 


Their Lordships of the Labour Appellate Tribunal observed in their decision 
“The learned lawyer for the Company contended that there should not have 
been any order for reinstatement of Bhutnath Bhattacharjee and Mohan 
Chandra Das, as they have heen re-employed by the Company. We are not 
aware if they have been reinstated to their old salary and if they have got 
hack wages for the period of unemployment. If they have been reinstated 
on their former wages with continuity of service, the question of reinstate- 
ment is not necessary for them, but they are entitled to wages for the period 
they have been out of employment. They are entitled to be reinstated in 
terms of the award but in calculating what they should get as unemployment 
benefit, the amounts they have got by the Company since re-employment 
shall be deducted’’. 


Now, keeping those two awards before me, let me see how T should 
answer the points referred to me for clarification by the order of the 
Giovernment. It should be borne in mind that in so doing 1 cannot read into 
the award what it does not contain, or take away from it what there is in it. 


3060 THE CAIQUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 22, 1957 [Parr J 


سسمسوسہ سد یھ وسو es eee‏ 
ss‏ ہے ওরস‏ 


So, my roll ia not to arnve at a fresh decision, but to interpret what I have 
already awarded. 


In this limited scope I find that both this Tribunal und the 00 
Labour Appellate Tribunal gave retrenchment relief during the period these 
men had been kept out of employment, i.e., from the Ist January 1953 up 
to the dute they were reinstated. But if they have already been reinstated, 
at least some of them, then the wages drawn during this period of 
re-employment should be deducted from the wages computed for this period. 
The idea is that the men should not get as compensation their wages plus 
compensation. They should not get it twice over. But if they had served 
during this period of unemployment elsewhere, the award did not make any 
provision that the said earning should also be deducted. Possibly, there 
was no allegation or evidence to this effect before the Tribunal. So that 
question did not ariae before the Tribunal, and it is needless to say that the 
Tribunal had not decided it. So I am unable to answer whether the said 
varning from any source other than the present Company should be deducted 
in the present case, if not for any other reason, at least for the reason that 
the award is silent about it. Re-employment is not the same thing as 
employment. It stands here for re-employment under this Company. 
Similarly, the question of having any declaration from the employees 
concerned cannot arise in the present case. For the self-same reason the 
question of the form of declaration is uncalled for. So, ] say by way of 
clarification that the Tribunal had in view while deducting wages, only 
re-employment under the present Company. So the point for clarification is 
mivdirected and cannot be answered as it 18, except as above. 


On the second point the Company contends that those who had declined 
reinstatement have forfeited their claim for compensation because the award 
rovided that those two conjoins relief. This interpretation of the Company 
is really taneiful, if not amusing. If two reliefs are given, unléss one is 
made dependent upon the other, the foregoing of one cannot result in the 
forfeiture of the other. 


That would be an absurd position. The Tribunal by its award found 
that those men were kept out of employment unfairly, and they were piven 
compensation for this period of শিপ unemployment. So that compensation 
they must have under the award. Over and above compensation, they were 
given reinstatement. If they declined reinstatement, they cannot have it. 
But for that reason, they cannot lose both. So my interpretation is that 
those employees who declined reinstatement must, at all events, get 
compensation payable under the award. 

G. PALIT, 


۱ Judge, Fifth Industrial Tribunal. 
The 24th July 1967.

DELHI ADMINISTRATION, DELHI 


NOTIFICATION 


No. F.110/57-C.—6th August 1957.—Wherens 
the issue of “Sarita”, a Hindi monthly 
magazine of Delhi, edited and published by Shri 
Vishwa Nath at the Delhi Press, New Delhi, has 
published in its July 1957 issue a poem captioned 
“Ram Ke Antardwad” by Arvind Kumar, which 
is deliberately and maliciously intended to out- 
rage the religious feelings ofa class of the 
citizens of India by insulting the religion or 
religious beliefs of that class und tbe publication 
of which is punishable under section 295-A of 
the Indian Penal Code; 


Now, therefore, on the above-cited grounds and 
in exercise of the powers conferred by section 
99.A of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Act V 
of 1898) the Chief Commissioner of Delhi hereby 
declares to be forfeited to Government every copy 
of the said issue of the ‘‘Sarita’’ and gill other 
documents contaming copies, reprints arfd transla- 
tions or extracts from the said issue. 


By order, 


PRAKASH KRISHEN,
