PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION, WEST BENGAL 


General instructions to candidates applying in response to 
advertisements issued by the Commission for recrult- 
ment to posts by ‘‘Selection’’. 


(1) Instructions regarding submission of application.— 
Applications are to be made on the prescribed form which 
weil be available from the offica of the Public Service 
Commission, West Bengal, Anderson House "টি 
floor), Alipore, Calcutta-27, personally or on sending a 
large selt-addressed envelope with stamps sufficient to 
cover the postage affixed to it. Candidates who are unable 
to obtam a ot the prescribed form may apply on any 
similar typed (not bandwritteon) form showing oxactly the 
wording and spacing of the pra os form published in the 
“Calcutta Gazette’ of the Ist September 1955, provided 
the blanks are filled up in the candidates’ own handwriting. 


(2) Partioulars and 06101708165 required.—Candidates 
should furnish evidenco of their age, qualifications and 
previous experience together with certificates written not 
more than one year prior to the date of their applications, 
trom responsible peraons, testifying to their private 
character. 


(3) Fee.--Candidates must enclose with their applica- 
tions a fee of Rs. 5 (for each category of posts) in the 
form of a poset chalan from @ Government Treasury 
or the Roserve Bank of India under the head ‘“XXXVI— 
Miscellaneous—Reccipts of the Public Servico Commiasion, 
Weat Bongal’’. Money orders, cheques, vtc., in lieu of 
troasury chalana ure not accepted. Postal orders, 
however, may be accepted from candidates. They should 
be crossed and made payable to “The Secretary, Public 
Service Commission, West Bengal’’. No application will 
be considered unless accompanied with the requisite 
application fee. 


Candidates in Government service should make sure 
before depositing fee that their applications will be 
forwarded by their superior officers. صا‎ no case will the 
fee paid with the application be refunded. 


The Commission may remit fee in case of genuinely 
indigent and bona fide displaced persons from Pakistan 


Note.—“(i) A displaced person lense age concession 
must furnish with his application satisfactory evidence 
that he is a bona fide displaced person from Pakistan. 
e.g., refugee registration card or ھ‎ certificate from a 

azotted officer or a Member of Parliament or State 
zogislature, in original. 


(ii) A member of the Scheduled Caste or Scheduled 
Tribe claiming age concession muat furnish with his 
application a certificate in original from a gazetted officer 
or a Member of Perliament or State Legislature belonging 
to the Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe, specifying the 
particular caste or tribe to which he claims to belong. 


(iii) A displaced person secking remission of the 
application fee must furnish besides the evidence required 
under Note (i) above, a certificate (in original) from a 
District Officer or a gazetted officer or a Member of 
Parliament or State Legislature to show that he is not in 
a position to pay the prescribed fae.” 


(4) Address.—Candidates should give their present 
address and should communicate at once any subsequent 
change of address. 


(5) Canvassing.—Any attempt on the part of candidates 
to enlist support of their applications through persons of 
influence or officials of Government will disqualify them 
for appointment. Spontaneous recommendation — from 
persons interested in the candidates or athorwise known 
to them will be disregarded. 


(6) Applications from candidates who are in permanent 
or temporary employment under any Government, a local 
or Statutory Hody (e.g., Damodar Valley Corporation), in 
India will he rejec unless they are submitted thropgh 
the appointing authority of their poste or service. 


Candidates serving under Government or a local or 
statutory body should submit an advance copy in the 
না form. The application fees should in such cases 

attached to the advance copy and not to the original. 
The candidature of such applicants may not however be 
considered if the original applications do not reach the 
Commiasion’s office within a fortuight from the closing 
date. Unless applications in onmginal or advance copies 
with application fees are received within the closing date, 
late applications may be rojected.

STATEMENTS OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 


The object of this Hill is to impose an annual tas on personal expendi- 
ture, above a prescribed level, of individuals and Hindu undivided 
families. Such o tax in addition to being a deterrent to excessive personal 
expenditure and an incentive for savings 180 forms a significant part of 
an integrated tax structure. 


T. T. KRISHNAMACHARI. 
NEw DELHI; 
The 16th May, 1957. 


FINANCIAL MEMORANDUM 


This Bill proposes a levy of tax with effect from Ist April, 1958, on 
expendituro of individuals and Hindu undivided families. Though this 1s 
a new tax, the procedure for assessment and collection of this tax is very 
much allied to that of taxes on income. It is accordingly proposed that 
for the time being the tax be administered by the Income-tax Department 
and that no separate administrative machinery need he set up. 


The existing pressure of work on the Income-tax Department, is huw- 
ever, already quite orig This pressure is likely to increase further on 
account of the proposed lowering of the minimum taxable limits. It will, 
therefore, be necessary to expand adequately the staff at various levels of 
the departmental cadres. 


The increase of personnel, along with incidental expenses of adminis- 
tration is estimated to cost Rs. 8 lakhs per annum ultimately. Actual 
recruitment of staff will, however, be made as and when it is found really 
necessary.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 
The object of this Bill is to impose o tax on fares payable by passengers

proceeds of the tax less the portion attributable to Union territories shall 
be assigned to the States concerned. The principles of such distribution 
wili have to be formulated by Parliament by law.

MEMORANDUM REGARDING DELEGATED LEGISLATION 


In the case of railways administered by companies, it 1s necessary to 
regulate the vollection of taxes under this law by means of rules made by the 
Contral Government. The tax may also have to be collected by other 
authorities on behalf of the Railways. Clause 6, therefore, authorises tho 
Central Government to make rules providing for the regulation of the 
collection of taxes, the uuthority to which the taxes so collected may be 
paid, the form in which returns should be made and the like. 


The rule-making power is of a normal character.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 


In a judgment delivered on the 27th November, 1956, the Supreme 
Court held that no retrenchment compensation was payable under section 
271. of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, to workmen whose services were 
terminated by an employer on a real and bona fide closure of business, or 
when termination oceurred as a result of transfer of ownership from one 
employer to another. Since then, a number ot undertakings have closed 
down or put up notices of closure for one reason or another. This has led 
and is likely to lead to a large number of workmen being rendered 


88 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 22, 1957 [Parr VI 


unemployed without any compensation. In order to meet the situation 
which was causing hardship to workmen, 16 was considered necessary to take 
immediate action and the Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Ordinance, 1957 
(4 of 1967), was promulgated with retrospective effect from 1st December, 
1956. 


2. The Ordinance provides that compensation would be payable to 
workmen whose services are terminated on account of the transfer or ػ۵‎ 
of undertakings. In the case of transfer of an undertuking, however, if the 
workman is re-employed on terms and conditions which are not jess favour- 
able to him, he will not be entitled to any compensation. This was the 
position which existed prior to the decision of the Supreme Court. In the 
case of closure of business on account of circumstances beyond the control of 
the employer, the maximum compensation payable to workmen has been 
limited to his average pay for three months. If the undertaking is engaged 
in any construction work and it is closed down within two years on account 
of the completion of its work, no compensation would be payable to workmen 
employed therein. 


3, This Bill seeks to replace the Ordinance by an Act of Parliament. 
Opportunity has been taken to amend the definition of ‘Tribunal’ as 
inserted by the Industrial Disputes (Amondment and Miscellaneous 
Provisions) Act, 1956 (36 of 1956). The amendment is merely formal and 
clarificatory.

August 1957.—This is an application under section 109 of the‏ ا121 
Representation of the People Act, 1951, dated 160) July 1994) = by‏ 
Shri Mohini Mohan Roy for leave of thig Tribunal to withdraw his Election‏ 
Petition. This application tor withdrawal was duly published in the‏ 
Calcutta (razette, dated 26th July 1957, us required under sub-section (2)‏ 
of section 109 of the Act giving notice thereof to all concerned fixing 8th‏ 
August 1901 for hearing. The petition for withdrawal was thereafter put‏ 
up for hearing in presence of the parties on 8th August 1957. Shri Mohini‏ 
Mohan Roy deposed on oath that he now prefers to withdraw his Election‏ 
Petition though he does not withdraw the ullegations made in the said‏ 
Election Petition, viz., that his Nomination Papers were duly signed by his‏ 
proposers and that the Returning (fticer illegally ond behind hia ‘back‏ 
rejected his Nomination Papers relying upon the er parte and untrue‏ 
statements of the respondent Shri Jagannath Kolay. The petitioner‏ 
Shri Mohini Mohan Roy does uot assign 815 cogent ground for bis prayer‏ 
jor withdrawal of the Election Petition except his verba] submission that he‏ 
wants to avoid further bitterness of feelings over this election. Shri Mohini‏ 
Mohan Roy has taken his oath to deny that he has received any considera-‏ 
tion for this step for withdrawal of his Election Petition and has also denied‏ 
of any bargaining with the respondent in respect of this withdrawal.‏ 

The respondent Shri Jagannath Kolay was present in Court but did not 
take his oath to assert that the Nomination Papers of the petitioner 
Shri Mohini Mohan Roy were not signed by his proposers, Of course, 8th 
August 1957 was not fixed for hearing the Election Petition on merits and 
Sj. Kolay appears to lave taken his oath before the Returning Officer 
asserting that the Nomination Papers of Shri Mohini Mohan Roy were not 
signed by his proposers.

ee er جا‎ ewe ee = 


ATE A A পা‏ بت ہ۳ سس ب٣ a‏ سسجت تچ شس سے کت 
The Nomination Papers of Shri Mohini Mohan Roy have not been‏ 
produced before this Tribunal and it is now too early to express any opinion‏ 
about the genuineness of the signatures of the proposers on the same. The‏ 
best person to prove the genuineness of the said signatures of the proposers‏ 
on the Nonunation Papers are the signatories themselves none of whom,‏ 
however, has been examined before me or before the Returning Officer.‏ 
The Returning Officer had no other option but to act upon the er parte‏ 
evidence of the respondent Shri Jagannath Kolay who took his oath before‏ 
him stating that the Nomination Papers of Shri Mohini Mohan Roy were‏ 
not signed by the proposers named therein. Apparently Shri Kolay’s‏ 
evidence was an opinion about the genuineness of the suid signatures 08‏ 
he had himself satisfied by usking the signatories as to whether they had‏ 
signed or not. It appears that one-of the signatories who figured as a‏ 
proposer in the Nomination Papers of Shri Mohini Mohan Roy was a son‏ 
of the petitioner.‏ 


ডি আজ 


Having perused the Election Petition, it does not appeur that there is 
any allegation of corrupt practice or any other allegation of similar nature 
and no material has yet heen brought to the notice of this Tribunal for 
refusing leave to withdraw this petition at this stage. The respondent does 
not also oppose the prayer for withdrawal. 


The main allegation in the Election Petition is rather against the 
Returning Officer for acting hastily and on insufficient data, viz., an 
opinion of the respondent, without calling upon the proposers to deny their 
signatures on the Nomination Papers of the petitioner or calling upon the 
petitioner to show cause. In such perspective, in my opinion, the Election 
Comniissioner is a vecessary party to vindicate the bona Ade and justifiea- 
1101) of the order of rejection of the Nomination Papers passed by the 
Returning Officer (a subordinate of the Election Commissioner). The act, 
however, doea not provide for impleading the Election Commissioner. The 
Act also is silent as to how the Tribunal can proceed if the parties refuse to 
participate in the proceedings or if the petitioner refuses to proceed any 
further. The provision of old section 89 for asking the Advocate-General 
to participate in the proceedings has been repealed by the Act 27 of 1956 
amending the Representation of the People Act, 1951. 


Sub-section (2) of section 110 provides the grounds for refusal of an 
application for withdrawal] where such application appears to the Tribgnal 
to have been induced by any bargain or consideration which ought not to 
be allowed. Similar considerations have to be made when refusing leave 
to withdraw under section 109, sub-section (1). At this preliminary stage 
when considering whether leave should be granted and whether the applica- 
tion for withdrawal should be granted or refused and in the absence of any 
material to suggest any bargaining or consideration which ought not to be 
allowed, and after giving my very careful consideration on the implication 
of such withdrawal, T see no reason to refuse the leave to proceed with thia 
petition for withdrawal, or to refuse this application for withdrawal of the 
‘lection Petition. 


Before I leave this matter I must observe that the learned Lawyer for 
the respondent Shri Jagannath Kolay advanced an argument that the 
Election Petition of Shri Mohini Mohan Roy itself was defective and ought 
10 have been rejected by the Election Commissioner as provisions of 
section 82 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, were not complied 
with. His contention, in short, was that all the candidates who filed their 
Nomination Papers, or at least those candidates who actually contested the 
election from the said constituency ought to have been joined as respondents 
tu this petition. He has drawn my attention to section 82 section 86 and 


3404 THE CAL, GAZ. EXTRY., AUGUST 22, 1957 [Part ] 
2:22 


to vection 90, sub-section (3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1991. 
Shri Mohini Mohan Roy was cross-examined to admit that there were other 
contesting candidates besides the respondent Sj. Kolay. The Election 
Petition did not udmittedly implead the other contesting candidates. 


T must at 0186 say that there is no substance in this contention of the 
learned lawyer for the respondent. The Klection Vetition of Shri Mohini 
Mohan Roy does not claim any further declaration than the election of the 
returned candidate Shri Jagannath Kolay is void. It is only where there 
is an additional prayer for declaration claiming the petitioner (in the 
instant case Shri Mohini Mohan Roy) as having been duly elected after 
declaring the election of the returned candidate as void that al] the contest- 
ing candidates ought to be joined, but “where no such further declaration 
is claimed’? only the returned candidates have to be joined in the election 
mtition. Admittedly in the instant case only Shri Jagannath Kolay is the 
returned candidate. Tlenee there can be no question of rejecting the 
Mrection Petition im dimine, under section 90, sub-section (3) for non- 
compliance with the provisions of section 82 of the Act. Hence, 


ORDERED 


Let leave to proceed with the petition for withdrawal of the Election 
Potition be granted under section 109, sub-section (1). The petitioner 
Shri Mohini Mohan Roy 1s further permitted to withdraw his Election 
Petition, under section 110 subject to the payment of costs to the respondent 
—10 gold mohurs including রি fev. Notice of the withdrawal he 
forthwith published in the Official Gazette, under section 110(3)(b). Any 
person who might have been a petitioner may, within 14 days of such 
publication, apply to be substituted as petitioner in place of the party with- 
Crawing and upon compliance with the conditions of section 117 as to 
security for costs shall he entitled to be substituted and to continue with the 
proreedings upon such terms as the Tribunal may think fit under clause (c) 
of sub-section (3) of section 110, Put up on 13th September 1967, after 
publication of the notice under section 110, sub-section (3), clause (b) for 
fixing a date for final orders. 


Let a copy of this order be forwarded to the Chief Election Commissioner, 
Tndia, New Delhi, for information.

Bhaduri, Shri Anath Nath Paul and Shri Aigoo, represented by J. and 
8. Hutchison Workers’ Union, 26/8 Dum Dum Road, Calcutta-12. 
(Case No. Vill-188 of 1966.) 


BEFORE THE SIXTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL. 


PRESENT : 
Sunt SAILESH SENGUPTA, Judge, Sicth Industrial Tribunal 


Appearances: 
For the Company: Shri N. M. Das Gupta, Advocate, 
For the Union; Shri Panchanan Bhattacherjee. 


During the pendency of o reference made to the Sixth Industrial 
Tribunal, by Government order No. 2342])is./1)/111.-183/52, dated the 
2062) August 1962, services of Sarbashree K. P. Bhaduri, Anath Nath Paul 
and Shri Algoo were terminated by Messrs. J. & R. Hutchison 1400. The 
discharged employees moved the Tribunal by an application under 
section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act. By his award published in the 
Calcutta Gazette, dated the 1161) June 1953, Shri S. K. Niyogi held that 
the discharge of the these workera was unjustified. Reinstatement with 
buck pay and dearness allowance up to the date of reinstatement with 
effect from the date of respective discharges was ordered. An appeal 
مک‎ by the Company concerning these three employees was dismissed 
xy the Appellate Tribunal on the 001 of June 1954 (Appeal No. Cal. 92 of 
1953). The directions given by the State Tribunal were upheld. The 
Company did not implement the award. The workera were not reinstated 
and the wages due were not paid. Thereafter the workers placed the 
matter before the Government. After some time the present reference 
ia oe by Government Order No. 2803Dis./D/6P-60/55, dated the 26th 

une 1990. 


The point submitted for decision by the Tribunal is:— 


“To what monetary benefits are Shri K. P. Bhaduri, Shri Anath Nath 
Paul and Shri 41000 entilted under the award of the Sixth 
Industrial Tribunal published in the Calcutta Gazette, dated the 
1161) June 1958, under order No. 195] Dis./D/ Sm ig dated 
the 26th May 1953, and subsequently confirmed by the Labour 
Appellate Tribunal 91 


On behalf of the Company an objection was taken that o fresh referenre 
is pot maintainable in regard to non-implementation of an award made on 
un earlier reference. This contention 1s perfectly sound. The matter has 
come to the Tribunal through a wrony channel as no reference could -he 
made in the circumstances stated above. Though Government thought fit 
to treat لا‎ as a dispute which could be referred under section 10. ہر‎ its 
true essence it is a matter for investigation and computation under section 0 
of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act. Tearned 00০16 
for the Company submitted that the Tribunal could not ignore the form in 
which matter has come before it and treat it 1s one covered by secion 20. 
I cannot subseribe to this view. Since the Tribunal has been called upon 


3472 THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., AUGUST 24, 1957 {Pant I 


| a RE A সস 


to ascertain the amount due to these employees under the award, the firm 
is immaterial inasmuch as the Tribunal has jurisdiction under another 
provision of the law to fulfil the requirements. In this view I deal with 
the matter as within the provision of section 20 of he Industrial Disputes 
(Appellate Tribunal) Act. The learned Advocate for the Company raised 
another objection that the law as amended confers jurisdiction upon the 
Labour Court alone to make computation under section 380. Government 
order was passed when the Industria] Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 
was still in force. Under the supplemental provision of the new Act if 
immediately before the commencement of the Act there be pending any 
proceeding in relation to an industrial dispute before a Tribunal conatituted 
under Industrial ]isputes Act, 1947, as in force before such commencement 
the dispute might be adjudicated and the proceeding disposed of by that 
Tribunal after such commencement as if the new Act has not been passed. 
The Tribunal is therefore to decide the issue under the law as it was 
before the amendment. Its jurisdiction cannot be held to have _ been 
ousted. Under the award these employees are to get wages from the date 
of discharge up to the date of reinstatement. As reinstatement has not 
been effected that terminus is interminate. Their dues up to this day can 
be calculated and I proceed to do so. 


From the evidence given we find that K. P. Bhaduri was drawing 
Ra. 210 inclusive of all allowances on the date.of his discharge on Ist 
November 1952. The wages due to him up to date amount to 
Rs. 11,929.35 ۰ 


Anath Nath Paul used to draw Rs. 70 inclsive of all allowances. His 
services were also terminated with 69806 from lst Janugqry 1952. The 
wager duc to him up to this day amount to Rs, 3,976.46nP. 


Algoo was drawing Rs. 65 per month. From the Appellate Tribunal 
Award we find that he was ھا‎ a with effect from lst September 
1952. The wages due to him up to date amount to Rs. ۵,204.16" 


Taken at my dictation and corrected by me.

Misconduct of IAcensed Contractor, Supervisors and Electrical Work men. 


80. (1) Report of neyligence.—When in the opinion of a person licensed 
under Part II of the Indian Electricity Act, 1910, to supply energy or of a 
person for whom any electrical installation work is being or has been 
carried out, any work carried out by a contractor licensed under the regula- 
tions is not in accordance with the Indian Klectricity Rules, 1956, und such 
licensee or other person desires to bring the facta to the notice of the Board, 
he shall make a report in writing to the Secretary. 


(2) A report made to the Secretary under this regulation by a person, 
other than a person Jicensed under Part IT of the Indian Electricity Act, 
1910, to supply energy, shall be accompanied by a deposit of Rs. 10 or auch 
larger amount as the Board may fix by special order in any case. If in 
the opinion of the Board the charge contained in the report is not substan- 
bated, the Board may direct that the deposit shall be forfeited. 


31. Malpractice ar infringement of Regulations to be reported.--If any 
person holding an electrical workman’s permit or a supervisor's certificate 
of competency or an electrical contractor’s license is found by the Board to 
be guilty of negligence, incompetence or a breach of these regulations or of 
she conditions of his license, the Bourd may suspend or cancel such permit, 
certificate or license. The decision of the Board shall be final. 


3148. Unauthorised entrits, mutilations or defacements of workmen’s 
permits, supervisor's certificate of competency and electrical contrartor’s 
licenses.-Any mutilation or deferement of, or any unauthorised entry in, 
any workmen’s permit or supervisor’s certificate of competency or electrical 
contractor’s license shall make the permit, certificate or license. as the case 
may he, liable to cancellation by the Board. The decision of the Board 
in this regard shall he final,

AWARD 


This reference was received in this Court on the 24th June 1957 and ط118‎ 
July 1961 was fixed for appearance and filing written statement by the 
Union. On 116) July 1957 the Union did not file any written statement and 
Sth July 1957 was again fixed for the written statement to be put in by the 
Union and the case was adjourned to several dates awaiting the statement 
from the Union. The Company put in appearance on 20th July 1957 
praying for time to put in a petition of compromise and the Company was 
allowed time till 30th July 1957 for this purpose. 

On 30th July 1957 a petition of compromise signed on behalf of the 
employers and the employee has been put in together with an annexure 
pie, the terms of compromise. I have read the terms of compromise 
which appear to be fair and reasonable. Therefore the compromise may be 


given effect to. The reference may thus be disposed of in terms of compro- 
mise which will form a part of award. 


Dictated and corrected by me.

This application under section 38۸ of the Industrial Disputes Act

& Co. (Private) Ltd. and their workmen of the Head Office, represented by 
the Babulal & Co., Ltd. Employees’ Union. The award on the aforesaid 
reference was made by this Tribunal on 5th June 1956 and was published 
in the Calcutta Gazette, on 28th June 1956. 


On 5th November 1955, Shri Sitaram Jaswal (Bania) filed an applica- 
tion under section 33A 04 the Act, complaining that the opposite party 
Company had dismissed him by its letter, dated the 8th June 1956, 
without obtaining previous permission of the Tribunal. It is stated that 
the petitioner prayed for leave to proceed to his native village in April

was an active member of the Union and his Trade Union activities were

offered himself for work at Panihati, which was also refused. The

aforesaid letter tou, and as such, it had to be sent to him per registered 
post. On receipt of his reply, he was given a last chance by letter,

this purpose another Durwan was detailed to accompany him to Panihati, 
and the workman was assured that the suspension order would be

withdrawn on his joining duty there. The Durwan was shown the

For the Union: Shri A. H. Bharatputra, Secretary of the Union. 
For the Company: Shri N. K. Mukherjee, Advocate. 


The Government of West Bengal, in the Department of Labour, by 
order No, 1113-1.R./IR/11L-112/57, dated 10th April 1947, referred 
under sections 7 and 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 
1947), the industrial dispute hetween Messrs. F. Hussain & Brothers, 
28 Strand Road, Caleutta-1, 00008 of their workmen, Shri Abbasbhoy 
Alibhoy Wadhwanwala, represented by the Paschim Bengal Gumasta 
Sabha, J-535 Paharpur Road, Calcutta-24, regarding matters specified 
in the second schedule of the Act, to this Court for adjudication. 


Schedule 


Whether the Management was justified in dismissing Shri Abbasbhoy 
Alibhoy Wadhwanwala? What relief is he entitled to? 


AWARD 


In this case the Union contends that Shri Abbashhoy Alibhoy 
Wadhwanwala (hereinafter referred to as the ‘‘workman’’ for the sake of 
brevity) went home on 2 months’ leave on_ receipt of the news of some 
ailment in his family with effect from Ist July 1956. The workman 
applied for an extension of leave which also was granted, The workman 
= i returned to Calcutta on 26th October 1956 to resume his duty but 
the Company did not permit him. The workman tried his hest to persuade 
the Company to take him in but all his efforts proved abortive. The 
Company thus wrongfully dismissed him from his service. Hence this 
prayer for reinstatement with other incidental relief. 


The Company denies the allegations in the Union's written statement 
and the specific case of the Company is that the workman voluntarily gave 
up his job and accepted all his dues in full and final settlement of claim. 
Therefore. the claim of the Union is unsustainable. 


DECISION 


This case was originally fixed on Ist July 1957 for hearing but on 
that date the Company prayed for time on the ground that their account 
books were retained in the Sales-tax Office without which they could not 
proceed with the case and 29th July 1957 was the next date fixed for trial. 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZFITE, AUGUST 29, 1957 3143 


On this date, however, the Company was ready to prosecute the case, 
but on behalf of the workman, the Secretary of the Union put in a 
petition stating that the Union is not willing to proceed with this case as 
the workmun failed in attending the Court on two dates successively. 
The Union therefore does not proceed with the case. Thus it 15 evident 
that there is no dispute outstanding between the parties. This case he 
thus disposed of.

AWARD 


This application under section 338A of the Industrial Disputes Act 
arises out of a proceeding based on G. 0. No, 2463Dis./D/11L-8/55, dated 
8rd June 1955, regarding an industrial dispute between Messrs. Kedar 
Nath Jute Manufacturing Co., J.td., Managing Agents, Messrs. Babulal 
& Co. (Private), Ltd., and their workmen of the Head Office, represented 
by the Babulal & Co., Ltd. Employees’ Union. The award of the 
aforesuid reference was made by this Tribunal on 5th June 1956 and wus 
published in the Calcutia Gazette on 28th June 1956. 


On 20th July 1956, Shri Deb Narayan Chatterjee, Shri Shibaram Roy, 
Shri Ajit Kumar Roy, Shri Sibnath Chowdhury, Shri Gopal Chandra 
Banerji, Shri Sushil Chandra Jutta, Shri Haripada Dutta and 
Shri Kanaiya Lal Kodal applied under section 33A of the Act, complaining 
against their discharge on various grounds. It is prayed that they may 
be reinstated with full wages for the period of their non-employment. 
The Company, in its written statement, opposed the claims on the ground 
that the workmen were surplus to requirement and they were retrenched 
on the pdinciple of ‘last come, first go'’ and that there was no victimisa- 
tion or unfair labour practice in retrenching the petitioners. It is prayed 
that the claim of the complainants should be rejected. 


On going through the record, it is noticed that out of the eight 
complainants, Shri Shibaram Roy, Shri Gopal Chandra Banerji, 
Shri Sushil Chandra Dutta, Shri Haripada Dutta and Shri Kanaiya Lal 
10018] never appeared before the Tribunal, nor were they represented by 
any body. The rest of the complainants being Shri Deb Narayan 
Chatterjee, Shri Ajit Kumar Roy and Shri Sibnath Chowdhury were 
present in person on the dates of hearing and_ were represented by 
Shri Panchanan Bhattacharjee, and Shri N. M. Das Gupta, Advocate, 
appenred for the employers. 


The hearing of the case commenced on 8:۵ January 1947, on which 
date documents were filed by both the parties. A number of adjournments 
were granted at the request of the parties to explore the possibilities 
of arriving at an amicable settlement. Ultimately on 24th July 
1957, a petition was filed by the employers in which it is stated that out 
of the eight applicants, five had settled their disputes previously and 
received their discharge benefits under section 25(F) of the Act and the 
remaining thyee applicants, being Shri Deb Narayan Chatterjee, 
Shri Sibnath Chowdhury and Shri Ajit Kumar Roy had also settled their 
disputes with the Company and received retrenchment benefits in full 
and final satisfaction of their claims and that they have no further 
disputes with the Company. The Union representative also testifies to 
the correctness of the petition. It thus appears that all the applicants 
have received retrenchment benefits in full and final satisfaction and they 
have no further dispute. This petition appears as Annexure A to thie 
award. It is, therefore, awarded that there is no সদা between the 
parties. The compromise petition in Appendix A shall form a part of 
this award.

The case of the workers as represented in their written statement is 
that no weekly holiday or leave was being granted and they were made to 
work for 14 to 15 hours. On representation being made to the Proprietor 
no relief was available. Thereupon the workers convened o meeting und 
decided to act in concert with the backing of a Union. With this object 
in view they joined the Calcutta Hotel and Restaurant Workers’ Associa- . 
tion which they left after a while to enlist as members of the Calcutta 
Hotel, Bar and Restaurant Employees’ Union. As soon as the Proprietor 
got scent of this enrolment of the workers as members of a Union, he cut up 
rough and treated them to rough talk seasoned with invectives. Shortly 
thereafter the Proprietor started terminating their services one by one, 
without any rhyme or reason. In this way the 10 employees whose case has 
been submitted for adjudication were all kicked out. ‘he claim is now 
made for reinstatement of these men with compensation and wages due. 
The Tribunal’s directions are also solicited in regard to holiday, leave and 
working hours. 


The Proprietor filed written statement stating that weekly holidays, 
working hours and leave were regulated by the provisions of the Bengal 
Shops and Establishments Act, 1940. The amenities provided by the said 
Act were being enjoyed in full measure. The Proprietor denied having 
terminated the services of any of these workers. His case is that in order 
to put him to trouble and bring the business to a stand-still the employees 
remained absent without notice one by one and did not return to duty. 
In order to keep the Hotel running he had to engage other men in these 
vacancies. As there was no termination of service by him but voluntary 
abandonment by the men themselves, no question of reinstatement or 
compensation can arise. Some wages are due for the short period before 
abrupt departure which the Proprietor has always been ready to puy. 


Issue Nos. 4 and 5: According to Issue No. 4 Ranjit Kumar (Ghosh 
was dismissed. He figures once again in Issue No. 5 as one of the men 
who had been retrenched. There appears to be some confusion. At the 
hearing the spokesman for the workers submitted that this is not a case 
of retrenchment but of dismissal of all the workers. Issue No. 9 suggest- 
ing as it does that retrenchment had been effected has not been correctly 
framed. I treat the case therefore as one of dismissal of these 10 workers. 


The workers’ view-point is that on their joining the Union the 
Proprietor saw red and abused them in foul language. Not content with 
such unseemly behaviour, he embarked upon a course of throwing them 
out of employment one by one. The Proprietor’s version is that he was 
not aware of the formation of any Union or the workers joining any Union

Union which was already in existence. Throwing these employees out of 
employment because of their membership of that Union the Proprietor 
could not expect to get any advantage. There was no guarantee ا ا)‎

issue Nos. 1, 2 and 3: A complaint was made to the authorities by

AWARD 


This is an application under section 338A of the Tudustrial Disputes 
Act, filed on 2nd January 1957, by workman Shri Balai Chand Mullick. 
He was a peon in the opposite party concern. On 7th November 1956, the 
Cashier of the opposite party made over an _ insured cover containing 
Rs. 1,000 addressed to one Shri N. N, Kapoor for sending the same by 
insured post from Rash Behar) Avenue Post Office. Sogn after at about 
11 a.m. on that date the petitioner returned and reported that he lost the 
said insured cover in the circumstances detailed in Ext. A. The Company 
could not believe his statement and it thought that it was a 
cuse of criminal breach of trust and accordingly made o report to the 
Oflicer-in-charge, Tollygunge police-station, on 7th November 06 
(Ext. B) for necessary action. The police arrested the petitioner on 8th 
November 1956 and produced him before the Police Magistrate on that 
date on a report (Ext. C). He was in jail custody from that date till 
29nd November 1956 (Ext. D). On 22nd November 1956, on the report 
of the police that there was no sufficient evidence to proceed against him, 
the petitioner was discharged by the Police Magistrate (Ext. D). After 
such discharge, the petitioner applied to the Company for permission to 


দে 1 TH CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 29, 7 315৭ 
এ নিলি: চিল 
resume duty. In reply the Company suspended him with effect from the 
date of arrest pending departinental enquiry against him on charge of 
gross and culpable negligence in the matter (Ext. FE). Departmental 
enquiry wa. held and a statement of the petitioner was recorded (Ext. F). 
On 17th December 1954, the Company passed order dismissing him for 
his gross and culpable negligence (Ext. Fl). This the Company cia during 
the pendency of adjudication proceeding سا‎ respect of an industrial 
dispute between the opposite party and their workman. The workinan 
accordingly made the complaint. He alleged that there was no justifica- 
tion for termination of his employment. 


The Company, on the other hand, pleaded that it wns justified to 
terminate his employment, as in any case the petitioner was guilty of 
gross and culpable negligence in carrying out his duties. 


The parties eventually filed a joint petition of compromise and prayed 
for an award in terms thereof. The terms appear to be fair. The 
opposite party agreed to take back the petitioner into ite employment ; 
while the petitioner agreed to pay the sum of Rs. 1,000 in instalments 
from his pay and allowances. In the circumstances, 1 make my award in 
terms of the petition of compromise. The petition of compromise is made 
part of the award.

The original reference out of which this present complaint under 
section 338A of the Industrial Disputes Act has orisen was made under 
Government Order No. 3996Dis./D/11L-126/55, dated Calcutta, the 7th 
September 1956. 


This is an application under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes 
Act, for termination of service without leave of the Tribunal when a 
reference proceeding was pending. 


The case of the applicant is that an order of retrenchment lauded on 
him out of the blue on 6th December 1955, terminating his service from 
Ist January 1956. The action taken by the employer was in contravention 
of section 33. 


The defence of the other party was that the applicant was a part-time 
compounder in the Company’s factory dispensary, which was abolished 
on account of the introduction of the State Insurance Scheme. As a 
result of the said closure the post held by the applicant as a part-time 
compounder was abolished. There was no substance in the application 
made by the employee. 


DECISION 


Parties have filed a petition jointly stating that the dispute has been 
amicably settled. In the circumstances the application is disposed of on 
the finding that no dispute 18 subsisting at present.

Suri G. PALIT, Judge, Fifth Industrial Tribunal. 


AWARD 


The original reference out of which this case has arisen was made 
under G.O. No. 5441-I.R./D/10L-116/56, dated 20th December 1956. 


I need not go into the facta of the case which have led up to the 
present dispute because the matter in question has heen settled by a 
vetition filed by the petitioner by which the case is allowed to be dropped. 

he ground which is urged for such withdrawal is that in view of the 
amendment of the order of reference by corrigendum order No. 1922-I.R./ 
187/101-457, dated 7th June 1957, by which the Head Office employees 
have been excluded from the pending adjudication and now as the present 
dispute was in respect of the Head Office in which the said workman waa 
concerned, the present case is not tenable in law under section 994 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1941. 


I accept the said contention and allow the case to be withdrawn. 
This is my award.

ANNEXURE 


In the matter of an industrial dispute existing between the Bus Owners and 
their workmen represented by the Haringhata-Kanchrapara-Birahi- 
Calcutta Bus & Transport Employees’ Union, P.O. Bara Jagull, 
district Nadia. (Case No. Vill-29 of 1957.) 


BEFORE THE FOURTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL 


PRESENT: 
Suri M. N. GAN, Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal. 


For the Union: Shri P. K. Nandi, Counsel. 
For the Company: Shri P. R. Mukherjee. 


The following two issues arising out of an industrial dispute existing 
between Bus Owners and their workmen represented by Haringhata-Kanchra- 
para-Birahi-Calcutta| Bus & Transport Employees’ Union, P.O. Bara 
Jaguli, district Nadia, was referred to this Tribunal for adjudication, by 
the Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 86-1.R. / 
D/4L-21/56, dated the 7th January 1957. 


The Employees’ Union filed a single written statement and the Bus 
Owners filed a joint written statement as also separate written statements 
in the dispute. 

Issue 

(1) Is the dismissal of the workmen mentioned in column B of the 
attached list by the employers mentioned in column A of the list, valid and 
justified ? 

(2) Are they entitled to reinstatement? 


FINDINCS 


IsSues Nos. 1 and 2, The Union’s case, as stated now, is that all these 
dismissals are invalid and unjustified, and that the dismissed employees 
should be reinstated in service with all hack wages. The contention of the 
Bus Owners is that only one employee wus dismissed, after proper enquiry, 
for Kis misconduct, and that all other employees had voluntarily abandoned 
their employment either before the strike or after it. Some of them, 
পা were re-employed, on former pay, on their own request long after 
the strike. 


Shri P. K, Nandi, learned Counsel for the Union, classified these cases 
of dismissal into three groups, viz.— 
(1) those who were dismissed before the strike; 
(1) Shri Sadananda Banerjee, Driver (26-9-51), 
(11) Shri Pran Gopal Kundu, Driver (10-12-55), 
(117) Shri Krishna Pada Ghose, Conductor (28-1-56), 
(iv) Shri Prafulla Kumar Kar, Driver (14/15-8-56), 
{2) those who were dismissed after strike but re-employed; 
(1) Shri Kasi Nath Kurmi, Conductor, 
(11) Shri Tapan Kumar Ghose, Assistant, 
(111) Shri Amira Dhobe, Driver, 


43) all the remaining employees dismissed after strike but not 
reinstated.

ae re পা 


At the time of hearing, Shri Nandi, on behalf of the Union, did not 
ress the cases of (i) Shri Sudhir Kumar Chakraborty, Driver, (1) Shni 
Sankar Kr. Bose, Conductor, and (iii) Shri Samiran Bikash Sarkar, 
Assistant. [In the written statement, bus number 1014 belonging to bus 
owner Shr: Sankar Mukherjee, it is stated that all of them were reinstated 
with back wages by the employer. 0. P. W. 6, Shn Sankar Mukherjee, 
admitted this in his deposition before the Tribunal. Accordingly, there is 
no outstanding dispute between Shri Sankar Mukherjee, bus owner, on the 
one hand, and his employees, viz., Shri Sudhir Kumar Chakraborty, Shri 
Sankar Kr, Bose and Shri Samiran Bikash Sarkar on the other. I make 
an award to that effect for intormation of the Government. 


J will now examine the cases of 15 other alleged dismissals, one by one, 
und record my findings thereon. 


It is in evidence of P.W. 1, Shri Amrita [Lal Mitra, the General 
Secretary of the Union, that his Union, of which the alleged dismissed 
employees in the dispute are members, was formed in August 1954. The 
Association 18 a registered one and is affliated to J.N.T.U.C. Shri Mitra 
sent a charter of demands to the Bus Owners on 4/5th January 1956. The 
demunds were not conceded and even no reply was given to the Union. 
Thereatter, the Union decided to call for o strike and after several postpone- 
ments, the strike took place on 24th March 1956. But the strike did not 
Inst long, and is said to be an unsuccessful one and the running of the 
buses was not even suspended, beyond a part of the day. These facts are 
established in this case, and we shall now consider the cases of dismissal 
against the background of these facts. 


(1) Shri Sadananda Banerjee.—The Union’s written statement, which 
runs into several pages, does not contain uny statement of his case. In 
fact, the written statement does not give out any details of cases except 
of two employees only. Shri Banerjee’s case us far as can be gathered from 
his evidence is that he was in service of Shri Sudhir Kumar Kundu. He 
was a bus driver and was dismissed towards the end of 1951 for his Union 
activities. He said that he was the President of the Union. He was not 
81৮61) any charge-sheet or written letter of discharge. He, however, 
complained to the Union towards the end of December last year, after an 
interval of 0 years. He admitted having purchased a lorry thereafter. In 
cross-examination he said that he came to Shri Sudhir Babu’s service after 
the sale of bus of Jamir Mia and he left service after 20th July 1951. Shri 
Mitra said that Shri Banerjee complained to him about his dismissal and 
the same was recorded in his complaint book (Ext. 1(a)]. This unfortunate- 
ly refers to a complaint of an alleged dismissal of Shri Banerjee on 22nd 

ecember 1955 by his then employer, Shri Sankar Kumar Mukherjee. 
0.۲۰۷۷ ۰ 6, Shri Mukherjee, was not asked any question about it. Besides 
that, that dismissal is not an issue in this case. 0.P.W. 5, Shri Kundu, 
anid that Shri Banerjee remained absent from work from the middle of 
1951. He was seen thereafter to drive a lorry. He left his job without 
notice. The Pay Register of 1951 shows that Shri Banerjee was absent 
from duty since 20th July 1951, but received payment by signing the 
Register (Ext. E). There is nothing on record to show that Shri Banerjee 
was ever elected as a President of his Union. On a consideration of all 
these, I find Shri Banerjee’s alleged dismissal from service in 1951 is not 
true. Accordingly, Shri Banerjee is not entitled to any relief in this case. 
He having left his employment long, long ago, without notice to his 
employer, is not entitled to reinstatement. 


(2) Shri Pran Copal Kundu, Driver.—The Union’s case is that Shri Pran 
(ropal Kundu, Driver, was discharged without any fault by one Jnan Sankar

Shri Kundu applied for fresh appointment, und in u letter (Ext. C), dated

tien, Shri Kundu admitted that one of the conditions of their services was 
that they did not get any pay for absence from work. ©.P.W. 4, Shri 
Chatterjee, said that he did not dismiss him from service. In fact. Shri

damaged, und went home. He did not return to work thereafter. He 
came only for fresh appointment on 6th October 1956. In fact, Shri

the conductor of his bus to that post, who had licence for it. There is no

from service created a furore and the Union made it a point for calling a 
strike. Accordingly, it is only reasonable to think that the issue is not so 
simple as the evidence now discloses. At the same time, it must be held 
that the Union had failed to make out a case of Shri Kundu as stated in 
his written statement. There, it was alleged that he was discharged by 
Shri Jnan Sankar for defective driving. That case has not been establish- 
ed, Shri Kundu is now continuing in service after re-employment since 
last October. He has no further claim on his employer. On this evidence 
and in the circumstances, I am inclined to hold that he was not dismissed 
from service, in the way alleged by the Union, and that he is not entitled 
to any relief. 


(3) Shri Krisna Pada Chosh, Conductor.—The Union’s written state- 
ment is silent about his case. He is P,W. 3. He was conductor in the 
service of Shri Jugal Chandra Ghosh. He said that he did not remember 
the date of discharge. He was not given any charge-sheet. He was asked 
to drive a car, which he refused, due to strike, He admitted that at 
times he was found short of cash. He did not, however, udmit that he left 
his service when he was found short of cash hy Rs. 1-15 on 28th J anuary 
1956. O.P.W,. 2, Shri Jugal Chandra Ghosh, said that he did not dismiss 
Shri Ghosh. On 28th January 1956, he was found short of cash by Rs. 1-15 
in one trip. At first, he refused to explain this shortage but later said 
that he purchased rice by it. Thereafter he left the place without turning 
up again. His way-bill, Ext. D, shows that he was found short of cash 
by Rs. 1-15 on 28th January 1956. There is no other evidence on this 
point. There is no corroboration of the Union’s case as now disclosed in 
the evidence of P.W. 3. I am, therefore, not prepared to accept the 
evidence of P.W. 3 as true. He resigned from service and, therefore, is 
not entitled to reinstatement in this case.

(4) Shri Prafulla Kumar Kar, Driver.—The Union's written statement

Shri Bandopadhya. The Association on a consideration of every thing 
before it came to the finding that the misconduct was proved but then it 
demanded only an apology trom him before ubsolving him of the charge. 
Shri Bandopadhya, however, declined to offer any apology. The Associa- 
tion, thereafter, appointed his own brother as a Starter in his place. 
Exhibit F series would show that the Association, his employers, was 
anxious to allow him full opportunity to appear and explain his conduct 
before the enquiry. The enquiry was properly «done, and Shri Bando- 
padhaya had every opportunity to defend himself. There was no viglation 
of the principles of natural justice. There is no good reason why this 
Tribunal should interfere with the finding of the Association in his case. 
Shri Mahabir Bandopadhya, therefore, is not entitled to reinstatement, or 
any other relief. 


Other employees participated in the strike. 0006 of them, P.W. 9,

left his service due to derangement of his brain. Shri Paul admitted that 
he was in mental hospital in Dum Dum for 3 months, only 10 days after 
the strike. This conclusively proves the employer’s case. He was not 
dismissed from service and was not entitled to reinstatement.

Accordingly, the question of his reinstatement does not arise.

2. After usual summons the parties put in appearance and filed their 
written atatements. The pleadings were completed on 4th January 1957. 
The parties were thereafter directed to file lists of documents. Then after

3. The matter of dispute as stated in the schedule to the order of 
reference is as follows: 


Whether the termination of service of Shri Mannalal Parekh was justi- 
fied? What relief is he entitled to? 


DECISION 


Paschim Bengal Gumasta Sabha (hereafter called the 7 examined 
the workman concerned, Shri Mannalal Parekh (P.W. 1), besides proving 
correspondences [Exts. 1 to 1(1) and 2 to 2(f)] Messrs. M. ."ا‎ Shahani & 
Co. (Cal.), Ltd. (hereafter called the Conpany), on the other hand, examined 
the Manager, D.W. i Shri Daulatram 5 Kripalani and a repre- 
sentative of Messrs. Pearline Paris Private Ltd., Bombay, D.W. 2 Shri 
A. 1), Shanbhha. 


The Company deals in various toilet goods, perfumeries, cosmetics and 
other luxury goods. It was formerly a proprietory concern which was estab- 
lished before 1987. In 1948 separate companies out of the said parent 
concern were formed and incorporated under the Indian Companies Act for 
Calcuttsu, Bombay, Karachi and Delhi. The Caleutta Company with which 
we are concerned under the present reference employed in all ahout 25 
to 30 workmen at the relevant time. 


P.W. ۱ Shri Mannalal Parekh was 0 salesman in the concern having 
had served for 8 years. His last salary was Rs, 167 per month. 


Kmployment of Shri Mannalal Parekh in this concern according to 
both sides ceased from 19th July 1955. According to the Company the 
workman submitted his resignation on 19th July 1955 and thus put an snd 
to his own employment, while according to the workman the Company 
terminated his employment on the false plea of resignation on 19th July 
1955 although, in fact, he did not resign. From the correspondences, oral 
evidencs and circumstances neither version seems to me wholly correct. The 
workman, it appears, was not satisfied with his lot in the Company and 
was giving vent to it by saying now and then that he would not continue. 
Although the workman denied having resigned on 19th July 1955, the 
evidence and circumstances rather show that having heen agitated .nd 
extited for reasons best known to him, he as in the’ past, expressed 6ا‎ 
intention to resign and accordingly made over the order book 10 the 
Managing Director on 19th July 19455. The fact that he admittedly 
returned the order hook on that day coupled with the fact that he left the 
office soon after and did not turn up for duty thereafter would support that 


Parr 1] THE 08147771148 GAZETTE AUGUST 20, 1957 3167 
১৯-১৯-০৬৯০ gp mm po ar na eR OR =~ ORC | 


there wags such expression of intention on his part to resign. P. W. 2 who 
was present at the time deposed that 2. W. 1 came to the Managing 
Director, had a heated discussion with him and the Manager of the 
Company and then said that he wauld not work with them any ۰ 
His evidence cannot be discarded merely because his principal has ۵ 
connection with the Company. The workman has no satisfactory explana- 
tion why he made over the order book on ]9th July 1955 more so when he 
had not admittedly done so in the past at the time of going on leave on 
the ground of illness (influenza). So the alleged illness on the present 
occassion eould not have been obviously the ground tor euch return of the 
order book. 11 rather appears that having expressed his intention not to 
continwe any more, he made over the order book in pursuance thereof. 
From the evidence I am also unable to believe that he left the office on 
19th July 1965 and continued to be absent thereafter due to his illness. 
According to his own showing he becume ill at home before coming to 
0170৪, and so it waa more natural for him to come to office fortified with 
a medical certificate as he had admittedly done on the previous occasion for 
taking leave on the ground of having got influenza. The story of ؤ۵‎ 
on 19th July 1955 2৪ afterthought and unreliable. Dr, ©. M. Saha who is 
alleged to have attended and treated him for alleged illness from 19th July 
1955 has not been examined and no explanation ۳۳ heen given for the 
aame. The evidence of the workman (P.W. 1) on the contrary shows 
that another doctor Shri Prokash Ghosh who had attended him on the ۹۷) 
oecusion and granted medical certificate is his close neighbour living at a 
distance of 5 to 7 minutes’ walk. So had he fallen ill on 19th July 1992, 
it was more natural that he would have been attended by self-same doctor 
who is hia close neighbour. 


This time the workman, however, got a medical ceitifieate 8 days after 
و‎ long after the controversy started on 21+ July 1955) from a different 
octor, shri C. M. Saha who lives not in the locality but in Lower Chitpore 
area more than § miles away from his residence. The said doctor, it has 
already been noted, has not either heen examined to support workman’s 
elaim of illness or to take responsibility for certifieate. The workman's 
evidence that he did not express his intention to resign on 19th July 1965 
eannot, therefore. be accepted as reliable in view of the circumatauces. 


At the same time the case of the employer Company that thete had 
been absolute resignation by the workman und the matter ended on 19th 
July 1955 and uo option was left to the workman to revoke it, cannot be 
accepted as making a full and correct disclosure. There can he no doubt 
from the circumstances that the workman although expressed himself on 
19th July 1955 not to continue in the employment of the concern, did so 
express not out of his own free will or volition but having had heated 
discussion with the Managing J)irector and the Manager of the Company. 
It further appears that the said verbal expression of not continuing any 
more was not accepted by the management on that date (19th July 1955) 
or until 218 July 1956 (wide Ext. 1), According to the management after 
the workman expressed his desire not to continue any more in their serviee, 
he was asked to reconsider and was eventually asked to tender his resigna- 
tion in writing. This would show that the matter was not concluded on 
19th Julv 19545 and the workman wus given option to review the matter 
and revoke resignation, if necessary. The workman admittedly did not 
thereafter tender his resignation in writing. On 2118 July 1955 fhe 
Managing Director wrote to inform the workman that in pursuance of the 
conversation which he had with the workman on 19th July ‘+955 his 
resignation was thereby accepted. The workman was also asked by the 
said letter to hand over the stationery and other office papers in his

protested having resigned, and questioned the right of the employer صا‎ 
terminate his employment. It was not unnatural. After having asked the 
workman to tender ie resignation in writing and thus having given him 
option in the matter, it was not fair or proper ou the part of the Managing 
Director to terminate employment of the workman on the allegation of the 
anterior verbal resignation when the letter of resignation as was required 
was not forthcoming. The fact that the workman did not send resignation 
in writing and on the contrary, protested immediately on receipt of ihe 
communication (Ext. 1), would show that he repudiated the resignation 
for which option was given to him by the management. The action of 
the management was not, therefare, bona fide. Tt is not unlikely that it 
did so having grown wiser in order to get rid of the workman, who was 
not satished with his lot in the concern though drawing a higher salary of 
Ra. 167 per month. That it was from an ulterior motive 14 apparent from 
the 170 that the action was taken prior to submission of the required 
resipnation letter in writing. The circumstances that the parties intended 
a subsequent letter of resignation to be made, are evidence to show that 
they did not intend the previous conversation on 19th July 1995 to amount 
to an agreement and to put an end of the matter. If one 1৭ permitted to 
say ہمہ‎ there was only proposal on the part of the workman not 10 continue 
in service of the Company on 19th July 1955. The said proposal according 
to the evidence and circumstances was not accepted and the Company 11 
ita turn made a counter-proposal whereby the workman was asked to 
reconsider the matter and he was eventually told to tender resignation ۴ 
writing, This amounted to nothing more than a new proposal or 88 ا‎ 
frequently called counter-offer and not absolute and unqualified acceptance. 
There can be no agreement without a complete acceptance of the proposal. 
Acceptance with a variation is no acceptance. So, the management in the 
absence of written resignation had no justification to terminate the emplov- 
ment of the workman a. it did on 21st July 1055. After having asked the 
workman to review and submit resignation لا‎ writing the managemont 
should not have niade anterior verbal resignation which aceording to their 
own witness (1). W. 2) was a result of heated discussion and = consequently 
not out of free will or volition as a basis for termination of the employment 
of the workman. So on examination of the whole of the correspondences, 
oral evidence and circumstances, it appears that the termination of service 
of Shri Mannalal Parekh was uot justified. As it, however, appears that 
Shri Parekh was dissatisfied with his lot in the Company and had 0) the 
past expressed himself not to) continue in’ the concern and hus since 
termination of employment got better joh with higher salary in another 
concern, T think that it will be to the interest of all concerned that there 
should he no order for reinstatement. Having regard to all facts ond 
circumstances, it appears that ends of justice will be met if the workman 
be awarded compensation equivalent to 4 months’ salary سص‎ last drawn by 
him in the concern, The Company 18 accordingly directed to pay the 
compensation within a month from the date the award becomes enforceable. 


Regarding preliminary objection taken by the Company that what has 
been roferred to ia not an industrial dispute within the meaning of 
aection 2(k) but 1s pure and simple individual dispute, T am unable to 
sustain it. The evidence no doubt shows that the workmen of the concern 
have no Union of their own nor are they members of Pnachim Bangal 
Gumasta Sabha nor did any of them take up the cause of the workman but 
this by itself would not take away the dispute out of the category of 
industrial dispute. An individual dispute may nonetheless develop into an 
industrial dispute as defined in section 2(k) of the Act ifthe said dispute

According to the written statement filed on behalf of the workers there 
was great irregularity in the payment of their wages. The workers did not 
receive their wages month by month or according to any fixed dates. This 


unsatisfactory state of affairs cannot be allowed to continue and payment 
should he directed to be made within 7th of every month.

is sought to secure relief in that regard. 


An artificial distinction was made treating some of the men as employees 
of the Company and 138 workers are supposed to be employees of contractors, 
In the written statement this was described as a ‘false contract system” 
designed by the Company to divide the workers into two camps. The 
ao-called contract system should be abolished and the 138 men should be 
treated as direct employees of the Company, 


Sixteen workers were illegally retrenched in July 1954. The Union 
demands their reinstatement together with compensation. 


The pia admitted in the written statement that wages could not 
be paid regularly. At present wages are being paid monthly but not on 
any fixed date. 


Regarding retiring benefit, it was pleaded that the business of the 
Company was going downhill. B. N. Railway used to give contracts to 
this Company but of lute no such contract is being given. The loss of this 
contract has resulted in loss to the extent of 60 per cent. of the total 
business. There were differences amongst the partners. One of the 
partners cut off his connection with the: business and another wanted 
dissolution. The other three partners however stuck to the business in 
expectation of fair days. For overdraft loans received from the Central 
Bank of India a suit was filed in the High Court at Calcutta and a receiver 
was appointed by the Hon'ble Court in 1949 who was in possession of the 
management of the business till March 1954. There were other liabilities 
which could not be discharged and various proceedings were started against 
this Company. Against this background demand for retiring benefits would 
be disastrous, 


This Company has a number of contactors. In regerd to certain types of 
work it engages the services of contractors who recruit their own employees, 
exercise control over them and get the work done. With regard ما‎ these 
men the Company has no responsibility and no power of supetvision or

DECISION 


issue No. 3: On a literal construction, the point as framed takes for 
granted that the 138 workers named in List A are not direct employees of 
the Company. The Tribunal has to give its decision whether they should 
be treated as direct employees. If the issue is construed in this limited 
gepse the Union has no case at all. Once it is admitted that there are two 
clusses of workers, one class being direct emplovees and another class 
employed by contractors, there must be very strong reason for the Tribunal 
to interfere with the internal management of the Company and dictate how 
its affairs should be conducted. Nothing has heen suggested or proved on 
behalf of the Union why the contract system should be abolished and the 
men employed by the contractors placed in service under the Company, 


The real intention appears however to be that the Tribunal should make 
an investigation as to whether the men supposed to be employees of the 
contractors are really employees of the Company kept apart by some con- 
trivance for ulterior motives. If this is an artificial distinction this may be 
removed if the Tribunal finds that as a matter of fact these people are 
employees of the Company. Reading the issue in this light I proceed to 
embank on an enquiry whether these workers are Company's men or 
employees of the contractors. 


That some sort of distinction is being made and the men are not being 
{reated as employees of the Company is admitied in the written statement 
of the Union. In paragraph 6 at page 1 the system is deseribed as ‘'falso 
eontract system’’. In second paragraph at page 3 it 1s stated that the Union 
had demanded abolition of the so-called contract system. The Company 
has in ils written statement at page 5, mentioned the names of the seven 
persons who are said to be contractora. According to the Union these men 
are Supervisors of the different sections. The men engaged in these dopart- 
ments work under them, not as their employees but as persons over whom 
{hev have got powers of supervision. Exhibits J and J(1) are the contractors’ 
rate books. The books are hallowed by age. On examination of the 
contents 1 find that there were contractors for different varieties of work. 
They engaged their own staff to carry out the work. As for instance, at 
page 184 of Ext. J in paragraph 11 the contractor stipulated that the Firm 
could pay his staff from his bills or he would himself pay his staff in 
presence of the Company’s accountant. Similar provision was made with 
another contractor at page 166. Similar provisions appear in other 
contracts recorded in Ext. J(1). Exhibit K series are bills submitted by 
contractors. Existence of the contract system has been proved. It will 
appear from Ext. J(1) that Motilal Gupta nomed in the written statement 
had obtained contract along with Mobarak Ali in 1935. Contract was again 
given to him in 1936 as will appear from the entry towards the end of the 
book. Tafazzal Hossain got a contract in 1950 as will appear from Ext. J. 
On behalf of the Union all this was sought to be rebutted pay books Ext. 2 
series in which Motilal Gupta and Tafazzal Hossain are named as employees 
drawing fixed salary. In Ext. 2 Motilal Gupta was described as compositor- 
in-charge drawing Rs. 125 inclusive of pay and allowances, In Ext, 2(a) 
Taffazal Hossain is shown as drawing Rs. 105 plus Rs. 22 as dearness

allowance. [6 was also pointed out that Motilal Gupta received increments 
of pny. In the pay sheet Ext. 2(b) for the year 1952, his pay is noted as 
Rs, 276 plus Rs. 22 as dearness allowance. Av argument was advanced 
that if le were a contractor there cannot be such wages and increment to 
boot. Learned spokesman for the Union referred also to the attendance 
registers in which names of all the workers were entered. So far as the 
attendance registers are concerned the Company’s reply is that under the 
Vactories Act names of all the persons working in the factor, must be 
recorded in the register. In regurd to the pay sheet, the learned Advocate 
for the Company offered the explanation that for purposes of calculating 
contribution due from the emplover under the Employeea? State Insurance 
Corporation Act some wagea were to be tuken 08 the basis. It was for that 
urpose alone that wages were recorded in the pay sleets. IT am _ not 
impressed with this argument because Employees’ State Insurance Act came 
into operation on the 14th of August 1955. Exhibit 2 is the pay sheet for 
the year 1940 and Ext. 2(a) is the pay sheet for the year 1952, sv is also 
the pay sheet Ext. 2(b). Wages were not certainly recorded ‘against the 
names of the contractors so far back for purpose of calculation of contri- 
bution os suggested. The truth appears to me to 119 in between the rival 
versions, That Motilal, Tafazzal and others were contractors admits of no 
doubt because of the entries in Kxts. J and J(1), It may be that these 
people alsu uccepted appointment under the Company and became their 
employees. While working as employees of the Company thay wgre also 
given the advantage of accepting contracts as before. So they filled dual 
capacity, viz., that of employees of the Company and at the same time 
Contractors to carry on business as a side line engaging their own staff for 
executing the orders. That seems to he the probable explanation of the 
conflicting position as brought out in the evidence. Stresa was laid on 
leave application made by Tofazzal Hossain (Ext. 1), Leave with pay 
was allowed. Since, in my view, he was both an emplovee and contractor 
there is nothing strange that he had to obtain leave for his absence. The 
Union spokesman referred to a case reported in 1955, L.A.C., page 686. 
In that case it was proved that the management paid bonus to the coolies 
who were said to be employees of the contractor just as ا(‎ paid bonus to its 
ether employees, Annual leave according to the Factories Act and leave 
en sustaining injuries were granted by the management to these coolies and 
payment for the same was also made. Qn these facts their Lordships held 
that they were inconsistent with the position that these men were employed 
by a contractor. The case before me can claim no parity with the case 
cited. Tt is not proved that any bonus was paid to the workers or leave was 
granted to the workers by the Company. Dearness allowance at the same 
rate was no doubt paid but it is not established that payment was made by. 
the Company out of its own funds. The materials availahle are not 
sufficient for the finding that the men, who admittedly were not treated 
as the Company’s employees, were really their employees. In this connec- 
tion reference may be made to a decision made by the Authority under the 
Payment of Wages Act before whom claim for wages was made by a large 
number of workers including some who were supposed to be the contractor’s 
men. The Company took up the defence with regard to those inen ۱۹ 
they were employees of the contractors and their wages had heen paid by 
them. The Authority under the Payment of Wages Act recorded a clear 
finding that they were the employees of the contractors (vide Ext. B at page 
18). Though the principle of res judicata is not fully applicable an 
analogous principle does in fact apply. The judgment Ext. B is a very 
strong piece of evidence in the present case. Taken in conjunction with the 
evidence [| have discussed above it clinches the issue. In my Judgment 
the Union has failed to prove that these workers are employees‘ of the

issue No. 4: ‘The Company has produced ita balance-sheets to prove

the Company collected the employees’ share of contribution under the 
[71019195669 State Insurance Act but did not pay the same. The Company 
recovered sales tax but did not make payment in discharge of its own 
liabilities. Jt was on account of its own acts of omission that proceedings 
for recovery of arrears were started. Though there is some force in this 
contention it must be borne in mind that a normal being does not make 
default in payment of inescapable liabilities and incur the risk of harass- 
ment by proceedings if it has the means to keep clear of all these trouble. 
Though the Company may have been guilty of acts of improvidence one 
cannot blink the fact that it was hedged او‎ by different kinds of liabilities 
for large amounts. The loss of 1). N. Railway contract made the situation 
still more precarious. V.W, 4 has admitted in his evidence that actually 
there was full in business. In these circumstances [ must hold that the 
Company had ample grounds for making retrenchment.

The next question is whether the retrenched employees are entitled to 
relief under section 25(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act. One of the 
arguments advanced on behalf of the Company was that some of the men 
were extremely old. They were not capable of further service. In their 
case section 25F cannot be applicable. Reference was made to the definition 
of retrenchment in the Industrial Disputes Act. Retrenchment means the 
{ermination by the employer of the service of a workman for any reason 
whatsoever otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary 
uction, but does not include— 


(a) Voluntary retirement of the workman, or 


(b) retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation 
if the contract of employment between the employer and the 
workman concerned contains a stipulation in that behalf, or 


(c) termination of the service of a workman on the ground of continued 
ill-health, 


Since there is no case of any stipulation in the contract of employment for 
retirement on attainment of any particular age, the retrenchment in the case 
of old employees must be held to be retrenchment as defined in the Act. 
There is no reason why they should not get relief as provided in section 25F.

serve an employer whose business according to lis own showing waa on 
the down-grade. ‘Their unwillingness to come back 0৮091 be @ ground 
for refusing the relief due to them under the law. 


The compensation awarded to the workers named above must he paid 
within three weeks from the date of publication of the award in the 
Calcutta Gazette. 


issue No. 1: It is agreed that the wages would be paid by the 7th of 
every English calendar month. This arrangement will be operative from 
the month of September 1957. 


Issue No. 2: Financial weakness was pleaded on behalf of the Company 
to avoid the responsibility of making provision for retiring benefits. It is 
admitted by both parties that the Employees’ Provident Fund Act applies 
to this establishment. The Company is therefore directed to introduce 
Provident Fund Scheme in accordance with the said Act within three months 
of the publication of the award {n the Calcutta Gazette unless exempted by 
Government from the operation of the Act. 


The Union representative urged that for the uncovered period gratuity 
should be made available. As I have already pointed that the concern 
18 fighting against heavy odds, so far as its financial position 1s concerned, 
it would not be expedient to grant the prayer for further relief in the form 
of gratuity.
