This industrial dispute existing between Messrs. National Motor Worka 
(Propriestor-—Shri Rajani Kanto Deashi) (hereinafter referred to as _ the 
Company), 66 Hazra Road, Calcutta and their workmen represented hy 
Automobile Engineering Workers’ Union, 249 Bowbazar Street, Calcutta, 
regarding the following issues, was referred to this Tribunal for adjudi- 
cation, by the Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, order 
No. 547-1.R./1R/10L-2/57, dated the 19th February 1957. 


Both parties filed written statements, adduced evidence—oral and 
documentury—and advanced arguments, in this case. 


(1) Whether the retrenchment of the workmen named in the attached 
list is justified. What relief are they entitled to? (The 
attached list is given as per Appendix A to this award.) 


(2) Whether the disciplinary action taken against Shri Gour Mohan 
Koley, Mistry, is justified? What relief is he entitled toP 


(3) Whether the discharge of Shri Narayan Chandra Dhara is justified ? 
What relief is he entitled to? 


FINDINCS 


A list of retrenched workmen, uttached to the order of reference, shows 
that 49 workmen were retrenched by this Company. Serial Nos. 1 to 42 
of the list were retrenched on 8th October 1956, and serial Nos. 43 to 49 
on 19th December 1956. The Union’s case is that the workmen had 
organised a Union in September 1956 for redress of their grievances against 
the Management of this Company. The Management, however, retrenched 
the ৪0110 workmen without notice, without charge-sheet, and also without 
assigning any reason whatsoever. The Company’s contention is that the 
retrenchment was done for bona fide trade reasons. This was necessary as 
there was reduction of work, and that some of the workmen had adopted a 
“‘go-slow’”’ tactics to put the Company into a loss in the business. In the 


I] TH) CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 29, 1957 3189‏ وط 


ely 


০ 
on এ 


or weed 


additjonal written statement the Company contends that the issue No. 1 
in the order of feference is bad im law, for, the dispute was finally settled 
and concluded by an agreement, dated 15th October 1956, and the workinen 
are, therefore, estopped from raising the issue again. The Union. on the 
other hand, denies the existence of such an agreement and puts the 
Company to its strict proof. The agreement is said to he embodied in the 
two documents, viz., Exts. 2 and 3, same as Exts. C and D. Exhibit © 
is u copy of a letter of demands which some of the workmen had placed 
before the Management on 15th October 1956. This appears to be signed 
and thumb-marked by 4] workmen. Exhibit D is the reply of the Munage- 
ment to the said letter of demands. Exhibit D appeurs to he signed by two 
witnesses besides the proprietor of the Company. The witnesses are (i) 
Shri Rajani Kumar Mitra, said to be a communist leader and (11) Shri 
Arabiundy Das, is the son-in-law of the proprietor. Shri Mitra 18 not an 
employee of this Company. His connection with the workmen in dispute 
could not he established. Only five workmen mentioned in the list attached 
to the order of reference are said to have signed this list of demands. The 
Union’s contention, however, is that none of the workinen actually signed 
this list. In this state of evidence, I fail to see how the two documents 
can be said to constitute an agreement binding on the workmen involved 
in this dispute. One broud point is that this was supposed to be made 
at a time when conciliation proceedings were pending. One further fact 
is that this alleged agreement refers to acceptance of demands made hy 
‘the striking employees’’ who joined duties at 1-30 p.m. on 15th December 
1996. It is not reasonable to helieve that the settlenent would be made 
privately, und not before the Conciliation Officer, before whom the mutter 
was then pending. Further, the striking employees who had joined on 
16th October 1956 could not be identically the same workmen who had been 
retrenched on 8th October 1956. Therefore, ] find that the two documents 
mentioned above, do not constitute any agreement which is binding on the 
workmen concerned in this dispute. Accordingly, the reference of Issue 
No. 1 cannot be said to be bad in law. 


Further, a valid agreement binds the parties only in respect of the 
issues specifically settled by it. It cannot have any application to matters 
extraneous to it. A glance at Ext. C, list of demands and Ext. D, the 
acceptance on behalf of the Management would show that among others 
the demand was made on behalf of the retrenched employees for payment - 
of wages for leuve due under the Factories Act. This cannot have any 
reasonuble connection with the justification or otherwise of the disputed 
retrenchment and puyment for compensation for that. In any view, the 
alleged agreement can never operate as a bar to the adjudication of this 


dispute. 


In the next place, it has been contended that the workmen are estopped 
from contesting this issue after having received payment in terms of the 
agreement from the Management. In this connection P.W. 1 proves a 
receipt of payment (Ext. Q) by Shri Talit Halder (serial No. 4 of the 
order of reference). The receipt shows payment of wages for 3 days’ leave 
for 1956 under the Factories Act. O.P.W. 2 Shri Halder admits this pay- 
ment. Under section 79 of the Factories Act, every worker who works 
for a period of 240 days or more in a factory during the calender year shal! 
he allowed during the subsequent year leave with wages for a number 01 
days. The said payment shows two things, viz., (1) Shri Halder worked 
for more than 240 days, i.e., 8 months in 1955 and (11) he must have worked 
in 1956 as well. Shri Halder’s evidence is that he had been in service for 
about 7 years before his retrenchment, whereas according to Ext. B, the 
Company’s statement on length of service, shows that Shri Halder only 


3190 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 29, 1957 8৮১৪

ny পপ রি প 


worked for 36 days before his retrenchment. This is inconsistent with the 
accepted position regarding his service under the aforesaid payment. 
Accordingly, this payment does not estop Shri Halder from raising the issue 
No. 1 in this case. The issue relates to different matters. 


Of 49 workmen, mentioned in the list, who were retrenched ىا‎ the 
Company, the Union does not press for adjudication of cases of the 
following workmen, viz., serial No. 3), Shri Sakhavath Roy, serial No. 32, 
Shri Suroj Sarkar and serial No. 42, Shri Suresh Karmakar. ہا‎ therefore, 
find that there is no outstanding dispute between these three workmen and 
the company and ] award accordingly. 


It is admitted that serial Nos. 7, Shri Brojen Das, 17, Shri Motleb 
Ali, 18, Shri Latif Ali were reinstated in service and actually working 
with this Company. So no question of reinstatement of these employees 
would in any event arise for consideration of the: Tribunal. 


Question now is whether the retrenchment of the remaining workmen 
for ‘trade reasons’’ is justified. The onus to prove this justification 1s now 
on the management. We are concerned with the retrenchment of two 
batches of workers made on 8th October 1906 and 19th December 1956. 
This-was done after short notice of 7 days. The first batch of 41 workers 
were retrenched purely on the ground of reduction of work, specially due 
to reduction in the number of orders received in the month of September. 
The second batch was retrenched on two grounds, viz., (i) for reduction of 
work, ond (ii) for adopting ‘‘go-slow’’ tactics. 


T can at once dispose of the additional ground of the alleged adoption 
of “go-slow’’? tactica hy seven workers by saying that none of them was 
charge-sheeted for the said ‘‘go-slow’’ tactics. No previous warning was 
given to them in writing in respect of the alleged ‘‘go-slow”’ tuctics to the 
workers. P.W. 1, proprietor, speaks of the ‘‘go-slow’’ movement without 
referring to any statement or register showing the extent of work done 
at the time of retrenchment, and that previous to it. Io am unable to 
necept the charge of ‘‘go-slow’’ against the retrenched workmen in the 
absence of further evidence to substantiate the charge. 


The moot question-ia whether there was any necessity to undertake 
this retrenchment at the relevant time, i.e., whether there was any real 
reduction of work due to alleged fall in the number of orders received in 
the month of September. The Union’s contention must also be kept in 
view, i.e., this retrenchment was made on extraneous considerations, 
They were victimised for their Union activities. 1১... ৯ Shri Lalit 
Halder, the only witness on the Union's side, on this point said that this 
retrenchment was effected about 2 or 3 days before the Pujas when the 
work in the Factory was going on in full swing, and that there was no 
reduction of work. He also said that the workers junior to him were 
retainéd in service whereas senior workers with longer period of service 
were retrenched. The witness was cross-examined, but not on this point. 
P.W. 1 Shri Rajani Kanto Deashi is the proprietor of this Company. He 
said. that in the month of September 1956 he had very few work to execute 
ut hand. He had smaller number of orders in hands in the previous month 
৬180, Accordingly, towards the end of September 1956 he decided to 
retrench some of his staff due to reduction of work, and issued a_ notice 
Ext. A. Exhibit A shows that the workmen were given 7 days’ notice to 
go on leave for paucity of work in the factory. The wording of this 
notice, strictly speaking, do not support the Proprietor’s evidence before 
the Tribunal. But then, the Ext. A need not be construed literally. . It 
may he taken as an intimation to the workers beforehand that their services 


Peer IT} THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 0 7 3191 


2 سس رر جح 


would not be required at the end of 7 days from the date of notice due to 
dearth of work. The notice falls short of the requirement of the statute. 
But then, it is there. P.W. 4 Shri Gthose, the Manager of the firm, does 
not speak anything useful on this point. He proves Exi. M, a statement 
01 work done in the year 1906, prepared from the Company’s books ot 
accounts. Hia other evidence is that the acovunts are maintained 10) 
submission of Income-tax statement, and that the Income-tax paid tor the 
year 1362 B.S. was more than what was paid in the previous year. He 
ulso said that no Income-tax was paid in 1363 B.S., viz., the year in 
dispute. It is, therefore, not possible to say whether there was any 
actual reduction of income in the year in question. It ig also not the 
Company's cave. The Company did not produce their accounts of the 
year. It produces a rough and ready hand book of orders supposed ٥ 
huve been received in 1906. EKxhibit N appears to be written afresh by 
P.W. 4, Shri Ghose. 


Actual orders received by the Company, which are in its custody at 
present, are not forthcoming to show the actual state of affairs. That 
would have corroborated Ext. N. in spite of its suspicious appearance. Ths 
important evidence has been withheld. The necessary presumption 14 that 
they would not support the Company's story if they were produced. 


Next, we come to the other evidence on the Company’s side on_ this 
point. ‘I'he Company has produced three Registers in this Case. Exhibit 
]. is the Attendance-cum-pay Register for office staff. It records the 
attendence of five employees actually employed in the office. Exhibit [ is 
the Bengali Attendance Register and Ext. R is the Register of adult 
workers, maintained under the Factories Act. These two Registers do not 
agree, Exhibit‘ R shows that the total number of employees working in 
each mouth 01 August, September and October was 27 only, whereas the 
Ext. ] shows that in September and October, corresponding to Bhadra and 
Aswin, 66 and 73 workers respectively were employed in the Factory. 
According to Ext. I, 29 workers worked in Kartic (equal to November) 
whereas Ext. 1 shows that 656 workers worked in that month. No 
endeavour was made to reconcile the discrepuncies in the two Registers. 
Exhibit M, the statement of work done in 1956, apparently prepared on the 
basis of Ext. N, shows that the total work done in August was worth of 
Rs. 37,377-15-6 only and in September Rs. 1,750 only, and in October 
Rs. 18.424 only. The value of total work done in 1956 is, according to 
Ext. N, about Rs. 2,81,108-2 only. The value of orders pending at the 
time of retrenchment of the first batch of 42 workers on 8th October 1956 
would he about Rs. 63,085 only. Therefore, it follows that at the time of 
retrenchment on the firal batch of workers, a substantial portion of ahout 
more than one-fourth of the total work done in 1956 was pending for 
execution in the workshop. This work was executed by the end of 
November. Further, if the Attendance Registers have got to be beliaved, 
the Company employed 66 and 73 workers in September and October 
respectively. There were new recruitments also. According to Ext. R, 
more than double the number of adult workers were employed in December 
and Junuary after the retrenchment. In fact, on 8th tale 1957 abont 54 
workers were found doing work in the workshop. I[t is said, on hehalf of 
the Company, that only 11 out of 54 workmen are in its direct emptoy- 
ment and that the remaining employees are in the service of contractors. 
That any work is done with the help of the contractor is not stated any- 
where in the two written statements filed by the Company. This is ‘a new 
case, and naturally the Union very seriously criticised it. We will come 
to it hereafter. It appears from Ext. H, a Jetter written by the Auto 
Thistributors Ltd., one of the principal customers of the Company, that a

were retrenched for extraneous consideration and not for bona fide trade

A ‘last minute attempt was made to prove that there was no work for 
the employees who were directly in employment under the Company at the 
time of retrenchment, and that the contractor’s workmen were doing the 
pending works as before. Question is whether this Company actually 
carried on business, on the relevant dates of retrenchment, through the 
agency of the contractors. As stated above, the Company did not say a 
word about it in its otherwise elaborate written 86961161765. It is after 
Shri Pathak’s visit and in course of the hearing of this case that the 
Company invented the story that work was heing done through confractor’s 
labour to explain away the employment of a large number of emplypyees. 
P,W. 1 said that his principal work was body building for huses, cars and 
lorries. His main work was confined to Carpenter's side. His own men 
did the timber work only and smith’s work was done by the contractor. 
He suid further that additional workmen were employed on temporary 
basis, paid at daily rates, whenever a large number of orders were received. 
These workmen were relieved as soon as the work was executed. In cross- 
examination he admitted that tinamith and blacksmith work were done 
by the contractor's men and that some work of the blacksmith were done 
hy his men and it was only the new work which was given to cortractor’s 
men and that his men did the repair work. At the same time he said that 
the tinsmith work was also done by his men. He examined P.W. 7, Shni 
Krishna Pada Naskar, to prove this. P.W. 7 said that he had been 
working as a contractor in this business for about 20 years. LHe received 
ordera verbally from the Company and paymenta were also acknowledged 
verbally, No bills were submitted for this work and no receipt wna signed 
or filed. He had no papers to show that he employed labour to do work 
in 11118 Company. No contract of employment was proved. P.W. 1 
contradicts P.W. 1. P.W. 1 said that he had received other papers, not 
produced here, to show that contractors were employed to do a part of 115 
regular work, On this evidence, it is not possible to accept the Companv’s 
storv as true. Further, it is not in evidence in this case that the 
contractor’s workmen do either overflow work, or specialized work, such 
work as cannot be done by the Company’s own men, or do it at cheaper 
rates. On the contrary, the evidence is that a part of the regular work 
is given to contractor’s men to exccute, P.W. 1 said that he never 
attempted to get rid of the contractor’s men before trying reduction of his 
own. I wns referred to a case reported in 1952 1.1.3. pp. 470-476 in 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 29, 1957 3193 


support of the proposition that it 1a one of the fundamental rights of the 
Management to get works done by contractors. In that case, the Labour 
Appellate Tribunal held that ‘‘im the circumstances of this case, whether 
the Company should carry on the work of tallying through contractors or 
hot, 18, 10) our opinion, essentially a management function and should uot 
be interfered with as it does not involve the discharge of any employee in 
3৬109, , ০,১১০, 7০ It ia true that the Management has the right to employ 
contractors to carry out any of its work but it is also true that it cannot 
do so at the cost of 818 own men. It 18 no argument to say that the 
Company 28 at liberty to disiniss his men on the ground of paucity of work 
and at the same time get the pending work done through the contractor’s 
men. In any view of the matter, the retrenchment in this case is 
unjustified. Lastly, it had been contended on behalf of the Company that 
the retrenched employees were temporary workers and, therefore, they 
could be discharged, at any time, without observing the formalities of section 
20(F) of the Industrial Disputes Act. The Union's contention, however, 
was that these men were not temporary, but permunent, with long years 
of service to their credit. O.P.W. 1, Shri Kalipada Datta, Secretary of 
the Union, prepared a statement (Ext. 8) on this point. This does not 
tally with the list (Ext. B) prepared on behalf of the Company. Some 
discrepancies in Ext. B have been pointed out. P.W. 1 said that none 
of the workmen had put in service nore than & year at the time of discharge. 
This has been abundantly proved to be incorrect by Ext. 4, and_ the 
evidence of Y.P.W. 2, Shri Halder. P.W. 1 said that these workers worked 
from LO or 12 days to less than a year, suggesting thereby that he employed 
them only when there was large number of orders, and discharged them 
uz soon xg the work was executed, on the ground of surplusage. Further, 
P.W. 1 adinitted, that he never told his employees, about the nature of their 
employment, at the time of appointment, It is now very easy to say that 
all such appointments ure temporary liable to termination at his pleasure. 
Further, *retrenchment cannot be made on the ground that the employees 
are all temporary men. The justice of the case for such retrenchment 
would still to be established. On all these points, I find the issue against 
the Company. 


have anxiously considered the question of relief in this case but find‏ آ 
no excuse, or remotest justification for disallowing the normal relief 10‏ 
the aggrieved workmen. They should be reinstated, except those whose‏ 
cases have been specially dealt with at the beginning of the issue. They‏ 
should be reinstated, within one month of the date of the publication of‏ 
this award. The Company would not be under any obligation of this‏ 
award to do so if any of the retrenched employees fails to report to duty‏ 
ut the Company’s workshop within the aforesaid period. I have also‏ 
considered the question of puyment of compensation and/or any other‏ 
suitable relief. It has not been proved before this Tribunal that these‏ 
employees or any of them suffered pecuniary loss, or damage ns a result‏ 
of this unjustified retrenchment. Apart from alleging that they were out‏ 
of employment since then, the Union did not make any attempt to prove‏ 
any such case. Accordingly, I find no sound reason for allowing any‏ 
compensation for this loss of employment. 13011 then, since these employees‏ 
were kept out of employment from the date of retrenchment, without any‏ 
justifiable reasons, this period of forced unemployment should be treated,‏ 
as if, these employees were on leave without pay. That is to say, their‏ 
services should be taken as continuing without any break. This issue 8‏ 
accordingly answered.‏

General Instructions to candidates applying In response to 
advertisements issued by the Commission for reorulte 
ment to posts by ‘‘Selection’’. 


(1) Instructions regarding submission of application.— 
Applications are to be made on the prescribed form which 
will be available from the office of the Public Service 
Commission, West Bengal, Anderson House round 
floor), Alipore, Calcutta-27, personally or on sending a 
large self-addressed envelope with stamps sufficient to 
cover the postago affixed to it. Candidates who are unable 
to obtain سوا‎ of the prescribed form may apply on any 
similar typed (not handwritten) form showing exactly the 
wording and spacing of the rags form published in the 
“Calcutta Gazette’ of the lst September 1955, provided 
the blanks are filled up in the candidates’ own handwriting. 


(2) Particulars and oertificates required.—Candidaten 
should furnish evidence of their age, qualifications and 
previous experience together with certificates written not 
more than one year prior to the date of their applications, 
from responsible persons, testifying to their private 
character. 


(3) Fee.—Candidates must enclose with their applica- 
tions a fee of Rs. 5 (for each catogory of posts) in the 
forn of a سار می‎ chalan from জে Government Treasury 
or the Roserve Bank of India under the head ‘““XXXVI— 
Miscellaneous—Receipts of the Public Service Commission 
West Hengal’’, Money orders, cheques, ৩10.) in lieu of 
{treasury chalans are not accepted. Postal orders 
however, may be accepted from candidates. They should 
he crossed and made payable to ‘‘The Secretary, Public 
Service Commission, West Bengal’. No application will 
be considered unless accompanied with the requisite 
application fee. 


Candidates in Government service should make sure 
before depositing fee that their applications will be 
forwarded a their superior officers. 2 no case will the 
fee paid with the application be refunded. 


_ The Commission may remit fee in case of genuinely 
indigent and bona fide displaced persons from Pakistan. 


Note.—''(i) A displaced person claiming age concession 
must furnish with his application satisfactory evidence 
that he is a bona fide displaced person from Pakistan, 
e.g., refugee registration card or o certificate from a 
perce officer or # Member of Parliament or State 

gislature, in original. 


(ii) A member of the Scheduled Caste or Scheduled 
Tribe claiming age concession must furnish with his 
application a certificate in original from a gazetted officer 
or a Member of Parliament or State Legislature belonging 
to the Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe, specifying the 
particular caste or tribe to which he claims belong. 


(iii) ۸ displaced person seeking remission of the 
application fee must furnish besides the evidence required 
under Note (i) above, a certificate (in original) from a 
District Officer or a gazetted officer or a Member of 
Parliament or State Legislature to show that he is not in 
& position to pay the prescribed fee.” 


(4) Address.—Candidates should give their present 
address and should communicate at onco any subsequent 
change of address. 


Part IT] 


(5) Canvassing.—Any attempt on the part of candidates 
to enlist support of their applications through persona of 
influence or officials of Government will disqualify them 
for appointment, Spontaneous recommendation from 
persons interested in the candidates or otherwise known 
to them will be disregarded. 


(6) Applications from candidates who are in permanent 
or temporary employment under any Government, a local 
or Statutory Kody (e.g., Damodar Valley Corporation), in 
India will be rejected unless they are submitted through 
the appointing authority of their posta or service. 


Candidates serving under Government or a local or 
statutory body should submit an advance copy in the 
rescribed form. The application fees should in such cases 
bs attached to the advance copy and not to the original. 
The candidature of such applicants may not however be 
considered if the original applications do not reach the 
Commission's office within a fortnight from the closinu 
ate. Unless applications in omginal or advance copics 
with application fees are received within the closing date, 
late applications may bo rejected.

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 


National Library 


IN response to public opinion, the working hours of the 
Reading Rooms and the Lending Section at Belvedere have 
been extended with effect from the 166) August 1953. The 
revised working hours are specified below:— 


Reading Roome— 
Week days (including Saturdays)—9 a.m. to 8 p.m. 
Sundays and holidaye—10 a.m. to 5 p.m. 

Lending Section— 
Week days (including Saturdays)—10 a.m. to 6 p.m. 
Sundays and holidays—10 a.m. to 1-30 p.m. 

The Reading Rooms and the Lending Section will. how: 
mbit مسا‎ entirely closed on the following days of the 


(i) fepublic Day, (ii) lndependence Day, and (iii) 
Mahatma Gandhi's Birthday. 


Persona above 18 years of age are eligible to make use 
of the Library. which is a free lending Library open to 
any one residing in any Ber of the Indian Union. There 
is no subscription to pay but secumty in cash is essential.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 


Pending the cousideration of the Budget proposals for the financial yeur 
1947-58, the Finance Act, 1957, provided for the continuance of the taxes 
on income and the duties of customs and excise at the 1956-57 rates with 
certain modifications. The object of this 131]] is to give effect to the financial 
proposala of the Central Government for the financial vear 1957-68. The 
notes on elnusea exploin the various provisions contained therein.

NOTES ON CLAUSES 


Clause 2 preseribes the rates of income-tax and super-tax for the financial 
year 1967-58 in supersession of the rates prescribed by the Finance Act, 
1957 : 

(1) The rates which have so far been expressed im tering of annas and 
pies are, as a consequence of the introduction of decimal coinage expressed 
iu terms of percentages. 


(2) kor individuale— 
(1) the tuxable minnnum has been lowered to Ra, 3,000, 


(ii) a decrease has been effected in the rates applicable to the lower slabs 
of income, 


(111) a more even rate of progression has been achieved by the introduc- 
tion of an intermediate slab between Ra, 10,000 and 15,000, 


(1) the maximum rate of income-tax has been maintained at 25 per 
cent., but it will operate above the level of Its. 20,000, 


(১) the super-tax free slab has been kept at Rs. 20,000, but a  com- 
paratively more even rate of progression is maintained with slight 
lowering of the maximum rate—which is reached at a level of 
Rs. 70,000. 


(vi) a basic surcharge of five per cent., an additional surcharge of five 
per cent. on earned income which exceeds rupees one lakh and a 
further surcharge of fifteen per cent. on unearned income have 
been introduced. 


(3) For Hindu undivided families— 
the taxable minimum has been lowered to Rs. 6,000 17) the case of 
families with more than two adult members. 

(3) For companies— 

(i) the basic rate of income-tax has been fixed at 30 per cent. as against 
the existing rate of 25 per cent., 

(ii) effective rate of super-tax on Jndian companies has been raised to 
20 per cent. t.e., by about 3 per cent., 

(iii) on bonus issues the additional super-tax has been raised from 1x4 
per cent. to 30 per cent., 

(iv) on excess distributions of dividends over the three levels of 6 per 
cent., 10 per cent, and 18 per cent. of the paid-up capital, the 
additional super-tax has been lowered from 12} per cent., 25 per 


cent. and $7} per cent. to 10 per cent., 20 per cent. and 30 per 
cent. respectively,

Clause T umends section 23A of the Income-tax Act. Sub-sections (1) 
and (2) of section 243A have been recast by sub-clause (i) with a view to 
fixing for various cutegories of companies the percentages of available 
profits which they should distribute im order to avoid the extra rates of

iM) per cent. in special circumstances, Where a company’s activities are 
partly industrial and partly non-industrial, the percentage applicable is 
& per cent. on industrial profits, and 60 per cent. or 90 per cent. as the case 
may be on non-industrial profits. For investment companies the percentage 
in 100 per cent.

Other sub-clauses carry out some consequential changes. 


Clause 8 nmends section 24 of the Income-tax Act in order to secure that 
١ loss shall not be carried forward for more than eight years. 


Clauses 9 and 10 replacing sections 48E and 58F' provide for the exclusion 
of employer’s contributions to a recognised provident fund, up to a limit of 
ten per cent, of salary, from the total income of the employee. Interest, 
subject to certain limits, on accumulated balances is already excluded. 


Clause 11 is a formal provision relating to the time from which the 
nmendments take effect. 


Clause 12.—Sub-clause (1), read with Parts I, II and IIT of the Second 
Schedule, proposes certain changes in import duties. These are intended 
mainly to rationalise the tariff rates, for example, by merging the existing

import duties—mostly on what may be called luxury itemse—have also been 
proposed.

RAJYA SABHA 


The following Bill was introduced in the Rajya Sabha 
on the 10th December, 1956:— 


Bint Nos XXIV or 1956 


A Bill to provide for the constitution of a Natiwnal Falin 
Board for the purpose of promoting the development of 
films as a medium of culture, education and healthy 
entertainment and. for the regulatwn of exhibitions by 
means of cinematograph. 


BE it enacted by Parliament in the Seventh Year of the 
Republic of India ৬৪ follows: — | 


CHAPTER I 


PRELIMINARY 


1, (1) This Act may be called the Cinematograph Act, 
1936. 


(2) Chapters I, II, 111, IV and VI extend to the whole 
of India except the State of Jammu and Kashmir, and 
Chapter 'V extends to Union territories only. 


(3) This Act shall come into force on such date as the 
Central Government may, by notification in the Official 
(tazette, appoint. 


2. It is hereby declared that it is expedient in the public 
interest that the Union should take under its control the 
cinematograph film industry, 


3. In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, — 


(a) “adult? means a person who has completed eighteen 
years of age: 


(b) ‘‘Board’? means the National Film Board consti- 
tuted under section 4; 


(c) “Chairman” means the Chairman of the Board 
appointed under sub-section (1) of section 6; 


(0) “Chief Examiner’ means the Chief Examiner 
appointed under sub-section (2) of section 18; 


(e) ‘‘cinematograph” includes any apparatus for the 
representation of moving pictures or serles of 
pictures ;

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 
The Cinematograph Act, 1952 (XXXVII of 1952), embodies in Part 11 


the scheme of centralisation of certification of films for public exhibition. 
The effect of the procedure for certification under the Act is primarily of a 
negative character in that examination is made mainly tor the purpose of 
eliminating objectionable features. ‘There has been a feeling that even 
fnder this procedure there is greater scope tor improvement of the moral 
and cultural standards of films. It has moreover been recognised that 
positive assistance, guidance and encouragement should be given in the 
production of films of better aesthetic and cultural standards. The Film 
Enquiry Committee recommended that a Production Code Administration 
should be set up to give advice to producers on scripts and other aspects of 
production and a Film Institute should be established for training and 
research, The Bill seeks to implement this recommendation. The Rill 
0180 revises the scheme of certification in the light of experience gained during 
the last five yeara. The revised scheme 1s made adequate for reflecting 
the established moral and cultura] standards, maintaining at the same time 
the principles of natural justice. 


Z. Accordingly, a new organisational set-up has been formulated. A 
Natiopal J'ilm Board will be established with threc constituent units, 
namely, the Film Certification Bureau, the Film Production Bureau and the 
Film Tnetitute. The object of the National Film Board, which will be an 
apex body, will be to promote the development of films as a medium of 
culture, education and healthy entertainment. The composition of the 
National Film Board is so devised as to include adequate representation of 
enlightened public opinion and also the various aspects of the film industry. 
Among its important functions will be the co-ordination and supervision of 
the activities of the constituent units and the guidance of their policy. The 
Film Certification Bureau will take over the work of the present censorship 
organisation, The Film Production Bureau will be a new unit and is 


146 THY CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 29, 1957 [Parr VI 
১৯ 
intended for giving on a voluntary basis, advice and assistance in matters 
connected with the production of films. A close co-ordination is to be 
maintained between the Film Certification Bureau and the Film Production 
Bureau, thus ensuring that positive guidance is made more practical and 
useful. The Film Institute wil] not only impart technical 6 10 
various aspects of film production but also conduct research thereby help- 

ing in the improvement of technical and aesthetic standards. 


3, Following the practice in many other countries, power has been 
taken to scrutinise, as part of the examination of films, posters which are 
intended for public exhibition through general distribution. 


4. Chapters 1١, 111 and IV replace the present Part IT of the Cinemato- 
graph Act, 1952, and Chapter V re-enacts the present Part ITI (which deals 
with the regulation of exhibitions by means of cinematograrh) for its 
application to Union territories.

FINANCIAL MEMORANDUM 


The Bill contemplates the constitution of ৮ National Vilm Board with 
three constituent units, namely, the Film Certification Bureau, the Film 
Production Bureau and the Film Institute. The Film Certification Bureau 
will replace the present censorship organivation. The Film  Preduction 
Bureau will be a new unit to give advice to producers on script and assist 
them in securing guidance on other aspects of film makiug, with a view to 
improving the standard of productions. There will be some special staff 
in the Bureau for this work. The Film Institute will be a iraining and 
research institution with the necessary staff and a building of its own includ- 
ing technical facilities and suitable equipment, use being also made of the 
facilities and equipment available in the Films Division. 


2. The National Film Board will have a Chairman who Will be a 
salaried officer of the Central Government and the members of the Board 
will receive only fees or allowances for attendiug the meetings of the Board. 
There will also be some staff attached to the Board. The Board will replace 
the existing Central Board of Film Censors set up under the Cinemato- 
graph Act, 1962, The additional expenditure in connection with the 
National Film Board will be roughly of the order of ninety thousand 
rupees. The ee on the Film Certification Bureau is expected to be 
approximately the same os the present expenditure on the censorship 
machinery which has an income by way of censorship fees. The annual - 
expenditure involved in the Film Production Bureau is estimated at Ra. 1.) 
lakh. In regard to the Film Institute, the capital requirements of which 
are estimated at Rs. 30 lakh spread over three to four years, it 1s proposed 
to moke an annual allocation of Rs. 12 lakh, to meet— 

(a) such requirements, 


(4) tha recurring expenditure on staff, stores and production of films at 
a part of the training and research, and 


(c) the non-recurring expenditure on furniture, vehicles, etc. 
It is proposed that engagement of staff should be deferred til] the fourin 


year, except for such staff as may be required in connection with tbe 
onstruction of the building or the purchase of equipment.

MEMORANDUM REGARDING DELEGATED LEGISLATION 


ye 

Clauses 42 and 49 of the Bill empower the Central Government tq make 
rules to give effect to the provisions of the Bill when enacted. Clause 49 
deals with the general powers of the Central Government to make rules in 
relation to the National Film Board, the Film Certification Bureau, the 
Film Production Bureau and the Film Institute. The matters in respect of 
which such rules may be made have been specified therein. They relate 
tu the allowances or fees to be paid to the members of the Board and the 
term of.pffice and conditions of service of members of advisory committees 
of the Roard and of advisory panela. They also relate to the procedure to 
be followed by the ha Certification Bureau in examining and certifying 
films and the procedure for filing on appeal against the decision of the 
Bureau. Rules may also be made relating to the manner in which illustrat- 
ed posters in connection with the exhibition of a film may be approved and 
the manner in which the Film Production Bureau and the Film Institute 
may perform their functions.Clause 42 of the 13111) on the other hand, 1s 
restricted in scope and deals with the powers of Central Government to make 
rules in relation to regulation of exhibitions by means of cinematopraph in 
Union territories. They relate to the terms and conditions and restrictions 
subject to which licences may be granted, the regulation of cinematograph 
exhibitions for securing public safety and the procedure relating to appeal 
syainst an order of o licensing authority. All these matters are of a pro- 
cedural and routine character. 


2. Under clause 50 of the Bill, the Board has been empowered to make 
regulations for regulating its own procedure. 


3. The proposed delegation of legislative power is of a normal 
character. z

CALCUTTA IMPROVEMENT TRUST 
NOTICE UNDER SECTION 63(2) OF BENCAL ACT V OF 1911 
Proposed Public Street No. ۷۱ (Cossipore) 
The 12th August 1957 
Notice is given under section 63(2) of Bengal Act V of 1911 that the 
Hoard of Trustees for the Improvement of Culcutta have prepared a plan of 
a proposed public street in Ward Nos. 4 and 0 of the Calcutta Municipality, 


known as Cossipore Aligument No. VI, for widening the existing Paikpara 


Ve Manindra Hoad from Anuth Nath Deb Lane to Barrackpore Trunk 
ad. 


The proposed public street will pass through the following municipal 
holdings :—~ 


Poikpara Raja Manindra Road: Nos. 1, 1/1, 2, 3, 3B, 5/1B, 5/2, 
9/2/4, 5/2/5, 5/38A, 01953, 6/30, 5/38D, 6, 7, 8, 9A, 980, 9D, OF, 
9G, 10, 11, 11/1, 12, 12/1, 13, 18/1/1۸, 18/1/2, 13/2, 1919, 
13/4, 13/5, 14, 164, 16B, 16/2, 16/3, 16/4, 16/5 and 16/6. 


Ranec Harshamukhi Road: Nos. 46, 47 and 48. 
Simlaiparo Lane: No. 27. 


The plan may he inspected and the lands traversed by the proposed 
public street ascertained at the office of the Trust, 10 Netaji Subhas Road, 
Calcuttu-1, on week days from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. and on Saturdays from 
11 a.m. to 12-30 p.m. 


٠ পা of the notice may be obtained for 12 nP. and of the plan for 
07১. 


Objections may be submitted on or before 8th November 1957. 
S. K. GUPTA, Chairman.

In the matter of an industrial dispute existing between Messrs. the Salkia

2, The reference was received here on <9th March 1956. The Union 
Bled written statement on 14th May 1956, The Company filed written 
objection on 25th June 1956. After several udjournments the case was taken 
up for hearing on Ist May 1957 and it continued on 3rd May 1957 when the 
evidence was closed. The argument was heard on 24th June 1967 and 27th 
June J957. The award was reserved. 


3. The issue contained in the schedule to the order of reference stands 
as follows:—. 


{f the discharge of Sharbasri Gour Mohon Ghosh and Mohadeb Kurmi 
was justified? What relief including reinstatement und/or com- 
pensation are they entitled to? 


AWARD 


4. According to the Union, the Transport Company in question is a 
highly prosperous concern. The workmen, however, were not given a fair 
deal, with the result that o Union, viz., the Howrah District Bus Workers’ 
Union, was formed tor collective bargaining. The said Union placed a 
charter of demands before the Company early in 1964. 
But, however, the said Union could not satisfy the aspiration of its members. 
So a new Union under the name of Domjur Bus Workers’ Union was formed 
by Shri Gour Mohon (thosh in the first part of March 1955. This Union 
placed a new charter of demands on 28th May 1955, 08 per Annexure A 
to the Union’s written statement. The Company, thereafter,. transferred 
Shri Gour Ghosh and his assistant Shri Mohadeb Kurmi from the route 
No. 60 (Kadamtala-Domjur) to route No. 54 (Ballykhal route) ostensibly 
to disrupt the Union. The workers of the route No. 60 are said to be 
members of the Union affiliated to the I. N. T. U. C., while the workers 
of the route No. 54 ore affiliated to the B, P. T. U. C. So the workers 
wanted to resist the transfer, but with no results. On 27th May 1957, it 
is the story of the Union, the bus in which Shri Gour Mohon (thosh was 
working, went out of order. Ou 28th May 1955, Gour Ghosh was ordered 
by the management to work in the bus No. WBU 407 plying“in rpute No. 
60. Gour Ghosh worked there up to 30th May 1955, but thereafter he was 
given no job. His name was placed in the ‘extra list’’. On 6th June 1955 
Gour Ghosh was asked to sign a blank paper which he refused to do. There- 
after the Company gave out that he stood dismissed from 8th June 1955. 6 
was given no charge-sheet, nor was there any enquiry held regarding him 
before the dismissal. 


Regarding the other worker, viz., Mohadeb Kurmi, he was also 
transferred from the route No. 60 to the route No. 64, On 12th September 
1955, at about 11-20 a.m., Mohadeb was involved in an accident with a lorry 
and his bus was damaged. The J.ine Supervisor Shri Chandrabali Upadhaya 
took him to the Bally police-station and lodged a complaint there agains 
the driver of the lorry involved in the said accident. A case under the 
Motor Vehicles Act was started. Mohadeb was not, however, alowed to 
join. On 15th September 1955 he was asked to admit his guilt in writing 
regarding the accident on 12th September 1955 which he refused. Mohadab 
was not even paid his earned wages from Ist September 1955 to 12th Sep- 
tember 1955. No charge-sheet was given to him.

According to fhe Company, tranafet of employees from one route to

owner, and that he was never asked to sign a blank paper. Gour Ghosh was 
diamissed with effect from 8th June 1965 due to his disobedience and insub- 
ordination. 


With regard to Mohadeb Kurmi, Shri Chandrabahi Upadhaya, the ۷

During the hearing, it appears, that the only charge against (Gour 
Mvhon Ghosh is that he worked in the bus No. WBU 407 on 28th May 1950. 
He did not attend the office of the &, T. A. from 29th May 1955 when 
he was in the “extra’’ list. On the 3lst May 1955 he was seen driving the 
bug WBU 40৫ in route No. 60 (vide Ext.D1). The explanation of Gour 
Ghééh ig.that he had worked in the Ballykhal route on 27th May 1955 up to 
6 p.m. in the bus No. WBU 263. After 6 p.m., as the bus got out of order, 
it was put into the workshop, and deposited there. He enquired of the 
Traffic Superintendent if the bus would move out that day. 116 referred him 
to the mistry who said that the bus would not move out for 3 or 4 days. سا‎ 
the written statement of the Union, at paragraph 17, it is said that on 28th 
May 1955 Gour Mohon was asked by the management to work in the bus 
No. WBU 407 in route No. 60, and he accordingly did it. From 29th 
May 1955 he was placed in the ‘‘extra’’ list and was given no work. Now, 
when I turn to the evidence, I find that it 1g nut disputed that on the 27tb 
May 1955 the bus which Gour Mohon Ghosh was plying went out of order. 
Shri Uma Sankar Singh, 0.1۳.۷۷۰ 5, says at page 3 of his deposition ٥, 
27th May 1955 Gour did half duty, as per the duty book. The bus was put 
into the warage at 5-30 p.m. The reason for putting the bus in the garage 
at that hour has not been mentioned here. It might have been for sume 
defect in the bus. This bus did not go out on the 29th May’’. So, (tour 
upparently .did nothing wroug on the 27th May 1955. On the 28th May 
1955 جا‎ 1s said to have worked in the bus No. WBU 407. This is also 
admitted by him. Exhibit Dl also proves it. Shri Narayan Chandra 
Mitra, O. P. W. J, has corroborated this. He says “Qn 28th May 1955 
Madan Chakraborty was permanent, and Gour Ghosh was on duty in the 
morning. Gour Mohon (thosh only worked for ihat day. Gour Ghosh 
worked in the morning in my bus without permission. I did not inform 
the polices JI asked him why he had done duty without my permission. He 
said that he was off duty, and so he did ply the bus. J kept silent. I kept 
silent for fear of the Union’’. Now, the charge against Shri (four Ghosh is 
that on 28th May 1955 when he was in the employ of the S,T.A., and was 
drawing his pay there, he should not have gone to work in the bus No. 
WRU 407 which belonged to another man. But Cour (thosh says by way of 
explanation that he did this at the instance ot the management. I accept 
this explanation of Gour Ghosh as correct, and for the following reasons: 

On the 29th May, as per the gurage register of WBU 263 (Ext. H) Gour 
Ghosh is shown as having worked for 8 hours. Shri Uma Shankar, 
0.1۲.۷۷۰ ر5‎ the Traffic Superintendent of the §. T. A. Ltd., says at page 3 
of his deposition that this entry is wrong. His reason is that the hus was

not moved out that day. Hut 1 think this explauation does uot stand. یں‎ 
Gour Ghosh was shown to have worked for 8 bolira on the 28th May 1953 in

duties in this Company for 8 heurn because his services were lent to the 
Bus No. WBU 407 in route No. 60.which belunged to Shri Narayana Mitra,

version of Gour Ghosh thut his services were lent to the bua No. W Bi AUT 
on 2811) May 1956. I do not accept the version of Shri Narayan Chandra

1954 without his permission. Madan (hakraborty was taken ill and so his

circumstances make it clear that Gour Ghosh’s services were lent to the bus 
No. WBU 407 on 28th Muay 1955. So the charge against him for working 
in another owner's bus on 28th May 1956 fails. 


Regarding the charge of working in other bus on some days in the week 
with effect from the 290) May 1965 the explanation of Gour Ghosh is that 
he was in the “extrn’’ list that week. To be in the “extra” list means, 
even according to the Company, that the man will have no pay if he is 
given no work during hat period. There is no certainty,—he may or may 
not be given work during the week when he happens to be in the ‘‘extra”’ 
list. So the position was that Gour Ghosh had absolutely no certainty 
of having a job during the week commencing from the 29th May 1955. 
In such circumstances, if he worked in another bus to earn something for 
hie maintenance how can the Company object to it? Tt is not a case of 
lay-off. In the case of lay-off, the employer has got to pay compensation 
for the period of involuntary unemployment. Tere the Company is under 
no obligation to pay any compensation for the loss of earning. How can it 
expect that the workers should sit idle and only record their attendance daily, 
and thus discharge their obligation to the Company unpaid? So the 
Company cannot take exception to the fact that Gour Ghosh did ply another 
man's bus within his permiasion during the week commencing on the 29th 
May 1955. So the charge ngainst him on this head cannot be sustained. 


Now the point that may arise in this connection is, why should the 
Company allow Gour Mohon Ghosh to work in another man’s bus and then 
level a charge against him for the same reason? The reason is not far: 
fo seek. Gour Ghosh was not in the good book of the Company. 110 was 
transferred from the Domjur route, where he had a Union, to the Ballykhal 
route where the Union had its affiliation to a different body of organisation. 
The Company takes shelter under the plea that such transfers are usual and 
for the exigencies of the service. That may be so, but in the present case, 
tuken with other facts, it hecomes significant. The other facts are that on 
“8th May 1955 Gour Ghosh submitted a charter of demands (aide Ext. 1) 
to the Company, and on the following day, i.e., 29th May he found his 
name in the “extra” list. I have already shown what is meant hy having

0081৮”, Shri Chandrabali, Upadhaya, O.1.W. 4, at page 2 ام‎ his ecross-

men are kept to meet contingencies when some drivera happen to be absent

Choudhuri and M. B. Rajan, These people do regularly double duties. It

with double duties, while those who are not so are put in the ‘extra’ 118, 
Thus it is clear that while some drivers were being given double duties,

when’ he submitted a charter of demands to the Company in his capacity 
as the Secretary of the Union. So, does it require much imagination to 
hold that Shri Gour Mohon Ghosh was in the bad book of the Company? 
Not only that, the Company was out to do him some mischief and chuck 
him out. It is for this reason, while other drivers were allowed to work 
in other buses, or their working in other buses was connived at during this 
period of 400 work’’ when in the “extra’’ list, in the case of Gour Ghosh 
the Company suddenly took exception to such working in other bus, and 
levelled a charge against him just to do away with his services under the 
Company with the object of getting rid of him. 90] am satisfied by the 
evidence on record that Gour Mohon Ghosh was guilty of no offence charged 
against him by the Company. On the other hand, the motive of the Com pany 
in the present case has been exposed. It had a nefarious design to erush the 
Secretary of the Union so that the charter of demands of the Union might 
be nipped in the bud. That is why he was given no charge-sheet. So I 
hold that the discharge of Shri Gour Mohon Ghosh was unjustified. He 
should be reinstated within une month of the award coming into operation 


Regarding relief, he ought zet wages which he would have had, had he 
been سد‎ employ during the period of forced unemployment minus any 
earning obtained by him meanwhile. About this earning the evidence ia 
meagre, and not much dependable, As the Company did not have the 
benefit of his services during this long period, I allow as compensation hhlf 
the average wages, I mean, earnings, thut Shri Gour Mohon (thosh used 
to draw during previous, 3 months prior to his discharge, with effect from 
Sth June 1955 up to the date of bis reinstatement. This should be paid in 
three equal successive mouthly instalments the first of which should be 
within one month of the award coming into operation. 


Regarding \Mohadeb Kurmi, the charge is that on 12th September 5 
at ubout 11-20 a.m. he wus driving the Company’s bua when a lorry 
(No. WBU_ 7354) dashed against it. According to the Wnion, Mohnadeh 
accompanied by Shri Chandrahali Wpadhya, the Tine Supervisor, went to 
the Bally police-station and lodged a complaint there regarding the accident. 
A case was started under sections 11%, 118 and 116 of the Motor Vehicles 
Act. Mohadeb was not allowed to join his duties thereafter hy the Com- 
pany. His name was put in the ‘extra’? list On 15th September 195h 
Mohadeb was asked to admit his guilt for the said accident stating that he 
was responsible for it in his atempt to overtake the lorry in question. 
Mohadeb’s refusal to do so has led to his discharge. He was not giyeu 
his wages for the period from Ist September 1955 to 12th September 1095.

hin guilt. He was suspended Sa ও of hia insubordination in refusing to

Turning to the evidence, I get the report of fhe Supervisor, marked as 
Ext. 1). I get from it that a cart was going on in front of the said bus, and 
the bus tried to overake it near about Hari Banerji Lane. But no sooner 
had the bus caught the cart and wanted to by-pasa it on the right hand side, 
the lorry approached quite suddenly and sruck against the right side of the 
bus causing damage to its body haul and peg. The bus was taken to the 
Rally police-station by a constable and there it was detained from 11-20 to 
4 p.m. An investigation into the matter as well as the verbal statement of 
the conductor of the bus revealed that the damage was caused due to the 
negligence of the driver. As I find from the remarks put on the body of the 
report, this driver was suspended because of his refusal to sign the said 
report. But the point is, can the Company ask the driver to countersign 
such report which would fasten the liability of the accident on him, and 
that at a time when the police case was sub judice. If the Company had 
any sense of responsibility, 1 would have not have demanded such a 
countersignature from the driver. It might ask for an explanation. But 
in the circumstances the Company should have refrained from doing even 
that, because the case of the driver would be prejudiced before the police, 


So T have no hesitation to find that the driver made no offence by refuaing 
to sign the report, Ext. D. 


Then I come to the question of the accident im question. Mohadeb, 
P.W. 2, says ‘On the 12th September when J stopped my bus for picking 
up passengers, a lorry, I mean, a loaded lorry, came from the Bally side and 
collided against my bus, and next collided against a rickshaw resulting in 
on ateident. It was 11-380 a.m. When the lorry was caught, the driver said 
that his brake failed and consequently he could not control the lorry.’”? Tn 
bis cross-examination it appears that this man joined the services of this 
Company in 1945 or 1946. He says that there was no case, not to speak of 
two cases, against him in the Howrnh Court for causing accidents. In the 
same breath he anys that in 1954 a man was run over by his car, but he wag 
absolved from blame by the Company, as well as by the Court. Trom the 
Court records filed before me it appeurs that in 1954 he was charged for 
having caused the death of one Murshed Ali by his negligent driving. 
Thus it iw clear that the Company had some sort of leitimate grievance 
against this driver in course of his service under it. In such circumstances, 
if the Company wants to terminate his services, as has been done, I do 
not think I should interfere with the said decision of the management. 
An employer may not very well like to have in his employ men who are 
frequently involved in accidents and thereby cause harassment and expenses 
to the employer, In this particular cuse T do not think that the Union 
has been able to show that the Company had any grudge against the man 
for lis Union activities. 1118 transfer from the Domjur route to the Bally- 
khal route in itself cannot he significant because such transfer might have 
been an incident of the service. The appointment letter, admittedly, does 
vot contain any restriction on such right of transfer. So, in the circum- 
stances, ] do not disturb the decision of the Company in terminating his 
services, But his will be a case of ‘discharge’ and not “‘dismissal’’. By 
this T mean that this man would be entitled to all retrenchment or retrial

benefits so far as are available in the preaent Company. I cannot give

But his discharge is justified in the circdmatances, I find no Union 
activities to his credit. J have granted him relief which I could grant in 
the circumstances on his discharge from the service but no compensation.

AWARD 


The case of these 18 workmen was taken up by Adam Motor Workers’ 
Union. The sum and substance of the contention of the Union is that the 
discharge of all these workmen is illegal, unjust und mala fide. They were 
discharged, simply because of their Union activities. Accordingly, the 
Union claimed their reinstatement with continuity of service and hack 
wages for the period of forced unemployment.

eT

The Company in its written statement has stated that the workers— 
Shri Rajani Kanto Biswas (serial No, 16), Shri Sidheswar Monda) (serial 
No. 17) and Shri Subhas Chandra Mondal (serial No, 18) were employed as 
Tinsmiths in the concern, and were retrenched by notices, dated 14) 
January 1956, for trade reasons, and also due to paucity of work in that 
department. Regarding other workers, it is the cause of the Company that 
the Management decided to close down the business, and accordingly served 
notices terminating the services of all the workmen on 30th July 1956. 
This Company was started originally on 15th June 1947 for the purpose of 
carrying on business of motor car repair, spray painting, etc., in the name 
and stvle of Adams Motor Works at 61A Theatre Road, Caleutta. It was 
a partnership business consisting of 3 partners—Mr. A. M. Adama, Mr. N. N. 
Adams and Mr. M. Apcar. The business being found to be not profitable, 
partnership was dissolved with effect from Ist July 1956 and Mr. Apcar 
sold his share to the other two partners, and cut off all connection with the 
firm. Tollowing the dissolution of partnership, the Management decided 
te close down the business. So, due to circumstances over which the 
Management had no control, the services of all the workmen serving then 
under the Company had to be terminated. After the said closure and 
termination of services of all the workers, partnership business was again 
started in September 1956 with two partners—Mr. A. M. Adams and 
Mr. .لا‎ N. Adams. Regarding 15 workers, the Company wanted to say 
that all these persons had lost their services as a result of closure, and all 
relationship of employer and employees ceased by notices served on them 
Individually on 30th July 1956. Regarding workers Shri Norottam 
Chandra Das (serial No. 1), Shri Austom Kumar 7916 (serial No. 7), Shri

———————————————— مب ہے مججً بت ےس ےکس‎ নু 
Abdul Rauf (serial No. 10) and Shri Kanai Lal Dutta (serial No. 14),¥the 
Company has submitted that there is no industrial dispute between them and 
the Munagement, inasmuch as they have been re-employed and are still 
working in this Company. Finally, the Company wanted to say that the 
present reference 1s bad in law, and not maintenable, and that the workers 

concerned are not also entitled to get any relief. 


At the very outset, I may aay that the workers Shri Norottam Chandra Das 
(serial No. 1), Shri Austom Kumar Hait (serial No. 7), Shri Abdul Rauf 
(serial No, 10) and Shri Kanai Lal Dutta (serial No. 14) have no dispute 
whatsvever with the Company. These workers through their lawyer filed an 
application to this effect before the Tribunal on 30th July 1957, and the 
said application has been duly signed by them. In the circumstances, their 
case needa no adjudication by the Tribunal. 


Regurding the remaining 14 workers mentioned in the list, they may be 
divided into two groups. The workers Shri Rajani Kanto Biswas (serial 
No. 16), Shri Sidhesawar Mondal (serial No. 17) and Shri Subhas Chandra 
Mondal (serial No. 18) fall under one group, and the rest under the other. 
The abovenamed three workers (.e., serial Nos. 16, 17 and 18) who were 
employed os Tinsmiths under the firm, were discharged by notices, dated 
3ist January 1956, due to paucity of work. They were, however, given one 
mouth’s notice, and this discharge was to be effective from 18٦ March 1900. 
They admittedly got the notices. 


As regards the workers coming under the second group, their case, as it 
appears, stands on a different footing. It is the contention of the Company 
that they were employed in the firm of Messrs. Adams Motor Works, which 
was a partnership business with three partners, viz., (1) Mr. A. M. Adams, 
(2) Mr. N. N. Adama and (3) Mr. M. Apcar, but on Ist July 1956 that 
vartnership was dissolved, as it was not found to be profituble, and the 
‘aed lop was ulso closed from that date. Ience, the said firm terminated 
the services of the workers including the present 14 workmen after giving 
one month's notice. After the said closure and termination of services of 
all the workmen, the partnership business was aguin started in September 
1956. But it was a new venture and a new business altogether with two 
partners only—Mr. A. M. Adams and Mr. N. N. Adams. Accordingly, 
a preliminary objection has been raised on behalf of the Company that the 
present reference is not sustainable. Learned lawyer appearing for the 
Company has voiced an argument before the Tribunal that there was no 
relationship of employer and employee between this Company and these 
workmen, Inasmuch as these workmen were never employed by it, and that 
as such there could be no industrial dispute between this Company and 
those workmen within the meaning of the Industrial Disputes Act which 
could have heen referred to the Tribunal for adjudication. T have given 
my careful and anxious consideration to the matter in the light of evidence 
as adduced before the Tribunal. In my estimation the preliminary objec- 
tion raised on behalf of the Company should be upheld. It cannot be said 
that the argument, as put forward by the learned ae er for the Company, 
is devoid of merit and substance. It is crystal clear کٹ‎ the materials on 
record that a partnership business consisting of three partners—Mr. A. M. 
Adams, Mr. N. N. Adams and Mr. M. Apcar was started originally on 
15th June 1947 in the name and style of Adams Motor Works, and that all 
the workmen mentioned in the list were employed and worked there, but that 
partnership business was dissolved with effect from Ist July 1956, and a 
new partnership business with two partners was again started in September 
1906. The services of all these workmen were terminated by the Manage- 
ment of the partnership business which was dissolved. It is neither party’s 


Part I] THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., 00১] 29, 1957 3497 
a a حجکہبہبب بب‎ ae POT hi TS A 


cage that after this they were taken back or re-employed in the new partner- 
ahip business, which was subsequently started with two partners. In my 
opinion, as svun as that partnership business wus dissolved, it must be deemed 
to have ceased to exist altogether in the eye of law. It is true no doubt 
that the new partnership business was started in the same place and under 
the sume name and style with two out of three old partners. But this Goes 
not necessurily mean that the old partnership hwainess has been continuing 
still un spite of its dissolution as evidenced by Ext. A. Such view cannot be 
entertained or accepted under the law. 


There should be an industrial dispute, before such a dispute is referred 
for adjudication. An ‘‘industrial dispute” according to the definition of 
that term in section 2(k) of the Industrial Disputes Act comprises any 
dispute or difference between the employees and the employera, or employers 
and workmen. ‘‘Workmen”’ means any person employed (including an 
টা in any industry to do any skilled or unskilled, manual or clerical 
work for hire or reward, and includes for the purpose of any proceeding 
under the Act in relation to any industria] dispute, a workman discharged 
during the dispute. The question is whether the present case can be brought 
under the category of × dispute between the employers and workmen. A 
decision of this question undoubtedly depends upon the relationship between 
these workmen of the old partnership business and the Management of the 
present partnership business. It is clear from the ovidence that these 
workmen were never employed by the Management of the present partnership 
firm. Before a dispute can be said to be a dispute between employers and 
workmen, the relationship of employers aud workmen should be established 
between the parties. That this is the correct position, appearr to have been 
authoritatively laid by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India in the case case 
of Dhrangadhra Chemical Works vs. State of Saurastra [1957(i), 181.۰ 
477). It was held that the essential condition for a person boeing a 
‘‘workman’’ within the terms of the definition in the Industrial Disputes 
Act, was that he should be in the employment of his employer, and that 
there should be relationship between the employer and es as between 
master and the servant. It may be that when such a relationship had 
existed at one time and there was termination subsequently of that 
telationship, the persons who was once in employment would come within 
the definition of ‘‘workmen’’. But when, as in the instant case, the persons 
concerned were never employed by the employer, such persons cannot be 
deemed to be ‘‘workmen’’. Im the result, I hold that there was no industrial 
dispute within the meaning of the Industrial Disputes Act, which could 
have been validly referred to the Tribunal for adjudication. Therefore, the 
Tribunal has no jurisdiction to adjudicate upon the alleged dispute. The 
preliminary objection accordingly succeeds. 


In the view I have taken regarding the preliminary objection, it is no 
longer necessary to go into the merits. Even if I am to enter into the 
merits, [ would hold that the discharge of these workers was justified, and 
that they were not entitled to any relief. The claim for reinstatement of 
these workmen is out of the question. It has transpired from the evidence 
of O.P,W. 1, Mr. A. M. Adams—one of the partners, that in the previous 
partnership busimess 35 workers were employed, and that the same number 
1s employed at present in the present business. This indicates that there 
is no scope for re-employing these persons. Moreover, many complications 
might arise if the present concern were asked to take these persons. In the 
interest of industrial peace, such complications should be avoided by all 
means. Then again, it bas transpired from the evidence that the services 
of majority of these workmen had to be terminated on dissolution of

partnership and cloaure of business. The Tribunal is satisfied from ws

were bona fide. It has been held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India 
in the case of Pipraich Sugar Mills, Ltd. vs. Pipraich Sugar Mills Mazdoor

discharged as a result of closure of a business, because retrenchment which

discharge on closure of a business. Hence, the workers who were discharged 
on dissolution of partnership and closure of business, are not entitled to

present concern cannot be directed to pay such compensation. 


earned spokesman of the Union has contended that if the facts leading

Issue No. 12 This issue relates to the claim of revision of the existiug

Turning to these initial objections raised by the Company I find that 
I am unable to accede to the said contentions. No doubt, under section 
10(4) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, as amended, the Tribunal cannot 
travel beyond the scope of the issue as framed. But at the same time the 
Tribunal has been permitted to look into incidental matters connected with 
the issue. So the pesition is that though I cannot under the issue framed, 
addresa myself to the revision of wage scales as such, still while revising 
the grudes if I find it necessary that the wage scales should be varied, [ 
think 1 would not exceed my jurisdiction or transgress the limit if 1 do 
ao. Regarding the second contention of the Company, the position in law 
ib really as has been indicated by it. But in the present case I find that 
the evidence makes it clear that there has been a material change of cir- 
cumstances. What is meant by ‘‘material change of circumstances’’ has 
not been clearly indicated in the aforesaid judgment of the Hon’ble 
Supreme Court. If by this, improved solvency of the Company is meant, 
then in the present case I find that it is ৪0. The increase in profits 19 an 
index of the growing solvency of the concern. If I compare the audited 
balance-sheets of the years 1954, 1955 and 1956, marked Exts. H to H2 
I find that there has been not only a steady increase in the profits, but also 
that the profit position reveals 2 material prosperity. For instance, in the 
year 1954, after payment of dividends the net balance that was carried 
forward amounted to Rs. 4 lacs 8 thousand and odd. In 1955, os per the 
audited balance-sheet, the net balance of profit stood as Rs. 9 laca 61 
thousand and odd. In 1956, though the aaid balance stood at Rs. 6 lacs 
and 73 thousand, the total balance retained the same figure of Rs. 13 lacs 
and odd, as in the previous year. The net balance in 1956 showed a little 
decline because of special appropriation under different heads. This 
makes it abundantly clear that the Company was making a headway 
towards increase 1 solvency.

But if the ‘material change of circumstances’ means that the cost of 
living index should show an upward variation, even then I find that there 
has been a considerable change. For instance, 1n December 1952 the cost 
of living index stood at 378.9 as per the State Statiatical Bureau 
No. 1615(2)1/10, dated 9th June 1953. In September 1956 this figure went 
up to 302.7 eid State Statistical Bureau No. 32(9)I, dated 18th January

Bureau No. 325(9)1, dated 4th July 1957]. As the year 1957 advances, this 
cost of living index maintains its upward trend. We are all feeling the 
pinch of it, and even the State Government is embarrassed in the matter 
of increase in dearness allowance on the basis of soaring prices of essential 
food commodities. Now, the wages in this country have been made to rest 
on the needs of the employees considered from the human point of view. 
So if the cost of consumers index rises, the wages are bound to be raised. 
Workmen should be enabled to make their two ends meet, and to maintain 
their efficiency. Of course, dearness allowance to ascertain extent tempo- 
rarily mitigates the sufferings of workmen. But when the prices of com- 
modities rule high and do not show any downward tendency, we may take 
it that the position is more or less permanent. If that is so, mere increase 
in dearness allowance will be equivalent to tinkering with the problem. 
We have to face the problem squarely and boldly, and increase the wages 
where the same is called for. So regard being had to the above, ۲ think 
o case has been made out for a material change of circumstances, and the 
wage levels are liable to be revised accordingly.

is nominal, and cases asking for such medical attention are very rare. ‘@f 
course, the Union has led evidence that it is difficult to get the assistance 
of private doctors except on payment of exhorbitant feas. But specific 
cases have not been enumerated where difficulties were experienced as 
anticipated. It will not do to forget that the Company is not under any 
obligation to bear the entire expenses of free medical treatment of ao worker 
and his family, The burden is shared also by the State. In the changed 
circumstances, consequent on the introduction of the State Employees’ 
Insurance Act, [ am unable to saddle the Company with further expenses 
on the score of free medical attention to employees’ parents, and other 
dependents, viz., brothers, sisters, ete., when strictly spenking, the 
Company is lable to defray the expenses of its employees only. So the 
claim under this head is turned down. 


issue No. 3: This demand is gradually becoming persistent in moat of 
the Companies. It can hardly be denied that dearness allowance has come 
to stay. There is hardly any near prospect of prices coming down to the 
pre-war level. If dearness allowance becomes a permanent feature, then it 
18 desirable that at least a fraction of it should go into the body of wages. 
But the difficulty is that this decision cannot be taken in a solitary case like 
the present one. If this decision is to be taken, it should be taken industry- 
wise, or steps in this direction may be taken by the Government on a 
comprehensive basis. The (Gadgil Committee’s recommendations, it is 
worth pointing out, waa not accepted by the Government on this score. 
Besides, dearness allowance being given in the Provident Fund 
contribution and also in gratuity, the importance of this claim has been 
minimised to a great extent. So in the present case I turn down this claim.

Issue No. 5: The Union here claims some casual leave. The Company 
submits that the privilege lenve and sick leave in vogue in this Company 
are more liberal than anywhere else. So the claim for further casual leave 
cannot stand. The Company has submitted a chart showing leave avail- 
able to the workmen. For the shift workers 30 days’ privilege leave in a 
year is given. For the non-shift workers 20 days’ privilege leave in a vear 
ia given. QOut of the above, 15 days are given under the Factories Act; 
12 Cavs as festival holidays, and 2 days as national holidays. Under the 
Second Engineering Tribunal’y Award the total period of leave was 30 or 
30 dave, and out of that 15 days were under the Factories Act, 10 days as 
festival holidays, and 5 or 6 days as other heads of leave. Even from the 
Company’s above statement it is clear that under both the awards of the 
Major Engineering Tribunal, 5 or 6 days’ other kind of leave was provided 
for, This seems to stand for casual leave. The Company’s stand seems 
to be that because the privilege leave and sick leave are ample here, the 
claim for casual lexve cannot be sustained. J om unable to agree to this 
idea. Sick leave may be admissible only on production of medical 
cettifionte in case a person falls sick. Privilege leave accrues on the length 
of service. But it can never be thought of that a man during the whole 
year would not require some davs’ absence for doing odd business for his 
family. Casual leave is provided for everywhere. In all systems of 
holidavs and leave, it has been recognised that there should be some 
provision for absence for doing one’s casual husiness. I can understand

ee سعتٹہمیٗبپووییپپپٗکپووچُِِٔویسٹچ‎ 


tha{ it should be curtailed to the minimum in an engineering industry or 
an industry where other kinds of leave are hberal. But there can be no 
reason why casual leave should be totally denied to the workmen. In the 
Standing Orders of the Company, I find in item No. LIE that the Power 
Station Superintendent or the District Engineer may, at his discretion, 
grant additional leave but without pay. This certainly does not answer the 
requirement of casual leave, nor was it meant to answer the same. This 
was meant to provide for additional leave where longer leave than under 
the provision was required, viz., in cases of privilege leave and sick leave. 
So I must take it that the Standing Orders of the Company do not provide 
for contingency of casual leave. Considering all these circumstances, এ 
award that 5 days’ casual leave with pay in a year must be granted to all 
employees. But such leave should not be claimed as a mutter of right, and 
must remain at the discretion ‘of the management, and must lapse after 


one year. 


isSue No, 6: This issue relates to retrenchment of Sitaram Mistry 
(carpenter). According to the Union, this man was working as a carpenter 
since 1953. He was put on probation for one year as a dependent of

probation was extended for 6 months. He was given a further extension 
of 6 months on the ground that he was atill a slow worker. On the expiry 
of the last extension period he was discharged from service. Annexure B 
to the Company’s written statement is the letter of appointment of Sitaram 
Mistry on probation from 5th April 1954. As per the Company's letter, 
dated 3rd July 1956, which is Annexure C to the Company's written state- 
ment, I find that he was discharged with the observation 4001 work was 
not satisfactory’. The Power House Superintendent issued several letters 
of warning for improvement of work, but with no effect. Shri B. B. Ghosh, 
O.P.W. 1, who was the Power House Superintendent, states before me, at 
page 2 of his deposition that Sitaram was taken as a probationer on the 
recommendation of the Works Committee. Sitaram was a casual labour 
for about 5.0۲ 6 months before he was taken as a probationer. Sitaram was 
verbally told and also written to that he worked slow. The Works Com- 
mittee was informed of this in writing. Tt appears that Sitaram was given 
ample trial. The fact that his period of probation was extended from time 
to time shows clearly that the Company was rather willing to retain him. 
But ultimately when it was found that he could not improve his work, the 
Company was compelled to discharge him, There is no motive alleged 
ayainst the Company. J find no mala fide in the present case. So I uphold 
the discharge order and reject the claim of reinstatement and compensation 
for Sitaram.

AWARD 


This 1s a case of summary dismissal of an employee of Messrs. De 
Penning & De Penning (hereinafter referred to as the Company for the 
sake of brevity) on the ground of disobedience and insubordination.
