1০-৮৯-১১০১ 


9 
The case of the Union is that the Company carries on business in 
Patent & Trade Mark Agency in India, Pakistun and all over the world. 
Shri (shose was an employee in the Accounts Department. The টা 
has no systematic terms and conditions of service. The employees forme 
u Trade Cnion of their own sometime in September 1956. Shm Chose took 
n lending part in the Trade Union activities which the Company did not 
take in good grace and became vindictive. On 19th December 1956, at 
about 4-25 p.m., Mr, De Penning called Shri (those to enquire as to who 
would du Mr Perie’s work as he was absent and why his (Perie) was not 
done by him. Shri Ghose in all courtesy told Mr. De Penning that there 
was no instruction from him to do Perie’s work for the day. This reply 
infuriated Mr. De Penning who ordered Shri Ghose to get out of the 
office and hurriedly caught him by the neck and pushed him out of the 
office. This was followed by a letter of «dismissal. No charge-sheet was 
given, nor was any enquiry held and this is opposed to ছায়ার নর of 
natural and social justice. The Union therefore alleges that this is a case 
of victimisation, pure and simple, and seeks Shri (Ghose’s reinstatement. 


The Company in their written statement denies generally the allega- 
tions in the written statement of the Union and contends, inter alia, that 
on 19th December 1956, Mr. G. M. Faulkner, a senior officer of the firm, 
‘came to Mr. De Penning and told him that there was an urgent report 
to be posted to the client with a debit note but as Mr. Perie was absent, 
he (Mr, Faulkner) requested Shri Ghose to write out the note who flatly 
and in an insolent manner refused to do the same saying that it was not 
his job; that Mr. De Penning agaiu and again requested him to do the 
work and explained to him that as on previous occasions he did _ write 
out the debit note in the absence of Mr. Perie and as the matter 
was very urgent he should do it, hut Shri Ghose still refused whereupon 
Mr. De Penning gave him a last chance with a clear understanding that 
if he did not write out the debit note he would be dismissed. Stil] Shri 
(those refused to write out the debit note and thereupon Mr. De Penning 
told him that he was dismissed from service and next day he might 
collect his dues; that Shri Ghose asked for a letter of diamissal and he 
was informed that he would be given it the next day; that the matter being 
very urgent Mr. De Penning himself wrote out the debit note which was 
sent to their client that very day. Thus the Company justifies the 
summary dismissal on the ground of insubordination and gross misconduct 
and repudiates the allegation of victimisation. The Company _ therefore 
seriously contends that in the circumstances the employee is not entitled 
to reinstatement. 


DECISION 


Admittedly in this case there was no charge-sheet, no enquiry, nothing 
of the kind. It is therefore seriously contended on behalf of the Union 
that the principles of natural and social justice had been violated and 
justice had heen denied to the employee by the orders of summary dis- 
missal, There. are numerous rulings wherein it has been laid down that 
if no enquiry were held by the management the Tribunal and/or Court. 
18 entitles to hold an independent enquiry and scrutinise the action of 
the Company on this point. The rulings reported in 1956 J..1..J., Vol, TT, 
page 67, 1990 (۰.۱۰٠۰٠٢ Vol, 11. page 433, 1957 T..1.J3., Vol. TI, page 387, 
1957 L..d., Vol. II, page 15, may be referred to. In all these cnses 
the trend of decision 1s that rules of natural and social justice require that 
the delinquent emplovee must he given o reasonable opportunity of being 
heard in his defence and that fundamentals of fair play and justice must 
he observed. This requires that a proper enquiry need be held by an 
impartial authority before an employee is found guilty. In the case 


۶× 1] THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., AUGUST 29, 1957 3513 


8 ১ ০৯৯ 
of Buckingham & Carnatic Co., Ltd., it is laid down that the Industrial 
Tribunals have been given the power to see whether the termination 
of service of a workman 1s justified. It is also laid down there that if 
there is evidence to support the action of the management the Tribunal 
will not substitute its own judgment for the judgment of the manage- 
ment. But the decision of the management with regard to a charge of 
misconduct against an employee will not prevail if— 


(i) there is want of bona fides; or 


(ii) it is 4 case of victimisation or unfair labour practice or violation 
of the principles of natural justice; or 


(iii) there is a basic error of facts; or 
(iv) there has been a perverse finding on the materials. 


Now, it devolves on the Court to arrive at an independent finding as 
the result of the enquiry held by this Court whether the instant disniissal 
is justified or not. 


Now, I come to the facts. The Company bases the order of dismissal 
on the incident that happened in their office on 19th December 1956 
round about 4-15 to 4-25 p.m. This incident relates to the preparation of 
a short debit note, photostat copy of which is murked Ext A(7). The 
debit note relates to the firm of Messrs. Smith Stanistreet & (Co., who 
entrusted the Company to make a search in the office of Registrar of 
Trade Marks and to communicate the result thereof to them. If the 
result of the search proved favourable, Company's customers would 
proceed to get the patent mark registered immediately. The Company 
therefore contends that this was a very urgent cen important matter 
which required immediate despatch to the client that very day (19th 
December 1956). The case of the Company is that Shri Ghose refused to 
prepare this debit note though asked intially to do so by Mr. Faulkner, 
9. senior officer of the Company, at about 4-15 p.m. and when he refused 
to carry ont Mr. Faulkner's orders Mr. De Penning, « senior partner of 
firm, asked Shri (rhose to prepare the debit note which he still refused 
und that even after Mr. De পট gave him a final ultimatum that 
he might disobey his orders on pain of dismissal. This warning even 
went unheaded and then Mr. De Penning said that in that case his 
service was no و‎ required and he was dismissed. On behalf of the 
Union it is seriously contended before me that this is a cooked up 
story, a myth, pure and simple, and nothing short of an unfair labour 
practice and victimisation because Shri (those was mainly instrumental 
in forming a Trade Union on or about September 1956 of which he was 
to treasurer and therefore the Company first axed Shri Ghose. In this 
behalf there is nothing beyond the sole evidence of Shri Ghose and his 
evidence 18 that at about 4-25 p.m. Mr. Faulkuer asked him to do_ the 
debit note which he could not carry out because there were the auditors 
examining his portion of the work that day and he had to attend to 
them. And it is also his case that there is no practice in the Company’s 
office that in the absence of one employee, another does his work. On 
the contrary, the Company has examined Mr. Faulkner and Mr. De 
Penning as well. As their evidences are very important I  pruceed_ to 
quote the relevant portion of their evidence in eztenso, Mr. Faulkner 
says as follows:— 


“T went to the Accounts Department and Mr. Perie was not present 
due to sickness. I asked Mr. Ghose to write out the debit 
note. He flatly refused stating that it was not his work. 
Then I went to Mr. De Penning to let him know what was 
happening. Then Mr. De Penning sent for Mr. Ghose in my 


3614 THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., AUGUST 29, 7 [Part I 


সপ کر چا‎ ×٠ ے.‎ awe 


presence. Mr. De Penning usked him to make out the debit. 
He refused. Mr. De Penning said that as Mr. Ghose was not 
prepared to do the work then ‘he must go’.’’ 

“It was between 4 and 4-15 p.m., I went to the Accounts Depart- 
ment. I asked Mr. (710046 to make out the debit. Mr. Bose and 
Mr. Barat (1 believe) were there. The seat of Mr. Ghose 18 
Just in front of Mr. Bose’s. Mr. Bose and Mr. Barat are in our

Accounts Department, nor 19 it a fact that I did not ask Mr. 
Gihose to make out the debit. In my knowledge there was uo 
coinplaint about Ghose’s work on that date.....,......... 


This version of Mr. Faulkner is corruborated by Mr. De Penning who

“IT sent for Ghose in the presence of Mr. Faulkner. I asked Ghose 
to prepure a debit note and give it to Mr. Faulkner to send it

I asked 11121) again to prepare it and I asked him twice and

The evidence of Mr. Faulkner thus supported by that of Mr, De Penning 
lenves no room for doubt in my mind that they gave the Court the 
truthful version of what actually happened in the office on 19th Wecember 
1956. And the evidence of Shri Ghose alene does not take awny the 
least from the truth of the incident as related by Company’s witnesses 
before me. I have absolutely no reason to disbelieve the testimony of 
Mr. Faulkner and Mr. De Penning and I om unable to hold that ‘they 
would stoop so low as to manufacture ao false story to sack Shri Ghose 
for his Trade Union activities. It is difficult to believe that nothing 
happened on that particular date to justify the dismissal of the employee. 
It 1s also curious that Ghose could not produce his colleagues Bose and 
Barat to support his version. It is pertinent to point out that the Union 
in their written statement alleged that Mr. De Penning hurriedly caught 
Shri i by the neck and pushed him out of the office and added 
“Bloody Bengalee, you shall have to go out and I will see what law can 
keep you in this office’. ‘But not a word was said in Court to corroborate 
this allegation. This omission is very materia] and this taken with other 
circiunstances of the case leads me to hold that the Union has not stated 
the whole truth. There is another circumstances which needs be referred 
to in this connection. The Union suggests that there is no practice in 
the Company’s office for one employee to do the work of another in his 
absence. But, the Company has produced certain photostat copies (Ext. A 
series excepting A-7) of debit notes prepared by Shri (those in the obsence 
of the assistant whose duty it was to prepare it. Admittedly Shri Ghose 
was an Assistant Accountant and it is contended on his behalf that it 
was no part of his duty to prepare the debit note in any circumstances. 
But as already proved by the Company which produced the photostat 
copies of debit notes sometimes prepared by Shri Bose, sometimes by 
Shri Ghose in the absence of Mr. Perie whose duty it waa to 70 the 
debit notes, I om convinced that as a matter of ordinary practice it was 
nothing unnatural for any other assisant to do the work of Mr. Perie in 
his absence especially when the work was short and simple. Undisputedly 
Mr, Perie was absent only on the 19th December 1956 and the work being 
very immediate and urgent the debit note had to be sent out on _ that 


Parr Uf THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., AUGUST 29, 1987 5518 
০৩০১১১১১১১2 00১0000১000 
very date and Shri Ghose was asked to do it. Shri Ghose has not heen 
able to show any valid or acceptable excuse to exoverate himself from 
the blame for his repeated refusal to do the s‘mple debit note. This 
debit note Ext. A(7) is a very short matter and admittedly it might take 
only two minutes to do it and it was only his dogmatic refusal which led 
to this trouble. If good rense had dawned on Shri Ghose he would 
certainly have agreed 10 do the debit note, but his obstinate refusal 
brought him to the present impasse. Then aguwin it is urged on behalf 
of the Union that this note was kept pending in the Company's office 
for the last 2 or 3 days but all on a sudden it strangely struck the 
Company that the matter was immediate and urgent and that the note 
must be despatched by that day’s mail. Jt is further contended that 
even if the search report were Immediate and urgent there was no 
urgency about the debit note which might have waited for u day or two. 
The debit note concerns the Company since it was their bill only and 
there was no apprehension of the Company's losing a petty amount of 
Ks, 16 only from a reputed firm hke Messrs. Smith Stanistreet & 09. 
Hlerein Mr. De Penning explained thai it was the invariable practice of 
the Company to despatch the debit note along with the search report. 
The question of urgency or otherwise of the debit note is immaterial. 
What concerns the Court is the disobedience of Shri (those to carry out 
the orders of the Company first through Mr. Foukner and ultimately 
through Mr. De Penning. There was the order and there was the 
repeated refusal of the employee to carry out the sume even on pain of 
dismissal and this was a clear case of gross disobedience and insubordina- 
tion which certainly merits dismissal. The present conduct of Shri (chose 
was clearly subversive of all discipline in the Company and it would he 
laying down a dangerous proposition of law, I am afraid, if it be held 
that such gross insubordination does not justify the orders of dismisaal. 
In this connection a reference may be made to the case of Messrs. 
Phagyaluxmi Insurance Ltd., published in Calcutta (Gazette. May 10, 
1951. In this case the Judge, Shri P. R. Mukherjee, found that the 
dismissal of Shri Bhabesh Chakravorty was justified. What happened in 
this case may be briefly stated thus :— 


“The driver employee was never punctual in attendance and had been 
in the habit of being absent without notice. 116 was warned 
several times for remaining absent without leave and warnings 
had no effect. Apprehending that he might not turn up at the 
appointed time the Managing Director of the Company cautioned 
him on the previous day to turn up punctually at 8 am., but 
strangely enough he obliged the Managing Director by putting 
in an appearance at 9-30 a.m. That waa an important engage- 
ment. What was most regrettable ond inexcusable was the 
impertinent conduct of the driver who when confronted by the 
Managing Director flatly on his face said that he (Managing 
Director) cannot expect better attendance from him (the driver). 
The Managing Director thereupon summarily dismissed him.’’ 


This dismissal was upheld by the learned Appellate Court and the case 
is reported in 1962 L.A.C., page 366. The flat refusal of the driver in 
the face of the Managing J)irector to carry out his orders was considered 
ما‎ be an act of insubordination sufficient to justify the reapers of the 
workman summarily. The insubordination displayed by the employee in 
Soi his is of a type of that displayed by the driver in the case referred 
0 above. 


Next, a word need he said about the Union’s allegation that this 
employee was axed for his Trade Union activities. The Union, it is stated,

Company’s cuse and not the 7 The Court does not like to speculate

displayed by the employee as referred to. above is sufficient just. fication

behalf of the Union that the punishment of summary dismissal 15 too 
severe to be upheld in the circumstance. But since the Court has found 
that the dismissal is justified, the Court cannot substitute its own, punish- 
ment for that imposed by the Company. It has been clearly laid down in 
the case of Buckingham and Carnatic Co., Ltd., reported in 1962 L.A.C. at 
puge 498 “that it would be open to the Tribunal to examine the findings 
of the munagement on the charge of misconduct to assure itself — that 
there is evidence to support the finding and that the decision of the 
سن سان‎ is a possible view on the evidence before it. In such a case 
the Tribunal should refrain from substituting its own judgement for the 
judgment of the mahagement, us in such matters the Tribunal does not 
uct lke a Court of Appeal but rather as a supervisory body, exercising 
what would ordinarily ۶ regarded as powers of revision for correction 
of basic errors which go to the root of the matter and of perverse finding»’’. 
Having carefully considered the entire case on its merits the decision 
of the Court is that it cannot hold that the decision of the management 
is lacking in bona fides or that it is a case of victimisation or an unfair 
labour practice or of violation of the principles of natural and social 
justice, nor can the Court say that there is a basie error of facets or that 
tue findings of the management are perverse on the materials. This is 
a clear case of gross insubordination and no useful purpose would have 
heen served if the Company had given a churge-sheet calling upon the 
employee to explain the charge and held an enquiry and arrived at a 
conclusion, The deplorable’ incident that happened on the fateful after- 
noon of 19th December 1956 in the presence of Mr. De Penning and the 
employee needed no charges to be framed, nor any explanation therefor 
and in the circumstances it cannot be said that any prejudice was caused 
ما‎ the employee in the absence of an enquiry, Absence of a regsonnble 
Opportunity given to the employee does not by itself vitinte the enquiry 
but in order to vitinte the enquiry it must be shown that prejudice was 
caused to the employee. In this case J must say that no prejudice was 
caused to the employee becouse he deliberately refused to carry out the 
orders of the senior officer and the senior Managing Partner of — the 
Company. In this connection reference may be made to the case of 
সিল জিন Tea Estate (70.  Ltd., and Kerala 07019100801 
Workers Union reported in 1956 L.5..J., Vol. II, page 434, wherein it 
has been ت10‎ down that “in a domestic enquiry one should not expect 
a rigid observance of the rules of procedure prescribed either by the 
Criminal or Civil Procedure Codes but when the standing order itself 
luys down that the particulars of the offence complained of should: be 


given in the charge-sheet, there can be no doubt that the enquiring officer

conducted according to rules of natural justice would be sufficient." 


In view of the rulings reported above and having regard to the case 
| must come to the finding that the dismissal in the present case is justified 
und that the failure to serve a charge-sheet before enquiry cannot be cousi-

employee was prejudiced in his defence,

1৭ that the case of the workman was taken up by the Patent and Trade

The conclusion therefore is that the dismissal of this employee 18

4, Before I take up the issue, I would like to give o brief history of the 
dispute. 

It is contended by the Union that the pay-scales in the existing grade 
system were fixed long ago, and that they و‎ » change for the better 
in the context of changed circumstances. The existing grade system 18 
also said to be defective inasmuch as there is nu yearly increment. There 
18 no job valuation, and so the pay system is defective. It is also

contended that here the workers have got to handle poisonous gas and 
chemicals, and this has an adverse effect on their health. In view of the 
above nature of work, it is urged that the wage acales should be jincrensed. 
Regarding bonus, it is contended that the bonus the workers are now 
getting is customary bonus payable annually. It is further contended 
that for the year 1954, over and above customary bonus, three months’ 
extra bonus should be given to the workers. 


The Company, on the other hand, contends that the business originally 
belonged to Messrs. Hadfields (India), Tid., which got involved in debts. 
The present Management took it over in 1948 along with debts 
of the old Company, and it has to fight against keen competition. It 
has still to fight against debts. Its total personnel will be nearly 200, 
Its wage scales are far in excess of what are being paid by similar 
concerns in the neighbourhood. There are other facilities available here 
unlike similar other concerns. The Company resists the granting of 
automatic incremental scales of pay for the workers. They, however, 
rive increments on the basis of satisfactory work and regular attendance. 
The minimum total monthly emolument of an unskilled worker is Rs. 89-6. 
The story of handling poisonous gas, etc., is said to be a myth. There 
has been no case of occupational disease, and unless one be careless 
one runs no hazard in handling chemicals. Regarding bonus, the 
Company denies the existence of customary bonus. The bonus which is 
iven is based on profits. The Company proposed to give two months’ 
asic wages as bonus for the year 1954. This was announced on the 29th 
March 1955, and the first instalment was given in March 1955. This 
quantum of bonus is claimed to be the highest bonus paid in the paint

paid for the first time in ۰ 


issue No. 1: Coming to the issue in queation, 1. must point out that 
the onus to prove the existence of customary bonus is on the Union. 
The Union has practically placed no evidence before the Tribunal in this 
respect which can be cal ed reliable. Besides, the Ext. B, which is the 
agreement reached in 1952, with the Union, shows that bonus was not 
customary. The paragraph 6 of the said agreement runs thus: 


“The question of paying a bonus in September 1952, will entirely be 
dependent on the business conditions of the Company then, and 
will be reviewed in August 1952 in consultation with the 
Secretary, Howrah Paint Workers’ Union’’. 


It wil] not do for the Union just to say that the agreement in question 
had been with another Union, unless it can be shown beyond doubt that 
the said Union had bartered away the rights of the workers, or that it 
acted in collusion with the Management. Regarding the claim of bonus 
for the year 1954, Ext. D shows that bonus equal to one month's basic 
wage was promised to be paid, as in the previous year, at the Puja time, 
according to the usual schedule. The remaining one month’s bonus was 
made payable subject to certain conditions. The workmen received bouns 
under this notice. So it is clear that the workmen did acquiesce in 
the conditions under which bonus was distributed as above. So it may 
be clearly said that they are estopped from raising a further claim for 
extra bonus in respect of the year 1954. Even if the question of estoppel 
is put out of account, still the claim of (a age bonus is practically 
buried as a result of this notice, Ext. D. So I hold that the claim for 
customary bonus for the year 1954 stands rejected.

AWARD 


The original reference out of which this case has ari 7 
سا‎ order No S0UDin/D/JUL-130/56,datol Bt Soptouber 186 


9. The petitioner contends that he has been made to retire pre 
at the age of 54 years, and that this has been done without ঠাস ক 
permission of the Tribunal in writing before whom the main case was 
pending for adjudication. So section 33 of the Act has been violated. He 
claims relief under section 33A of the Act. 


The Company resists the claim on the ground that under the Standing 
Orders, a man is liable to retirement on completion of 30 years’ service, or 
on his reaching 55 years of age, whichever is earlier. In the present 
case the petitioner was appointed on the lat April 1924. So he completed 
80 years’ service on 9186 March 1954. Consequently he was liable to 
retirement on Ist April 1954. He was, however, allowed to continue in 
his service, on the basis of an agreement in a conciliation proceeding, up 
to 818: March 1957. So when he retired on that date, no permission of the 
Tribunal was necessary. 


Turning to the evidence on record, I find that the Company has 
ت000‎ the service card of the petitioner, and in that card I find that 
is age was 21 years at the time of this appointment in March 1924. 
From this, it is clear that on lst April 1957, he did not reach 55 vears of 
age, but he completed hia 30 years of service long before that. Now, as 
the Standing Orders stand, he is liable to retirement on his com letion of 
80 years’ service because that is earlier than his attaining the age of 
68 years. So the Company did not violate the Standing Orders in this 
matter of his retirement, It is the contention of the Union that thie 
man was in the service of some other Company in 1928, and that this 
fact can be proved by evidence. But I do not go into that evidence. 
find it superfluous. The petitioner has been made to retire not only on 
his completion of 30 years’ service in this Company, but on maturity of 
the agreement term entered into before the Assistant Labour Commissioner. 
How can he avoid this agreement? So he was justly retired after end of 
March 1957. This petition under section 33A ر18‎ therefore, liable to be 
rejected, and I reject it accordingly.

ORDER 


No. Eas.Com. /Rice/Paddy(1) /b492F.8.—30th August 1907.—In  exer- 
cise of the powers conferred by section 3 of the Essential Commodities 
Act, 1955 (10 of 1955), read with the Government of India, Mimistry of 
Food and Agriculture, Order No. 8.2.0,1477, dated the 29th April 1957, 
notified at pages 988-989 of Part II, section 3 of the Gazette of 1768 of the 
116৮ May 1957, the Governor, ‘with the prior concurrence of the Central 
(Giovernment, is pleased to make the following Order, namely سے‎ 


ORDER 


1. Short title, extent and commencement.—-(1) This Order may he 
08111 the West Bengal Rice and Paddy Control Order, 1991. 


(2) Jt extends to the whole of West Bengal. 


(3) It shall come into force in the areas specified in the Firat Schedule 
ما‎ this Order at once and the Order or any part of it shall come into force 
in other areas on such date as the State Government may, by notification 
in the Ofieial Gazette, appoint and different dates may be appointed for 
different areas. 


2. Definitions.—In this Order, unless there is anything repugnant in 
the subject or context,— 

(a) ‘Director’? means the J)irector of Food, Department of Food, 
Relief and Supplies (Food and Supplies Branch), Government 
of West lise or any other officer authorised by him to perfori 
the functions of the Director under this Order;

(b) ‘‘Form’’ means a‘form us set furtb in the Second Schedule to this 


Order; 
(c) ‘Specified areas’? menns the areas specified in the First Schedule 
to this Order; : 


(d) ‘Rice’ does not include Chira, Muri or Khoi but includes broken 
rive (Khud). 


3. No person shall engage in any undertaking which involves the 
yroduction or manufacture of rice, or the purchase, sale or storage for sale 
in wholesale quantities of any rice or paddy except under and-ig accordance 
with a licente issued under paragraph 6. 


Eeplanation.—In this paragraph, the expression ‘‘purchase, sale or 
storage for sale in wholesale quantities’? means purchase or sale in 
quantities exceeding ten maunds in any one transaction or storage in 
quantities exceeding ten maunds for the purpose of sale, as the case may 
be, and the expression ‘‘production or manufacture of rice’? means 
manufacture of rice by any process of removing the husk from paddy (rice 
‘in রা husk) at a rice mill or with the aid of a power-driven husking 
machine. 


4. Transport of rice or paddy into specified areas.——No person shal! 
move or transport or cause to be moved or transported into the specified 
areus by land, water or air any rice or paddy except under and in accordance 
with a transport permit issued in this behalf under paragraph 7: 


Providing that nothing in this paragraph shal] apply to the movement 
or transport of rice or paddy— 


(a) not exceeding five seers in weight by a buna fide traveller as part 
of his or her luggage or not exceeding two maunds in weight 
by a bona fide consumer on any one occasion, or 


(b) under and in accordance with Military Credit Notes, or 
(c) on Government account, 


Keplanation.—A bona fide consumer under this proviso means a person 
who ordinarily resides within the specified areas and who carries 
the foodgrains for his or her consumption or for his or her 
family’s consumption, the onus of proving which shall lie on 
of him or her. 


9. Transport of rice or pady out of certain areas.—The Stute Govern- 
ment may, by notification in the Oficial Gazette, direct that with effect

transport or cattse to be moved or transported out of such area as may be 
specified in the notification by land, water or air any rice or paddy except 
under and in accordance with a permit issued in this behalf under 
paragraph 7: 

Provided that nothing in this paragraph shall apply to the movement or 
transport of rice or paddy— 


(a) not exceeding five seers in weight by a bona fide traveller as part 
| of his or her luggage, or 


(b) under and in accordance with Military Crodit Notes,’or 
(9) on Government acoount.

10. Suspension and cancellation of licences and permits.—If any 
person being the holder of a licence or a transport permit granted under 
this Order contravenes any of the provisions of this Order or any of the 
conditions of such licence or permit, then, without prejudice to any other

by order, after giving him an opportunity of being heard in his defence, 
guapend or cancel the licence or permit. On the cancellation of a licence 
or permit under this paragraph, the holder of the licence or permit shall 
surrender the same to the State Government or to such person as may be 
specified in this behalf in the order cancelling the licence or permit. 


[1]. Powers of entry and search.—(1) Any person authorised by the

Provided that in exercising the powers under this sub-paragraph due

(2) Any person authorised by the State Government to make search in

West Bengal Ordinance No. VIII of 1957 


THE TRANSFERRED TERRITORIES (APPLICATION OF 
WEST BENGAL TAX LAWS) ORDINANCE, 1957. 


WHEREAS it is expedient to apply to the transferred territories 
certain tax laws in force in the rest of West Bengal; 


AND WHEREAS both Houses of the Legislature of West 
Bengal are not in session and the Governor is satisfied that 
circumstances exist which render it necessary for her to take 
immediate action; 


AND WHEREAS the instructions of the President under the 
proviso to clause (/) of article 213 of the Constitution of India 
have been obtained; 


The Governor is pleased, in exercise of the power conferred 


by clause (/) of the said article, to make and promulgate the 
following Ordinance, namely: — 


Short titlo 1. (1) This Ordinance may be called the Transferred 
and Territories (Application of West Bengal Tax Laws) Ordinance, 
commence- 1957 

mont 


(2) It shall come into force on the date of its publication 
in the Official Gazette. 


Definition. 2. In this Ordinance, “transferred territories” mean the 
territories transferred from the State of Bihar to the State of 
West Bengal by section 3 of the Bihar and West Bengal (Transfer XL of 


of Territories) Act, 1956. 1956. 
Repeal of 3. As from the date of the commencement of قالطا‎

The Assistant Labour Commissioner (Statistics), Weat Bengal, will act 
as the Secretary of the Committee. 


The functions of the Committee will be to examine the schemes of 
rationalisation in the various Jute Mills in the State and to make recommen- 
dations to Government on the following : -- 


(1) Outlining a phased programme of rationalisation so 08 to cause no 
retrenchment. 


(2) Apportionment of. work-load and increase of wages, if justified, 1 
increased work-loads. 


(3, Fixation of cadres, permanent and temporary, for each of the 
rationalised establishment. 
(4) 11158510701) of retiring age for each category of workers. 


The Committee may also take in Assessors possessing expert knowledge 
for such assistance as may he deemed necessary.

NOTIFICATION 


No. GOl9/M.SE-15/57.—29th August ۰0967. 
Whereas the Corporation of Calcutta have, by a 
resolution passed unanimously at its meeting held 
on the 5th July 1957, made = a recommendation 
under clause (xxi) of section 526 of the Calcutta 
Municipal Act, 1061 (West Bengal Act XX XIII 
of 1951), that the expenditure incurred in -endiag 
a delegation consisting of the Mayor and the 
Chairman of the Standing Finance Conimittee of 
the Corporation accompanied by the Chief 
Engineer of the Corporation and the personal staff 
of the Mayor to New Delhi tor obtaining financial 
assistunce from the Government of India for the 
project for construction of quarters for the 
sweepers, methors, mazdoors, etc., in the 
Corporation service, as well as other projects, is a 
matter likely to promote the public health, safety 
and convenience of the persons resident in Calcutta. 


Now, therefore, the Governor, in exercise of the 
power conferred by the said clause, is pleased to 
declare that the said matter 1s one which is likely 
to promote the public health, safety and 
convenience within the meaning of the said 
clause. 


By order of the Governor, 
N. M. BARDHAN, Jt. Secy.

Special provisions relating to procedure in appeala against ordera of

where he or they can be served.

up according to the provisions of Rule 35, Chapter V, Part 11 of the

paper-book as there are respondents, to be served together with three extra

(XIV ot 1947), for udjudication. The said Fifth Industrial Tribunal was

2. The reference was received here on 28th April 1956. After usual 
notices the Union filed written statement on 2156 May 1956. The Company 
filed written objection on 1161) June 1956. After several adjournments for 
interlocutury matters such as inspection, etc., the case was taken up for 
heuring on oth Murch 1957, and the evidence was concluded on that day. 
The argument was heard on 17th June 1957, and the award was reserved. 


3. The issues contained in the schedule to the order of reference stand 
as follows سے‎ 


(1) Pay and scales of pay. 
(2) Dearness allowance. 
(3) Provident Fund. 

(4) Overtime. 


AWARD 


4. According to the Union, this Company is u well-known firm of Jong 
stunding dealing in all kinds of provisions such as Jams, Sauce, Pickles, 
Meata, Butter, Cheese, Fruits, Vegetables, Liquors, Tuilets, Razor Blades 
and sundry stationery articles. This Company being a member of the 
Bengal Chamber of Commerce and Industry, introduced in March 1947 tor 
its employees scales of pay and dearness allowance on the lines recommended 
by the said Chamber of Commerce at that time. The employees, however, 
were not satisfied with this, and they went on agitating for better 
emoluments and amenities till the Omnibus Tribunal (Mercantile Tribunal) 
was set up by the Government under its order No. 135Lab., dated 17th 
January 1948. The workmen, however, withdrew participation from the 
suid Tribunal on a tacit understanding from the Company that the Company 
would implement whutever is eet by the anid fribunal. But the 
Company was not as good as its promise, and did not redeem the said 
pledge. Now, though the cost of ving index hus gone up from 401 to 410 
points in respect of the middle-class cost of living index and from 321 to 
330 points in respect of working class cost of living, the Company refused 
to increase the amount of D.A. Accordingly, the Union which was formed 
in October 1955, submitted a charter of demunds to the Company on the 6th 
December 1955. The present reference is the result of that, when 
conciliation failed to produce any tangible results. 


According to the Company, it is faced with serious difficulties due to the 
uncertain nature of the import policy of the Government for the pust few 
years. The result has been that the Company has been forced practically 
to cut down its import programme and under-sell its commodities. It is 
denied emphatically that that it was ever a party to the Mercantile Tribunal 
aforesaid, or did give any assurance to the workmen to make good the 
award that would be passed by the said Tribunal. On the other hand, 
the Company contends that at the time of adjudication of the dispute before 
the suid Mercantile Tribunal, the employees of the Company recorded in 
writing that there was no pending dispute between the present Company 
und its workmen. Even before that, the Company further says, there had 
been an agreement entered into between the Company and its employees in 
which dearneas allowance was put on a progressive scale according to the

rise in the cost ef living index up to a certain point. This was confirmed 
by a circular, dated Ist April 1958. Tho Company pleads its inability to 
increase the dearness allowance on the ground that it is struggling against 
q crisis. For the saine reason it is not in a position to increase either thé 
wage scales or the grades of pay. Whatever profit the Company did make 
in the past was largely due to the help the Company received from other 
sources and on having loans of capital without interest and other advantages. 
At the present time due to certain extraneous factors beyond control, the Com- 
pany has been forced to fall buck upon its own resources with the result that 
the Company finds itself in a very tight corner. It was contemplated to have 
recourse to retrenchment and drastic economy in all matters of expenses. Due 
to hard competition in the market, the Company cannot raise the prices of 
commodities with the result that it has to defray duties practically unaided. 
Regarding the Provident Fund, the Company says that it is unable to increase 
the rate. It allowed what it could permit having been to that extent under

the Company resists it on the gorund that there are slack periods when the

rush periods. To crown this, the employees have started ‘‘go slow’ 
tactics, says the Company, and it apprebends that overtime allowance would 
merely set 2 premium upon it.

Issue No. 3—Provident Fund 


Regarding the Provident Fund, the Union olaims that the rate of 
contribution should be at 10 per cent. in place of 6} per cent. of the salary, 
as at present. Besides, there should be compensation at the rate of half 
month's salary for each completed year of service for the period uncovered 
by the Provident Fund. 


The Company contends that it grants Provident Fund contribution by the 
employees and the employers at 6} per cent. of the salary only because it is 
exempted from the income-tax. It cannot increase it, and thereby increase 
the amount of income-tax. But this contention I am unable to accept 
an toto. Contribution to the extent of 6} per cent. is no doubt immune from 
the liability to pay income-tax. But that does not mean that the 
contribution cannot be higher. Lots of other companies, and even 
engiveering firms, are allowing Provident Fund contribution at a higher 
rate than 1018 6} per cent. Even the Government Provident Fund Act 
contemplates for the workers 10 per cent. as the contribution out of the 
salary of the workmen. 6} per cent. as the amount of contribution to the 
Provident Fund was originally given in the Major Engineering Tribunal’s 


Part I} THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 5, 1957 324] 
i a neers 


Award. But that has aleo been altered. So I make the Provident Fund 
contribution to be 8 per cent. of the salary of a workman having in it an 
equal share of contribution by the Company. This will come inta operation 
from the first of the month following the month when the award becomes 
operytive ~The Company should not grudge the extro amount of income- 
tux it will have to pay consequent on this small enhancement of the rate 
of contribution to the Provident Fund. It should be borne in mind that 
Provident Fund has a great salutary effect on the industry itself. It 
teaches the workmen to ae by something for the future. That also serves 
as a retiral benefit in old age. It also checks frequent turnovers which is 
a bane in most of the companies. It cuts down absenteeism. So in the 
long run the Company does not stand to lose by such contribution to the 
Provident Fund. 


For the period uncovered by the Provident Fund, there should be some 
compensation. It may be that there are many old employees who do nut 
get much benefit of the Provident Fund because of its introduction towards 
the end of. their service period. So J] grant them in lieu of Provident Fund, 
compensation at the rate of half month’s salary for each completed year of 
service just before the imtroduction of the Provident Fund system. This 
should be paid during the retirement when they leave the service as a retiral 
benefit. 


Issue Ne.4.—OQOvertime 


This relates to the claim for overtime allowance. Overtime is allowed 
under the Factories Act. As this concern is not a factory, the Company 
resists the -claim on this head. The Company is, no doubt, justified in 
that view, -But even in commercial concerns overtime allowance is 
provided for udder uwards of Tribunals. They are treated as units 
governed by the Shops and Establishments Act. So if the workmen have 
to work beyond the scheduled houra, they are entitled to get some over- 
time allowance. The scheduled hour of departure in this Company is 
9 p.m. on week days, and it is 1 p.m. on Saturday, as I get in evidence. 
For one hour after the scheduled hour of departure no overtime will he 
payable. But beyond that, for each hour of work the workmen will 
get 14 tintes their wayes,—I mean, salary and D.A. It is contended by 
the Company that the workmen are going slow, and overtime allowance 
would only encourage it further. No evidence has been placed before me 
showing that the workmen are guilty of ‘‘slow down’’ tactics. So, I do 
not see how the granting of the legitimate overtime wages would encourage 
slow down on the part of the workmen. The Company next says that there 
is slack season as well as brisk season in the business. So no overtime 
should be granted. I find no force in this contention. If there is any 
slack period, the question of overtime allowance then does not arise. But 
if during the brisk period the workmen are detained longer than the 
scheduled hours of work of the Company, why should they he deprived of 
overtime wages? They cannot be held answerable for slack and_ brisk 
business. So the contention of the Company is overruled and _ overtime 
allowunce is allowed as above.

die ich 


How is the gratuity awarded by the first Omnibus Engineering 
Tribunal by way of retirement benefit for the period uncovered by 
Provident Fund to be calculated ? 


After usual notices both parties filed written stutements, 


AWARD 


Iesue No. 1: On the question of interpretation of the award of the 
first Omnibus Engineering Tribunal, Shn J. N. Chatterjee, appearing on 
behalf of the Company, at the outset, contended that the reference was bad 
in law, and the Tribunal has no jurisdiction to entertain it. Shri Patit 
Paban Pathak, on hehalf of the Union, referred to paragraph 7 of the agree- 
ment, dated 9th February 1997, and pointed out that this issue was, by 
common consent, submitted to the Government for its reference to a 
Tribunal, Therefore, Shri Chatterjee cannot raise that objection in this 
case. Apart from the legality of the question it was contended that it would 
be improper to question a course of action settled by an agreement, which 
was binding on the parties. Shri Chatterjee, in view of the terms of the 
agreement, agreed not to press the legul objection, and did not press it. 


The question involved in the dispute is a short one. The parties before 
me hold different views, and the matter was made more complicated at the 
stuge of conciliation. Hence the necessity of an adjudication for clarificution 
of the point. This Company has introduced a Contributory Provident 
Fund, with effect from March 1949, apparently, in terms of the said award 
in reference. It had a gratuity scheme already in operation. It appears 
from the written statement of the Union, and the arguments advanced by 
the learned representatives of the parties, that the question in dispute lies 
within a narrow compass. The directions given i the Tribunal, at 
1086 112 of its award (Government publication—awards made by Major 
পা বিলিন Tribunal during 1948, Vol. 111)) relevant for our purpose, 
are: 

(i) On retirement after continuous service for not less than 2) yeara— 
Gratuity at the rate of half a month’s pay for each completed 
year of service, subject to a maximum of 15 months’ pay. 


(17) On retirement before completing 25 years’ continuous — service, 
owing to illness, old age or any other sufficient cause, with the 
written consent of the employer—Gratuity at the rate of half 
» month’s pay for each year of completed service. 


(111) For the period for which the Contributory Provident Fund has 
been in operation, the employees falling in clauses (1) and (11) 
will receive the whole amount of the employees’ contribution to 
the fund; but in calculating the gratuity payable, the period for 
which the Contributory Provident Fund has been in existence 
will be deducted from the total period of service. The maximum 
period of service for those failing in clause (i) will be deemed 
to be 30 years for the purpose of this clause. 


3244 THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 5, 1957 [Part I 
aa nr eesrecemerner een িঠা 


It is evident from the above that the award directed a method for 
calculating the gratuity payable in a case, as here, where both gratuity and 
contributory provident fund are in operation. The award decided that the 
workmen are entitled to claim only one kind of retiring benefit. Accordingly, 
it directed that the period for which the contributory provident fund has 
been in existence, will he deducted from the total period of service and 
that the maximum period of service for employees falling in clause (i) will 
be deemed to be 30 years for the purpose of-clause (ii1). The parties have 
no difference of opinion regarding this. ‘They have differences only on the 
question whether the gratuity should be calculated on the basis of the 
wagetrate prevailing prior to the introduction of the provident fund, or, 
us at the date of the retirement. The Company’s case is that since the 
employees are not entitled to double benefits, of both gratuity and provident 
fund, on retirement, under the award, it is only reasonable to hold that 
the wages should be calculated for payment of gratuity at the rate 
prevalent before the introduction of the contributory provident fund, i.e., 
at the rute paid in February 1949. I have considered the arguments 
advanced by the learned representatives of both sides, and have also 
carefully considered the relevant portion of the award, and I find that: 


(1) the award does not say that the wages should be calculated at 
the rates as they stood in February 1949, i.e., at the rate just 
before the introduction of the scheme of the _ contributory 
provident fund, 


(11) the only direction made in this respect is that in calculating 
gratuity payable for the period, for which the contributory 
provident fun has been in existence, that period shall he 
deducted from the total period of service, 


(ili) it would not We proper to make any anticipation, assumption or 
surmise in this respect, 


(iv) the payment of retiring henefit is dependent on retirement and no 
one can either claim it or get it before he actually retires from 
service. Therefore, the only relevant date in this connection is 
the date of retirement. 


It is, therefore, reasonable to conclude that the retiring benefits should 
be calculated on the basis of rates of wages as they exist at the time of 
retirement. This view appears to get some support from the earlier 
provisions made, at page 111 of the said award, regarding the method of 
calculation of gratuity under a gratuity scheme for small companies, 
employing less than 100 men. There it is stated as followa: 


“Gratuity is to be calculated on the basis of average substantive pay 
during the last 12 months of service.”’ 


This seems to me to be the implication of the directions given at page 112 
of the award, This is also in conformity with the universal practice, which 
prevails everywhere, where similar payments are made on retirement. It is, 
therefore, not reasonable to think that the award by implication directs 
payment of gratuity, calculated on the basis of average substantive pay as 
it stood before the date of the introduction of the contributory provident 
fund, It would be fallacious to say or suggest that, on retirement, the 
dute, on which the gratuity system ceased to he in operation, ia to be taken 
into consideration for the purpose of payment of retiral benefits, and not 
the date, when an emplovee actually retired. It would he equally wrong to 
anv that for payment of gratuity the rates of wages, as they stood, year 
after year, before the period when the contributory provident fund came 
into existence should he taken into reckoning. 


Birt I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 5, 1957 3245 


Ee ee Ee = die 
oi ame ip eI TD TERESI ০০ সাপ 


In my opinion, gratuity 1s to be calculated under the award in question, 
on the basis of average substantive pay during the last 12 months of service 
immediately before the date of actual retirement. ١ answer the issue 
accordingly. 
This is my award.

AWARD 


This ia a case arising out of termination of services of certain employees 
as surplus by the Chhayabani Cinema. 


The case of the Union is that the aforesaid Cinema Company had no 
fixed terms ond conditions of service. The employees therefore formed a 
union, This enraged the company who started victimising employees one 
after another. These 6 workmen were victimised purely for their trade 
union activities and the termination of their services is unjust and mala 
fide and they should be reinstated. 


The Company denies the allegations in the written statement of the 
union and its case is that the Cinema House was opened on 26th March 
1956 and the employees concerned were employed on a temporary basis and 
they had to be retrenched because the Company was suffering heavy losses 
and could not afford to retain these workmen in services. Other objections 
in the written statement are not pressed. The Company has emphatically 
denied the allegation of victimisation. 


This Cinema House was started on 26th March 1956. There is no 
dispute that these workmen were employed on a temporary basis since the 
formation of the Company. It is admitted by the office Secretary (Sibnath 
Chatterjee) of the Bengal Motion Pictures Employees’ Union that the 
financial condition of the Company is not good. This Secretary has simply 
stuted that these workmen were victimised because of their trade union 
activities. Beyond his bare verbal stutement there is nothing else to 
corroborate it. Curiously enough some of the disimssed workmen who were 
present in Court were not examined. Thus there is no evidence worth the 
name to substantiate the allegation of victimisation. On the other hand, 
as admitted by the office Secretary, the financial condition of the Company 
is not good. The Proprietor also produced Account Books before the Court 
and examined two other witnesses to prove the condition of the Company and 
I have no reason to disbelieve them. I am therefore satisfied that the 
Company 3s not in an affluent position to retain these workmen in their 
services. It is also in evidence that the Proprietor raised a loan to the 
tune of Rs. 15,000 for starting the Cinema House. If the business were 
brisk we would expect that the Company would certainly maintain the full 
complement of the initial staff. This being the nature of the evidence and 
there being no proof of ill-feeling between the Company and workmen, I 
cannot hold that these workmen were victimised simply for their trade union 
activities, There is also no proof that these workmen vigorously took up 


7۸31 Ij) THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 5, 1957 3247 
ee SS SSS sss سم سے سس س ےے وو‎ 
trade union activities so as to alienate the sympathy of the Proprietor. 
The Company knows its financial conditions quite well and obviously for 
rationalisation of the staff and economy the Company was obliged to effect 
thia, retrenchment and the: Court should not ordinarily interfere with the 
আগে of the Company. It is a prima facie right of the Management to 
determine its labour force and the Management would be the best judge to 
determine who would become surplus on the ground of rationalisation. 
economic or other reasons on which retrenchment can be sustained and if 
the Management acting in a bena fide manner effects the retrenchment, the 
Court should not interfere with the retrenchment which the Management 
may effect [৭৪ the case of Viswamitra Press reported in 1952 L.A.C., 
pages 20-33]. Then there is one other fact that criminal cases are pending 
against some of these workmen and some are absconding even now. In 
the present state of things even if there be orders for reinstatement of 
some of them they cannot be expected to venture to appear publicly tu 
take up the job. The Court in the circumstances cannot interfere with 
the termination of services of these employees which therefore stands 
justified. 


These workmen ure not entitled to reinstatement but they must, how- 
ever, he awarded the retrenchment benefits under section 25F of the 
Industrial Disputes Act as they have been in continuous service for not less 
thun a year. Having regard to the present financial condition of the 
Company I award these workmen only one month’s wages in lieu of notice 
and 15 days’ wages for the completed year of service under the Company. 


Another point was taken though not pressed during trial, namely, that 
this is an individual dispute becuuse these workmen are not members of 
any union but this point has ultimately abandoned. O.P.W. 2 has admitted 
in crosa-examination that the dismiased workmen are members of the union 
and the office Secretary has also deposed that some of the dismissed work- 
men are members of the Bengal Motion Pictures Employees’ Union who 
have espoused their cause. So there is no substance in the contention of 
the Company that thia is an individual dispute. 


The Company will therefore pay these workmen their wages for a month 
and au half within a month of the pubheation of this award. 
This is my award.

in the matter of a complaint under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes

Cycle (Factory No. 2) Mazdoor Union, 130 Narikeldanga Main Road, 
Caloutta-11, against the aforesaid company has arisen was made under 
Government order No. 4712Dis./D0/11L-210/55, dated the 28th 
September 1955. (Case No. 7 of 1957 under section 33A.) 


BEFORE THE SIXTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL 


PRESENT : 
ٛت8‎ SAILESH SENGUPTA, Judge, Sixth Industrial Tribunal. 
For the Company: Shri Sailesh Sen, Advocate. 
For the workmen: Shri Parimal Das, President of the Union. 


~ 


This application under section 383A of the Industrial Disputes Act was 
preferred by three workmen who are under suspension under on order made 
by the India Cycle Manufacturing Co., Ltd., on 26th July 1988. 


Charge-sheets were drawn up against these workers and several others 
on various heads. Qne of the incidents in which these workers were 
supposed to have been involved was riotous disturbance in the Company's 
factory. ‘The workers’ case is that they were perfectly innocent and have 
been wrongly placed under suspension. No enquiry was held 11060 the 
allegations made aguinst them. They requested the management time and 
aguin to 1116 the suspension and permit them to resume their duty. The 
management turned a deaf ear to their importunities. 


The Company submitted in its written statement that following disturb- 
ances in the factory these three workers were suspended pending enquiry 
into the charges. No enquiry could however be held us they did not turn 
up. The order of suspension had been passed before commencement of 
proceedings before the Tribunal. There can be hence no contravention of 
section 33 as at the date of suspension no proceeding under the Industrial 


Drsputes Act was pending. 


There was disturbance in the factory on the 25th of July 1955. On 
the next day charge-sheets were drawn up against a number of workers 
including these three men. Exhibit 2 is a specimen of the charge-sheets. 
These workers could not he served with charge-sheets before November of 
that year as letters addressed to them by registered post came back 
undelivered [wde Exts. B, 1301) and 1302)], They were however traced 
through the help of the Union President and a date for enquiry was fixed. 
The evidence of P.W. 1 is that they had attended the enquiry and had 
denied the charges. Manmotho Babu who held the enquiry asked them 
to come on another date. No further enquiry was however held. The 
evidence of the Company’s witness O.P.W. 1 is that Ratan Sen and 
Jagadish Mitra attended some day in February 1956 when he was holding 
enquiry but they refused to reply to questions and took up a highly defiant 
attitude. He asked the men to go away. The President of the Union 
was informed and requested to be present at another enquiry that was 


Part I} THE CAIAUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 5, 1957 3251‏ 
وےےےےس-۱۱ح و 6ڑ ےے سے سے سے سے سے سے ے سے گے سے 


proposed to be held later. He did not however come. In the result no 
enquiry could be held. 


The order of suspension was in fact passed hefore proceedings under 
the Act had started. There could hence be no contravention of section 33 
at that stage. The point for consideration now is whether thereafter the 
suspension took the form of punishinent. Learned Advocate for the 
Company relied on the case decided by their Lordships of the Supreme 
Court which is reported in 1957 1, L.L.J., page 17. Their Lordships held 
that suspension without pay even for an indefinite period pending enquiry 
or pending permission of the appropriate Tribunal to dismiss workman 
would not be punishment requiring permission of the Tribunal. Though 
this particular order of suspension was not punishment at its inception, 
circumstunces gave a different turn later on. O.P.W. 1 admitted that all 
hopes of enquiry had been given up. Last attempt to hold enquiry was 
made in February 1956. Since then the matter is at o standstill. The 
workers applied more than once to the management for permission to 
return to duty but no reply was given. Their prayer was not granted. 
The dictum of their Lordships of the Supreme Court relied on by the learned 
advocate is of no assistance to him as after the idea of holding enquiry 
was given up, the suspension cannot be said to have been pending enquiry 
or permission of any Tribunal. This suspension assumed a_ different 
complexion and cannot but be regarded as punishment. ‘I'he workers are 
deprived of their wages and no indication was given that they will be 
taken back, I'he Company by its attitude demonstrated that relationship 
of master and servant had ceased to exist. This change in the churacter 
of suspension took place during the pendency of the reference proceeding. 
Accordingly, section 33 must be held to have been contravened. 


Learned Advocate for the Company argued that refusal to employ these 
men might be construed as lock-out as defined in the Act. Lock-out 
implies continuance of relationship of master and servant. The manage- 
ment does fot however regard these people as their workmen. Neither are 
they paid their wages nor are they called upon for performance of duty. 
Strictly speaking this cannot be taken as lock-out, for a lock-out 18 
generally adopted as a security measure and not on account of any offence 
committed by the workmen. A lock-out would also be punishment if the 
refusal to employ is attributable to any offence or misconduct. In my 
view therefore though suspension in this case did not contravene section 22 
at its commencemenf, it did so when the Company decided not to hold an 
enquiry and to let matters remain hanging indefinitely. 10 my thinking 
they are entitled to relief on the finding that by the course of events this 
paricular suspension wus converted into punishment by the final decision 
of the management not to hold any enquiry, and not to allow them to 
return to duty. The application is accordingly allowed. The manage- 
ment is directed to allow them to join their duty and to pay their ا‎ 
from March 1956 till the date they are taken back, which must be 
accomplished within fifteen days from the date of publication of the award 
in the Calcutta Gazette.

An industrial کس‎ in respect of the following issues, between

Bengal, Labour Department, order No, 676-I.R./D/11L-274/55, dated the 
4th March 1957. 


Both the parties filed written statements, adduced evidence, oral and 
documentary and advanced arguments in the case. 


(1) Whether the workers are entitled to receive any additional bonus 
over and above what has already been paid for the year 1064-7 
If so, at what rate? 


(2) Whether the termination of services of Shri Makhan Lal Das was 
justified? ‘To what relief is he entitled? 


FINDINGS 


Issue No. 2: The services of P.W.1 Shri Makhan Lal Das were 
terminated with effect from 26th April 1956. The Company’s case is that 
this was done as there was no work for him, i.e., for dearth of work. Shri 
Das, in his evidence before this Tribunal, said that he did not slesire to go 


Part I} THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 7٦ 3253 
0ٹ ِ ,00080۳ مس مصییسسمس 9٭د‎ 


back to work, and claimed compensation for retrenchment. He frankly 
stated that there was no work in office for him, and that in the matter of 
retrenchment, the Company followed the normal rule of “last come, first 
go’, Hia elder brother, the only other Polisher in the service of the 
Company, who entered service 8 or 9 years before him, remains in service. 
Shri Das is an ordinary member of the Union and, therefore, the Union 
did not rightly press the claim for reinstatement on the ground of victimisa- 
tion. We take it that the retrenchment, in his case, is justified, and Shri 
Das is entitled to retrenchment relief. In fact, the Company, in_ its 
letter (Eat. ©), dated 26th April 1956, offered him viz., (i) earned wages 
up to date, (ii) one month’s pay in lieu of notice, and (iii) retrenchment 
conipensation at the rate of 15 days’ for each year of service. The offer 
was considered inadequate and refused. The Union further demanded 
gratuity in terms of Shri M. C. Banerji’s award and_ retrenchment 
compensation at the statutory rate for 32 years of service, i.e., for a total 

eriod of service not only before this Company but also before its predecessor 
in the business. Shri M. C. Banerji’s award was published in the Caleutta 
Gazette on the 14th Muy 1953. Gratuity, it appears, is payable ouly on 
retirement from service and on death, and not in a case like this, when the 
services of an employee are terminated by way of retrenchment on 1119 
ground of dearth of work. There is nothing in the award to supwort a 
claim for gratuity on retrenchment over and above the statutory ‘ompensa- 
tio: on this account. The claim for gratuity should, therefore, fail. 


P.W. 1 Shri Das said that he was in service of this Company for the 
last 32 years before his retrenchment. 11٦ did not get any appointment 
letter but he proved a certificate (Ext. 1) which he received from a former 
partner Mr. Binns of this business. The certificate is dated 15th April 
1947. In it, it is stated that Shri Das, when he was a young lad, entered 
service of this business over 20 years ago, that is to any Shri Das joined 
this husinese while a young man more thap 20 years before 15th April 1947. 
He has put in another 9 years of service before his retrenchment. That 
makes a total of 29 years, in place of 32 years, spoken of by him in his 
deposition. There is no evidence on the Company’s side to show that this 
evidence of Shri Das is untrue. That he continued in service till his 
retrenchment without any break is also extablished in this case. There hans 
been, it is ulleged by the Company, two changes of employers, viz., (1) when 
Shri Khemka purchased this partnership business from Mr. Biuns and 
Mr. Deeks and (11) when the business was converted into a public limited 
company aa it 1s at this day. Apart from the brief recital of this fact in 
Shri শি. C. Datta Gupta’s award (Ext. B), dated the 12th June 1948, there 
ig no evidence on the Company’s side to show when and how the original 
business was transferred to this Company. That there had been a transfer 
was partly conceded by Shri Das, but as a worker he was not interested in 
the change. His service was uninterrupted and the service conditions 
remained as they existed before, with a very slight alteration in hours of 
attendance. He continued in service for over 29 years in this business. It 
appears from the Ext. B that the business is still being carried on 01) the 
name and style of ‘‘Cook & 79156514100. with the goodwill and assets of 
the partnership business. It is, therefore, idle to talk on the basis of & 
finding, with reference to a case of another employee, in Shri Datta Gupta’s 
award, that the service of Shri Das should be taken to commence only from 
the date of incorporation of this Company into a limited company im 1946. 
The findings on any particular issue in the award of Shri 8. ©. Datta Gupta 
cannot be taken to be relevant and binding upon this Tribunal in a different 
case. Shri 9.0. Sen, Advocate for the Company, also did not contend that 
they were binding in the present case. Shri M. C. Banerji had to consider 


3254 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 56, 1957 [Parr I 


this question in g general way in answering the issue of পা in his 
award. He came to the conclusion that the Company should take into uccuunt 
the services rendered by workmen to his predecessor in title for the purpose 
of calculating gratuity, where there is continuity of service. I nm also of 
the sume opinion. Whether the services continued under different employers, 
without break, is a question of fact which J] have answered in favour of the 
workmen. There is nothing in law which should support the contention of 
Shri Sen that with every change of employer the service must be held to be 
terminated whether, in fact, they were or not so. In this case, Shri Sen 
referred to the provisions of section 24h(FF) of the Industrial Disputes Act 
in support of his contention that Shri Das was not entitled to any retrench- 
ment compensation for the period previous to the date of the incorporation 
of the Company into a public limited company. Admittedly, the services 
of Shri Das were terminated on account of dearth of work, that is to say 
he was found te be surplus to requirements in the office. It is not the 
Company’s case that his service was terminated on account of any change 
of ernployers fo: transfer of business. Therefore, section 25(FF) either 
before or after amendment has no application here. Neither the provisions 
of the said section by implication supporta Shri Sen's contention. In my 
opinion, a contrary view seems to be implied in section 25(F¥) of the 
Industria] Disputes Act. Shri Das is entitled to retrenchment compensa- 
tion for the total period of service done in this business, namely for 29 

enrs. He 3s entitled to 144 months’ pay at the rate of Ra. 71 per month 
8 in Ext C). He is further entitled to Rs. 61-9 on account of earned 
wages and Ra. 71, i.e., an amount of one month’s pay in lieu of notice 
(as in Ext. C). Shri Das did not ask, as stated already, for reinstatement 
and, therefore, he is not entitled to it. The Company will pay him the 
said 110101111 of compensation, etec., under this award within a month from 
the date of its publication. I answer the issue accordingly. 


issue No. 1; The Company paid its workers 15 days’ basic nay as 
bonus for the year 1954-55. The UWnion demands an additional nmount of 
1? months’ wages os bonus in addition to what was already paid. The 
Company’s case is that the workers are not entitled to it and that the 
amount already paid was not only adequate but generous too. 


Shri Sen relied upon the balance sheet Ext. A series. Income Tax 
Assessment Order, Ext. E and o chart under the Full Bench Formula to 
show that after deducting the prior charges under it there is a deficit of 
of Rs. 15,483 and no aurplus profit for distribution among the workers. 
Balance sheet (Ext. A) for the relevant year shows that the net profit is 
Rs. 60.689-5-10, There is nothing on the Union’s side to challenge either 
the halance sheet or the chart drawn up under the Full Bench Formula 
to be wrong. Additional bonus is claimed out of profit for the year in 

uestion and as there is no surplus profit available under Full Hench 
‘ormula, after deducting the admitted prior charges, the workers are not 
entitle to any additional bonus in the year in question.

AWARD 


This is a complaint made by as many as 20 persons. Their case is that 
they were ull workmen of Messrs. Leonard Biermans Societe Anonyme— 
Opposite Party, but the Opposite Party during the pendency of the aforesaid 
proceedings before this Tribunal wrongfully dismissed them without the

The Company—Opposite Party—contested the application. It is the 
contention of the Company that the present application must fail in linine,

because the petitiqners were never the workmen of the Company. The 
version of the Company is that all these persons were allowed to work as 
apprentices in the ‘Company’s factory by Mr. Palaria at the instance of the 
mortgagee Company—National Playing Card Company, Ltd., which 
financed this Company to the extent of more than one lakh against hypo- 
thecation of some of its plants, machineries and other assets. Mr. Palaria 
had to be appointed as the Factory Manager.of this Company for protection 
of the interests of the National Playing Card Company, Ltd., in the plants 
and machineries, etc., mortgaged to the said Company. When in the 
beginning of January 1957 Mr. Potti took over charge of this Company, 
he came to know of the position of the prétent petitioners, and 55160 the 
mortgagee Company to withdraw them from the Company's factory. 
Accordingly, the petitioners were not allowed to work when they upproached. 


The parties have adduced evidence—both oral and documentary. 
After giving my anxious and careful consideration to the evidence and 
circumstances, I feel no doubt or hesitation in saying that these 20 persons 
are to he deemed to be workmen of the present Company. It did not 
matter much whether they were taken in or appointed by Mr Palaria at the 
instance of the mortgagee sean” et ا‎ Playing Card Co., Ltd. It 
is clear from the materials on record that Mr. Palaria wag acting as oo 
Manager of this Company at the relevant time. Even if it be assume 
that these persons were taken in by Mr. Palaria at the instance of the 
mortgagee Company, it must be held that they were taken for and on behalf 
of this Company. The present Company will be certainly bound by what 
was done through its agency or by its agents. The stubborn fact remains 
that Mr. Palaria while acting as Factory Manager of this Company, took 
these persons in its factory, and that they were emploved in the said 
factory, and not in the concern of National Playing Card Company, Ltd. 
It has also been proved that these persons while employed, used to get their 
pay or wages from the present Company, and that the Pay Register for 
them as well as for other workers of this Company was the same. Then 
again, it appears from Ext. A that gate pass was issued to one of these 
persons, namely Shri Shyam Sundar Joshi by this Company, and it was 
signed hy the above Factory Manager. So, there is no escape from the 
conclusion that these persons were appointed for and on hehalf of this 
Company. Accordingly, I hold that these persons were the workmen of 
the present Company. 


Next point for consideration is whether there was contravention of 
section 33. Tt has been admitted by the Company in its statement in reply 
that these persons were not allowed to work, when they called on the 
Company's factory on 7th January 1957 (vide paragraph 6). It is also a 
fact that since then they have not been allowed to resume their duties in 
the factory. So, the position comes to this that during the pendency of the 
original reference before this Tribunal, all these workmen were discharged 
by the Company without taking permission from the Tribunal. An 
argument has been advanced by the learned lawyer of the Company that 
these persons were taken in as apprentices, and as such no permission of the 
Tribunal was required for terminating their services. I would say 
straightway that there is no merit or substance in this argument. A pro- 
bationer or a temporary workman comes within the definition of “workman” 
in section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act. Even an apprentice is 
included in the definition. It is well settled that even a temporary workman 
is entitled to the protection afforded by sections 33 and 33A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act. Merely because the employee was only an 
apprentice or a temporary workman, the emplover could not. in: diaregurd 
to the provisions of section 33, discharge him without the permission of the 


Pant I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 6, 1997 3257 


Tribunal. For this authority, | rely on the decision of the Labour Appellate 
Tribunal of India reported in 1967(1) 15... page 93. 


So, the last point for consideration is about the nferits. It has been 
held by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India that not only the fact of 
contravention, but also the merits of the case must be gone into, and the 
mere fact of contravention will not help an employee. The scope of investi- 
gation made by a Tribunal under section 33A into the merits of discharge 
or dismissal is exactly the same ‘‘as if it were a dispute referred to it” by 
an independent reference under section 10 of the Act. Therefore, a duty 
ia cast upon the Tribunal to gnter into the merits of the case and to give 
the employees appropriate consequential relief. It is an established 
principle of law that where a Court or Tribunal is called upon to decide a 
matter, it must decide in a complete way, in order that the rights of the 
parties may be settled. These persons, who have been working in the 
Company’s factory were not allowed to work when they کر‎ on 7th 
January 1957, and this fact stands admitted. The burden of proof is on the 
employer to show that their discharge or termination of service was 
justified. On a consideration of the entire evidence, I find that the Company 

an not succeeded in discharging the burden that lay heavily on it. The 
only plea that was taken on behalf of the Company is that these persons 
were not the workmen of the Company, nor were they ever employed by it. 
But that plea has not been accepted by the Tribunal for reasons already 
stated. So, the point boils down to this fact that the present petitioners 
were discharged wrongfully from their service. They were refused work 
without any rhyme or reason. There was also violation of the principles of 
natura] justice. So, the discharge or termination of service of the peti- 
tioners cannot be upheld. 


The question next is about the relief, which the petitioners are entitled 
to. JT am of the opinion that they are entitled to reinstatement and to be 
restored to their respective jobs in the factory of this Company. Even the 
fact that they were apprentices or probationers does not stand in the way of 
their being লিসা No circumstances have been established for deny- 
ing them relief of reinstatement. 


So far as back wages are concerned, I am not disposed to awurd the same, 
because it is alleged that these persons were taken as upprentices. IT refrain 
from expressing any opinion in the present complaint as to whether the 
present petitioners were really taken in as apprentices or temporary work- 
men. This point may be pursued, if necessary, at the time of hearing of 
the original reference which is still pending. 

In the result, the application is allowed. The petitioners must be 
reinstated without any break in their service. They shall report themselves 
for duty in the factory of the Company within 10 duys from the date of 
publication of this award in the Calcutta Gazette. They will not, however, 
get any back wages or allowances. 


This is my award.

AWARD 


The case of the Union is that these eleven workmen concerned were 
laid off for a month from 28th November 1956 to 27th December 1956 
unjustly and were not given any wages for the period. This was purely 
due to the Trade Union activities of the workmen which the Company did 
not like. So non-payment of due compensation for the period they were 
laid off is purely an unfair labour practice. The Union therefore claims 
due wages of these workmen for the period of lay-off. 


The Company in their written statement contends that these workmen 
were laid off for valid reasons as there were no works in the factory for 
these workmen to do during the period they were laid off. Other allegations 
in the written statement of the Company are not pressed during trial. 


DECISION 


The trial in this case has been simplified. Admittedly these workmen 
were laid off for the period from 28th November 1956 to 27th December 
1956. There is no dispute that the lay-off was justified. The Union made 
no attempt to show that this lay-off was unjust. That being so, the work- 
men are entitled to 50 per cent. of the wages for 26 days during the period 
of lay-off minus the wages for the weekly holidays that intervened. Both 
parties agree that these workmen are entitled to 60 per cent. of their 
wages for 26 days during the period of lay-off. 


The Company must pay the aforesaid wages, 1.e., 60 per cent. of the 
wages for 26 days to the workmen according to their respective wages 
within a month of the publication of this award. 


This 1s my award. 
Dictated and corrected by me.

The issues as contained in the schedule to the order of reference ure as

(1) Wages and dearness allowance.

AWARD 


The case of the Union as stuted in the written statement is that the 
workmen employed in this concern are required to work all the days of the 
week, and they work 14 hours a day. The mimimum pay for a workman 
is Rs, 56 per month. There is no dearness allowance, no esta no holiday

(1) Minimum basic pay of 15. 90 and dearness allowance of Rs. 40 
per month. 


(ii) 192 working hours in a month.

casual leave in a year. 


(iv) Gratuity at the rate of 15 days’ wages for each year of service, and 
sickness benefit on the basis of Employees’ State Insurance Act. 


The Company contests the demands of the Union. In reply, it states 
that it is a very small concern, and employs only about 8 workmen. The 
conditions of service of the workmen employed in this concern, their wages 
and other privileges are in line with those of similar concerns in the locality. 
The grievances of the Union are fantastic, and should be rejected. It is 
further stated that out of the 8 workmen, 6 were dismissed for misconduct, 
and the remaining 2 were given cliance to work, if they gave undertaking 
of good conduct. One of them, Shri Protap Tewari, gave such undertaking

Now I would take up the issues, one by one. 


issue No. 1 


This concern deals in lime, brick and surki for which coolies and ۵6ء‎

present concern and need no revision. No case has also been made out for 
giving separate dearness allowance. J)earness allowance is allowed only to 
supplement the basic waye. But here in the present case, the basic wage 
that is being paid to the workers is quite adequate and fair. So, no separate 
dearness allowance can be fixed. Hence, the demand of the Union in this 
respect is refused. No document was produced before the Tribunal on 
behalf of the concern to show that wages at the rates as deposed to by

issue No, 2
