considering the nature of business of the concern and also the number of 
workmen employed by it. If this concern is to grant such paid arnual

stand-still. So, the existing leave and holidays appear to be adequate and 
auficient for the workers of a concern like the present one, particularly 
regard being had to the nature of its business. This concern must continue 
to give such leave and festival holidays to its workers, and the workers 
should remain satisfied with this. This issue is thus disposed of. 


From the evidence of 0.P.W. 1, Shri Purna Chandra Parel, it appears

to disturb the existing working hours. The existing working hours are fixed 
as deposed to by O.P.W. 1 Shri Parel. This concern must see that the 
workers are not compelled to work beyond the said working hours. 
However, if the concern needs their services beyond the existing working 
hours, it should pay overtime allowance to them. This issue is decided 
accordingly.

This demand appears to be not only unreasonable but also fantastic. In. 
such a small concern no retiral benefit in the shape of gratuity as claimed 
can be introduced. So, this demand 18 refused. 


It 1s not necessary for this Tribunal to make any provision for sickness 
benefit in view of the operation of the Employees’ State Insurance Act. 
This issue 1s decided accordingly. 


Regarding the demand for ‘nlleged arrears of wages nos contended on 
behalf of the Union, I may say that it cannot be entertained as this point 
is not covered by the issues as framed. Moreover, the claim for recovery 
of arrears of wages cannot be entertained by an Industrial Tribunal. The 
remedy on this score lies elsewhere.

By order No. 6299-1.K./ 1D / 111-326 '56, 19151 the 12th December 1990, 
the Government of West Bengal, in the Labour Department, referred under 
section 160) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the industrial dispute 
between Mesers. Kusum Brick Works, post office and village Makhala, 
distriet Hooghly, and their workmen represented by Bally Khal ٣اا‎ ٤(۱ 
Masdoor Union, 11 Bally Station Road, post office Bally, Hooghly, regard- 
ing the matters specified in the achedule, to the Third وا‎ Tribunal 
constituted under section 7 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, by notifica- 
tion No, b92Dis.;D/121-5/52, dated the 23rd February 1953, for adjydica- 
tion 

< After usual summons the parties put in appearance and filed their 
written statements. The pleadings were completed on 26fh Maveh 1957. 
The parties were thereafter directed to file lists of documents. Then after 
adjournmenta the case was fixed for hearing on 3lat July 1957. 


3. The matter of dispute as stated in the schedule to the order of 
reference is a4 follows: 


The amount that the boatmen are entitled to as their lagal dues. 


Bally Khal Entakhola Mazdoor Union on behalf of one Majhi and five 
daries sought to recover a sum of Ra. 1,122 said to be in arrears for supply 
of sand to the brick-field on piece-rate system. It was said that there was an 
ugreement between the majhi and the management to the effect that the 
majhi would supply sand in his own bout No. ©-8747 to the brickfield during 
the season ot the rate of Rs. 2-6 per dari for 11710001705 of sand and at Rs.4-12 
for the majhi aud 2 onnas as sand tax per ton. Accordingly it was said 
that sand was supplied on different dates from 4th November 1954 to 13th May 
190; that they received advances against the said supply from time to time 
und that the aforesaid sum of Rs. 1,122 was in arrear. Kusum Brick 
Works, on the other hand, denied liability and pleaded that the status of 
the 17719111103 und the daries was that of independent contractors and not of 
workmen and that the State Government wus not competent to refer the 
dispute for adjudication under section 10. On the date of hearing on 
')181 July 1957 the learned Advoeate for the Company intimated that he 
had no instructions from his client. The case was accordingly taken up 
for er-parte hearing under rule 15 of the Bengal Industrial Dispute Rules. 
The Union examined the boatman Shri Banshi Majhi besides proving khata 
(Ext. 1). On the evidence and circumstances it does not appear that majhi 
und the daries were workmen within the definition of that term in section 
2(s) 01 the Act. The supply of sand, if any, it appears from the evidence 
wus 0010৬ purely on the basis of contract and that there was no relation of 
master and servant between the parties. The principal requirement of the 
contract of service is the right of the master in some reasonable sense to 
control the method of doing the work. In the present case the evidence 
shows that the majhi was to supply sand at the stipulated rate and the 
owner of the brickfield had nothing to do in the manner of execution of the 
said work. Tho majhi, according to his own showing, was the owner of the 
boat in which the sand was supplied and it was he who employed the duries. 
The Company did not employ any of them but was merely concerned to get 
the supply and the majhies and daries had the full liberty to do their work 
as they liked. The contract was not one of service but for services. ٣ 
a contract for services the work, although done for the business, is not inte- 
grated into it but is only accessory to it. In such a case the employers need 
only see if the work has been done according to specifications and within 


Part I] THE CALCTTITA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 5, 1957 3267 


the given time, and the men engaged are not really employees; while under 
a contract of service;-a mpn is employed us part af the business, and his 
work is done us an integral part. of the business. In tho present case the 
evidence shows that none of the majhies and the daries was so employed. 
Merely because the men were to be paid on piece-rate basis, thia would not 
convert them into the category of “‘workmen’’, when the evidence reveals 
that the owner of the brickfield had no power of supervision and control at 
any stages of the work from beginning to end. So, on the evidence I find 
that there was no relation of employer and employees between the parties 
and that the men were independent contractors. It, therefore, follows that 
the reference is incompetent. Besides, a claim solely for recovery of arrears 
as here, cannot be an industrial dispute within the meaning of section 2(k) 
of the Act, In.this view of the matter the Tribunal has no jurisdiction ta 
enter into ths reference. 


It is awarded accordingly.

For the Company: Shr 8S. (×× Bhanja Chowdhury, ..L.B., Labour 
Adviser, Howrah Manufacturers’ Association, 


The original reference, out of which this application under section ۸ 
arises, was made to this Tribunal by the Government of West Bengal, 
Labour Department, under its order No. 3144Dis./1D/107.-98/56, dated 
th July 1946. The said reference was disposed of by this Tribunal on 
Oth December 1956, and the award has been published in the Calcutta 
Gazette, dated January 3, 1957. 


AWARD 


It is the ense of the workman concerned, Shri Dhananjoy Chakrabarty, 
that he was a workman in the Moulding Department of Messrs. Bose 
Brothers—opposite party—but on 7th August 1957 while the main reference 
wos pending before thia Tribunal, he was discharged by the (‘umpany— 
opposite parly—without the express permission of the Tribunal. So, it is 
contended that section 798 of the Industrial Disputes Act has been contra- 
vened thereby. 1) is further alleged that the said discharge has been illegal 
and unjustified. So, remstatement with back wages has heen claimed. 


The application was contested by the Company—opposite party. The 
main contention of the opposite party is that the applicant—Shri Dhananjoy 
Chakrabarty—is not a workman of the Company, but he was employed 
under Shri Jaladhar Singh, who is a contractor under them. ‘That being 
as, the present application should fail in limine. 


is very curious that the petitioner himself, who made this apphuwation,‏ :ا 
haa not appeared before the Tribunal to Wepose. As a petitioner, he should‏ 
have turned up before the Tribunal to give evidence. The Union, which‏ 
represented the petitioner in this case, examined its Joint Secretary—Shrt‏ 
Satven Das. But the evidence of Shri Das is not at all helpful. He‏ 
coull not make any positive statement that Shri Dhananjoy Chakrabarty‏ 
was not employed under the contractor, Shri Jaladhar Singh. The‏ 
Company, on the other hand, has examined the said contractor and has‏ 
produced documentary evidence to show that Shri Dhananjoy Chakrabarty‏ 
was employed under the said contractor and not under the Company.‏ 
O.P.W. 1—Shri Jaladhar Singh, who is contractor of the Company—has‏ 
لت deposed on orth that he was an independent contractor, and that‏ 
Dhananjoy Chakrabarty was employed under him and not under the‏ 
Company He has further stated that he used to exercise control and‏ 
supervision over Shri Dhananjoy Chakrabarty while employed undor hin,‏ 
and that the Company—opposite party—had no concern with him in this‏ 


Part I} THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 6, 1957 9269 


Sp, 


respect. He has also deposed that he used to pay wages to Shri Chakrabarty. 
The bills produced and proved by this contractor as also the attendance 
register, which are marked Fxts. A-serics und B-series, respectively, gu to 
prove unmistakably the version of the contractor as correct. ‘There 18 no 
rebutting evidence on the side of the applicant. In the cireumstances, I 
find nu justification for not accepting the oral and documentary evidence as 
adduced on behalf of the a gree party. So, on a consideration of the 
evidence as it stands, [ hold that Shri Dhananjoy Chakrabarty was not a 
workman of the Company—opposite party ,—but he was emp oyed under 
the coutractor—Shri Jaladhar Singh. That being so, it must be held that 
thure wus no relationship of employer and workman between the opponite 
part, and the applicant. The essential condition of a person being a 
‘“scorkman’’ as defined in section 2(8) of the Act is that he should be employ- 
el to do the work in an industry, that is, there should be employment of 
his by the employer and there should be the relationship between employer 
and him as between employer and employee or master and servant. For 
the reasons stated above, the question of contravention of section 33 does not 
Grise in the present case, and as such the application must foil in 16 
It is accordingly ordered that the application be rejected.

The case of the Union is that Shri R. C. Bhattacharjee, an Assistant 
Chemist in the employment of Messrs. Kilburn & Co., Ltd., since 13th 
September 1948, was discharged from his service all on a sudden on 
4th June 1956 on the ground that the Company had no confidence in him. 
There was no charge-sheet, nor was any enquiry held. The Company 
offered no opportunity to this workman to explain his conduct. 'Thus 
the discharge of the workman is unjust, illegal mala fide and an unfair 
dabour practice. The Union seeks reinstatement of the workman with 
other reliefs. 


The Company controverts the allegations in the written statement of 
the Union and resists the claim of the Union on the following grounds, 
enter alta: 


That the Kilburn’s Employees’ Union hns no locus standi to

the technical staff is nc member of the Kilbuen’s Employees’ Union; that 
the workman was engaged in experimental work in connection with the 
manufacture of disinfectants under the name of “Ail-Rao.’’: that the 
Company received information that the workman owned or was connected 
with a manufacturing concern “Bhattacharjee Cheimcal Works” of dis- 
infectant which wos being sold under the name “Bac-Kil’’: that the 
Company has in their contemplation various Wevelopments and iit was 
essential in the interests of Company’s existing business to prevent 
leakage of trade informations for protecting Company’s business. In the 
circumstances the Company discharged this workman who was given

DECISION 


In addition to the point referred to this Court for determination, 
another tok arises, namely, whether this is nn industrial dispute. This 
point will be taken up after the point of reference is first determined. 


The moin question is whether the discharge of this workman in justi- 
fied and what relief he is entitled to. 


Admittedly in this case there was no charge-sheet, no enquiry, nothing 
of the kind. Thus obviously the principles of natural and social justice 
have been violated in this case. tte was not given an opportunity to 
explain his conduct and the principle of “audi alteram partem’’ has been 
violated. If there were a proper enquiry by the Management the Court 
could judge whether the decision arrived at by the Company was a 
possible view in the circumstances. There are numerous case-laws on the 
subject and the case of Janata Pictures and Theatres Ltd. and Amulya 
Chakravarty reported in 1956 L.L.J., Vol. II, page 67, may be referred to. 


Next, the Court proceeds to enquire, as the Court is quite competent 
to huld an independent enquiry, on the evidence adduced before it, whether 
the termination of his service is justified and what relief he is entitled 
to. Beyond dispute this workman received due treatment from the 
Company since the commencement of his service and he enjoyed additional 
remuneration of Rs. 50 during Manager’s absence and his pay was Rs. 185 
aus D. A. when his service was terminated. It 1s common ground that 
uring these 8 years only once there was a charge-sheet ogninst him and 
he way warned after enquiry. The Company did not then throw him 
overboard, The climax was, however, reached when the Company found 
that this workman’s brother who ia a non-Matric was manufacturing 
Kac-Kil, a disinfectant (something like phenyle) and selling the same in 
open market. rage a supervisor, Nripendra Nath (those, O.P.W.1, 
urchosed a bottle (Ext. B) and he was told that it was being manufactured 
۱ the workman's brother living together in 16/1 Iswar Ganguli Lane, 
Ralighat, Caleutta. The Union has tried to show that the workman’s 
two sister’s sons who are graduates in Science have helped 1719 brother 
towards manufacturing this cdisinfactant. The Union has not produced 
these two nephews whose evidence might have clarified the position. 


The Union further contends that this disfectant is so common and the 
formula of its preparation is so easy that anybody and everybody 
can prepare it. After all, the disinfectant is a او‎ preparation and 
I cannot persuade myself to believe that anyohe without a modicum of 
scientific knowledge can prepare it. This workman is a B.Sc. and 
employed in Company’s laboratory where Azl-Bac. was manufactured and 
marketed and the inescapable natura] suspicion is that he picked up the 
fornia from there and used the same at home in preparing the disinfectant 
under a different name and passed that off in the Bazar. Azil-Bac. was 
the name given by the see and the name given hy Bhattacharjee 
Chemical Works is Bac-Kil, only the position of the syllables Kil and 
Bac has been reveraed in the new name. It struck me _ very atrange 
indeed that the workman did not hesitate in trying to hoadwink the Court 
by saying that the contents of the bottle (Ext. B) were purchased from 
Bazar and his brother simplv bottled it and sold it in the market. This 
Is nothing short of a bare lie and the Union did not dare to put the

workman's brother in the witness .سط‎ His evidence was very material 
in this cose and the Unon in not producing him before the Court 
suppressed the truth which reflects a good deal of Jisoredit on the veracity 
and conduct of the workman. Furthermore, of all persona in the world, 
no explanation 1s forthcoming as to how this workman’s brother devoid 
of any scientific education would be able to manufacture this disintectant 
whieh i the product of the Jaboratory of ١٣×۲ Company where this 
workman was ot lute an assistant chemist. The hand of this workman 
beh.nd the preparation of this disinfectant by Bhattacharjee Chemical 
Works is so clearly perceptible that it would be nothing short of a 
perverse finding to bold that this workman is wholly unconnected with 
the aftair und that his conduct does not savour of any sort of bad faith. 
As tightly contended the workman has forfeited Company's confidence 
nnd he does not deserve to be retained in the service of the Company. 
The Company plans to manufacture various other chemical substances 
aud there is no knowing when this workman will pick up an important 
formula in future and do something which may اس‎ disaster to Compuny’s 
business. The Company rightly apprehends further evil from this 
workman in future and the Court cannot foist him upon it. The present 
behaviour of the workman is certainly prejudicial to the interests of the 
Company which he serves and he proved hnuself false to the Company. 
In the case of Municipal Corporation, Greater Bombay and another = and 
Labour Appellate Tribunal of India and another reported in 1957 L.1.J., 
Vol. 11, page 37, at page 41 it is laid down as follows: ‘An employer at 
best may he lable to pay to his employee damages for wrongfut *termina- 
tion of employment, hut normally he cannot be compelled to retain an 
employee when he does not desire to retain him in his employment’. ا‎ 
have been referred to a case (Goodlass Wall Ltd., Bombay vs. workmen 
employed under it) reported in the Industrial Court Reporter (Bombay), 
1991, at page 66, In that case the employees entered into competitive 
bitsiness with their emplovers and the Judge observed as follows: “I am 
of the opinion that emplovees who enter into competitive business with 
their employers fail in their impled duty, which is engrafted on their 
contracts of service, to serve their employers with good faith and fidelity 
and any employees who are guilty of bad faith ond infidelity to their 
employers are guilty of misconduct for which dismissal would be the 
proper punishment to award them’’. The element of bad faith is a 
common feature in both these cases. The Company lost faith in this 
workman. Good faith is a very essential requisite in a chemist and want 
of it makes him undesirable to be retained further in service. The 
Jompany alwavs entertain suspicion about his actions, so the Company 
cannot feel happy to be compelled to retain him, nor will he feel happy 
to work in the Company where everybody will look upon him with sus- 
ا‎ and where all his actions would be under surveillance. Fe it said 
efore parting that Company’s stopping the manufacture of Aul-Pac. 
since 1954 makes no difference in the position so fur as want of good faith 
on the part of the workman is concerned. 


In the circumtances of this case and having regard to the demeanour 
of the workman in the witness box who in his evidence very much prevari- 
cated, IT must find that the termination of the service was quite justified 
and this I say on the basia of the enquiry held by the Court. The 
reinstatement of the workman is thus inconceivable and must be refused. 


Next, I take up the other question whether this is an industrial dispute. 
The definition of the term ‘‘workman’’ has been much widened iu the 
emended Act of 1956 (Act XXXVI of 1956). “Workman” means any 
person (including an apprentice) employed in any industry to do any 


3278 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 5, 1957 [Pari I 
— سو‎ ৭ 
skilled or unskilled manual, supervisory, technical or clerical work for 
hire op reward, ete. The Oxford Dictionary meaning of the term 
“terhnical’? ٭ز‎ “of, or in a particular art, science, baudiciaft, ete., as 
technical terms, skill, difficulty, ete’’. Jn the light of the amended defini- 
tion 1 have no hesitation in finding that a “chemist” ja now وع‎ workman 
within the moaning of the ‘‘workinan”’ as given in the amended Act. 


‘Lhe Company pext raised the question that the workman is not a 
member of the Kilburn’s Employees’ Union. The Union has proved that 
he ia. a member of the Union representing his case before the Court. He 
became a member 01) 2od June 1956 and his service was admittedly 
terminated on 4th June 1996. May he he got scent that his service was 
going to be terminated, and so he enlisted himself as a member 01 the 
Union, As the fact stands out he had been 2 member of the Union before 
his service was terminated however suspicious his membership might be und 
as his case has been taken up by the Union, J must hold that this is an 
industrial dispute. This question has been elaborately dealt with in the 
recent case between Newapapers, Ltd. ond I.T., Uttar Pradesh and others 
reported in 1967 L.U.J., Vol. II, page 1 and nothing cun be usefully added 
to it. I would only quote the following: ‘‘Having regard to the modern 
condition of society where capital and Jabour have organised themselves 
into groups for the purpose of fighting their disputes and settling them 
on the basis of the theory that in union is strength, and collective bhargain- 
ing has come to stay a single employee’s cnse might develop into an 
industrial dispute, when as often happens, it is taken up by the Trade 
Union of which he is a member and there is a concerted demand by the 
employees for redress. This view is in consonance with the basic idea 
underlying modern industrial legislation’. Here the case of the work- 
man has heen espoused by the Union of which he is a member and so this 
is held to be an industrial dispute. 


In view of my above findings the termination of the service of the 
workman is held to be justified and he 18 entitled to no relief as he has 
been paid notice pay and 4 months’ pay equivalent to 15 days’ pay for each 
padi re yeur of his 8 years’ service.

Schedule. 


Whether the suspension of Shri Hanuman Singh is justified? What

AWARD 


Decision 


The case of the Union is that the Indian Marine Service, Privute, Ltd. 
(hereinafter referred to as the Company) is a ship repairing industry. 
The Union submitted demands for Puja bonus and revision of wage 
structure, etc. This exasperated the Company which therefore tried to 
crush the Union. Jn so doing the Company first victimised Shri Hanuman 
Singh and served charge-sheets on some other workmen as well. This 
Hanuman Singh was placed under suspension and an enquiry was held by 
the Company, which did not communicate their decision to the Union. 


Hence the dispute. 


The Gompany has denied the allegations of the Union and states that 
on 19th October 1956, they served a charge-sheet on Hanuman Singh for 
his threatening to assault Mr. Richard Hendrick and obstructing the 
vun in which Mr. Tubbs left the workshop and thus prevented Mr. Tubbs 
117 proceeding. It is thus alleged that the workmen resorted to 
obstructive tactics with show of violence to Mr. Richard Hendrick and 
inteyfering with the liberty of movement of Mr. Tubbs. The Company 
justried the order of suspension of the workmen. 


On the eve of the case being taken up the Union thought it prudent 
to accept the offer of reinstatement in service which the Company ۶۶ 
out to him on condition of his giving an undertaking that he would be 
of good behaviour. The Company also agreed to reinstate him on that 
condition and the parties put in a petition of compromise. The terms of 
compromise appear to be fair and reasonable and may therefore be given 
effect to. The dispute is therefore disposed of in terms of the petition of 
compromise which do form a part of the award.

Schedule 


Is the discharge of Shri Prakash Chand Aluwallah and Shri Harchand 
Singh justified? To what reliefs are they entitled? 


AWARD 


The case of the Union is that the Company is a_ highly prosperous 
concern and manufactures aerated water of various kinds and has got an 
extensive business all over India. The Company neglected the reasonable 


3284 THE 05147701104 GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 5, 1957 [Part I

grievances of the workmen who therefore formed a Union and placed a 
charter of demands to the management. This enraged the Company which 
therefore started victimising the employees one after another. The instant 
two workmen Shri Prakash Chand Aluwallah and Shri Harchund Singh 
were charge-sheeted on 15th November 1956 on frivolous grounds and a 
sham enquiry was held wherein the principles of natural and social justice 
were হলনা নী and 91177886615 these two workmen were dismissed. ‘lhe 
Union therefore urges that the dismissals of these two workmen were 
arbitrary, illegal and mala fide and seeks their reinstatement. : 


The Company denies the material allegations in the written statement 
of the Union and contends that on 14th November 1956 Shri Prakash Chand 
was at the Inspection Point No. 1, and Shri Harchand was at Inspection 
Point No. 2 of the Plant, that on a report that both of them were engaged 
in breaking bottles at random, a foal وم‎ was made to tha Plant Superin- 
tendent who forbade them to do so but to no effect. Therefore these two 
workmen were charge-sheeted and due enquiry was held wherein they were 
given all reasonable facilities and found guilty and so dismissed. The 
Company therefore contends that there waa no mala و‎ nor any act of 
unfair labour practice. The workmen are not entitled to reinstatement or 
any other reliefs. 


The principal point referred to is whether the discharge of these two 
workmen is justified. The Company justifies the discharge of these two 
workinen on the basis of charges as tramed in Ext. A und Ext. A(1), duted 
15th November 1956. The charge ia that these two workmen did acta 
subversive of discipline by way of sabotage causing damage ؛‎ the 
Compuny’s property by breaking bottles on 14th November 1956 deliberately. 
There is also a super-added charge that they did acts of similar misconduct 
on other occasions also. These two workmen ‘were therefore called upon 
to show cause which they did and their explanations will be found in Exts. 
B and B(1), dated 16th November 1956. Their explanations are in the 
same vein, They have stated in their explanations that they did not break 
the broken bottles wilfully and deliberately but there were some broken 
pieces of bottles found at their places and the new foreman asked them 
wherefrom these broken pieces came and they replied that 90708 were. 
broken by the operators if they were defective and that this was as per 
Manager’s previous instruction pursuant to the previous practice obtaining 
for a long time. The workmen thus explained that they were not guilty 
This explanation did not satisfy the Management and the Manager Daljit 
Singh (0.P.W. 1) held an enquiry which was admittedly attende? by 
these two workmen. The proceedings of the enquiry have been marked 
Ext. E in this case. It appears that the Manager recorded the statements 
of as many as six witnesses in the presence of these two workmen who 
nlso were exumined. On behalf of ٠ union it is stated that this enquiry 
stands vitiated because the workmen were not supplied with the copies of 
the statements recorded during the enquiry, nor did the workmen sign the 
statements of the witnesses and cross-examine them. On behalf of the 
Company it is contended that the workmen were allowed all reasonable 
facilities to cross-examine the witnesses and they were also asked to sign 
the atatements but they deliberately refused to do so. The Manager has 
taken oath in this case and he in his evidence has given full details about 
the working of the machine and the procedure adopted by him in holding 
the enquiry. In spite of Manager’s asking the workmen to sign the 
atatements and to cross-examine the witnesses examined on behalf of the 
Company the workmen deliberately refused to do. So it is not the fault

of the Company, nor for that reason the Court will be justified in holding 
that the present enquiry by the Company stands vitiated. As is well 
known all principles of natural and social justice should be observed in 
holdiug enquiries wherein the delinquent wrokmen should be afforded 
all reusonable facilities with an eye to no prejudice being caused to them. 
Bearing these fundamental principles in mind the Court is not in a position 
to hold that the workmen in this case were denied reasonable oppor- 
tumties or anything else occurred which occasioned failure of justice. 
Independently of the findings arrived at by the Management the Court in 
this case also held un enquiry wherein the Manager (O.P.W. 1), Plant 
Superintendent (U.P.W. 2) and Assistant Plant Superintendent (O.P.W. 3) 
have been examined and nothing has transpired in their evidence which 
will yustify the Court in holding that the enquiry was held in o manner 
prejudicial to the workmen. It is also noticeable in this case that the 
charge-sheets, dated 1661) November 1956, followed closely upon the

carefully scrutinised cannot be described as perverse on the materials 
sroduced before the Management or there was any basic error of facts. 
۲ this connexion Ext. J, dated 14th November 1956, may be referred to. 
Shri S. P. Singh (O.P.W. 2), the Plant Superintendent, reported to the 
Manager that on the information received from Sucha Singh he enquired

but they said that Mr, Malan (previous Plant Superintenedent) instructed 
them to break the bottles. Shri S. P. Singh, however, advised while

the parties mean those which are defective or unfit for use. Thus in Ext.

the issue of such previous instruction by Mr. Malan. Furthermore, such 
instruction 28 incompatible with the automatic working of the machine as 
testified to by the Manager (O.P.W. 1) in his deposition. The relevant 
portion of his deposition is as follows: ‘‘When the bottles come out the 
defects, if any, are seen. From there the bottles come at the inspection 
Berk No. 1 where there is a mirror which points out any defects in the 
ottles and the defective bottles are removed for rewashing. Bottles then 
proceed for the 2nd ''.امنم مر‎ The working of the machine is automatic 
and this is a case of deliberate breaking of bottles at random by these two 
workmen. This is a huge concern and a daily report about bottles has 
got ta he submitted to the Head Office of the Company at Delhi and they 
maintain a stock register of bottles showing how many bottles are defective. 
Having regard to the evidence on record and the automatic working of 
the machine 1 must hold that these two workmen were rightly found 
guilty of deliberately breaking the bottles on 14th November 1956 on their 
own admission and in the absence of the proof of the Management’s 
previous instruction to that effect. Mr. Malun is no longer in the service 
of the Company and so the Company could not produce hiss hefore me. 
Therefore as the result of the independent enquiry held by the Court these 
two workmen are rightly found guilty of deliberately hreaking the bottles. 
This is an act not only prejudicial to the interests of the Company but it 
is also 0 misconduct subversive of discipline in the entire management.

On behalf of the Union it Kas been contended that the Company 
victimised these workmen os Prakash is the Vice-President of the Union 
but no ill-feeling or animosity is proved to have existed between the 
Union and the Company, nor is there any allegation. of any overt act 
pursuant thereto. Prakash stated that the Manager offered him a sum of 
Rs. 700, 800 if he left the Union but there is no independent evidence 
beyond hia verbal statement to corroborate this. I am therefore unable to 
believe this allegation. So the plea of victimisation fails. 


I shall now conclude with the aspect of the law involved in cases of this 
type. It has been laid down in a recent case of the High Court of 
Allahabad reported in 1957 L.1.J., Vol. II, page 15, that the Industrial 
Tribunal must in such cases consider three questions, namely, (1) whether 
the workmen were found guilty of misconduct by the employer, (2) whether 
the correct procedure was followed by the employer 1n arriving at the 
finding, and (3) whether the misconduct could be visited with the 
diamissal. All these three tests have been fulfilled in the instant  caae. 
Punishment is deemed justified as the Company lost all faith in the work- 
men who were found guilty of committing such misconduct, It is there- 
fore found that the discharge of the two workmen is fully justified. 


As regards relief—reinstatement is out of the question. The Company 
do not want such workmen nor can such workmen be foisted upon them. 
They forfeit retrenchment benefit on account of their misconduct. Their 
wages for November 19456 are admittedly outstanding. The Company must 
pay the workmen the same within a month of the publication of this award. 


This is my award.

DECISION 


Issue No. 1: Employment of Shri Ramayan Singh was terminated 
from 29th July 1953 in the circumstances as below: 


He was a lorry driver for 8 years in the Hakery Department of the 
Great Eastern Hotel J.td. Before that he was a cleaner. 00 110) August 
1952 the workman Shri Ramayan Singh (P.W. 1) while driving Company’s 
lorry ۲٢ 1(1 1316 knocked down at Beliaghata a girl aged 6/7 years killing 
her. Police arrested him and started a criminal case under section 304A, 
I.P.C., in the Court of Magistrate, Ist Class, Sealdah, for having caused 
death of the girl by rash and negligent driving. The workman was 
released on hail on Company’s surety on 12th August 1952. On thet very 
date his departmental head Shri Sudhir Kumar Mitra (D.W. 2) served the 
original of the notice (Ext. B) on driver Ramayan Singh. By the said 
notice the driver was told that the Director took a serious view of the 
accident yesterday in which he was invalved and a child of 6 years was

killed. He was further told that if he was found guilty ty the Court of 
Jaw his -ervices with the Company would come to an end ‘from the date 
of conviction. On that condition be was allowed to continue in service. 
Contrary to his case as made out in the lettera of his- Advocate and the 
Union, the driver had to admit that he was allowed to continue in service 
on release on bail and was paid his salary up to 28th July 1963. 


On 29th July 1953 Ramayan Singh was convicted under section 304A, 
I.P.C., and was sentenced to 3 months’ R.J. and a fine of Rs. 200 by the 
Magistrate, 1st Class, at Sealdah. Appeal against the same to the 
District ond Sessions Judge, Alipore, was dismissed. The workman was 
admittedly allowed to continue in Company’s quarters till conviction. 


On conviction on 29th July 1953 his employment according io the 
revious notice was terminated by the Company from 29th July 1953 and 
his name was struck off from the muster-roll. The case of the workman 
that his employment was not terminated hut he was refused employinent 
and locked out, 18 not borne out by the evidence. 


Therenfter on 19th August 1950 the workman Ramayan Singh claimed 
to have written a letter ns in Annexure A to the written statement of the 
Union to the Managing Director of the Company intimating that he had 
preferred appeal against his conviction in the Sealdah Court and that his 
license was in tact and so he should be permitted to resume work. The 
Company denied having received such letter. 


On 12th July 1964 the High Court pronounced judgment on appeal 
maintaining the conviction but modifying the sentence to one of fine of 
Rs. 400 only (Ext. 6). 


On 16th August 1964 the workman claimed to have written to the 
Managing Director as in Annexure B to the written statement of the

On 4th September 1964 the workman repeated his prayer for permission to

(Eat. (۰

refused employment and was not paid his wages or expenses of criminal 
casos, whereupon conciliation started. As no settlement was evontually 
poasible, the dispute was referred to this Tribunal for adjudication. 


Against this background it was urged on behalf of the workman on the 
hasia of sections 17 and 18 of the Motor Vehicles Act that when the Court 
did not cancel ‘he license on conviction and when the workman was not 
disqualified from driving, the Company had no justification to terminate 
the employment of the workman. I am unable to sustain the contention. 
When the workman was convicted for killing a girl by rash and negligent 
driving, it was absolutely Company’s option whether to keep such دہ‎ man in 
the employment or not. As a matter of fact, the Company gave notice 
forthwith about such intention to terminate his employment if he wes 
convicted by competent Court. The workman was not only convicted but

۱ کتہكسعسسھمکھمکت عحس ھ ھا جج سس کٹ ے‫‎ আআ 
his convietiot’ was tpheld up to Hon'ble High Court. No question of 
violation of the principles of natural justice arises as the fact of conviction 
in a ,۹ھ 1مانی‎ case 4s by itself sufficient ground for termination of employ- 
ment without furthet enquiry. Consequently the Company was within its 
rights to terminate employment of the workman on conviction and to main- 
tain it. Tho fact that hia license was not cancelled on conviction under 
section گا‎ :) the Motor Vehicles Act would be of no avail againet the 
Company. He might not have been disqualified but this would not oblige 
the Company to retain in its service one convicted of rash and negligent 
driving and killing a girl thereby. The option was with the employer and 
it appears that the Company acted in the matter bona fide in the interest 
of the Company. There was no question of victimisation as sought to be 
made out in tae letter of the Union or in the written statement. The 
workman himself gave direct lie to the same in his deposition before this 
Tribunal. He not only did not claim to have had any Union activities 
but he 0180 denied having had any connection with his brother who is 
said to be Treasurer of the Union. The fact that the Company not only 
stood surety and got him released on bail but also paid his salary till 
conviction and allowed him to remain in Company’s quartera would show 
that the Company had no grudge against him and accommodated him as 
far as it could. ] am, therefore, of opinion that termination of employ- 
ment of Ramayan Singh was bona fide and justified. 


As, however, the delinquency for which employment of the workman 
was terminated is not one of those specified in Company’s standing orders 
As amounting to misconduct for which punishment by dismissa) can be 
meted out iv terms of puragraph 14 of the standing orders, the action of 
the Company in terminating the employment must, in the circumstances, 
be deemed to he discharge and not dismissal. The workman should, there- 
fore, get gratuity, bonus and other benefits as admissible to him at the 
time of termination of employment on 29th July 19538. The Company is 
accordingly directed to pay gratuity at half month’s salary for each 
completed year of service with the Company proportionate honus and pay 
for the period nt privilege leave due according to the rules as then current 
in the Bakery Department. The amount is to be paid within one month 
from the date the award becomes enforceable. 


Regardiag claim of the workman to get recoupment of cost of criminal 
cases and the amount of fine, I am unable to sustain it. After conviction 
and maintenance of the same up to the Hon’ble High Court, there can be 
no foundation for such claim. There ia also nothing to show that the 
Company had or has any obligation whatever in this respect.

The following issue, arising out of an industrial dispute between Mesars. 
Ganges Rope Co., Ltd., Shibpore, Howrah (hereinafter referred to as the 
Company) and their workmen represented by the Rashikal Mazdoor Sabha, 
101 Cowies (that Road, Shibpore, Howrah, was referred to this Tribunal 
for its adjudication, by the Government of West Bengal, Department of 
Labour, by order No. 682-1.R./D/11L-267/55, dated the 4th March 1957. 


If the wages of the workmen should be increased and if 80 te what 
extent? 


Both purties filed written statements, adduced evidence, oral and dagu- 
mentary, and advanced arguments in the case, 


FINDINGS 


Issue No. 1: The Union claims (i) a flat increment of 10 per cent. of 
wages subject to a minimum of Rs. 10 per month, (01) grades as referred to 
in Annexure @ to its written statement, (111) attendance bonus at the rate 

f Rs. 6 per month, etc., and (iv) house-rent allowance at 10 pet‘ cent. of 
the wages, subject to a minimum of Rs. 10 per month, 7 that with 
retrospective effect from the date of the Third Jute Tribunal’s Award. 


The Company's contention is that the Union’s demand for grades, 
attendance bonus and house-rent allowance are outside the scope of the 
present reference and, as such, they are not maintainable in the present 
case, Further, there is no justification for demanding any increment for 
the Company pays the highest wages in the rope industry, and the total 
emoluments of an employee of this concern compare very favourably with 
the total emoluments paid in the other industries in the region. The 
Company, despite its disadvantageous position for higher cost of produc- 
tion in the competitive market, had introduced a production bonus scheme 
which was subsequently liberalised. As a result of this an employee is now 
varning more than what he used to do previously. The finances: of the 
Company are incapable to bear any further increase in wagea. 11059 
Company also contends that it is under no obligation to pay its employees 
in terms of the Third Jute Tribunal’s Award to which it was not a party. 


I think that the Union’s demands for grades, attendance bonus, and 
house-rent allowance in the present dispute are not maintainable as they: are 
outside the scope of the present reference. The only dispute referred to 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 5, 1957 3297 
22 


the Tribunal is, whether or not the existing wages of the employees should 
be increased and, if so, to what extent. The said three demands have no 
direct connection with the fixation of wages. It cannot be said that they 
are matters incidental to the above issue in question. That being the 
position, the prayer of the Union for grades atténdunce bonus and house- 
rent allowance should be rejected. IJ reject them accordingly. 


Now, the point for consideration is whether the existing rate of wages 
should be increased and, whether the UWnion’s claim in this respect for a 
flat increase of 10 per cent. of the existing rates of wages subject to a 
minimum of Rs, 10, should be accepted. A total complement of 773 
workers were employed by the Company on the week ending 15th June 
1957. Calculated on this basis, the Union’s minimum demand is likely tu” 
cost the Company about Rs. 92,760 a year. The increment as demanded 
on the basis of the Third Jute Tribunal’s Award would cost, according to 
the Company, about Rs. 58,668 a year. The estimated expenditure on this 
account has been worked out by the parties as above. 


The admitted position is that the existing rates of wages came to be last 
revised when the Company allowed the benefits of the Second Jute 
Tribunal’s Award to its workmen sometime in 1951. Before that, the 
Company had given effect to the First Jute Tribunal Award, so far it related 
10) wages and dearness allowance. It is in evidence of O.P.W. 3, Shri A. K. 
Ghosh, the Assistant Manager of the Company, that the production bonus 
scheme "has been in operation since 1949 or 1950. ‘The scheme was then 
revised iu 1953 when it was considerably liberalised. Excepting officers, 
everybody employed in the factory enjoyed the benefits of this scheme. 
The quantum of production bonus paid last year umounted to three months’ 
basig wages. ডি 2, Shri Wahi, Manager-in-charge of the Company, 
and P.W. 1, Shri Apurba Sen (iupta, the General Secretary of the Union, 
depose tw the same effect. The Union demanded that the wagea should be 
increased at the rates given in the Third Jute Tribunal’s Award. The 
Company did not accede to this request. The demand for increment of 
wages was not conceded. Accordingly, the Union now asks for a general 
increment of 10 per cent. of the existing rates of wages subject to a 
minimum of Rs, 10, on the ground that the Company is bound by the agree- 
ment to phy in terms of the Third Jute Trmbunal’s Award. It has paid 
increment according to the First and the Second Jute Tribunal Awards. 
It is, therefore, in the fitness of things, says the Union, that (i) the Company 
should allow an increment in terms of the Third Jute Tribunal’s Award, 
and (11) that the Company should also pay living wages to its employees, 
particularly, as they are required to exercise greater degree of skill in work 
than their counterparts in any Jute Mill, and also (111) on the ground that 
the cost of living had gone up with the rise in the prices of foodstuffs and 
other essential commodities. The Company’s defence however, is that there 
was no ayreement, or assurance given to pay in terms of the Jute Tribunal’s 
Award and, as such, it would not pay in terms of the same. The Union has 
not made out any case for payment of living wages or for a general rise in 
wages, either on the ground of performance of greater skill by the workers, 
or on the ground of rise in the prices of foodstuffs and/or rise in the cost of 
living index. The Company is already paying more than what other 
coucerng In the same industry are paying in the locality. 


۴ 
The agreement, relied upon by the Union, is mentioned in paragraph 2 
of the Manager Mr, Robertson’s letter (Ext. 1), dated 7th September 1961, 
to the President of the Union. We do not get the text of the Agreement, 
which was not produced before this Tribunal. But it is sufficiently clear 
from the letter, Ext. 1, that there was a longstanding agreement between 


3298 THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 5, 1957 [Part I 


the Union and the Management of the Company providing among others, 
that the terms and conditions of service for workers here should be on lines 
of the awards by the Jute Textile Tribunal in respect of the Jute Mill 
workers. It is stated in the aforesaid letter, Ext. 1, that the First Jute 
Tribunal’s award was implemented, and that an assurance was given that 
the Second Jute T keke Award would be implemented in due course. 
We have got it in evidence that the 2nd Jute Tribunal’s Award was also 
fully implemented, The above reply of Mr. Robertson waa given on receipt 
of the charter of demands from the Union, on 28th August 1951 [Ext. 
I(a)}]. The Company’s case now is that the Union did not stand by the 
agreement und, in fact, in a letter, dated the 14th December 1951 (Ext. A), 
the Secretary of the Union made it clear that the workers would not accept 
the award of the Jute Tribunal. It further appears that the Union, 
however, accepted the uward, despite its letter (Ext. A) to the contrary 
and that both parties treated this agreement as binding on them to the 
knowledge of the Government. IJt appears from Ext. 2, the letter, dated 
the 17th February 1954, written by the Assistant Secretary, Government of 
West Bengal, Labour Department, to the Secretary of the Union, that there 
wus ap agreement between the Union and the Management for observance 
of the terms and conditions of the Jute Tribunal’s Awards. Thereufter, 
the Union again demanded for the implementation of the Third Jute 
Tribunal’s Award but the Manager in his reply, dated 2let November 1955 
(Ext. 2b), categorically denied giving effect to it on the ground that the 
Company was no party to it. The Manager also regretted his inability 
to take cognizance of the findings of the said award, as it did not concern 
his company. In this state of evidence, it is idle to contend that the agree- 
ment which existed between the Union and the Management, as mentioned 
in the Manuger’s letter (Ext. 1), dated the 7th September 1951, was no more 
binding on the parties, and had ceased to be operative in law. It is one 
thing to say that the rates of wages under the award would not satisfy the 
workers at the moment, but it is quite a different thing to assert that the 
Company is no more under any obligation to honour the agreement 
regarding Sais Sa pee to of the said award. In my view, the Company, 
after having held out hopes to the workers, cannot now ignore the said 
agreement—much legs—to back out from it. The Union, however, asks for 
wore than whut the workers are entitled to under the award by virtue of the 
৭১10] agreement. The Union cannot blow hot and cold at the same breath, 
It must either stand by the agreement or lawfully terminate it. It can 
only have more than one proof of change of circumstances. The award of 
the Third Jute Tribunal was made on 20th September 1955, ond was 
published in the Calcutta Gazette, dated 6th October 1955. This award was 
wodified to some extent in appeal by the Labour Appellate Tribunal. The 
decision of the Labour Appellate Tribunal was reported in 1956 (November), 
Labour Appel cases, p. 790. No endeavour was made to prove that, since 
the date of the last award there had been material changes in the circum- 
stunces justifying further revision of the findings of the said award, relevant 
to the issue in question. On the other hand, the Company has succeeded in 
establishing that the cost of living index was 370 pointa in 1951, and the 
average figure of it for the year 1956 was 347 points. It is true that the 
cost of living index has gone up to 469 points in the month of June 1957, 
hut even then this does not show an overall increase over the cost of living 
index of 1951, when the rates of wages were last revised. The Union’s chart on 


this point appears to be erroneous for, it referred to figures of Asansol, and 
not of Calcutta. The Company, in the next place endeavours to show by 
evidence, including the chart, Ext. 0, that it pays to its employees & basic 
poy and dearness allowance, which taken together, amount to more than 


Pant 1| THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 5, 1907 3299 
০৯৯৯৯ 


what are actually paid to the employees of the sister concerns in the same 
industries, und in the same locality. The Shalimar Rope Works pays basic 
pay and dearness allowance amounting to Rs. 57 per month and Messrs. 
Hartons, 1১80.) also pays an equal amount. The শী ell Rope Works pays 
a production bonus amounting to Rs. 5-7 a month in addition to basic pay 
and dearness allowance. The Ganges Rope Co., Ltd., also pays a produc- 
tion bonus amounting to Ra. 6-8 per ee 


The question now, is whether the production bonus paid to the employees 
by this Company can be treated as a part of wages. Mr. Justice Ramaswami 
of the Madras High Court in a case reported in 12 F.J.R., p. 238, held 
on a review of all the cases on this point, that bonus is not a regular part 
of wages, deferred or otherwise, and it 1s in a sense an ex gratia payment, 
but by the statute or by agreement, it can assume permanency, and become 
part of wages. Practically, the same view was taken by the Labour 
Appellate Tribunal in Coal Appeals where it held that it is the normal 
concept that the minimum wage is a fixed amount which a workman must 
receive for the work that he does. The present bonus scheme has been 
outlined in the Ext. E(2). The payment of this bonus 1s dependent on 
production, regular attendance, and also on approved service. Therefore, 
by its very nature, it can never be looked upon as a regular part of wages. 
This has to be earned hy putting in extra eftorts. In my opinion, it may 
be taken into consideration to ascertain, us in the Metal Box’s case, the total 
emoluments of an emplovee, but it should not be so done in judging the 
adequacy or otherwise of the amount of wages. If the amount of produc- 
tion houws ts deducted from the total emolument as stated in the Ext. C., 
16 will be seen that this Company is paying Ka. 635-6 in basic wages und 
dearness allowance to its employees as against Rs, 67-2-9 allowed in the 
Third Jute Tribunal’s Award, whereas the Shalimar Rope Works and the 
Harton Co. are paying a total of Rs. 57 only. It is the Union’s case that 
the Shalimar Rope Works and Harton Co., cannot be compared with the 
Ganges Rope Co., Ltd., for, the Ganges Rope Co., Ltd., holds a unique 
position which the other two companies, much smaller in size, can never 
aspire to reach. We do not get the balance-sheets of all these three 
companies referred to above and, therefore, are not in a position to make 
any correct estimate on this point. But it is abundantly clear that the 
Ganges Rope Co., Jitd., manufactures quality products, and employs a 
larger রি ও of workmen in their work. 


On the question of production, the parties differ in their estimates. The 
Union’s evidence is that the production has gone up under the production 
bonus scheme, whereas the Company’s case is that it remains practically 
the same. It, however, appears that except in the last six months of 1956, 
the sale position remains very satisfactory in some years. There were 
record sales. As nothing is claimed on the basis of increased productivity, 
this question does not detain us long nor present any difficulty. 


Except on the issue of introduction of grades, the Company did not 
plead its financial incapacity to grant an increase in wages. Nevertheless, 
1 should be seen whether it has the capacity to bear any additional financial 
burden on this ground. Although the sales were increased in 1956, the 
corresponding profits showed a downward trend. There was less profit in 
1956. Roughly, 1t was one-fourth of the profits of the previous year. But 
then, the Company paid a dividend to its share-holders, much higher in 
relation to the amount of profits earned in that year. O.P?.W. 2, Shri Wahi 
attempted to give an explanation on this point. He said that the reason 
for low profit against the high figure of sales is that the cost of production 
was high. We have not got any detailed explanation on this point. It is 


3300 THE CAILUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 5, 1957 [Part I 


জর সপ কে সবলে 


however clear from the evidence of the balance-sheet (Ext. GQ) with Ext. را‎ 
that the Company had earned handsome profits in the past, and that due to 
increased cost of production it earned Jess profit in the Jast year. This does 
not show that the Company’s financial position is unsound, or that it 18 


incapable of bearing increased financia] burden on the score of imereased 
wages, 


Next, the question now to be considered is whether the employees can 
succeed in getting an increased wage on the ground that they are required 
to display an extra amount of skill in work under this Company, much more 
than what an employee in a Jute Mill is required to do. The evidence in 
this reapect on the Union’s side is given by Shri Sen Gupta, P.W. 1, who 
has no experience of work either in this Company or in a Jute Mill. He 
admitted that he had no knowledge about the work of Jute Mills. He does 
not possess more than elementary knowledge on the subject. He is an 
employee of Howrah Municipality. It is not possible to hold, -on this 
evidence, that an employee in the service of this Company is required to 
show greater amount of skill in work than that of a Jute Mill worker. 


Lastly, as ] have stated above, the agreement on which the present claim 
for the increment of wages is based, is binding on both parties. That being 
ao, the Company is bound to give effect to the 3rd Jute Tribunal’s Award 
which allowed an increased rate of basic pay but a lower rate of dearness 
allowance. Exhibit C shows that the aforesaid award of the 3rd Jute 
Tribunal allowed a total of Rs. 67-2-9 to a worker, whereas this Company 
is at present paying a total emolument of Ks. 63-6 per month. 


On a consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case I find that 
the wages of workmen in this Company should be increased, and brought 
in line with the Third Jute Tribunal’s Award. The weekly-paid employees 
should get an increment of Ra. 3-12-9 and monthly paid employees should 
get an increment of Rs. 3-2 only as in the Third Jute Tribunal’s Award. I 
answer the issue accordingly. 


This is my award.

The dispute sought to be resolved by adjudication on this reference 
made by Government order No. 4828Dis./D/101-32/55, dated the 27th 
September 1956, relates to some of the salient conditions of service applicable 
to workers serving under the India Industrjal Works, Ltd. 


The points formulated in the order of reference are as follows :— 


(1) Revision of grade and increment, 
(2) Dearness allowance. 


(3) Leave, 
(4) Modification of attendance bonus rule. 


The Union in ita written statement referred to the history of the 
dispute and pointed out that there are no grades of pay for the workers and 
for last five years no increment has been granted. The cost of living 
index number has moved upward sharply and no step has been taken to fill 
up even in a small measure the yawning gulf between the wages and the 
cost of living. The Company grants no privilege leave, casual leave or 
sick leave. The grievances of the workmen in this respect should also be 
redressed. The attendance bonus rule is extremely stringent. Its modi- 
fication is indispensably necessary. 


The Company in its written statement asserted that the terms and 
conditions of employment were much more favourable than those obtaining 
‘n similar industries. The minimum wage for unskilled and semi-skilled 
workera was determined by an agreement during the pendency of a 
refercnce proceeding before the Fifth Industrial Tribunal and the said 
agreement was made part of the award. There has been no materiul change 
in the circumstances since the date of the award which might warrant 
disturbance of the wage structure built up by the award. The financial 
position of the Company has in the mean time suffered serious decline. 
In the present finanoial condition the Company cannot be made to under- 
take any further liabilities. No incremental 80016 is prevalent in any 
Enginecring Industry and none should be fixed for this particular unit. 
Dearness allowance is being paid at a flat rate of Rs. 90 on the basis of the

10 duys’ festival holidays with full poy. Sick leave previously allowed 
has now been discontinued as the Employees State Insurance Scheme has 
been put into operation. Existing leave facilities are satisfactory and do 
not require any revision. Attendance bonus was introduced by the Company 
on its own initiative to encourage regularity in attendance. The Union 
demand for relaxation of some of the conditions 15 unreasonable, as such 
relaxation would put a premium upon laxity in attendance. 


issue No, 3—Leave: ‘The Union demand is that privilege leave to the 
extent of 15 days which might accumulate for three years and casual leave 
for 15 days should be granted in addition to the leave admissible under 
the Factories Act. Reference was made on behalf of the Union to the 
award of the Second Major Engineering Tribunal Award. At page 246 
of the volume of awards made ىا‎ Tribunule for the quarter ending 
September 1940, published by the Government of West Bengal, 14000 
Department, directions given by the Tribunal regarding leave may 09 
found. For employees according to the Factories Act, 1948, the Tribunal 
allowed annual leave with wages for 10 days or more which may _ be 
permissible under section 79 of the Factories Act, such leave being allowed 
to accumulate in the manner provided by that Act. In addition the 
Tribunal provided for six or five days other leave with wages according as 
there would be two Sundays or one Sunday within the period of the first 
10 days of the continuous annual leuve under section 79 of the Factories 
Act, such leave being allowed to accumulate in the manner provided by 
that Act. Since the publication of the award, the Factories Act has been 
amended and at present leave up to a period of 14 days may be earned by 
a factory worker. As under the old Act only 10 days leave could 1১৬ 
earned, the Tribunal had to supplement the leave by udding five or six 
days’ other leave. Since that position does not hold good at present and 
the Iactories Act itself makes adequate provision for annual leave there 
is not an iota of justification for making separate arrangement for 
privilege leave. The period available under the Factories Act 19 properly 
speaking privilege Jeave. I am not prepared, therefore, to accede to the 
nion prayer for allowing privilege leave in addition to the statutory 
leave. 


The other item of claim is casual leave. The Second Major Engineering 
Award allowed 7 days’ casual Jeave with full pay to clerical and supervisory 
staff. No such leave was granted in respect of the workers, skilled or 
unskilled. It has not been shown that casual leave is being enjoyed by 
workers of any factory. I am not prepared to make a departure. The 
claim, for casual leave is accordingly rejected. Leave that is heing granted 
by the Company at present will continue. 


Issue No. 4--Modification of attendance bonus rule: Attendance bonus 
is available in the shape of one day’s wages to those workers who are in 
attendance throughout the whole month for full working hours. If any- 
body goes on leave for any day or part of a day he forfeits the privilege. 
The Union submitted that 21 days’ attendance in a month should be held 
sufficient to qualify a worker for drawing attendance bonus and the rate 
should he Rs. 3. Attendance on all the working days in a month should 
ontitle the worker to two days’ wages. The Company stoutly opposed 
modification of the attendance bonus rules on the inane suggested hy the 
Union. This bonus was the creation of the Company for discouraging 
absenteeism. The object was to provide some sort of reward for regularity

Taking Rs. 5 per month us the pre-war expenditure on food per month

By fixing the minimum at Rs. 55 per month, we are increasing 
the averuge wages by Rs. 5 or Rs. 6 per month, and in our

to bear at present, when the industry is pussing through difficult 
times owing to short supply of steel and other raw materials. 
For the unskilled worker, therefore, we fix the minimum basic 
wage at Rs. 30 per month or Rs. 1-2-6 per day. 


Since the making of that award, the question of minimum basic wage 
in Engineering concerns has come up _ before other Tribunals. The 
minimum basic pay as fixed by the Major Engineering Tribunal has been 
consistently accepted for guidance. Shrijut Sengupta cannot expect me to 
ignore the Major Tribunal award and other awards which followed the 
lead. An additional reason for not responding to the appeal for a 
departure from the beaten track ia that industrial peace would be 
imperilled if I were to follow the course advocated by Shrijut Sengupta. 
It should also be borne in mind, that in May 1952, the parties to this 
dispute had themselves adopted the minimuin basic pay as settled by the 
Mujor Engineering award as adequate under the then existing conditions. 
The Union did not then take the view, as is now done by its spokesman, 
that the Major Engineering Tribunal had done injustice to the workers.

turn back the hand of the clock and introduce rates of pay which the

Minimum basic pay was fixed at Rs. 30 in May 1952 by compromise 
which formed part of the award made by the Fifth Industrial Tribunal. 
In Burn Company's case reported in 1957, 1, L.I..J. page 226, the Hon’ble 
Supreme Court has held that though terminated by notice under section 
19(6) of the Industrial Disputes Act the decision of a Tribunal will 
preserve its strength unless there is change of circumstances. In the 
resent case the Company has served notice to terminate the award. 

evertheless, the fixation of basic wage made by the award will not dis- 
appear unless change of circumstances is proved. The Union argument 
is that the cost of living has heen rising in a steady orescendo. The index 
number is now 390, is 1s however no ground Jor effecting changes in 
the basic minimum wage. The rise in the cost of living is to be met by 
adjustment of dearness allowance. It follows therefore that the basic 
minimum pay as determined by the 1952 award must remain intact. 


The second line of the Company’s defence is that the business is not 
having plain sailing. It is struggling againet heavy odds, and 18 just 
keeping its head above water. The auditors’ report Ext. B, 20019 
balance-sheets Exts. B(1) to B(8) reveal a highly embarrassed financial 
position. ‘lhe share capital was five lakhs of rupees. Borrowings from 
bank amount to 1] lakhs. All the ossets of the Company are mortgaged 
to the Bunk. No provision could be made for depreciation and no reserves 
have been built up. No dividend has been paid since 1951. The state- 
ment Ext. A(2) shows that up to 1956, total profits umounted to Rs 25,708 
whereas the losses amounted to Rs. 2,91,278. Tin plates and galvanized 
wire ure the staple raw materials required by the Company for its produc- 
tion work. Exhibit C(1) shows that for the third quarter of 1957/7, the 
yompany could secure 80 per cent. of its sanctioned quota from the 
authorised dealer, the Tin Plute Company of India, Ltd. Government 
letter Ext. C shows a further cut in the quota by 50 per cent. It is true 
that same quantity of raw materials could be procured from local markets. 
But that can hardly be counted upon as a sure and perennial sourae of 
supply. Cost of materials has also gone up considerably as will appear 
from the statement Ext. A(3). The business of the Company is undoubtedly 
passing through heavy travail. The outlook is depressing in all conscience. 
According to the Company’s spokesman neither basic wage nor the 8ء‎ 
allowance can be enhanced without dealing a serious blow to the industry, 
as under prevailing conditions the business has not the capacity to ط٣‎ 
any further burden. The cases reported in 1954, 1..A.C. page 10, 1954, 
1, L.L.J. page 766 and 1954, 2, L.I.J. page 221 were cited in support 
of the: proposition that capacity to pay is a severeign consideration. 60 
behalf of the Union Shrijut Sengupta controverted the proposition on the 
plea that for fixation of minimum pay capacity to pay deserves no considera- 
tion as un industry which cannot pay the minimum has no right to exist. 
The view propounded by Shrijut Sengupta is not, in my estimation, 
universally applicable. In the case reported in 1951, 2, L.L.J. page 221 
it has been held that the Company ۰ has not been able to build up 
any reserve requires special consideration. In the Buckingham and 
Carnatic Mills, Ltd. case reported in 1952, L.A.C. page 490, their Lordships 
observed at page 517 that capacity to pay is to be considered in fixation 
of basic wages. The First Major Engineering Tribunal had 0180 taken 
the capacity to pay into consideration as wil] appear from the following 
observation at page 97 


“The fact that we have been induced by consideration of the prevailing 
wage rate and the capacity of the industry to pay, to fix a lower

minimum wage than we might otherwise 0%5৬- done is no doubt an

This point is more or less academic in the present instunce since the task

do not apply as in the case of first-time fixation of minimum wage. It may

New Delhi, the 12th August, 1957 


RESOLUTION 


No. 1(7)/56-Policy,—In the Government of India, Ministry of Irrigation 
and Power, Resolution No. 1(7)/56-Policy, dated the 19th June 1967, the 
following amendments shall be made :— 


A.—Under the heading ‘‘Co-crdination Committee of Irrigation and 


Power Seminar’’: ‘ 


(i) In serial No. 19, for the words, ‘‘Additional Chief Engineer, 
Andhra’, the words, ‘‘Chief Engineer, Nagarjunasagar Canals, 
Andhra Pradesh’’, shall be substituted. 


(ii) In serial No. £0, for the words, ‘‘Chief Engineer اس سو‎ 
Andhra’’, the words, ‘Special Chief Engineer (Irrigation 
Andhra Pradesh’’, shall be substituted. 


(iii) In serial No. 22, for the words, ‘‘Chief Engineer, Public Works 
Department, Rajshahi’”’, the words, “Chief Engineer, Irriga- 
tion, Rajshahi’’, shall be substituted. 


(iv) In serial No. 34, for the words, ‘‘Chrief Engineer, Public Works 
Department, Kerala’, the words, ‘Chief Engineer, General 
and Irrigation, Kerala’’, shall be substituted. 


B.—Under the heading, “Co-ordination Board of Ministers” ۰ 


(i) In serial No. 16, for the words, ‘‘Minister for Public Works, 
Kerala’, the words, ‘‘Minister for Law, Kerala’’, shall be 
substituted. 


Order 


Orvernmp that this Resolution be communicated to all State Governments, 
the several Ministries of the Government of India, Prime Minister's 
Secretariat, thea Private and Military Secretaries to the President, Cabinet 
Secretariat, Parliament Secretariat, the Planning Commission and the 
Comptroller and Auditor-General of India. 


Orveren also that the Resolution be published in the (42265. of India 
and that the State Governments be requested to publish it in the State 
Gazettes for general information,

CONDITIONS 


1. No blasting operation shall be carried out between the hours of sunset 
and sunrise. Blasting operations shall only he carried out between thie 
hours*® 


2. The preparation of charges, the charging of holes and the firing of 
shots shall be carried out by or in the presence of o responsible person with 
experience of handling explosives, 


3. No smoking or any source of light or fire shall be allowed in or near 
the place where cxplosives charges are being prepared or kept. 


4. Not more than 8 holes shall be loaded and fired at any one time. 


9. For charging or steaming a shot hole, no person shall use an iron 
or steel tool, scraper or tamping rod, nor shall forcibly press the explosives 
into a hole of insufficient size. A tamping rod made entirely of wood shall 
be used, 


G. Before exploding any blasting charge, a strong wooden lattice 
sufficiently weighted shall be placed immediately over the drift so as to 
prevent, as for as possible, the projection of fragments of stone by the 
explosion of the blasting charge. 


7. No person shall re-bore or tamper a hole that has once been charged 
or attempt to withdraw a charge either before firing’or after a misfire or 
deepen or tamper with empty holes or sockets left aiter blasting. 


8. Before commencing shot firing, the licensee shall give sufticient 
warning to the public by an efficient system of signals and by putting up 
red flags in the danger zone, namely, 200 yards from the place of blasting. 
He shall see that all persons in the vicinity bave taken proper shelter and 
shall 8180 take suitable steps to prevent any person approaching the shot. 


9. The licensee shall warn the public not to approach the site of blasting 
operation ut least within an hour after explosion or in the case of an open 
quarry, not to aproach such quarry within half an hour after explosion. 


10. The number of shots which explode shall be counted and unless it 
is certain that all the shots have been exploded, no person shall approach or 
be permitted to approach the place unti] 30 minutes after the firing of 
shots. 


11. In the event of w misfire, a portion of the tamping may be sludged 
out with compressed air or water under pressure, but no kind of tool shall 
be used for this purpose. The hole shall thereafter be reprimed and fired. 


১১১১১ ০ 
*Tho licensing authority should endorse the hours during which the blasting operations may 
be carried out.

_ 13. The licensee or his agent shall remain present at the place and

14. The licensee shall be responsible for all blasting operations 
conducted under this licence. 


15. The licensee shall produce his licence, if required to do so, before 
any officer authorised under rule 106 of the Explosives Rules, 1940, and 
shall afford free access to such officer to any place at which any blasting 
operation 1s carried on, so as to ensure that all necessary precautious have 
been taken to guard against danger to the public.

DIRECTORATE OF ACRICULTURE, 
WEST BENCAL 


Culcutta, the 18th February 1957. 


Forecast of Kharif Pulses (other than Cram and 
Tur) of West Bengal for 1956-57 (excluding 
territories transferred from Bihar). 


Season.--The weather conditions have on the 
whole been fair for the cultivation of the erup in 
all the «districts of West Jdengal except 
24-Parganas, Naudia, Murshidabad, Burdwan and 
Midnapore. 


Area and yield.—The total uren under difterent 
kharif pulses (other than gram and tur which are 
published separately) is estimated at 42,100 acres 
this yeur compared to $5,400 acres last year. The 
total outturn of different kharif pulses for the State 
ws & Whole is estimated at 9,800 tons this year 
compared to 9,400 tons last year. 


The average yield yate per acre of different 
kharif pulses for the State as a whole is estimated 
at 6.31 maunds this year compured to 7.24 maunds 
last year. 


Mung.—5,700 00168 are estimated to be under 
“Mung” this year compared to 4,600 acres last 
year. The total outturn of the crop for the State 
an a whole in estimated at 1,400 tonsa this year 
compared to 1,100 tons last year. The average 


SCTPPLEMENT TO THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 5, 1957 


yield rate per acre of the crop for the State us a 
whole is estimated at 6.51 maunds this year com- 
pared to 6.71 maunds lust year. 


Mashkalai.—24,2U0 ucres are estimated to be 
under ‘‘Mashkalai’’ this year compared to 22,500 
acres last year, The total outturn of the crop for 
the State as a whole is estimated at 5,700 tons this 
year compared to 6,200 tonsa of last year. The 
average yield rate per acre of the crop for the State 
as a whole is estimated at 6.42 maunds this year 
compared to 7.6] maunds last year. 


Moth.—500 acres are estimated to be under 
“Moth” this year and the total outturn of the crop 
for the State as a whole is estimated at about 73 
tons. The average yield rate per acre of the crop 


for the State as a whole is estimated «at 4.00 
maunds. No acreage was shown with ‘‘Moth” last 
vear. 


Other pulses.—11,7U0 acres are estimated to be 
under “(ther pulses” this year compared to 8,400 
acres last year. The total outturn of other pulses 
for the State as a whole is estimated at 2,600 tons 
this year compared to 2,100 tons last year. The 
average yield rate per acre of other pulses for the 
State as a whole is estimated at 6.10 maunds this 
year compared to 6.81 maunds last year. 


S. N. MUKHERJEE, 
for Virector of Agriculture, West Bengal.

Notices were issued on both parties who filed written statements setting 
forth their respective cases. 


The case of the Union on the issues is as follows: 


The Company was a well-equipped Silk Textile Industry in West Bengal 
und it used to employ about 1٦6جب‎ workmen. The Company gradually 
retrenched 72 workmen as shown in the list attached to the order of ۰ء‎ 
Prior to the notice retrenching 72 workmen, the situation in the Company 
was such that the workers were neither paid their wages for months together, 
nor were issued letters of termination of service, nor were they given any 
retrenchment compensation. They were verbally retrenched by Shri K. C. 
Biswas, Managing Director of the Company, and the workmen were told 
that they would paid their retrenchment compensation and other dues 
when he would get money from the Goverument or would be in a position to 
urTrange finunce. 


The rules of leave in the Company was to pay full wages for casual leave 
and sick leave availed of, but this sum has not been paid as shown in 
Annexure A to the Union’s statement. It is prayed that the issues may 
be answered in favour of the workmen and the dues shown in Annexure A 
be awarded in full. 


The Company, in its written statement, states as follows: 


That 00 industrial dispute is maintuinable inasmuch as the alleged 
dispute is not an industrial dispute within the meaning of the Industrial 
Ihsputes Act that the employment of the workers in question being terminated 
from the 2lst May 1955, they are not competent in law to have their alleged 
کت‎ adjudicated in Industrial Tribunul and that their petition is bad 
in law for misjoiner of parties, as the employees in question ure not entitled 
to have their individual claim adjudicated jointly and as such this Tribunal 
has no jurisdiction to adjudicate their claim jointly, that the claimants of 
the Union were not workmen within the meaning of the Act, inasmuch as 
they were ‘not in the employment since 218 May 1965, and as such they are 
not entitled to have their claims adjudicated by this Tribunal. It is also 
stated that the Pravati Textile Mills Labour Union is not entitled to repre- 
sent the said claimants as they were neither workmen within the meaning of 
the Act, nor were they members of the Union since 218٦ May 1955. পচ is 
further stated thet the award given by Shri M. C. Banerji between the Com- 
pany and its workmen in 1952 having expired, the claimants are not entitled

ما‎ any sick leave or casual leave wayes or gratuities. The Company submits

The appearances for the parties were as follows :— 
For the workmen: Shri M. Saha, Advocate and Shri H. Roy, Pleader.
