The issues framed for the decision of this case are the same as that men- 
tioned in the order of reference and are as follows: 


Issues 


(1) Whether the 72 workmen mentioned in the list appended to the 
schedule to the order of reference are entitled to sick leave and/or casual 
leave wages? 


(2) Whether the said workmen are entitled to gratuities in conformity 
with the rules which were in force at the relevant time? 


AWARD 
Decisions 


Issue Nos. 1 and 2: On the date of hearing, the Company did _ not 
appear and the case was heard in their absence. 


The Union’s case is that according to the rules of the Company, the 
workers were allowed casual leave with pay for five days in the year and 
medical leave at seven days per year. Medical leave used to be accumulated 
for three years. It 1s also stated that payment of the wages for sick leave 
und casual leave uvailed 01 was to be made at the end of the year. The 
72 men mentioned in the list attached to the order of reference, it is claimed, 
enjoyed medical leave and casual leave before the date of their discharge, 
but they were not paid wages for such leave. The Union, therefore prays for 
ক্র wages for casual and medical leave availed of by the workers and not 
paid for. 


P.W. 1 Shri Santi Ranjan Banerji, deposed for the Union. It appears 
that workers Nos. 44 Kali Charan Manna, 28 Jugesh Ch. Das and 5 Narendra 
Nath Dus of the order of reference are since dead, No award may there- 
fore be made on their behalf. All the workers were discharged between 
January and March 1954. They availed of the medical leave for seven 
days in the year in 1952 and 1969 and the casual leave for 5 days per year 
also in those years. Casual leave cannot be accumulated. TT ey shall, 
therefore, get wages for five days’ casual leave in 1952 and 14 days’ medical 
feave in 1952 and 1953. The statement attached to the Union’s written 
statement shows the wages payable to these workmen. The entitlements 
of the workers in wages for medical and casual leave as stated above has been 
shown in Annexure A to this award. Issue No. 1 is accordingly answered. 


Rart I] THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., SEPTEMBER 5, 1957 3589৩ 


According to the agreement between the workers and the Company, 
dated 22nd April 1949, the workers are also entitled to gratuity at 15 days’ 
basic wages for every year of service from 22nd April 1960 till the date 
of the introduction of the Provident Fund Scheme. It appears that the 
Government Provident Fund Scheme was introduced in 018 Company on 
138th March 1953. The workers who were in the service of the Company 
for more than three years are, therefore, entitled to three years’ gratuity at 
16 days’ basic pay per year. It appears that some of the workers are in 
the service of the Company only for 2 years. They should receive gratuity 
at 15 days’ basic wage per year for two years. The entitlements of the 
workers in gratuity is also shown in Annexure A, which shall form a part 
of this award, The workers mentioned in serial Nos 6 Narendra Nath Das, 
28 Jugesh Ch. Das and 44 Kalicharan Manna in Annexure A are excluded 
from the award as they are since dead. Annexure A shall form a part of 
this award. These issues are accordingly answered.

ORDER 


No. 3219-I.R./D/11L-69/56.—22nd August 1957.—Whereas under the 
Government of Wert Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 4568Dis. /D/ 
11]-69/56, dated the 24th October 1956, the industrial dispute between 
Messrs. Anderson Wright Ltd., 7 Wellesley Place, Caleutta and their work- 
men represented by Anderson Wright & Co. Employees’ Association, 
7 Wellesley Place, Caleutta-1, regarding the matters specified in the schedule 
thereto was referred for adjudication to the Fifth Industrial Tribunal; 


And whereas the suid Fifth Industrial Tribunal has submitted to the State 
Government ita award on the said industrial dispute; 


Now,.therefore, in pursuance of the provisions of section 17 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the Governor is pleased hereby 
to publish the said award as shown in the annexure hereto. 


ANNEXURE 


in the matter of an industrial dispute existing between Messrs. Anderson 
Wright Ltd,, 7 Wellesley Piace, Calcutta, and their workmen represented 
by Anderson Wright & Co, Employees’ Association, 7 Wellesley Place, 
Calcutta-1. (VIII —318/56.) 


BEFORE THE FIFTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL 


PRESENT: 
Suri (0. PALIT, Judge, Fifth Industrial Tribunal. 


Present for the Union: Shri D. L. Sen Gupta, Advocate, with 
Shri M. Saha, Advocate. 


Present for the Company: Shri M. Ghosh, Labour Adviser of the Indian 
Engineering Association and Shr R. Goswami, Junior Legal Adviser of 
the Bengal Chamber of Commerce. 


By (rovernment order No. 4568)is./D/111-69/56, dated the 24th 
October 1956, the aforesaid dispute has been referred to the Fifth Industrial 
Tribunal, presided over by me, for adjudication under section 10 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947). The said Fifth Industrial 
Tribunal was constituted under section 7 of the Act by the notification 
No. 3581Lab., dated the 9th June 1951. 


2. The reference was received here on 27th October 1956. The Union 
filed written statement on 15th November 1956. The Company filed 
written objection on 15th December 1956. After several adjournments the 
case was taken up for hearing on 29th July 1957, and the evidence was 
concluded on that date. The argument was heard on 30th July 1957. The 
award was reserved, 


38. The only issue contained in the schedule to the order of reference 
stands as follows :-— 


Whether those members of the subordinate staff, employed by Messrs. 
Anderson Wright Ltd., who were granted an increment of Rs. 10 
per month with o corresponding decrease in their dearness 
allowance according to the Mercantile Tribunal Award, published 
under Labour Department order No. 22d38Lab., dated the 7th May 
1949, in the Calcutta Gazette, Extraordinary, dated the 12th May 
1949, are entitled to restoration of the above deduction in dearness 


007 I} THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., 7 3583k 


ei 


allowance in view of the principles Jaid down in the award in 
respect of Messrs. Balmer Lawrie & Co. and their employees 
published in the Calcutta Gazette, dated the 2nd June 1905, and 
the award in respect of Messrs. Duncan Bros. ۸۹۸4ا‎ and their 
employees published in the Calcutta Gazette, dated the 26th 
January 1956. If so, from what date? 


AWARD 


4. The issue as framed is rather verbose. Not only that. To ask the 
Tribunal to decide a particular dispute according to the principles adopted in 
some other Tribunal adjudications is, perhaps, more than what is proper. 
When a dispute is referred to a Tribunal, the Tribunal is free to decide it 
in the manner it thinks best. Awards being judgments, cannot be made 
to orders. I am inclined to think that it will be ultra vires of the Govern- 
ment to ask the Tribunal to adjudicate a particular dispute according to 
certain reported decisions. The reason is obvious. The said decisions may 
have been based on particular sets of facts distinguishable from the facta 
[10,090 before the present Tribunal for adjudication of the present dispute. 
Besides, such decision is not binding on a court of concurrent jurisdiction. 
In that case the Tribunal can very well come to a decision contrary to what 
it is asked to contorm. A particular judgment, either of a High Court, or 
of the Supreme Court, is an authority for particular sets of facts involved, 
though such decisions are binding per sa on the subordinate courts. But 
still, if the facts are different, the subordinate court may very well give a 
contrary decision avoiding the binding .force of the rulings of the said 
judgment. This is the legal position which is accepted on all hands. So, 
judged in this light, the issue in the present case is anything but happy. 
The Tribunal has absolute freedom in the matter of giving its award, 
‘taeda gr it is not capricious or arbitrary. So, though the Tribunal is 
১010 to confine itself to the issue framed by the (Government, as _ per 
section 10(4) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, still it has its absolute 
and unfettered power to decide the particular dispute referred to it in the 
manner it thinks best. The Tribunal may accept the decisions referred to 
in the issue, if it is satisfied that.the said decisions are correct in the present 
sets of facts. With these preliminary observations I proceed to decide the 
issue. 


The Mercantile Tribunal by its award published on 12th May 1949 in the 
Calcutta Gazette, Extraordinary, at page 406, has given a decision which 
has led to the present dispute. It runs thus: 


“For the subordmmate staf—We replace the existing scales by the 
following: 139. تا‎ 0 7 


Dearness allowance is paid according to Bengal Chamber of Commerce 
scheme. All belonging to the subordinate staff shall be given 
an increment of Ry. 10 with a corresponding decrease in_ the 
dearness allowance without altering the total emoluments. For 
new entrants the dearness allowance according to the Bengal 


Chamber of Commerce shall be reduced by Rs. 10”’. 


This award was given effect ta, and continued till August 1904. In 
September 1954 a notice was issued by the Company intimating its 
intention to link dearness allowance of the subordinate staff with ‘ithe 
working class cost of living index. Prior to this it was Jinked with the 
middle-class cost of living index. This resulted in the reduction of dear- 
ness allowance from Rs. 61 to Rs. 58 per month, on the basis of the two 
sets of cost of living index as it stood at that time. A dispute arose over 


35831 THE CAL. GAZ. EATRY., SEPTEMBER 5, 1957 [Parr آ٢‎ 


পল্লি সে 


this switching over of dearness allowance from the hasis of middle-class 
cost of Jiving index to the basis of working class cost of living index. 
That dispute was referred to late 9. K. Neogi, Tribunal, for adjudication. 
The said Tribunal by his award in October 1952, decided that the working 
0188৭ cost of living index should govern the subordinate staff. The Union 
grudged this reduction in the amount of dearness allowance by this change- 
over of basis to determine the same. So a dispute again cropped up over 
this matter, and that dispute was referred to Shri M. N. Gan, Tribunal, 
for «adjudication. His award in the matter was published in_ the 
Caleutta Gazette, dated 2nd June 1955. Before that Tribunal the Union 
agitated that 30 per cent. of the total remuneration should constitute dear- 
ness allowance, and 70 per cent. of it should be merged into the basic pay. 
Shri Gan did not uphold this contention of the Union. 1106 decided in 
the case of Messrs. Balmer Lawrie & Co. and their employees, that the 
deduction of the amount which went up to make the minimum basic wage 
as Rs. 30 should not be done from the dearness allowance under the working 
class cost of living index. Shri J. N. Moitra, Tribunal, who decided the 
dispute between Messrs. Dunkan Bros. Ltd. and their employees, went 
further and decided that not only the amount of deficiency to make up the 
minimum basic wage of Rs. 30 per month should not be deducted from 
dearness allowance, but that refund should be made of such deductions 
from March 1954. His award was published in the Calcutta Gazette, dated 
26th January 1956, at page 369. So it is clear that in both these decisions 
of Shri Gan and Shri Moitra, they decided against this cut in dearness 
allowance under the working class cost of living index. So if these 
decisions are followed then this Tribunal mtat decide that the decrease in 
dearness allowance of a corresponding amount which was given as an 
increment in Messrs. Anderson Wright Ltd. should not be permitted. So, 
if I decide under the issue, as framed, my decision will be as above and 
that there ought to be restoration. 


But as I have already stated, I have to scrutinise whether the facts 
involved in the present case differ in any way from the facts involved in 
the aforesaid two decisions. The learned representative of the Company 
in the present case has made an endeavour to distinguish the facts of the 
present case from those of the aforesaid two decisions by pointing out that 
in the case of Anderson Wright Ltd. Rs. 10 per month was given to all 
employees irrespective of whether their wages were below Rs. 30 or above 
it. Arguing further, he contended that those employees who at that time 
were having a basic salary of Rs. 30 per month or above, had also this 
increment of Rs. 10. So the dearness allowance should be reduced by this 
amount. If this is not permitted, he said, those people stand to gain double 
advantages. They do not disgorge the amount of Rs. 10, but at the same 
time enjoy the benefit of the working class cost of living index in its 
entirety. This is argued to be unfair to the Company. But I must say 
that this is really no distinction of facts. If it 1s a distinction, then it 1s 
a distinction in degree, and not in kind. It cgnnot weaken the force of the 
decision. But I am afraid, there is some confusion in understanding the 
matter in ity proper perspective. Under the award of the Mercantile 
Tribunal when Rs. 10 was given as a fint rate inferement سا‎ respect of 
Messrs, Anderson Wright I.td., the said lenrned Tribunal must have found 
that not only the minimum basic wage was low here, but the basic wage 
of other employees and the subordinate staff was also low. So, the Tribunal 
granted relief in the shape of Rs. 10 general increment to all the members 
of the subordinate staff without discrimination. So, as a result of it, after 
that decision, the basic wage had a particular grade. Dearness allowance 
was, however, reduced by this amount. That means that dearness 


Part [[ THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., SEPTEMBER 5, 1957 3583m 


allowance was yiven less than what was warranted by the middle-class cost 
of living index, Now, when this standard of middle-class cost of living 
index was taken away from the subordinate staff, and they were made to 
submit to the lower standard of working olass cost of living index, all 
that we understand is that the basis of dearness allowance was changed. 
So there can be no point in retaining the tag-end of deduction of Rs. 10 
from the middle-class cost of living index to be tagged on to working clasa 
cost of living index. Shri .لا‎ N. Gan and Shri J. N. Maitra, Judges of 
the aforesaid Tribunals, found that by this change-over of the basis aforesaid 
the subordinate staff was subjected to reduction of Rs. 3 in the dearness 
allowance per month, calculated on the previous standard of living index. 
So it is cleur that their existing benefit was curtailed. Shri M. N. Gan 
objected to this. The Union contends that the condition of service was 
thus altered prejudicially. Now, whether I take this to be a change in 
the condition of service or whether it merely stands for curtailment of the 
existing benefit, the position is clear that the subordinate staff cannot be 
penalised twice over. Dearness allowance under the Mercantile Tribunal’s 
award on the middle-class cost of living index reduced by Hs. 10, was an 
integral whole as much as the working class cost of hving index. Now, 
the former cannot be split up, und one portion of it, viz., Rs. 10 cannot 
go over to the working class cost of living index to further reduce it. If 
this is allowed, then the benefit which was given under the Mercantile 
Tribunal’s award, would to a certain extent be negatived. 


The learned representative of the Company contends that the Union so 
long did not demur or object to this cut. So after this length of time it is 
estopped from claiming refund of the amount already paid in the shape of 
this cut. But this contention does not impress me. It will appear that 
the Union never acquiesced in this cut after the subordinate staff was 
subjected to the working class cost of living. First of all, it attempted to have 
70 per cent. of the dearness allowance being merged in the basic wage. 
When that was turned down by the Tribunal presided over by Shri Gan, 
it wanted to*have the middle-class cost of living minus this cut. When that 
was also turned down by Shri J. N. Moitra, Tribunal, it raised the present 
dispute. Now, when we consider that the Mercantile Tribunal represented 
the group of those commercial firms of which this Company was a member, 
os also other companies, then the fact of series of disputes will show that 
the Union did never submit to this cut without protest. But as the payment 
of salary, as much as dearness allowance, rests with the employer, the 
Union cannot do anything more than raising protests through one company 
or another, who are members of this mercantile body. So I can never 
accept the position as contended by the Company that the Union accepted 
this cut without demur and, as such, 18 estopped from agitating it. I 
reject this contention of the Company. 


So, considering the matter from an independent angle, apart from the 
said two decisions mentioned in the issue, I come to an identical finding 
that the dearness allowance under the working class cost of living index 
as is available to the subordinate staff of this Company, cannot be reduced 
by Rs. 10 because of the general increment given under the Mercantile 
Tribunal’s award, to the extent of this amount. 


Next, I come to the concrete relief which is available in the present 
circumstances. I find as above that the Company was not justified in 
making deduction of dearness allowance by Rs. 10. But this became 
untenable only when late 9. K. Niyogi, Tribunal, gave his award in October 
1952, subjecting the subordinate staff to the working class cost of living 
index. When the middle-class cost of living index governed the matter, 


3583n THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., SEPTEMBER 5, 1957 [Part ] 
ہے‎ 2 0১0 
the deduction was in order. So I] award that the Company is made liabie 
to refund Rs. 10 per month which it had imposed on dearness allowance 
after the working clasa cost of living index was introduced regarding the 
subordinate staff in this Company. That must be subsequent to the uward 
af late S. K. Niyogi in October 1992. Shm J. N. Moitra in hit award in 
the case of Messrs. Duncan Bros. Ltd. granted a refund from March 1904 
though his award was published on 26th January 1956. In the present case 
I have not been supplied with the date when the Company subjected the 
subordinate ataff to the working class cost of living index. But my award 
is that the restoration of Rs. 10 per month in dearness allowance will be 
effective from the date when the cut was given effect to. This amount is 
made puyable in two equal successive monthly instalments after my award 
becomes operative. 


Dictuted and corrected hy me.

presence of the parties on the date fixed, i.e., on 29th August 1957. 
Shri Mahitosh Saha has deposed on oath that he now prefers to withdraw 
his Election Petition on grounds of ill-health and on medical advice due to 
an attack of high blood-pressure and coronary insufficiency (vide medical 
certificate filed in support of his petition). He has further deposed that in 
view of his ill-health he requires absolute rest—physical and mental—for 
at least two months next and as such it is not possible for him to continue 
his Election Petition and to bear the strain and anxieties thereof. 
Shri Mahitosh Saha, in answer to this Tribunal, further conceded that 
he was not only withdrawing from the Election Petition but also was 
withdrawing the allegations made in the Election Petition regarding false 
personations of dead and absent voters by the respondent No. 1, the 
successful candidate, and that he had made those allegations under bona 
fide belief and that he had no materials at this stage to prove them. 
Shri Mahitosh Saha has further deposed that he has not entered into any 
contract or bargaining with the و‎ দা (No. (1), whose election has 
been challenged, for withdrawing this Election Petition. He denied to 
have received or to have been promised any sum in consideration of his 
present withdrawal. 


The respondent No. (1), Shri Pramatha Nath Dhibar, the successful 
candidate from the Galsi Assembly Constituency for the Reserved seat, does 
not oppose this রর for withdrawal but presses for costs to the score 
of Rs. 1,000. Shri Pramatha Nath Dhibar has taken his oath to depose

before this Tribunal on the preliminary point whether leave would be 
granted to the petitioner for withdrawal of his petition on the ground of 
ill-health as stated above. He denied to have caused the custing of votes 
for dead persons or for absent voters. He further deposed that he has not 
induced Shm Mahitosh Saha to filo thia petition for withdrawal to his benefit 
nur has he bargained with him in making him to withdraw his Election 
Petition. He has further deposed thut if this Election. Petition is 
allowed to be withdrawn by this Tribunal and if no other person appears 
and is permitted to continue this Election Petition then he would also 
withdraw his Recrimination Petition making counter-alleyations against 
Shri Mahitosh Saha, viz., of Shri Mahitosh Saha having caused votes for 
dead persons and for absent persons being cast by false personation. 


Having perused the Election Petition of Shri Mahitosh Saha I find that 
the only material grounds taken for declaring the election of respondent 
No. (1), Shri Pramatba Nath Dhibar, were that (a) some electors died long 
before the daté of poll and respondents Nos. (1) and (2) managed to get the 
votes of those dead persons recorded in their favour resorting to corrupt 
practices (vide particulars given in Schedule A), (b) that fulse personation 
wus resorted to with the help of and connivance of respondents Now. (1) and 
(2) and votes of absent electors were recorded (vide particulars stated in 
Schedule B) and that the reception of void votes in favour of Shri Pramatha 
Nath Dhibar materially affected the petitioner adversely in this election. It 
may be noted here that the result of the election was that the petitioner 
Shri Muhitosh Saha lost to reapondent No. (1) Shri Pramatha Nath Dhibar 
in the Reserved seat of the Galsi Assembly Constituency by only one vote. 


‘‘Personation 18 no longer a corrupt practice but votes cast by personation 
are void votes and will avoid the election if they have ss affected 
the result of the election. A person is said to vote by personation when he 
votes in the name of another person, whether living or dead, or in a fictitious 
name, or in his own name when by reason of the fact that he has already 
voted in the same or some other constituency, he is not entitled to vote.” 


Sub-section (2) of section 110 provides the grounds for refusal of an 
application for withdrawal where such application appears to the Tribunal 
to have been induced by any bargain or consideration which ought not 
to be allowed. Similar considerations have to be made when refusing 
leave to withdraw under section 109, sub-section (1). At this preliminary 
stage when considering whether leave should be granted and whether 
the application for i te should be granted or refused on the ground 
of ill-health of the petitioner and in the absence of any materials to 
suggest any bargaining or consideration which ought not to be allowed, 
and after giving my very careful consideration on the implication of 
such withdrawal, I see no reason to refuse the leave to proceed with this 
petition for withdrawal, or to refuse this application for withdrawal of 
the Election Petition. 


Shri Mahitosh Saha is a respectable retired Executive Engineer and 
considering his old age there can be no doubt, in the absence of any 
denial to the contrary, that he is really suffering from high blood pressure 
and coronary insufficiency which has induced him bona fide to withdraw 
his Election Petation on medical advice to avoid the necessary strain— 
both mental and physical—resulting from prosecuting this Election 
Petition further. (Refer Burdwan Division, South, 2 H.I.E.P., 82; 
L.D.E.C., 287). I am satisfied that this withdrawal petition has not been 
induced by any bargain or consideration and os such this petition must 
be allowed subject to payment of costes to contesting respondents Nos. (1), 
(2) and (4). No cost is allowed to the other respondents (3) and (5), who 
have not appeared. ۱ 

Respondent No. (1), Shri Pramatha Nath Dhibar, has deposed that he 
has incurred costs to the extent of Rs. 1,000 in drawing up his petition 
in Recrimination and in contesting the Election Petition. He has not,

however, filed any accounts or receipts to show the actual costs incurred 
by fim. ig agi the fact that the success of Shri Prumatha Nath 
Dhibur wos by a solitary vote in excess to the votes secured by the 
petitioner, there can be no doubt that there were reasonable grounds for 
filing this Election Petition. However, considerinig all these cireum- 
stances and in view of the fact that the petitioner Shri Mahitosh Saha 
has sought for withdrawal of his Election Petition at the very early stage 
before 01 evidence has been taken, I think the ends of justice will 0 
met by allowing twenty gold mohburs as costs payable by Shri Mahitosh 
Saha to respondent No. (1), Shri Pramathe Nath Dhibar. 

Respondent No. (4) Shri Phani Bhusan Roy, one of the unsuccessful

of the Reserved seat from the said Constituency. He gppeared in 
persun and pressed for costs on the ground that he has been unnecessarily 
dragged in this proceeding. Under section 82(a) of the Representation 
of the -People Act, 1951 (as amended up to date), all the contesting 
candidates other than the petitioner are necessary parties where the 
petitioner in addition to claming a declaration that the election of all or 
uny gf the returned candidates as void, claims a further declaration that 
he himeelf or any other candidate has been duly elected, as here. 
Therefore, it cannot be said that he is an unnecessary party and has been 
dragged for harassment. Wowever, under section 110, sub-section (3), 
respondent No. (4) is also entitled to some nominal costs. He is thus 
allowed one ‘gold mohur as costs, to be paid by the petitioner ‘Shri Mahitosh 
Saha. Respondent No. (2) was impleaded as having colluded with 
respondent No, (1) in the said election campaign. Respondent No. (2) 
has been-elected to the General seat from this Constituency. Shri Mahitosh 
Saha shall pay two gold mohurs as costs to respondent No. (2). 

Ordered 

Let leave to proceed with the petition for withdrawal of the Election 
Petition he granted under section 109, sub-section (1), The petitioner 
Shri Mahitosh Saha is further permitted to withdraw his Election 
Petition under section 110, subject to the payment of costs to the 
respondents Nos. (1), (2) and (4)—twenty gold mohurs [Rs. 340 (including 
pleader's fee)] to respondent No. (1) Shri  Pramatha Nath Dhibar, 
two gold mohurs (Rs. 84) to respondent No. (2) Shri Fakir Chandra ltoy 
and one gold mohur (Rs. 17) to respondent No. (4) Shri Phan) Bhusan 
Roy. Notice of the withdrawal be forthwith published in the Oficial 
Gazette, under section 110(3)(b). Any person who might have been ‘a

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 
DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH 
Public Health, 


NOTIFICATION 
No. P.H. /4297/2R-45 /57.—6th September 1957.—Whereas the Gover- 


nor is satisfied that oreas in the district of Jalpaiguri, not constituted muni- 
cipalities under the Bengal Municipal Act, 1992 (Bengal Act XV of 1982), 
hereinafter referred to as the said areas are threatened with an outbreak of 
Influenza being a dangerous epidemic disease; 


And wherens the Gdvernor is satisfied that the ordinary provisions of 
law, for the time being in force in the enid areas, are insufficient for the 
purpose of preventing the outbreak and spread of the said disease ; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the power conferred by section 2 of the 
Kpidemic Jiseases Act, 1897 (III of 1897), the (fovernor is pleased to 
prescribe for a period of three months the following temporary regulations 
to be ovserved by the public and by all persons affected thereby for prevent- 
ing the outbreak and spread of the said سر‎ in the said 8۰: 


Regulations 


1. (1) These regulations shall apply to the areas in the district of 
Jalpaiguri, not constituted municipalities under the Bengal Municipal Act, 
1932 (Bengal Act XV of 1982). 


(2) They shall come into force at once. 


2 In these regulations, unless there is anything repugnant in the 
subject or context :— 
(a) ‘Board’? means a Jalpaiguri District Board constituted under the 
Bengul Local Self-Government Act of 1885 (Bengal Act IIT of 
1885) ; ۱

issue 


What should be the rates of wages and dearness allowance for the 
workers of the Listing Department (Ribon Loom workers)? 


AWARD 
Decisions 


issue No. 1: The two Unions in their written statements put forward 
the same grievances. Their claims as set up in their written stgtements 
will be detailed below. 


The Ribbon Tooms are narrow looms inatalled in a separate department 
culled the Listing Department for the manufacture of what is called webbing 
or ribbons from jute fibres. Till about 1952, the Eastern Manufacturin 
Co. was 7 tactory doing webbing only. Since 1952, it has also installe 
broad looms of a standard Jute Mill for the manufacture of hessian and 
sacking. The other mills involved in this reference are standard Jute Mills 
primarily engaged in producing hessian and sacking with a Listing Depart- 
ment fur manufacture of webbing. 


There have been three nwards hy three Major Tribunals on the wage 
structure of{-the workers in the Jute Textile Industry in West Bengal. There 
are more zhan LOU Jute Mills in West Bengal. Phe First, Scond and the 
Third Mayor dute Textile Tribunal Peale, mude respectively in 1948, 
1951 and 1955, formulated the wage structure of all categories of workmen 
in the Jule Textile Industry. The wages of the workers in the Listin 
Department which existed in some of the Jute Mills, ا‎ those mentione 
in the present order of reference, were not the subject-matter of any of the 
three Major Tribunal Awards mentioned above. 


The Government of West Bengal, by order of reference, dated 17th 
Noyember 1948, referred the industrial dispute between the Eastern Manu- 
facturing Co., Ltd. und their workmen to Shri S. N. Modak, 1.٥.۵. (Retd.), 
as the Tribunal for adjudication. The award of this Tribunal was 
publisiféd by Government of West Bengal, notification, dated 16th March 
1949. At this date, this Company was mainly manufacturing webbing cloth. 
The learned Tribunal in the award mentioned above fixed the wage atruoture 
of all (৮৮০70118801 manual workers in the decision of Issue No. 2. There 
were other questions raised in the proceeding and there were 22 issues in all. 
The learned Tribunal adopted the level decided upon by the First Jute 
Textile Tribunal and observed that the decisions in the award should be 
- more or less on a par with the decisions and directions of the Jute Textile 
Tribunal’s award دہ‎ far as practicable. The learned Tribunal also observed 
that it was of the utmost importance that the level of decisions and directions 
in the award which he was going to make should be more or less on a par 
with those involved in the Jute Textile Tribunal’s award as far as practi- 
enable, as workers of mills of similar character should be treated for practical 
purposes in the same way. The case of the Unions in their written state- 
ments is a3 follows :— 


Shri Modak fixed the wages for different categories of pieve-rated and 
time-r1ated workers more or less in line with the wages fixed for the corre- 
sponding categories of the workers In a standard Jute Mill hy the First Jute 

extilé Tribunal Award in 1948. But in most cases the wages fixed were 
slightly less than the corresponding wages fixed for the Jute Mill operative. 
The dearness allowance was fixed at the rate formulated for the Jute Mill 
operatives by the First Major Jute Award. The wages of the weaver fixed 


6 10d THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., SEPTEMBER 7, 1957 [Paxt I 


on the basis of two looms for a weaver. The Second Major Jute Textile 
Tribunal increased the dearness allowance of the Jute ill worker by 
Re. 14۔1‎ and all the mills concerned with a Listing Department granted a 
similar increase of dearness allowance to the workers of that department. 
The award of the Third Major Jute Textile Tribunal in 1955, which was 
upheld by the Hon'ble Labour Appellate Tribunal of India, allowed a nett 
increase of 48. 3-12-9 in the total emoluments of every Jute Mill worker. 
This crease was not given to the Listing Department workers by the mills. 
It is stated that the ভিজতে of the various Jute Mills concerned with 
the Tasting Department maintained different weaving work-loads and in one 
mill 4 looms per weaver was the rule. In the result, the Listing Departmont 
workers in the various mills began to agitate for uniformity of wages and 
conditions of service amongst the Listing Department workers in the several 
mills as also for similar wages, dearness allowance and conditions of service 
as are applicable to the corresponding categories of workers in tho standard 
Jute Mil An industrial dispute was raised and conciliation proceedings 
were started for the settlement of this dispute. As conciliation failed, this 
reference was made, The Unions pray for the following remedies :— 


(1) The overall] nett increase in emoluments of Rs. 3-12-9 per month 
awarded by the Third Omnibus Jute Tribunal should be granted 
to the workmen of the Listing Department of the Eastern Manu- 
facturing Co, with retrospective effect from Ist November 1955. 


(2) The resulting wage rates of the Eastern Manufacturing Co. should 
be accepted as the uniform standard, to which the wages in the 
remaining six specified mills should be made to conform with 
immediate effect. 


(3) The said standardised wage rate structure should be made applicable 
on the basis of standardised work-loud of two ribbon looms per 
weaver as was prevalent nt the time of Shri Modak’s award. 


(4) For every additional ribbon loom operated by a weaver above two 
looms, subject to a maximum of 4 looms, he should be paid the 
full earnings of the production of each additional loom. 


(5) Sardars’ and weavers’ piece-rates for ribbon looms should be 
calculated on the basis of 100 yards unit of each variety of fabric 
and the winders’ rates on the basis of 100 Ibs. of yarn or twist. 


The Indian Jute Mills Association in its written statement states as 
follows :— 


The Eastern Manufacturing Co. was not a party before the First Jute 
Tribunal and the First Jute Award, which was published in 1948, was not 
binding in this Company. There was a separate Tribunal for the Eastern 
Manufacturing Co. and this Tribunal accepted the award of the First Jute 
Tribunal as the standard and made an award accordingly in 1949. Some 
rates fixed by the Company, as observed by that award, were definitely higher 
and for this reason, there was a slight variation in some rutes between the 
Firet Tribunal Award and the award by Shri S. ই, Modak on the Eastern 
Manufacturing Co. The award of Shri Modak was not binding on other 
Jute Mills engaged in the manufacture of Listing as one of the items of 
their production. These Jute Mills implemented the successive Jute Awards 
in the matter of wage fixation of all the categories of workmen including 
those of the Listing Section. Excepting the workmen of the Winding, 
Beaming, Weaving, Ribbon Reeling (Cloth Rolling) Departments of the 
Listing Sections, all other workmen engaged in the manufacture of Listing in 
the Jute Mills are common and correspond with the workmen engaged in the 
manufacture of hessian and sacking goods in Jute Mills. The Agarpara Jute 
Mills followed the wage rates of the Modak award for these workmen: Since 


Part I} THE (ঠা, GAZ. EXTRY., SEPTEMBER 7, 1957 36199 


the publication of the Modak award in 1949, the Eastern Manufacturing Co. 
has developed itself into a Jute Mill producing hessian and sacking goods 
us well and this Company was a party before the Third Jute ‘Textile 
Tribunal. All the Jute Mills who were parties in the present reference have 
implemented the directions of the Third Jute Award in respect of the 
standardisation of wage rates. The Eustern Manufacturing Co. and Agar- 
para Milla made necessary adjustments in the basic wages and dearnesa 
allowance in respect of workmen doing common jobs after the publication 
of the award of the Third Jute Textile Tribunal. ‘No change was made by 
these two mills in the basic wage or dearness allowance of workmen solely 
engaged in Listing and these rates continued to be more favourable to the 
workers. Listing operation is not also covered by the Third Jute Award. 
In the mills who also manufacture Listing, the operation of 3 hsting looms 
by one weaver has been a common feature since before 1949 and in some 
mills one weaver started to look after 4 looms or more. The work-load in- 
volved in operating one listing loom is very much lower than operation of 
one hessian loom. In a normal listing loom operation there are at most 
only 45 warp threads whereas in a normal hessian loom operation there are 
more than 400 warp threads. Furthermore, in the listing loom, breakages 
of warp threads are very infrequent, in view of the fact that these threads 
are double ply or more. Considering these facts, operation of at least 4 
listing looms per weaver cannot be said to involve heavier work-load than 
the operation of a single hessian loom. Operation of at least 4 listing looms 
per weaver should, therefore, be 11810 down as a standard work-load, and the 
wages should be standardised accordingly. The wages for Winding, Beam- 
ing, Reeling and Packing should be standardised so that they may not be 
out of proportion with the wages of workers of similar designations in Jute 
Mills. The demands made by the Unions are divorced from the realities 
of the situation and if the demands are accepted, financial burden of the 
Industry would be increased considerably and there 18 the danger that the 
market for the manufactured products will be adversely affected. The 
demands of the Union should be rejected so that the future of ]8 
production is not jeopardised. 


The written atatement of the Bharat Jute Mills alan shows that they 
have adjusted the wages of the Winding, Beaming, Weaving and Ttibbon 
Reeling workers of the Listing Section of the mill. It is stated that the 
work-load should not be reduced as the market will be seriously affected. 
The Company further states that working of 3 listing looms by one Winder 
is & commoa feature in the Industry and one Weaver can very easily operate 
4 کت‎ This Mill also prays that the demands of the Union shall be 
rejected, 


The award of Shri Modak on the Eastern Manufacturing Co. was 
published 1» March 1949. The Eastern Manufacturing Co. was then only 
a webbing mill with no standard Jute Mill operation of the manufacture of 
hessian and sacking goods. This mill has, however, since developed into a 
standard Jute Mil] for manufacture of hessian and sacking goods since 1952 
and 1963. The First Jute Award was made in September 1948, which 
standardised nomenclature and wage atructure for all categories of work- 
men in a standard Jute Mill. Shri Modak in making the award for the 
Eastern Manufacturing Co. followed the First Jute Award and attempted to 
formulate a similar wage level as were awarded for corresponding workers 
in a standard Jute Mill by the First Award. This fact will appear from 
the learned Tribunal’s observations at pages 260, 2%2 and 264 of the award 
(vide West Bongal Government publication of awards for the quarter ending 
March 1949). The Eastern Manufacturing Co, is one of the seven Jute

ANNEXURE 
in the matter of an industrial dispute existing between Messrs. Modern 
Art Press, 6 Bentinck Stroet, Calcutta-1, and their workmen represented 


by Press Workers’ Union, 19-M Panchanantola Lane, Calcutta-12 
(Case No. Vill—142 of 1956.) 


BEFORE THE SIXTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL 


Pore 


PRESENT: 
Surt SAILESH SENGUPTA, Judge, ১:০6) Industnal Trbunal.

For Lad 171,707: Shri Panchanan Bhattacherjee, Vice-President of the 
nion, 


For the Company: None. 
By order No. 3993Dis./D/13L-28/56, dated Calcutta, the 7th Septem- 


ber 1956, Government made this reference for adjudication of a dispute 
between Messrs, Modern Art Press and their workmen in regard to the 
question of dismissal of ten employees. 


‘he point for adjudication as per schedule is as follows :-— 


Whether the dimissal of the following persons was justified? What 
relief are they entitled to P— 


(1) Mr. G. Albin. 

(11) Shri Gouri Sankar Dey. 

(111) Shr Biren Ghosh. 

(iv) Shri Banamali Misra. 

(v) Shri Brojen Bose. 

(vi) Shri Baidyanath Chakraborty. 
(vil) Shri Deben Ghose. 
(viii) Shri Subhas Ch. Bose. 

(ix) Shri Krishna Kr. Debnath. 

(x) Shri Moni Mukherjee. 


The ease presented on behalf of the 10 employees is that their services 
were terminated on the 9th of July 1955, on the false plea that they were 
negligent in discharging their duty, and were not oxerting নিত ডি to 
their utmost to provide normal production. As a matter of that they were 
not receiving their wages for months together. A case was started before 
the Authority under the Payment of Wages Act on complaint made by the 
workers. Certain grievances were (placed before the Management by a 
signed petition, The grievances were not redreased, Qn the other hand, 
the Management was highly incensed at the conduct of the workers in 
starting un agitation for amelioration of their conditions. For these reasons 
these employees were thrown out of omployment all on a sudden. They 
are entitled to reinstatement and wages for the entire period. 


The Company filed written statement alleging that these workers were 
responsible for disturbing the peaceful atmosphere of the establishment. 
They had deliberately resorted to tricks to avoid giving normal production. 
No improvement was noticed even after warnings had been issued. As the 


Part 1] THF CAL. GAZ. EXTRY.. SLPTEMBER 7, 1067 3610 
2 ১ সস ہے ہے‎ 
financial condition of the Company deteriorated and these workers could 


not be controlled there was no other alternative but to dispense with their 
services. 


Another point was raised that no dispute was subsisting at the 0866 of 
termination of their services. ‘They were not therefore workmen within 
the meaning of the Industrial Disputes Act. 


Shr N. M. Das Gupta who had been representing the Company 
intimated on Ilth April 1957 that the Modern Art Press had gone into 
liquidation. The spokesman of the workers categorically danied the truth 
of the statement, 1109 was still given time to make enquiries and take 
steps jf the information given by the leurued Advocate was correct. Another 
date .ا حالص‎ On that date none uppeared for the Company and the 
Union led ,evidence that the Press had not gone into liquidation. It was 
conducting its normal business as before. In view of the sworn testimony 
denying the allegation that the concern had gone into liquidation, hearing 
of the case was taken up. As none represented the Company the hearing 
Was cv parte. 


The view was taken in some cases that the term ‘‘workman"’ cannot 
he applied to a former employee who has been discharged or dismissed 
otherwise than during an industrial dispute. This view has not been 
upheld by later decisions. Reference may be made to a decision of the 
Bombay [hgh Court reported in 1986 1, 15,151.) page 492 and a decision 
of the Supreme Court reported in 1957 1, L.0.J., page 27. 


by the evidence adduced by P.W, 1 the fact has been established that 
the services of these 10 employees were suddenly terminated without any 
reasonable ground. The witness denied that they were negligent in 
in performance of their duty or had avoided giving normal production. 
No warning had ever been administered to them. On the other hand, 
Ext. 100) shows that the workers had grievances which they wanted to be 
removed. This upplicution apparently caused irritation and action was 
shortly taken by way of retaliation. There was no charge-sheet or enquiry 
in regard to the allegations made against the workers in the written ۰ 
ment. The Tribunal must accordingly hold that their dismissal was 
unwarranted. The dismissed workers ure entitled to reinstatement and 
wages. They must be reinstated and paid their wages for the period of 
unemployment within 13 days from the date of publication of the award 
in the Caleutta Gazette.

No. PH. /4447/2R-45 /57.—11th September 1957.—Whereas the Gov- 
ernor ig,satisfied that the Municipalities of Kalimpong, Darjeeling, Siliguri 
and Kurseong are threatened with an outbreak of Influenza, bemg a 
daterous epidemic disease ; 

۶ And whereas the Governor is satisfied that the ordinary provisions of 
law, for the time being in force in the said Municipalities, are insufficient 
for the purpose of preventing the outbreak and spread of the said disease; 

Now. therefore, in exercise of the power conferred by section 2 of the 
Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 (III of 1897), the Governor is pleased to 
prescribe for a period of three months the following temporary regulations 
٥۵ be observed by the public and by all persons affected thereby for prevent- 
ing the outbreak and spread of the said disease in the said Municipalities. 


Regulations

Darjeeling, Siliguri and Kurseong. 
(2) ‘Shey shall come into force at once.

subject or context—

(c) ‘‘Medical Practitioner’? means any person practising the medical 
profession ; 
(0) ‘‘Patient’’ means a person suffering from or suspected to he 
suffering from Influenza;

Transport 


NOTIFICATION 


No. 5571 W.T.—6th September 1967.—In exercise of the power conferred 
by section 68 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 (IV of 1939), the Governor 
is pleased to make the following amendments in the Benga] Motor Vehicles 
Rules, 1940, published under notification No. ۰. 
tember 1940, at pages 2665-2829 of Part I of the Calcutta Gazette of the 
10th October 1940, as subsequently amended, namely :— 


dated the 21st Sep- 


Amendments 


For rule 52 of the said rules, substitute the following rule: — 
192. State Transport Authonty— 


(a) The State Government shall appoint an officer in the service of the 
State Government to be the Secretary of the Authority. 


(৮) In the State Transport Authority the number of membera whose 
presence shall constitute a quorum shall be— 


(i) in the case of un Authority consisting of not more than three 
members, the total number of members constituting the 
Authority, or 


(52) in any other case, three. 


(c) Where the State Transport Authority consists of more than three 
members, the Authority may, at its first meeting, elect one of 
the members to be the Deputy Chairman. At any meeting of 
the Authority where a quorum is present, the Chairman shall 
preside and if the Chairman is unable ٤ attend, the Deputy 
Chairman shall act as the Chairman of the meeting and in the 
absence of both the Chairman and the Deputy Chairman, the 
members present shall elect one of their members, to act as the 
Chairman of the meeting. 


(d2) The Chairman or the .Deputy Chairman or any member acting as 
Chairman of a meeting under sub-rule (6) shall have 0, second or 
casting vote in all cases of equality of votes. 


(6) The State Transport Authority shall meet at such times and at 
such places as the Chairman may appoint: 


Provided that the Authority shall meet not less than once in each of 
the periods of three months of January to March, April to June, 
July to September, and October to December unless the State 
Government otherwise directs. 


(f) Not less than ten days’ notice shall be given of any meeting of the 
State Transport Authority. 


(y) The period of ghee of the State Transport Authority shall 
ordinarily be three years: 


Provided that the State Government may, if it considers necessary to 
do so, reconstitute the Authority at any time before the expiry 
of the said period of three years or extend the said period to more 
than three years. 


(h) The State Government may, at any time, after giving any member 
of the State Transport Authority an opportunity of being heard, 
remove him from office for— 


(i) misconduct in the discharge of his duties, or 

(ii) any disgraceful conduct, or 
(tit) persistent failure to attend meetings of the Authority, or 
(w) any other cause deemed sufficient by the State Government. 


(£) When a member of the Authority dies, or is removed from or 
vacates his office, the State Government may appoint another 
member in hia place who shall, subject to the provisions of the 
proviso to sub-rule (g) and sub-rule (7৮), hold office for the re- 
mainder of the term of the Authority. 


(1) A member of the State Transport Authority shall receive a daily 
fee of fifteen rupees for every day on which he attends a meeting 
of the Authority and shall further be entitled to receive travelling 
and halting allowances at the scale and on the conditions apph- 
cable to members of the West Bengol Legislature, and any 
such member performing any journey in connection with the 
business of the Authority, otherwise than to attend the meeting 
of the Authority, shall, with the sanction of the Chairman, be 
entitled to receive travelling and halting allowances likewise: 


Provided that the daily fee of fifteen rupees for attending meetings of 
the Authority shall not be admissible to an official or to a 
member of Parliament or the State Legislature.”’ 


By order of the Governor, 
B. K. SEN, Asst. Secy.

OFFICE OF THE ACCOUNTANT-GENERAL, WEST BENGAL

Subject: Submiesion of statements of foreign nationals employed in 
departmonts of the Covernment of India and occupying Covernment 
accommodation. 


No. TM/630.—27th August 1907.—To facilitate the expeditious issue 
of “No Demand Certificates’? in respect of foreign nationals employed in 
the vuricua Ministries / Departments of the Government of India it has been 
decided that all departments of the Goverament of India will have to send 
to the Estate Officer, Government of India, in the first week of April each 
year, statements showing the names and designation of foreign nationals 
employed by them together with particulars of Government accommodation 
کہ‎ their occupation till the end of February of the year to which the 
statements relate. To begin with, the statements referred to above for 
the period from the date the Officer joined the department up to 28th 
February 1957 have to be sent to the aforesaid Officer. 


If during the course of the year it becomes known that the services of 
a foreign national are due to be terminated from a certain date the office 
concerned should send intimation to this effect to the Estate Officer, as early 
ag possible, through a demi-official letter to enable him to take action for 
cancellution of the allotment. A copy of that communication should also 
be endorsed to the F.A. to the Estate Officer with the request for issue of 
a “No Demand Certificate’, 


All heads of offices of the Government of India under the audit contro! 
of this office are hereby requested to note the above instructions for 
compliance. 


Subject: Corrections to Treasury Rules. 


No. TM/63).—27th August 1957.—All Treasury Officers and Sub- 
Treasury Officers in West Bengal, the Mannger, Reserve Bank of India, 
Caleutta, and all heads of offices of the Government of India under the 
audit control of this office are hereby informed of the following further 
corrections made in the Central Government Compilation of the Treasury 
Rules, Volume I, First Edition, Third Reprint :— 


(1) Page 190: Rule 624— 
Add the following as a sub-paragraph below the existing rule:— 


“Balances in the Personal Deposit Accounts do not lapse to Govern. 
ment under rule 635 if outstanding for more than three complete 
Account years. In coses, however, in which the Personal Deposit 
Accounts are created by debit to the Consolidated Fund, the same 
should be closed at the end of the financial year by minus debit 
of the balance to the relevant service heuds in the Consolidated 
Fund, the Personal Deposit Accounts being opened next year 
again, if necessary, in the usual manner. If a Personal Deposit 
Account is not operated upon for a considerable period and there 
is renson to believe that need for the Deposit Account has ceased, 
the same should be closed in consultation with the Officer in whose 
favour the Deposit Account has been opened.’’ 


(2) Page 32: Rule 92-- 


Number the existing Note below this rule as ‘‘Note 1'' and insert the 
following as Note 2:— 


‘‘Note 2.—Any person paying money into a treasury or the Bank on 
Government account to the credit of the Central Public Works 
Department shall present with it a memorandum or chalan m form 
Ne. T.R. 6 with the letters ‘C.P.W.D.’ superimposed diagonally 
in red ink on the chalan.’’

By Government order No. 4842Dis./D/11L-123/56, dated the 28th 
September 1956, the aforesaid dispute has been referred to me under section 
10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947). The said Fifth 
Industrial Tribunal was constituted under section 7 of the Act by the 
notification No. 3381Lab., dated the 9th June 1991. 


2. The reference was received here on 22nd October 1956. The Union 
filad written statement on 15th November 1956. The Company filed 
written objection on 15th December 1956. After several adjournments the 
case was taken up for hearing on 17٤ط‎ July 1957 when the evidence was 
সস The argument was heard on 18th July 1957, and the award was 
reseryed. 


3. The only issue contained in the schedule to the order of reference 
atands as follows: 
- Are the employees entitled to any bonus for the years 1904 and 1965? 
If so, what should be the quantum? 


3352 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 12, 1957 ھ۲۸]‎ 1 
১৯৯১ ১০১ ০০৯ 
AWARD 


The Company has filed its balance sheets audited by Messrs. George 
Reod & Co., Chartered Accountants, for the years 1953, 1954 and 1999. The 
Company contends that it has hardly any margin of profit left for giving 
bonus for those two years in question, viz., 1954 and 1955. If the formula 
of the Labour Appellate Tribunal, as given in the Rastriya Mill Mazdoor 
case, is followed, then as per the Ext. ,لا‎ it will appear that the Company 
has no available surplus for giving bonus. Rather, there will be found 
a deficit to the extent of Rs. oF 000 and odd in 1954 and Rs. 19,000 and odd 
in 1955. The Union has filed a chart working out the same formula m 4 
manner in which it is shown that even after payment of three monthis' 
salary as bonus for the two years in question, there will still be profits 
to the extent of Rs. 22,000 and odd in 1954 and Rs. 82,000 and odd ju 
1955. This chart of the Union working out the formula of the Later 
Appellate Tribunal has heen marked as Ext. 1 in this case. 


I must point out that this Labour Appellate Tribunal’s formula for 
finding out available surplus for bonus does not, strictly speaking, apply 
to firms other than manufacturing concerns. The present firm دا‎ in 
importing business mainly, and also in locally manufactured commodities. 
At all events, it does not do any manufacturing business itself. In that 
view the above formula 18 out of place in its application here. 


Next, even if I find that the said formalu is applicable to the present 
case, I shall find, even according to the Union as per its chart, Ext. 1, that 
the prior charges in 1954 amounted to Rs. 85,000 and odd and Rs. 76,000 
and odd in 1955. Regarding the profit and loss account, which is not 
disputed, I find that the income in 1904, including income from other 
sources, was Rs. 72,000 and odd and in 1995 it was Rs. 69,000 and odd 
(vide Ext. B). So, regard being had to the admitted prior charges, the 
balance shows a deficit in both these yeurs. To obviate this, the Union 
has taken that in the Calcutta branch of the Company the net profit 1s 
Rs. 1,20,000 in 1954 and it is Rs. 1,70,000 in 1955. Taking those figures 
into the reckoning, it is shown that there is available surplus in each of 
those years in question. But this method of calculation of the Union 
cannot be accepted. Firstly, there is no separate account for the Calcutta 
branch. The Company made some provisional accounting to ascertain 
the profits of the Calcutta branch, excluding the profits in the Calcutta 
Head Office, only to determine the commission that is payable to the 
Branch Manager Shri K. N. Roy. Shri K. N. Roy is entitled to certain 
commission on profits of the Calcutta branch, excluding the Head Office, 
as it will appear from the confidential letter, dated 18th May 1951. The 
Union, from the oral evidence, has ascertained what percentage the Calcutta 
branch office should get out of the profits. But this, to say the least, is 
highly speculative, and no reliance can be made on it. So, I cannot hold 
that the profits of the Calcutta branch office are as stated by the Union in 
its chart as per the Ext. 1. Besides, when there is only one consolidated 
balance sheet for the whole Company, audited by Chartered Accountunts, 
there having been no separate audited balance sheet for the particular 
branch, and when the profits of that particular branch are merely matters 
of speculation or so, I cannot apply the formula of the Labour Appellate 
Tribunal for ascertaining the available surplus for the purpose of bonus 
with reference to profits of that particular branch, namely, Calcutta 
branch. In that view also the calculations made hy the Union are 
unacceptable. 

Next, if I scrutinise the audited balance sheets of 1954 and 1958, 1,6, 
the years in question, I get that in 1954, 9৪ per the balance sheet, Ext. Al, 


١٣۲11 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 12, 1957 3353 


পু 
the balance thut was carried forward to the next year was Rs. 5,000 and 
odd after payment of taxes and dividends. In the year 1955, as per the 
Ext. A2, the balunce sheet reveals that only Rs. 1,500 and odd was 
carried forward to the following year after payment of taxes and dividends. 
This clearly shows that the bulance of profits is extremely meugre, taken 
as a whole of the business. This is hardly sufficient for payment of bonus 
which, for a single month even, roughly amounts to Rs. 3,800. In the 
Muir Mills case decided = the Hon’ble Supreme Court in January 1956, 
bonus was made মা fag only when the profits are huge, or at least sufficient. 
The Labour Appellate Tribunal systematically held that bonus is payable 
as a matter of policy or as a matter of principle only when the Company’s 
finuncial position is sound, and its capacity to earn profits for some years 
to come cun be depended upon. But here in the present Company, due to 
restrictions imposed by the stringent import and export policy of the 
Government, it is faced with a crisis. I have got in evidence that the 
Company has been forced to cut down its imports, and the necessary result 
hus been that the profits are dwindling down. Of course, it has got an 
agency of Amul butter recently, but it still remuins to be seen how far it 
can help tiding over the present critical position. In this view of the 
matter, to grant bonus sa result in accelerating the ruin of the Company. 
That is certainly not desirable even from the workmen’s point of view. 
So the workmen will be well advised not to claim bonus at least for some 
time to come till the Company bas improved its position such that its profits 
become. more or less dependable and adequute. So the present claim for 
bonus is rejected. 


Dictated and corrected by me. 


G. PALIT, G. PALIT, 
Judge. Judge, Fifth Industrial Tribunal.

Ry (zovernment order No. 66-I.R./D/10L-93(A)/56, dated the 5th 
January 1907, the aforesmd dispute has been referred to the Fifth Industrial 
Tribunal, presided over by me, under section 10 of the Industrial Disputes

2. The reference was received here on 1161) January 1957. The Union 
filed written statement on 9th February 1957. The Company filed written 
objection on 23rd March 1957. The case was taken up for hearing on 27th 
June 19)7. The evidence was taken on 5th August 1957 and 6th August

3. The issues contained in the schedule to the order of reference stand 
as follows :— 


(1) Whether the workmen of Berapukur Iron Works are entitled to 
any additional bonus for 1955? 


(2) To what quantum of bonus the workers of Berapukur Iron Works 
are entitled for the financial year ending on the 380th September 
1956? 


AWARD 


According to the Union, the Berapukur Iron Works is an establishment 
under Messrs. Martin & Burn Ltd. About 200 workmen are employed at 
Berapukur Iron Works, and about the same number of workmen are 
employed in the Head Office and depots including the depot at Kidderpore 
under the same managing agency. The workmen of the Berapukur Iron 
Works were granted 14 months’ basic pay as bonus for the year 1956, and 
one month’s basic pay as an advance tor the year 1956. The Head Office 
staff and the depot staff were granted three months’ basic salary as 
bonus in the aforesaid years. The workmen of this establishment opposed 
this discrimination in the matter, of bonus. It now claims six months’ 
basic ر0‎ as bonus for the said two years, or all events, what was 
granted for the Head Office staff and men in other depots under the same 
managing agency. 


Pant I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 12, 1967 3355 


আপস পা دی‎ A A دیج رجح تھی رس را‎ SS PE LE a A OE AL ETS, 


‘he Company opposes this claim for bouns by the Berapukur staff. 
It admits thut the Berapukur Iron Works is u workshop fabricating light 
structural materials under Messrs. Martin Burn Ltd. who have managing 
agency, selling agency and numerous other activities. This workshop is 
situated at Kidderpore, and is registered as o factory. It was a purty to 
the Major Engineering Tribunal. The Company says that there is no 
separate accounts for this establishment at Berapukur, but there is one 
consolidated balance sheet for the whole Company including the Works. 
Up to 1953 the employer did not pay any bonus to its workmen. On Oth 
January 1953 9 settlement was arrived at in a conciliation proceeding under 
which one month's 1)00810 sulary was given as bonus for that year's and also 
the same amount for previous years. This amount of bonus was also given 
in 1954. In 1955, however, the workmen claimed bonus at a higher rate. 
After some negotiations with the workmen, the Company gave 1/8th of 
the basic salary as bonus for the year 1955. The workmen accepted that 
bonus in satisfaction of their claim. In 1956 the Union demanded a still 
higher bonus, and also included in its claim an additional bonus for the 
year 1955. This has led to the present dispute. 


issue No. 1: This issue practically resolves itself under two heads, 
viz., (1) whether the workmen are entitled to any bonus higher than what 
was given for the year 1955, and (2), whether such claim is barred legally. 


Regarding the first branch of the contention the Union claims bonus on 
the profits of Messrs. Martin Burn Ltd. It contends that Messrs. Martin 
Burn 1500. granted 3 months’ basic salary, subject to a maximum of Its, 750, 
as bonus to the clerical staff for the year ending on the 30th September 
1955, having at their credit service of one year and over. Rupees one 
hundred was given on a flat basis to staff having Jess than one year’s 
service at their credit in that yenr. For the subordinate staff, it gave 3 
months’ basic salary to people who completed one year’s service in 199d, 
and Rs. 50 was given on a flat rate basis to people who put in service less 
than one year in the said year 1955. Later on, the amount of bonus was 
enhunced a bit in September 1955 on representation. The Company resists 
the claim of the Union on the ground that the Berapukur Iron Works is a 
registered factory, and bonus here must he governed by the profits it makes. 
The entire profits of Martin Burn Ltd., which is the managing agent of 
the Berapukur Iron Works, cannot form the basis of calculation of bonus 
available in this particular establishment. But, I am afraid, on the 
evidence on record I um unable to uphold this contention of the Company. 
I refer to the Ext. 106), dated 19th May 1956, which is a letter addressed 
by the Director of the Company to the General Secretary of the Union. 
It runs thus: 


‘We regret to note that the Union is raising objections to this bonus 
and are demanding that bonus should be computed according to sume 
formula used at Court some vears ago. We must point out that application 
of such a formula is hardly possible in the case of a small Structural Unit 
like the Berapukur Iron Works, which is not a separate Company, but 28

There is another point from which the matter should be viewed, i.e.. 
from the point of view of social justice. Social justice condemns discri- 
mination among workmen and workmen generally, and particularly in the 
matter of bonus when, to earn the total profit, ce put in conjoint and 
co-operative effort. As the Company has granted honus to the extent of 
three months’ salary in respect of the years 1954-55 and 1905-56 to the

no reason for denying it to the workers of the Berapukur Iron Works the 
profit of which department was, admittedly, included in the consolidated 
balance sheet of Martin Burn Ltd. Besides, discrimination in the matter 
of payment of bonus can never conduce to industrial peace. Industrial 
Tribunals exist for peace in the industrial sphere, and so discrimination 
except where merit and efficiency are involved, is condemned by them. 
Here it 1s not a case of merit and efficiency. So I hold that the workmen 
of the Berapukur Iron Works are legitimately entitled to bonus of three 
months’ basic salary for the years 1955 and 1956 like the workmen of the 
Head Office and the Entally Depot.

The Union case is that the workers of the Company are not receiving a 
square deal in regard to their service conditions. The wages paid to them 
are very low and stand no comparison with emoluments enjoyed by workers 
of other concerns of the locality. Dearness allowance is not given separately. 
As the Management did not respond to the Union appeal for rationalisation 
of the wages and other conditions of service the dispute had to be submitted 
to the Government. Ultimately this reference has resulted. 


The Company’s reply to the Union demand is that this concern is in the 
textile group but of much inferior status to the cotton mills. Wages that 
are heing paid compare favourably with wages paid by other concerns 
engaged in the same industry. Besides fixed wages, the Company has 
introduced an incentive bonus scheme so that workers applying themselves 
to improve production may earn more money. The Company has been 
suffering tremendous loss year after year. It has not the capacity to bear 
the brunt of any further enhancement of wages. The Company grants 
statutory leave according to the Factories Act, and some festival holidays. 
Regarding medical facilities, the Company’s reply is that the factory is 
governed by the Employees’ State Insurance Act. No special provision for 
medical facilities can therefore be claimed. Provident Fund scheme has 
been introduced under the Employees’ Provident Fund Act. In view of the 
straitened circumstances the Company cannot be made to introduce a 
gratuity scheme over and above the retiral benefit available under the 
said Act. Having suffered losses in all the years concerned the Company 
cannot be made liable to pay any bonus. Regarding service conditions, the 
Compuny stated that a draft standing orders was drawn up which would 
soon he submittéd for certification. Canteen facilities cannot be legitimately 
demanded as the number of workers is very small. Lastly, switching over 
from the system of daily wage to monthly wage system is resisted as 
unwarranted. 


A preliminary objection was takeu on behalf of the Company that in the 
order of reference the dispute is atated as having arisen between Messrs. 
Commercial Bureau, 9 Brabourne Road, and their workers. The adress 
given is that of the Head Office. The factory workers are intolved in the 
present dispute. The workers of the office at 9 Brabourne Road are not at 
all interested. According to the learned Lawyer for the Company the 
reference is bad inasmuch as the persons who are before the Tribunal, are 
not the employees of the Head Office. In support of his contention the

at page 2285. In the order of reference in that case the dispute was 
described as between Messrs. Butto Krishto Paul and Co., Ltd. (Head 
(fttice), 1 and 3 Bonfield Lane, Calcutta, and their employees. As some of 
the workers in the list attached to the reference were employees in the Sova 
Bazar Branch and some 11) other places the Tribunal held that theae men 
wer not concerned in the dispute, not being employees of the Head Office. 
In the present reference there is no question of any Head Office. The Com- 
pany has only one office and one factory. The factory workers are emplovees

say with any show of reason that the factory workers are not employees 
of the Commercial Bureau. The workers of the factory are within the fold 
of the reference. The objection raised is untenable.

Thy Company pays consolidated wages. Exhibits A and A(1) are charts

increments which came into effect in 1957. The Union case is that the wages

wages paid by other industries of same or similar nature. The Company 
relied strongly on its fast deteriorating financial position. Its কি 
sheets Ext. B series show a gloomy picture of loss in successive years. The

raised but that was not a good ground for repecting the audited balance

sheets must be treated as correct even though there might be some features 
which might breed suspicion. In 1956, the Company granted certain 
increments. 009 can safely say that the Management was satisfied that the 
existing wager were below the mark. Increments were given in order to 
cover the deficiency to some extent. Even after these increments we find 
that the wages actually paid are on the starvation line. In Exhibit A

Issue No, 4—Bonus for 1953, 1954 and 1955.

The balance sheet for 1955 has not yet been prepared. No decision can

The charts Exts. A and A(1) show that the number is 68. No direction for 
starting a canteen can be piven for such a handful of workers, specially 
when there is no evidence that Cafe and eating houses are not within easy 
reach. ‘Ibe financial position of the Company also forbids any action being 
taken to incrense the strain.

paid system, 


The Union wanted the daily-rated workers to be converted into monthly 
pnid workers. No reasona were given why this change should be made. 
Nothing was suggested in course of the argument in support of the claim. 
I find no reasonable ground to make any alteration in the existing system

An industrial dispute in respect of the following issues between Albion 
Plywood, Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as the Company), 11 Clive Row, 
Calcutta-1, and their workmen represented by the Albion Plywood Work- 
men’s Union, 6 Mahatma Gandhi Road, Budge Budge, 24-Parganas, was 
referred to this Tribunal for adjudication, by the Grovernment of Weat 
Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 1128-LQ. /IR/11L-129/57, dated the 
1160 April 1957. 


(1) Grades and scales of pay for each category of workers. 
(2) Dearness allowance. 

(3) Provident Fund. 

(4) Leave (sick, casual and festival). 

(5) Bonus for 1955. 


Both parties filed written statements, adduced evidence, oral and docu- 
mentary, and advanced arguments in the case. 


FINDINGS 


Issues Nos. 1 and 2: These two issues relate to grade and acales of pay 
aud dearness allowance. At present, there is no grade or scale of pay with 
provisions for annual increment. There is no dearness allowance, Provident 
Fund, etc., in this Company. The minimum earnings of an unskilled 
worker are Rs. 1-12 a day, all inclusive. The Union, therefore, demands 
that the minimum wages for a workman should be Rs. 85 to Rs. 100 per 
month, and that wages and dearness allowance at the enhanced rate should 
be paid with effect from August 1954. 


In contesting this claim, the Company states that it employs 150 
permanent hands and 160 temporary hands, and that the minimum conaoli- 
dated wages paid to an unskilfed workman is Rs. 12 per week, i.e., Rs. 2 
per day. Some of the temporary hands are paid below the said rates but 
their number is very small. No separate dearness allowance is paid. 
There is no justification either to split up the dearness allowance and basic 
wages, or to increase the rate of dearness allowance. The total wages paid 
compare favourably with those paid by other units of this industry. 


Learned representatives of both sides did not adduce any evidence 
directly on this point. It appears from their arguments and materials on 
record that this Company started its business in 1951. It is still in a 


3366 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 12, 1957 [Parr I 


nascent state and, therefore, it badly needs protection from all quarters. 
Shri Sen uppearing on 09151 of the Company contends that there are only 
two other big companies—one 19 Sitaman (U.P.) and the other in Bombay— 
and that this Company is not paying less than other companies in the same 
industry. At the same time, Shri Sen files oll the balance sheets of this 
Company since ity incorporation aud contends that it suffered a total loss of 
Rs. 7,69,949 up to 900) September 1954, and that it had earned some profits 
only in the years 1999 and 1956. The Company has a capital of Rg. 5,00,000, 
and borrowed a loan of Rs. 17,00,000 to run its business. The outstanding 
loss at the end of 30th September 1906 appears to be Rs. 4,98,748. Shri Sen 
invites the Tribunal to ounsider the issue against the background of the 
Company's position in the industry and of its finance. We are not in a 
position to suy, in the absence of any direct evidence on this point, that this 
Company is paying what others are paying elsewhere in this industry. On 
its own admission, it is paying a minimum of Rs, 2 per day to an unskilled 
worker, who is in permanent dervice. A temporary worker gets little less 
than a permanent hand. There is no separate dearness allowance.’ 
Admittedly, the wages paid are not adequate. Further, there is some amount 
of discrimination made between a permanent and a temporary worker, doing 
equal work in equal circumstances. But considering the question of the 
present finances of the Company, and of its position in the industry, it is 
not desirable to place any substantive financial burden on its resources. 
At present, there are no scales of pay, and no deurness allowance is paid 
separgtely. It is also difficult on the materials before me to split up wages 
into two. J am, therefore, not much in favour of introducing grades and 
৪8169 of pay, and separate dearness allowance at present. 


But at the same time, it must be said that the general index number of 
wholesale prices went up froin 360.4 in 1955-56 to 421.3 in March 1957. In 
week ending June 15, 1957, this has further gone up to 440.0. The 
working class consumer-price index recorded a rise of more than 7 per cent. 
over 1956-67, In this situation the workers can reasonably demand a 
substantial rise in their wages to neutralise the rise in the present cost of 
living. I have anxiously considered this matter and find that a flat increase 
of Rs. 6 per month for all categories of workets, including temporary hands, 
will give relief, to a considerable extent, to the distress of the workers. [, 
accordingly, award a flat rate of increase of Rs. 5 per month for all workers 
with effect from August 1957. These two issues are answered accordingly. 


Issue No. 3: There is no Provident Fund at present in this Company. 
A compulsory Provident Fund scheme under the Provident Fund Act has 
not been introduced as yet. The Company is still not out of its present 
difficulties. It is true that it made profits in the last two years but then, 
it has a huge loss yet outstanding. Therefore, this is not the proper time 
for introducing a Provident Fund scheme for the benefit of the workers. I 
answer the issue accordingly. 


issue No. 4: At present the workers get 168৪ under the Factories Act, 
and also get 9 days’ festival holidays in a year. The Union asks for 15 days’ 
sick leave with full pay and another 15 days’ sick leave with half pay in a 
year. It also asks for 7 days’ cnsual leave, and 5 more festival holidays in 
a year. In all an additional leave for forty-two days has been claimed in 
this dispute. This Company is located in the neighbourhood of the Jute 
Mills area in Budge Budge. The Jute Mills do not allow any casual leave to 
the workers but allow 15 days’ sick leave with half pay. I think that 
similar provisions should be meade for sick leave for the benefit of the 
permanent workers in the service of this Company. They will get 15 days’ 
sick leave with half pay in a year on production of a medical certificate.
