Medical certificate will be taken either from the Company’s Doctor, or from 
a registered medical practitioner. | answer this issue accordingly. 


issue No. 5: ‘This issue refers to the claim of bonus for 1955. No bonus 
was previously paid by the Compauy as it suffered losses in the business up 
to 1904. The balunce-sheet for 1955 (166, B) shows یح‎ net profit of 
Rs. 72,249-14-2 only, after providing Rs. 56,104 only as depreciation on 
block assets of the Company. The production and oles are nearly double 
of the previous year during the year under review. It appeurs from the 
Auditors’ report of the tala sheet for 1956, that no depreciation was 
provided for in that yeur, for in the opinion of the Directors, the deprecia- 
tion provided for in the past was excessive, as initial and special depreciation 
under Indian Income Tax Act was provided in the accounts up to the year 
ended 30th September 1954, and special depreciation as.per Income Tax Act 
was provided during the year ended 30th September 1955. So it is 
ubundautly clear that excessive depreciation was deducted and _ special 
depreciation under Income Tax Act was provided for in the balance sheet 
for 1955. Both parties file charts drawn up under the Full Bench Formula 
of the Labour Appellate Tmbunal. Shn P. R. Tatia, the Accountant for 
the Company, introduces Ext. C, upparently prepared under the instruction 
of the Management, and says that the initial and development rebates 
amounting to hs. 60,098-3 were not shown in the balance sheet. There is 
no evidence before this Tribunal how the Company could claim any such 
deduction in addition to normal depreciation which, in the opinion of the 
Directors, was excessive, and allowable under the Income Tax Act in the 
normal amount of 15. 56,104 only. On that ground alone, this amount of 
Ra. 60,093-3 should be disallowed from Ext. C. Under section 10(2), 
development rebate can only be allowed for machinery purchased after 9181 
day of March 1954. There is no such evidence on record to show that any 
of the new machineries was in fact purchased after March 1954. In these 
‘circumstances, the Company is not entitled to initial and normal rebate 
of Rs. 60,098-8 in this case. If from the gross profit of Rs. 1,28,511-6-2, 
the amount of depreciation, viz., Rs. 56,104, the amount of Income Tax 
Rs. 5,649-15-6 and Rs. 80,000 for return on capital at 6 per cent. of Ra. d 
lakhs are deducted, then it leaves” ao balance of surplus profit exceeding 
Ra. 37,000. 1۲ will leave a amaller balance if the income-tax of Rs. 31,864 
as in the Union’s chart, is deducted from the gross profits. In any case, 
it will still leave sufficient margin of profits for payment of a bonus amount- 
ing to 15 doys’ wages only. The permanent workers are only entitled to 
this bonus, and the payment should be made _ within a month of the 
publication of the award. This issue is accordingly answered. 


This is my award.

Is the refusal by the Management to allow the following workmen to

(i) Ghurthari Ram, (1) Chandrika Ram, (ili) Bhikhari, (iv) Seo

hunari. What relief ure they entitled to? 


The dispute relates to the alleged refusal by the Management to allow 
the workmen mentioned in the issue to work. 


AWARD 


The sum and substance of the Union’s contention is that the Management 


was not justified in این‎ work to the workmen concerned. But the 
version of the Company is thut those workers wilfully stopped work under 


Part 1[ THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 12, 1957 3371 


‘ie ahs পাপ ے- وہ ہے۔‎ পি 
মত oF رر ہت‎ সপ সস” চুরির" سس‎ রা A

this Company, and were not discharged by them. The Company’s conten- 
tion is that these workers were 7hitka workers or  job-rated workers, and 
were never whole-time workers under them, They used to make shoes for 
the Company on contract basis and get making charges at specified 
and ugreed rates on delivery of the fintshed shoes at the Company’s 
shop at 36 Bentinck Street, Calcutta, where they used to come 
for taking necessary materials for making shoes. These’ workers 
were at liberty to go to their native villages without any notice 
ta the Company for any indefinite period. Thev were also at 
liberty to work for other concerns at any other place. They used to make 
shoes in a room rented by the Company at 14 Prinsep Street, Calcutta. 
Certain grievances were raised on behalf of those workers, and the matter 
was taken to the Labour Directorate. The Conciliation Officer held a joint 
conference on 27th January 1956, when a settlement was arrived at between 
the parties. The terms of settlement were that the workers should. stay and 
work in the Prinsep Street Workshop, pending final shifting of the 
workers ip a new premises, if necessary, with proper arrangement of bath 
and lavatory. It was further agreed that the Management should pay all 
arrear wages and make regular payment of wages to the workers in future. 
Besides, it was also agreed that the Management should provide sufficient 
materials for the maunfacture of shoes, and the workers also should make 
shoes according to the standard laid down by the Management. In 
pursuance of this agreement, the Company made payment of all arrear wages 
to the workers concerned. In March 1956, the Company alao secured a room 
at 42 Metcalf Street, Calcutta, with common bath and lavatory in the 
groundfloor of the premises for accommodating the workers for making shoes. 
The workers were duly informed of this, but they failed to shift there 
in apite of repeated requests by the Management. The workers also did 
not approach the Management, nor did they do any work of the Company. 
Accordingly, the Company on 2nd May 1956 informed Mr. Neson, from 
whom they wanted to take a room in premises No. 42, Metcalf Street, that 
they would not take the said room. The workers stopped coming to the sho 

of the Company for taking materials for shoes, nor did they do any wor 

for the Company. Even they could not be found for a sufficiently long time 
at the workshop room of the Company at 114 Prinsep Street, Calcutta, 
where they used to work formerly, and it was also found that the said room 
was kept under lock and key by them. At this, the Company gave a notice 
to the landlord of the said room at 114 Prinsep Street, Calcutta, terminating 
the tenancy on the expiry of the last dav of June 1956. So, the Company 
wanted to say that the workers concerned wilfully stopped work under this 
Company, and that they were not refused work by the Management as alleged 
by 6 Union. In the circumstances, the workers concerned were not 
entitled to get any relief whatsoever. 


In this case, two of the workers have deposed on behalf of the workers 
coneerned, while on the side of the Company one of its proprietors, who 
is O. P. W. 1, was examined. Besides oral evidence, the Company 
produced documentury evidence, which are Exts. A to K(1), and they have 
been marked on admission by the Union. The workers concerned were 
cobblers, and they were admittedly getting work from this Company on job- 
work basis. The rates of making charges were different for different types 
of shoes, and they used to get such making charges on delivery of the 
finished shoes at the shop of the Company at 35 Bentinck Street, Calcutta. 
They ৮150 used to take necessary materials fur making shoes from that shop. 
In the circumstances, the workers concerned ادوس‎ be deemed to be whole- 
time workers of the Company. They were rather its Thika workers. 
These workers admittedly used to work in a room at 114 Prinsep Street, 
Calcutta, the rent of which was paid by the Company. But the workers 


3372 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 12, 1957 [Parr 1 


raised a dispute regarding certain grievances, and the matter went to the 
Labour Directorate. It is both parties’ case that a settlement was arrived 
at before the Conciliation Officer, as a result of the joint conference which 
took place on 27th January 1956. Exhibit A(1) is the memorandum of 
settlement, It appears therefrom that one of the terms of the settlement 
was that all workers would stay and work in the Prinsep Street Workshop, 
pending final shifting in the new premises, if necessary, with proper 
arrangement of bath and lavatory. It is abundantly clear from the materials 
on record that in accordance with this term of agreement, the Company 
found out a room for the workers in Mareh 1956 at 42 Metcalf Street, 
Calcutta, where there was 18186) arrangement for common bath and privy in 
the groundfloor, P. W. 1, Shri Chandrika Ram, one of the workers, who 
deposed in this case has also admitted in his evidence that there was 
urrangement for bath and privy at 42 Metcalf Street. The workers concerned 
were asked to shift to the new premises, but they did not. It appears from 
the materials that the workers were duly informed of this through their 
Union, and the Labour Officer was also apprised of this fact. When the 
workers concerned did not shift to that premises at 42 Metcalf Street, 
Calcutta, the Company was at last ات‎ to give up possession of the 
room in that premises. The workers stopped coming to the Company’s 
shop for taking work. The room at 114 Prinsep Street, Calcutta, where 
they used to work, was alao found to be under lock and key by the workers. 
In this state of things, the Company had no other alternative but to 
terminate the tenancy of the room at 114 Prinsep Street, Calcutta, by 
the end of June 1956. Exhibits B(1), 001), 1)01) and 1001) will prove 
this. Exhibits G(1) ond K(1) will also prove that the Company paid 
rent of the said room at 114 Prinsep Street, Calcutta, up to June 6۰. 
On a consideration of the entire evidence and circumstances, and having 
regord to the nature of work of these workers, conclusion follows that 
these workers had wilfully stopped work under this Company, and there 
is no escape from it. The. Tribunal is not prepared to believe that the 
Management discharged them or refused work to them. It is patent 
from the facts and circumstances that the workers concerned took an 
attitude for not doing any work for the Company, and that is the reason 
why they for a sufficiently long time did not come to the Company’s 
shop for taking shoe materials, refused to shift to the new premises at 
42 Metcalf Street, Calcutta, which was proposed to be taken by the 
Company for the workers, and put the workshop room at 114 Prinsep 
Street, Calcutta, under lock and key and went away. This Company 
carries on shoe business. So, in the interest of business, it could not 
wait ad infinitum for these workers. Pluced in such a precarious 
position, if the Company had engaged new workers in a room at Chadni 
Chak for making shoes, it cannot be blamed. That these workers were 
not discharged or dismissed by the Management has also been admitted 
by P.W. 1, Shri Chandrika Ram, one of the workers, who deposed in 
this case. There is also the positive statement of 0.P.W. 1, who 18 one 
of the proprietors to the effect that the Company did not stop to give 
work to these workers. We further get from his evidence that these 
workers did not come to the Company’s shop for the last 18 months. On 
n consideration of the matter, it is decided that the Management nevor 
refused to allow the workers concerned to work, but they themselves 
stopped work under this Company. That being the position, the question 
as to whether the refusal by the Management to allow the workmen 


mentioned in the issue to work is justified or not, does not arise at all. 
As the workers concerned stopped work under this Company wilfully 
and deliberately, they are not entitled to any relief whatsoever under the 
Act,

The issue as continued am the schedule to the order of reference is as 
follows: 


Whether the Management was justified in dismissing Shri Safi 
Abmed from his service? What relief is be entitled to? 


AWARD 


It مد‎ the case of the Union, which took up the cause of the employee 
concerned, that Shn Safi Ahmed worked in Messrs. National Cloth Stores 
from 1949 to J65th November 1956. Though Shri Safi Ahmed put 01) 
satisfactory service there, his wage was not increased. So, he demanded 
an ifférement in his wages. At this, the proprietor got ungry and 
summarily dismissed him from service. So, reinstatement with back 
wages for the period of forced unemployment wus claimed. 


The Company’s version in short 1s that Shri Safi Ahmed was never 
appointed as a salesman in this concern, but was actually appointed as 
n domestic servant of the propnetor at his house. Only on 186 November 
1956 he was appointed as 10 salesman in the cloth shop, where he worked 
for 16 days. He left the shop all on a sudden without giving any intima- 
tion to the proprietor and did not report for duty since then. 


In this case, Shri Safi Ahmed hag deposed, while on behalf of the 
Company Shri Basir Ahmed, the proprietor of the concern, has given 
evidence. ‘The proprietor, who is U.P.W. 1, has stated on oath that Shri 
Safi Ahmed was appointed as a domestic servant at his house 11) 1949 
on a pay of Rs. 10 per month plus fooding and clothing, and that he 
wos appointed as a salesman in the cloth shop 01) Ist November 1946. 
Shri ass Ahmed (O.P.W. 1) has further stated that after working 
for a few days in the shop, Shri Safi Ahmed asked for a loan of Rs. 600) 
from him for building o house but os that loan was refused, he left the 
shop on 14th November 1956 and did not turn up since then. O.P.W. 1, 
Shri Basir Ahmed, has made a positive statement that Safi Ahmed, the 
employee concerned, left his service of his own aceord. Ile has categori- 
cally denied that Safi Ahmed was dismissed or discharged by him. It 
is interesting to note that Shr Safi Ahmed himself has also admitted 
clearly und unequivocally in his statement before the Tribunal that the 
proprietor did not discharge him, but he himself came away of hia own 
accord. In this state of evidence, 1 have no doubt 11) saying that this 
concern did not terminate the services of Shri Sofi Ahmed, but he 
himself threw up the job and went away of his own accord. Such a 
case 18 beyond the bounds of the Industrial Disputes Act. In view of 
the above finding, the employee concerned can have 100 grievance, for 
which the Tribunal may be called wpon to grant relief. If he has any 
claim for arrear pay, he may seek remedy olsewhere, because such claim 
for recovery of arrear pay cannot be entertained by any Industrial 
Tribunal.

Assistants’ Grade (AFHQ) Examination, December, 1957 


THE Union Public Service Commission will hold at 
Delhi and London, some time in December, 1957, a limited 
competitive oaxamination fer recruitment to permanent 
vacancies of Assistants in the Armed Forces Headquarters. 
The examination is open only to certain categories of (i) 
departmental candidates working in the Armed Forces 
Headquarters, and (it) employees of the AFHQ who are 
on deputation to other offices. Full particulars and 
application forma obtainable either from the Secretary, 
Union Public Service Commission, Dholpur House, New 
Nelhi, or fram the Chief Administrative Officer, Armed 
Fores Headquarters, New Dellu. Completed applications 
must reach the Secretary, Union Public Service Commis- 
sion, by the 5th October 1957 (19th October 1957 in the 
case of candidates residing abroad).

Yaleutta, the 12th April 1957 


Forecast of Cinger Crop of West Bengal for 1956- 
57 (excluding territories transferred from 
Bihar). 


Season.—The weather conditions have generally 
been favourable for the cultivation and growth of 
the crop in all the districts except Nadia, Burdwan 

and Birbhum. 


Area and yield.—The total area under ginger 
crop in the State has been estimated at 1,400 acres 
this year compared to 1,330 acres of last year. The 
total outturn of fully dried ginger for the State 
ax a whole is estimated at 600 tons this year com- 
pared to 580 tons of last year. The average out- 
turn per acre of fully dried ginger for the State 
as a whéle is estimated at 11.74 maunds this year 


compared to 11.77 maunds of last year.

ear have been taken from last year's final forecast 
eed on the results of sample survey and crop-

Dearness Allowance 


issue No. 1: [t is contended by the contesting Union that the dearnes~ 
allowance as applied to the workmen of the motor vehicles workshops was 
as follows سے‎ a: | 


April এসি For workmen having puy tange below Rs. 0, D.A. was 
Rs. 29 per month. For the pay range from Rs, 31 to Ra. 100 it 
was Rs. 3); for the pay range ubove Rs. 100 and below Rs. 150, 
the dearness allowance was Re. 40 per mouth, wad for the pay 
range above Rs. 150 the dearness allowance was Rs. 43 per month. 


— Lhe Union claims increase in D.A. on the grounds that (a) there is 
discrimination in the rate of D.A. in different departments of the Corpo- 
ration, (b) there should be full neutralisation of the cost of living index, 
und (9) that the cost of living index as applicable to the middle-class - 
people should be applied in the present case, — ০৮৮৮ 


Corporation denies any discrimination us alleged by the Union.‏ مل 
It upposes neutralisation of the cost of living index on the ground that‏ 
the Corporation is not a profit making concern, and that the previoua‏ 
Tribunals have turned down such claims. The appheability of the cost‏ 
of living index applicable to the middle-class people will be out of place‏ 
because the bulk of workmen here constitutes the working class.‏ 


If T look to the history of payment of D.A. in the Calcutta Corporation, 
1 shall find that it has systematically msen from Rs. 3 to Rs. 20 during 
the years 1942 to 1948 in the lowest stratum of the pay range, viz., up to 
Rs. 50 (vide paragraph 13 of the Union’s written statement), The annual 
cost for payment of D.A. to the entire staff of the Corporation was nearly 
90 Juks of rupees. This was move than what the Corporation could pay. 
When Government was moved in the matter, it came to the rescue of the 
Corporation by undertaking to pay 80 per cent. of the burden on the score 
of I).A. The condition for such grant was that the Corporation should 
pay D.A. to the employees just on the scales allowed by the Government 
for its own employees. Under that distinct undertaking the Corporation 
received the subvention from the Government. So the position is elgar 
that the Corporation is not in a position to increase the dearness allowance 
beyond the limit of what is paid by Government to its employees. This 
displaces the claim of the Union that the dearness allowance should be 
shaped by full neutralisation of the cost of living index. The other claim 
of the Union ia that the Calcutta Corporation should give D.A. on the scales 
us given by the Calcutta Electricity Company, Ltd., and the Culeutta 
Tramways Company, 1400.) because all are public utility concerns. Though, 
undoubtedly, these are all public utility concerns, the latter two are profit- 
making concerns. But the Calcutta Sonoran is fundamentally not: مد‎ 
In lieu of taxes it receives from the rate-payers, the Corporation 1s under’ 
an obligation to look after their amenities. Besides, as I have already 
shown, ita finances are extremely limited. It is running practically at the 
mercy of.¢he State Government. Then regarding the linking up of D.A. 
with the coat of living index figure, I must point out that 0 claims were 
(lixcarded by the two successive Tribunals in the past, presided over by 
Shri S. K. Sen and Shri S. N. Modak, and for good reasons. Dearnesg 
allowance, after all, must depend as much on the cost of living index figure 
as on the capacity of the concern to pay. Here that جو‎ ٠٥ sadly 
wanting. So this contention of the Union is liable to fuil, This claim of 
the Union would entail an extra expenditure to the tune of Rs. 31 laca, 
if not mote. So the claim is untenable on its face.

Now the point is whether the Tribunal should allow D.A. to be 
increased or keep it as itis. | cannot shut my eyes to the tact that the 
Corporation euployeea in the Motor Vehicles Departments ure as much hit 
by the rising tide of pricex of essential commodities as anybody else. — 
Everyone of us is feeling the pinch in consequence of soaring prices of 
commogties, Even the State Government, whose attitude is more often 
than not adamant in this respect because of it being the biggeat employer 
in the land, could not any more blink at the facts and ignore the reality 
of the situation. In August 1996, the Government of West Bengal, by 
the Finance Department memo, No. 3dd08F] F /2A-110/56, dated 20৮৮ August 
1956, granted un increase of Rs. 2 in the dearness allowance to its employees. 
This was further revised by the Finance Department memo. No. Ud4F/2A- 
60/57, dated 80th March 1957, by allowing au increase of 1).A. to the tune 
of Rs. 7) per month for staff having pay range up to Rs. 200 per month. 
So, in March 1957 Government did allow D.A. to be حا‎ by Rs. 2 
per ‘month. Now the point is whether the Corporation ought to be liable 
to pay this fucreased D.A. As it is admitted that the Corporation 
employees have been practically put on par with Government employees 
drawing salary up to Rs. 250 per month, so far as 1), is concerned, I 
really find no reason why in the present case the Corporation should with- 
hold this benefit to its employees. I ullowed this benefit of D.A. to the 
workers of the Palta Water Works under the Calcutta Corporation. The 
Yorporation may plead that unless Government sanction is secured, it 1s 
not in a position to allow this increase in D.A. But I must say that it 
should be the duty of the Corporation to secure the necessary sanction 
from (tovernment. As the Government did sanction such benefit in the 
past, and as the condition that was imposed on the Corporation 1s fulfilled 
here, I think the Tribunal will be justified in granting an increase of 
Rs. 4 in the existing D.A. as has been granted by the Government as per 
the aforesnid circular of March 1957. So 1 grant this increase of Rs: 4 
in the dearness allowance of the employees. do not make this award 
retrospective heyond the aforesaid Government circular, because the 
Corporation might be in a difficult position to secure sanction of Govern- 
ment for back expenditure. In the result the dearness allowance will stand

‘maximum of the grade was such that it was easily reached after 3 or 4 
increments. So the result is said to be that by the said scheme the 
Corporation wanted to perpetuate a low grade scale for all time to come. 
When it is remembered that the workmen in this factory mostly belong 
(0 the middle Bhodralok class, the injustice is said to be greater. These

Bhadraloks, as is well known, are hard put to it to keep up appearances

‘The pay and grades of the employees must necessarily depend on two 
primary factors dmong others, viz., (1) the capucity, to pay of the 
employer, (2) the needs of the employees. Keeping these two elements 
in view, I should point out that I have already exposed how melastic -the

basis of the present pay scale and grades, went deep into the matter. It 
had gone into the exact conditions under which the workers had worked 
and had tried to assess the valne of the jobs as much as it could ascertain. 
Of course, I uccept the contention of the Union thut these workers at the 
top or very near to the top had,the least to be benefited by the scheme. 5o 
it went hard with them. They reached the top of the grade by 3 or 4 
increments. Then they were faced with stagnation. Fj have got in 
evidence that many of these people had to wait at the top of the grade for 
nearly 7 or 8 years (vide Annexure A to the Union’s written statement 
which is not much disputed). Exhibit 1 and Ext. 1(a) also corroborate 
this. I always feel that if there is a stalemate at the top for a number of 
years, the workers there ure liable to lose all zest in their work. That 18 
certainly not desirable either for the employer or for the employees. So 
the grade must always have something to give for the workers at different 
times. I do not say that efficiency bars should not be there. That is 
salutory and must be maintained. So it becomes clear thut only the top 
of the existing grade requires some interference. 


Regarding the needs of the employees there can be no gainsaying that 
they are pressing. But for that reason to disturb the pay scale would not 
be proper and admissible. That should be offset as much as possible by 
the increment in the dearness allowance. Ihave already considered this 
matter when I dealt with the issue about dearness allowance. I have 
granted, an increment of Rs. 5 all round in the existing dearness allowance 
to the .pxtent allowed by the State Government concerning its 0 
employees. The Corporation has no choice in the matter of further 
increment on that count as J have already shown. So the’ claim of the 
employees to revise the grades and pay on the basis of rising prices, of 
‘essential commodities cannot be sustained. 7

Leave and Holidays 


Issue No. 3: The contesting Union says that the workers in te 
Motor Vehicles Departments have to work 46 houra in a week, & hours a 
day on week days and 6 houra on Saturday. Sunday is a paid holiday. 
They enjoy 8 festival holidays on sectional 07818. By this it is meant 
that when there is a Muhammadan festival, only 016 Muhammadan 
eniployees ure allawed to enjoy that holiday, and the rest non-Muhammadan 
employees have to work for 6 hours on that day. Similarly 
regarding the other communities of employees. The employees here are 
also grunted three half holidays on three ocensiona, viz., on Netaji’s 
birthday, Republic Day and Independence Day. The Union contends 
that there is discrimination in the matter of leave. Workers in these 
factories enjoy 21 days’ privilege leave on full pay while workers in other 
departments enjoy 31 days’ privilege leave which is cumulative for three 
years. The workers here are not granted any casunl leave while:'other 
workers enjoy casual leave for 15 daya in a year. The workers heré ‘get 
Ohly 15 days’ sick leave with half pay, while workers in other depart- 
ments get one month’s sick leave on half pay, and thereafter three months 
on quarter pay. The existing privileges of the workers here regarding 
sick leave have further been curtailed by the introduction of the 
Employees’ State Insurance Act. The Corporation, of course, denies any 
such discrimination in the matter of leate to the workers. I am afraid, 
the Union seems to have misconceived the situation altogether and mixed 
up the matter with the clerks. The clerical section stands on no different 
footing from the workers. This is so in every concern in general, and in 
all factories in particular. Regarding the total working hours, 48 hours 
work is scheduled to be the maximum under the Factories Act. Two 
hours’ less work is allowed here by way of an incentive. That is a benefit, 
oud must be taken ua such. ۸ gifted horse should not be looked in the 
face. The Union, later on, has developed many hairsplitting arguments 
on the score of its grievances. But I must tell it plainly that the 
working hours ure, strictly speaking, not within the issue addressed to 
me. The workers enjoy 8 festiva] holidays, and half holidays on three 
acasions in a year. This cunnot be 8710 to be inadequate. The 
statement of the Union that others enjoy 31 days of holidays in a year 
can never refer to workers in factories. That ostensibly refers to the 
clerks and other staff. Twenty-one days’ privilege leave in a year 18 ۵ 
little more than what is allowed under the Factories Act. It can never 
be 31 days, as claimed by the Union. But J make the said privilege 
Jeave on full pay cumulative for two years. The people here mostly hail 
from other countries. When they go on leave to their native places, they 
stuy there a little longer just to manage the affairs at home and also as an 
offset of the expenses of the journey to home. 


Regarding casual 16856) I think, there should be some. Even in the 
Major Engineering Tribunal’s Award 5 days ‘‘other leave’? was provided 
for. This ought to stand for casual leave. Besides, sick leave and 
‘sae e leave can never be a substitute for casual leave which can be 

ad ouly on production of medical certificate, and when one is actually 

sftk. Privilege leave is meant for other matters. One must have 
. casual business in the yedr to attend to. So I allow six days’ 20809] leave 
"an a year to the workers in these Motor Vehicles Departments. This 
leave will be strictly at the discretion of the authorities, and this will 
lapse with the end of the year. This leave will not be allowed to be 
affixed and prefixed with other holidays unless the autlorities so 
sanction at their discretion.

House Rent 


Issuo No. 4:3 ‘I'he contesting Union makes a grievance. of the fact in 
respect of inadequacy of the house rent allowance. The Government of 
West Bengal, in its Finance (Audit) Department memo. Nos, 1920F./F/ 
2A-86/47 and 92517, 7128-11195, dated 21st October 1948 and 4th April 
1956, respectively, granted house rent allowance of Rs. 10 per month on 
a flat rate for the basic pay range from Hs. 41 to Ra. 100 (superior service), 
and Rs. 4 per month on a flat rate for the basic pay range from Rs. 5 to 
Rs. 40 per month (inferior service). But the Calcutta Corporation, 
although it adopted the said notification «in toto, allowed only 318. 4 as 
house rent allowance in this department ignoring completely the difference 
between the superior service and the inferior service. Originally they 
were given Rs. 1-8 per month from April 1946, but later on it was 
enhanced to Rs, 2 per month from April 1954. As the rental in the 
Calcutta area went up very high, this pittance of house rent allowance 
proved to be merely an apology for it. The Corporation was pleased to 
sanction a further increase of Rs. 2 per month on the head of house rent 
allowance. 


According to the Corporation, before 1945, there was no house rent 
allowance ae tou ita employees except those who were entitled to 
uarters but could not be so provided with. It was on Ist January 1946 
that the Corporation granted house rent allowance for the first time at 
the rate of Rs. 1-8 per month per head to the skilled labour staff working 
in pumping stations, electricity generating stations and sub-stations. 
Thés benefit was further liberalised on Ist January 1947, when it was 
extended to the unskilled ataff as well. A marked step in_ advance was 
taken on 26th August 1955, when the Corporation sanctioned payment of 
house rent allowance on Government scales as they stood on Ist April 
1984) and subject to rules and conditions in force in Government of West 
Bengal. This took effect from Ist April 1954. On the Ist April 1999, 
Government of West Bengal, further revised their scules for certain 
categories of employees only. 


Now, coming to the evidence, I find that the Union was not accurate 
in its statement about the Finance Department circulars. The first 
circular already referred to, no doubt, was dated 2ist October 1948, and 
the second one was dated 4th April 1955. But for the inferior service, 
the pay range was from Rs. 5 to Rs. 45 por month. They were given 
Rs. 4 per month as house rent allowance. The superior service wns iD 
respect of higher pay range, 1.e., from Is. 49 and upwards, und their 
dearness allowance was Rs. 10 on a flat basis, So in the present case, I 
award that the employees in the Motor Vehicles Department will get the 
benefits 08 the aforesaid Government circulars. Their pay will decide

whether they belong to the superior service or to the inferior service 
regardiug the payment of house rent allowance as indicated above. The

Regarding the claim of the Union fof house rent allowance at 10 per

Before parting with the records of the case, I must point out one 
legal difficulty. It consists in the fact that out of 15 Unions before me, 
14 Unions have entered into » compromise with the Corporation. That 
compromise I have recorded, and ] accept it as part of my present award. 
Regardinig the contesting Union in the Motor Vehicles Department, 8 
it did not agree to join the said compromise, I have given the present 
adjudication. I had no choice in the matter. I could not stop these 
14 Unions from entering into a compromise with the Corporation and 
amicably settle their disputes any more than I could ask the contesting 
Union to drop the present contest. Similarly, I cannot legally thrust 
the benefit of mv present adjudication upon those Unions which did not 
contest and which prefer to abide by the compromise. So the only legal 
consequence which follows in the present case is that these 14 ane 
who were a party to the said compromise with the Corporation, should 
be bound by the said compromise while the Union and the employees 
regarding the Motor Vehicles Department should be bound by my present 
adjudication. As it is desirable that in the same Management, there 
should not be any great disparity in the scale of pay and other amenities 
unless the nature of work ie fundamentally different, I can recommend 
to the Corporation, not by way of any binding direction, but 00] by way 
of a suggestion, that the benefits arising from my present award, 1 they 
are in excers of the benefits under the compromise, may be extended to the 
other employees also. The agreement with the Corporation finds place 
in the Appendix JJ to this award, so far as the 14 non-contesting Unions 
‘are concerned, I incorporate it as a part of my present award.

No. 6529WT.—4th September 1957.—The following draft of an 
amendinent, which in exercise of the power conferred sub-section (1) 
and, in particular, by clause (1) of sub-section (2) of section 68 of the Motor 
Vehicles Act, 1939 (IV of 1939), the Governor proposes to make in the 
Bengal Motor Vehicles Rules, 1940, published with notification No. 1930P1., 
dated the 2lst September 1940, at pages 2655-2829 of Part I of the Calcutta 
Gazette of the 10th October 1940, as subsequently amended is hereby 
published, as required by sub-section (1) of section 133 of the said Act, for 
the information of persons hkely to be affected thereby. 


2. The draft will be taken into consideration on or after the 7th 
October 1967 and any objection or suggestion with respect thereto which 
may be received by the undersigned before that date shal] be considered :— 


Draft amendment 


In the proviso to rule 66 of the said rules, for the figure ''35”’ substitute 
the figure 44511, 


No. 5607W.T.—7th September 1957.—In exercise of the power conferred 
by sub-section (1) and, in particular, by clause (s) of sub-section (2) of 
section 29 read with section 73 of the Inland Steam-Vessels Act, 1917 (Act I

No. 6205/M.1C-49/65.—9th September 1957.—In exercise of the power 
conferred by sub-section 8 of section 531 of the 0189100066৮ Municipal Act, 
1951 (West Bengal Act XX XIII of 1951), the Governor is pleased to sanc-

Calcutta under clause ee of section 527 after complying with the require- 
ments of section 530 of the said Act and the same are hereby published as 
required by section 635 thereof. 


By-laws under section 527(46) of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951, 
regulating the use of Municipal Slaughter Houses in Calcutta. 


1. No person, whether a butcher or not, not being the Veterinary 
Surgeon in charge of the administration of the West Bengal Animal 
Slaughter Control Act, 1950 (West Bengal Act XXII of 1950), or any other 
officer of the Directorate of Veterinary Services and Animal Husbandry, 
West Bengal, shall have access to a slaughter house except for the purpose 
of slaughtering animals intended for human food or for the purpose of 
skinning, cutting up and clearing carcasses of animals so slaughtered therein 
or purchasing meat, heads, skin or offal aa hereinafter provided. 

2. No person shall, without or otherwise than in conformity with the 
terms of a license granted by. the Superintendent of a slaughter house in this 
behalf, have the right to slaughter animals in such slaughter house,

16. Every animal found to be suffering from an infectious or contagious

17. A dying or dead animal brought to a slaughter house shall be

18. The carcase of every animal which has been slaughtered in a

19. Every carcase or skin which upon examination is found to be

oY, Skinned carcases qualified for stamping shall be grouped into three

class each carcase is to be assigned, and in the event of any dispute the 
matter shall be referred to the Flealth Officer whose decision shall be final: 


Provided that the carcases of she-goats and ewes shall in no case be

No. 3038L.W./LW /5B-18/57.—3rd September 1967.—The Governor 18 
pleased to constitute with the undermentioned personnel a Regional Alloca- 
tion Committee, which will be responsible for the allotment of tenements 
built under the Subsidised Housing Scheme fur Industrial Workers at 


Motijheel, Dum dum :— 


(1) Deputy Labour Commissioner 


(Administration), West Bengal, 


ew Secretariat Buildings, No. 1, Hastings Street, Calcutta— 


Chairman. 


(2) Shri A. C. Ganguli, Executive Engineer, Housing Construction 
Division, No. 1, Anderson House, Alipore—Secretary. 


(3) Inspector of Factories, Barrackpore—Member. 


(4) Shri A. K. Thakur, Chief Accountant, Messrs. Jessop & Co., 
63 Netaji Subhas Road, Calcutta-l1—Member. 


(5) Shri Kanailal Das, South Sinthee Road, Dum Dum, Calcutta-2— 


Member. 


(6) Shri .کا .کا‎ Shukla, M.L.A., 


Rashmoni Ghat Road, P. QO. 


Talpukur, 24-Parganas—Member. 
2. The functions of the Committee will be (i) to convene meetings of 


the Committee at a place and time to be 


fixed in consultation with the 


Chairman und submit the applications received in response to the 
advertisement for letting out the tenements issued by the Department of 
Housing of this Government. The Committee will consider the individual 
applications and draw up a list of candidates to whom the tenements, in 
their opinion, may be 811 ~The list should be drawn up in order of 
preference and the number of candidates included in the list should be 
25 per cent. in excess of the total number of tenements available for 
allotment. (ii) In making the selection the Committee should make into 
consideration the following factors as also such other factors as_ they 


consider necessary :— 


(a) The size of the family of the candidate. 


(b) Monthly wages of the person. 


(c) Instance of the factory in which he works from the quarters to he 


allotted. 


(d) Recommendation of the employer. 


(iii) The proceedings of the meetings of the Committee together with the 
list mentioned above and all the applications will thereafter be submitted 
by the Secretary to the Department of Housing of this Government. 

Allotment of tenements to individual workers will then be made by the 
Department of Housing on the basis of the recommendations of the 
Gommuittee. Government reserve the right to over-ride the recommendations 
of the Committee in any individual case. |

Resolution be forwarded to other 


departments of this Government and the Directorate of Housing, Labour 


and Factories. 


By order of the Governor, 


K. C. CHAKRABORTY, Dy. Secy.

No. 1147M.—9th September 1957.—Whereas it 
appears that both Ward Nos. I and ITI of Bans- 
beria Municipality are of almost equal commercial 
Importance and though Ward No. T has a larger 
number of voters than Ward No. ITI, the popula- 
tion of Ward No. T is less than half of that of Ward 
No. TTT. So Ward No. TIT should have greater 
representation than Ward No. IT; | 


Now, therefore, in partial modification of this 
office notification No. 997M., dated 12th ۸۷ 
1957, I hereby determine, in exercise of the powers 
conterred by section 20 of the Bengal Municipal

mentioned place;

Act, 1950, and as delegated to me under section 38

“No. 2170P/80-9/50, dated 1th April 1950, I, 
8. Samaddar, I.A.8S., District Magistrate and 
Deputy Commissioner, Cooch Behar, do hereby 
sei that all buyers and sellers attending the said 
Hat Dhaprahat in Mekliganj subdivision shall 
complete all transactions before sunset and all 
shopkeepers, vendors and customers attending the 
Tat at shops shall leave the Hat by that time.

law,

REGULATIONS. 


In exercise of the powers couferred on him by sub-section (3) of section 
15 of the City Civil Court Act, 1953 (West Bengal Act XXI of 1953), the 
Chief Judge is pleased to frame the following 79701901988 prescribing the. 
duties of the ‘Registrar, clerks and ministerial officers of the City Civil 
Court, Calcutta, nimely :— a 


PART 1 
CHAPTER I 


Proliminary short title and commencement of the regulations 


1. These regulations may be called the Calcutta City Civil Court. 
Regulations, 1957. They shall be deemed to have come into force on and 


from the 23rd February 1957. 


PART 1 
Chapter ۱۱ 


Duties of the Registrar 


2. The Registrar shall be responsible to the Chief Judge for efficient 
administration of the various departments of the Court, viz., the English 
Department, the Accounts Department, Cash Department, the Copying 
Department, the Nazarat, the Forms and Stationery Department, the Record 
Room and the Library. He shall exercise all the powers and functions with 
which the Judge-in-charge of each of these departments in a Civil Court is 
vested under the Civil Rules and Orders, Volume I. Some of the more 
important powers and functions are set out in Appendix A_ ما‎ these 
regulations. 


3. He shall, in consultation with the Office Superintendent, allocate the 
dutiea of the clerks, ministerial officers and inferior servants including the 
menial staff appointed for the City Civil Court and deal with all matters 
relating to leave, pay, promotion and pension of all grades of the Govern- 
‘ment servants on the GCourt’s establishment. | 


4. He shall be the Drawing and Disbursing officer in গড a of both 
clerical and non-clerical staff of the Court and exercise disciplinary juris- 
diction over them according to the prescribed rules. 


5. He shall keep a close watch on the work of the staff and report to the 
Chief Judge whenever, in his opinion, the volume and the nature of the 
Court’s business warrant an increase of strength of the staff, 


6. He shall inspect the departments and offices under him from time 
to time and submit all periodical returns, statements and reports as required 
by the rules, to the High Court or to the Government. | 


7. He is authorised to be the Licensing Authority in ¢he case of clerks 
of Advocates, Pleaders, Attorneys-at-Law and Mukhtars, ordinarily practise- 
ing in the City Civil Court in terms of rule 81 of the ‘‘Rules of the Calcutta

EN পাত‏ سج سے TE‏ سر ہے بیج ہے سیت کس مرج ہے

City Civil Court, 1066’, framed by the High Court. He shall also deal 
with all matters relating tv issue, renewal and returns of certificates to the 
legal practitioners. 


The Registers to be maintained and the procedure to be adopted in this 
connection have been described in Appendix B to these regulations. 


8. He shall frame the annual budget for the City Civil Court and put 
up for the approval of the Chief Judge. 


9. In addition to the duties already assigned to him under ‘‘The 10189 
of the Calcutta City Civil Court, 1956’’ and the powers that may hereafter 
be conferred on him according to law, the Registrar shall also exercise 
the powers and perform the duties set out below in relation to— 


(A) Institution of Suits and Proceedings 


(i) The Registrar is the officer appointed under Order 4, R. 1, C.P.C., 
to receive plaints. 


Provided that where under Order 1, R. 8, Order 2, R. 4, section 20, 
C.V.C., or any other provision of the C.P.C., or under the provision of any 
other law, loave of the Court is necessary to sue, such leave shall be obtained 
before the plaint is presented before the Registrar. The plaints on accept- 
ance by the Registrar shal] be examined, under the supervision of the 
Office Superintendent, by the Plaint Clerks whose duty it ৪1001] be, among 
other things, to enter thom with all necessary particulars, in the relevant 
Nogisters and to make necessary endorsements on the plaints about the 
sufficiency or otherwise of the court-fees paid. In case of any doubt or 
dispute, the mutter shall be referred to the Registrar for directions. 


(ii) The Registrar shall refer to the Court for orders such plaints which 
in his opinion should be rejected. 


(iii) Every alteration in a plaint shall be initialled by the parties or 
by their lawyers with the leave of the Registrar, before registration thereof. 
After registration of the plaint, no alteration shall be made therein without 
the order of the Court in writing. 


iv) Where the plaints do not conform in all respects to the Rules in the 
Civil Rules and Orders, Volume 1, the leave of the Registrar will have to 
be tnken for their acceptance. 


(v) The Registrar may call for translation of documents submitted along 
with the plaint, where necessary. | 


(vi) The Registrar may receive defective affidavits of all kinds after 
obtaining appropriate Memoranda on the affidavits themselves mentioning 
the defects, from the parties concerned. 


(vii) When a plaint has been accepted the word ‘‘accepted’’ shall be 
endorsed thereon over the dated signature or initials of the Registrar. The 
Registrar shall mark the plaint according to the nature of the cause, such 
ns Money (Commercial), Money, Title, 0.0. and so on, and _ thereafter, 
it shall be numbered serially according to classification under the Rules 
in the Civil Rules and Orders, Volume I, and entered in the _ relevant 
Registers by the Plaint Clerks. 


(vii) The foregoing regulations in respect of plaints shall apply 
mutatis mutandis to all original applications except that an application to 
sue in forma pauperis shall be presented before the Judge presiding over the 
particular Bench taking the cause to which it relates.

What is supposed to be the statement of its case by the Union 1s 
nothing of the kind, It would be a misnomer to call it a written .state- 
ment. Phe elementary rule of pleadings is that all material facts nust 
be fully expressed so that no surprise can be sprung. The Union has

cannot throw out a callenge for boxing and then start kicking taking the 
adversary ۵۰ | | 


Mossrs. Angelo Brothers, Ltd., have in the written statement marshailed 
their objections to the demands supported by reasons. The gist of the 
defence is that the conditions of service applicable to the workmen دی‎ 
eminently fuir aml more favourable than the conditions prevailing in other

by sundry allowances substantially strengthening the total emoluments. 


DECISION 


Unlike mauy othor concerns I have to deal with in course of adjadi- 
cation proceedings, Messrs. Angelo Brothers, Ltd., appear to 5 broad- 
minded, practical idealists, fully conscious of the vital role played hy 
jabour in the working of the organisation. Two agreements Exts. A and — 
A(1) concluded between the Union and the Company in 1951 and 1954 
respectively bear eloquent testimony to its sympathetic and benevolent 
uttitude (owards the employees. Concession and improvements of terms 
were cordially granted. One of the points raised by the Company in its 
written stutement is that all the issues raised in the present reference 
are covered by the agreement reached in 1954. Since the agreement was 
not terminated in full conformity with the procedure prescribed by law 
it is still holding sway and hence the Union cannot re-agitate identical 
points so long as the agreement remains operative. The Company pleaded 
in the alternative that circuinstances remaining unchanged since the date 
of the said agreement, no occasion has arisen for reconsideration or revi- 
sion. Drawing my attention to the letter Ext. D jointly addressed by 
the two parties to the Assistant Lubour Commisisoner, Shrijut Bhattacharjee 
replied on behalf of the workers that having agreed to ao reference under 
section 10(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act the Company had repudiated 
the agreement. ‘The issues were accordingly amenuble to adjudication 
by the Tribunal. The argument is plausible but the view may also be 
taken that assured by the conviction that the agreement was still binding 
the Company wanted a pronouncement to that effect by the Tribunal in 
relation to self-same issues. I feel however that I should deal with the 
points under reference on merits. :

Issue No. 3—-Annual Bonus: The point for adjudication is annual 
honus. In terms of the agreement of 1951, renftirmed in 1954, the Company 
has been paying bonus to the daily rated workers at the same percentage 
us dividend paid to share-holders. Monthly rated staff are paid at half 
the rate subject to a minimum of one month’s basic pay if any profits are 
made in the out-going financial year. Shri Bhattacharyya stated 
categorically that the claim of the workers was not for bonus to be 
ascertained on the Full Bench formula. Asked to explain what was the 
nature of the claim, he said that the demand was for bonus ag stipulated 
in the agreement supplemented by 50 per cent. of the total profits made by 
the Company. He was actually approbating and reprobating in the same 
breath inasmuch as he wanted to milk the agreement he has  defimtely 
repudiated. Over and above that he wants to collect a moity share of the 
profits. [I am afraid the point as formulated reflects some confusion of 
ideas. Annual bonus may be payable as a condition of service. arising from 
express or implied agreement or by virtue of a customary right. Unless 
such a right has accrued a Tribunal cannot make bonus payment compulsory 
for future years as no claim can be sustained unless the trading results are 


۲۸2٢۲ 11 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 19, 1957 3449 


leaving sufficient surplus for distribution. In the decision‏ کے 


reported in 10952, 2, L.L.J., page 484 their Lordships pointed out that 
claim for bonus normally arises only in the event of trading profits in a 
particular year, A general and precise formula defining bonus for all years 
to come should not be laid down in advance unless it 1s clear that there 
would be profits every year and the profits would be such as would bear the 
burden of bonus according to the formula. Shrijut Bhattacharyya has 
no use for the Full Bench formula. I fail to comprehend how without the 
aid of the formula the workers’ claim to appropriate a share of the profits 
can be adjudged. It was argued that by consent of parties the award 
made by this ‘l'ribunal would be effective for three years. The claim for 
bonus therefore extends to some years still resting in the womb of 
futurity. I am led to the conclusion that the claim as made is untenable. 
I am anxious however to relieve the workmen of the consequences of the 
wrong step they have been misdirected to take. Since the Compan 
maintains that the agreement is still binding I direct that the bonus will 
be paid at the same rate as heretofore. ; 


Issue No. 4—House Rent: Rupees 10 is claimed as house rent on 
behalf of each of the workers. Some house receipts have been produced 
by two witnesses. They gave evidence that they have to pay house rent 
for hired houses. Ordinarily the employer is under no obligation to provide 
living quarters or house allowance in lieu thereof. The employee accept- 
ing an appointment is not blind to prevailing conditions and cannot ask the 
employer to find lodgings for him. Industrial housing is supposed to be 
a problem for the State to tackle. In determining the amount of basic 
wages expenditure on house rent is taken into account and 19 woven into 
texture as an integral component. 10 per cent. of the basic pay is 
estimated as fair. In the case reported in 1952, 1, ..L.J, page 31, Their 
Lordships held that house rent cannot be separately allowed. Angelo 
Brothers have been paying wages and salaries found by the Tribunal to he 
very [1], House rent is included in the wages. This Company was not 
floated yesterday. Workers employed therein huve been living in their 
houses from which they do not appear to have been evicted. No evidence 
has been given that the rent has shot up abnormally and the present rates 
form a crushing burden. Circumstances have not changed. In this state 
of things the present demand for separate house rent is unreasonable, It 
is accordingly rejected. 


Issue No. 5—Cratuity: A gratuity scheme is already in existence. A 
new scale was introduced under the agreement of 101. The last page in 
Ext. B supplies full particulars. The Union asked for— 


1 days’ wages for 5 years’ employment, 14 days’ wages for work up 
to 10 years, 21 days’ wages for a period reaching 15 years, J 
month’s wages for service put in beyond 15 years but up to 20 
years and 6 weeka’ for work beyond that period. 


The language is defective. The Union probably wants 7 days’, 14 days’, 
21 days’, and a month’s wages for each year of service. On behalf of the 
Company the plea was taken that it is paying 6} per cent, of the basic pay 
‘and dearness allowance and food allowance under the Employees Provident 
Fund Act. The gratuity scheme might have been dropped on the Provident 
Fund Act coming into effect. It was allowed to continue. The terms of 
the gratuity scheme should not be tightened up as the Company 108 
voluntarily given the scheme a perpetual lease of life concurrently with the 
benefits ensured by the State. Reported cases face both ways. 1۱8 the 
case reported in 1956, L.A.C., page 266, their Lordships held that when 
a concern is capable of giving dual benefit of Provident Fund and gratuity, 


3450 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE: SEPTEMBER 19, 1957 [Parr 1 


re aE ec 


both should be granted. Contrary view prevailed in the awards published 
in the Calcutta Gazette, dated the 8th September 1955, page 107 and 22nd 
September 1955, at page 133. No question of abolition of gratuity scheme 
in view of the enforcement of the Employees’ Provident Fund Act arises 
here. Both of them will remain operative. My task is to decide if the 
provisions of the gratuity scheme should be enlarged in order to secure 
yreater advantages to the employees. (Giving the matter close attention 
] am persuaded that as a new type of financial obligation has been placed 
on the Company which will bring substantial henefit to the employees the 
liability for gratuity freely undertaken should not be rendered more 
onerous. In this view I hold that the gratuity scheme will remain us it is.

FINDINGS 


Issue No. 1: At the outset Shri 13. N. Choudhury, Counsel for the 
Union, stated that the Union will not press the cases of the last four 
workers of the list for adjudication by this Tribunal, for they received 
payment of compensation from the Company, und had left the eee 
service. Shri Chowdhury at the sume time conceded two more points, 
viz., (1) that there was real need for retrenchment, 1.e., the Company had 
estublished a case for retrenchment of staff, and (11) that the number 
retrenched is also accepted as fair and proper. His two-fold objections 
however are (i) that in effecting retrenchment, the Company did not 
observe the normal rule of “last come, first go’? which by itself 1s an act 
of unfair labour practice, and (ii) that in the matter of payment of 
compensation, the Company did not take into consideration the past 
service of the retrenched personnel under the sterling Company and, 
accordingly, the offer of payment of compensation was 11 ۰ 


Shri S. K. Mullick, on behalf of the Company, contended that the 
rule of ‘“‘last come, first go’? was observed, as best as possible, and that 
the slight departure therefrom was mude on the ground of ethciency of 
the staff retained after the retrenchment. The compensation offered was 
fair and adequate, and made in terms of the previous awards, We are 
concerned with the cases of retrenchment of (i) Shri B. N. Roy Chowdhury, 
and (ii) Shri Jagannath Sarkhel. The cases of other four employees are 
disposed of with the observation that there is no outstanding dispute 
between them and the Company. 

The question now is, whether Shri Roy Chowdhury and Shri Sarkhel 
were retrenched with any improper motive. The Union’s case is that 
they were victimised for their Union activities. Shri Roy Chowdhury 
‘was the General Secretary of the Union for a long time, and Shri Sarkhel 
was an active member of the same. It appears from the evidence of these 
two workers, as also of Mr. Brown, the present Manager of the Trading 
Department, that Shri Roy Chowdhury had ceased to be the Genera] 
Secretary of the Union since 1955 and that both were members of the 
Executive Committee at the time of their retrenchment. It also appears 
that both the former and the present Secretary of the Union had 


3452 «= THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE SEPTEMBER 19, 1957 [Parr fT 


سح 


রি 


পার 


been continuing in service of the Company, and that there had been less 
— of industrial disputes during the time when Shri Roy 
Chowdhury held the position of Secretary of the Union than at the time 
when he was discbarged. Shri Sarkhel could not show any particular 
Union activities to his credit justifying any special treatment from the 
Management therefor. Shri Sarkhel has been re-employed in service of 
this Company only about a month ago, when Shri Roy Chowdhury did 
not accept the offer of re-employment made to him by the Company. 
According to the present Union Secretary, Shri Sarkhel, who is younger 
of the two, was more suitable for the post. Mr. Brown says that 
Shri Roy Chowdhury, as a Secretary of the Union, was more co-operative, 
aud that there had been less number of disputes when he held the office 
of the Secretary of the Union than at the present moment. So, there 
could not be any reasonable ground for inference that Shri Roy Chowdhury 
was specially selected for retrenchment because of his past association 
with the Union as its Secretary. There is still less reason to infer in the 
case of Shri Sarkhel that the Company proceeded against him because 
of his Wnion activities. T am, therefore, unable to find that any of these 
two gentlemen was victimised for his Union activities. 


Recuuse of considerable fall in the number of imports due to restric- 
tions imposed by the Government of India, it was found that there was 
very little, or no work at all either for Shri Roy Chowdhury or for 
Shri Sarkhel. Mr. Burleigh, the then Manager, and Mr. H. N. Nicholls, 
the Managing Director, after due consideration, prepared a list for 
retrenchment of staff (1986, B), and notices (Ext. ©) were issued to all 
concerned on the 1101) January 1957. Exhibit A is the complete list of 
the clerica) staff of the Trading Department as on 818۲ December 1956. 
It appears therefrom that Shri Roy Chowdhury and Shri Sarkhel had a 
number of juniors in other departments at the time of the retrenchment 
in question. Shri Roy Chowdhury joined the service of this Company 
m 1988, when 1 was a sterling Company, and not a rupee Company as it 
Is pow, and Shri Sarkhel joined in 1940. The four other gentlemen, who 
were retrenched along with them, had joined service in 1945 and 195d. 
It is not true to say that Shri Roy Chowdhury and Shri Sarkhel were the 
topmost men selected for retrenchment. There are at least half a dozen 
xenior employees in the list, as per the Ext. ‘A, who were not retrenched. 
Shri Roy Chowdhury worked in the Ovaltine Department, and 
Shri Sarkhel in the Provisions Department. The former was a Matriculate 
while the latter was a non-Matriculate. There has been, as stated above, 
some slight departure from the rule of ‘‘last come, first 8011, But 
then, this rule is not an inflexible one. Under section 25(2) of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, ordinarily, in case of retrenchment, the person 
last employed in a category should be retrenched first unless there 1s 
good reason for leaving him out. Under the Mercantile Tribunal’s award, 
exceptions in the application of the above principle have been made in 
cases of persons holding exceptiona] merit and ability. Now,- this rule 
is applicable other things being equal. It appears from the evidence of 
Mr. Brown, the Manager of the Trading Department, that in the case 
of these two gentlemen, other things were not equul, One was pretty old 
in service to poe afresh uny new work that might be assigned to him, 
on readjustment of duties. The Ovaltine Department, as a separate 
unit, was practically closed due to imposition of heavy duty enhanced 
from 314 per cent. to G0 per cent. This department is now heing carried 
on with the help of another clerk belonging to a different department 
who does the work in addition to his own duties, Workers who, in the

DECISIONS 


Issue No. 1: The Company’s case is that it is a emall hotel employing 
only 28 workmen and earns very little profit. It is stated that the 
workers are paid cash wage as follows and also are allowed free fooding 
comprising of two principal meals, tea three times a day and nasta 
(tiffin). The cash wages paid to the workmen are mentioned in the 
Annexure to the written statement and are as follows:— 


(1) Handiwalla—lts. 40 per month. 

(2) Cook—Rs. 50 per month. 

(3) Mate of cook—Rs. 40 per month, 

(4) Musalchi—Rs. 25-12 per month, 

(5) Tea mate—WRts. 22 per month. 

(6) Mate of Rotiwalla—Rs. 35 per month. 
(7) Platter—Rs. 19-12 per month. 

(8) Boys—Rs. 20 per month, 

(9) Tea Master—Rs. 30 per month. | 
(10) Rotiwalla—Rs. 40 per month. 


The evidence of the Manager, Shri Khoda Box, shows that the value 
of food, ten and tiffin will amount to Rs. 40 to Rs 45 per head per month. 
Even on a moderate estimate of these umounts, I -consider that the value 
of the food concessions as allowed to the workmen was at least Rs. 30 per 
month. It appears from the evidence on record that some of the workmen 
of the hotel assaulted some Kabuli customers that resulted in a criminal 
case and the whole batch of workmen left the hotel ond a new set of 
employees were engaged. Considering the fact thut the minimum cash 
wage is only Rs. 20 per month, the cash wages of ‘the workmen as 
mentioned above are increased by Rs. 2 per head per month. No other 
cash allowances are payable to the workmen. This issue is accordingly 
answered. ۱ | 


Issue No. 2: O.P.W. 1, the Manager states in evidence that the 
workers have to put in 74 to 9 hours’ work a day and that overtime 19 
counted in excess of work of 8 hours a day. The Union Muslim Hotel is 
ا‎ eating house and is, therefore, an establishment for publie entertain- 
ment under section 2(5) of the Bengal. Shops and Establishments Act, 
1940. The daily hour of work in such an establishment is governed by 
section 10 of the Bengal Shops and Establishments Act, 1940, and the 


Parr I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 19, 1957 3457 


wages for overtime work are governed by section 13 of the said Act. It 
is, therefore, awarded that the dasly hours of work and wages for overtime 
work shall be governed by section 10 and section 13 of the Bengal Shops 
and Kstablishments Act, 1940, respectively. This issue is accordingly 
answered, 


issue No. 3: 0.1۰.۷۷. 1 states in evidence that the workers of the 
hotel get 14 day’s holiday in a week and one month’s privilege leave in a 
রি The leave fucilities for employees of a hotel are to be governed 
y section 12 of the Bengal Shops and Establishments Act. They ure as 
follows: ‘A person নি in a shop, commercial establishment or 
establishment for public entertainment or amusement shall be entitled— 


(a) after every twelve months’ continuous employment, to privilege 
leave on full pay for fourteen days, 


(an) in every year, to sick leave on half pay for fourteen days on medical 
certificate obtained from a medical practitioner registered under 
the Bengal Medical Act, 1914, and 


) in every year, to casual leave (on full pay) for ten days; 
rovided that— : 


(i) Privilege leave admissible under clause (a) may be accumulated 
up to a maximum of not more than twenty-eight days, 


(1a) sick leave admissible under clause (aa) may be accumulated up 
to a maximum of not more than fifty-six days; and 


(11) casual leave admissible under clause (b) shall not be accumulated.’’ 


In view of the fact that the workers of the hotel are getting one 
month’s privilege leave in & year, I consider that they are not entitled to 
wny extra sick Sane. but they shall be entitled to casual leave on full 
pay for 10 days in a year. It is, therefore, awarded that over and above 
the privilege leave for one month on full pay allowed to the workers in a 
year, they shall get casual leave on full pay for 10 days in a yeur. 


Issue No. 4: The evidence of O.P.W. 1, the Manager shows that the 
Management did not refuse employment to any workmen as alleged 
and that the workmen left service of the hotel in fear of arrest by the police. 
There is no evidence on record to justify the conclusion that any workmen 
was refused employment by the employers, as alleged. It is awarded 
that the Management did not refuse employment to any workmen as 
mentioned in the list in the order of reference and the present issue 1s 
accordingly answered.
