Schedule 


(1) Whether the dismissal of Shri Ajit Mukherjee is justified? To what 
relief is he entitled ? 


(2) Whether the workmen are required to maintain Job Time Cards. 


(3) Are the workmen entitled to any relief during the stoppage of work? 


AWARD. 


The case of the Union is that the Company Messrs. Small Tools Manu- 
facturing Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as the Company for the sake 
of brevity), 18 an Engineering unit, engaged in manufacturing various kinds. 
of tools and implements for use in the mechanical processes; that the 
Company had no ascertained terms and conditions of the service of their 
workmen and during the course of the discussions of the charter of demands 
the Company unjustly dismissed one Shri Ajit Mukherjee on 15th February 


Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 19, 7 3459 


পারার ররর 


195% The Company further arbitrarily insists on introducing a system 
of maintaining Job Time Cards by the workers from 18th February 1957 
against which the workmen registered their protest in staging a stay-in- 
strike with effect from the noon of 18th February 1957. The Company 
suspended as many as 14 workmen—all leading members of the Union— 
-und declared a lock-out on 20th February 1957 most illegally. As the dead- 
lock continued Government issued an order under section 10(3) of the 
Industrial Disputes Act directing that 14 persons would not be allowed to 
join which made the situation worse. The Union therefore seeks reinstate- 
ment of Shri Ajit Mukherjee with full compensation for the period of forced 
unemployment and a further direction to the Company for not insisting 
on the writing of Job Time Cards by the workmen themselves and further 
reliefs on behalf of workmen who were not allowed to join their work. 


The Company denies the material allegutions in the written statement of 
the Union and contends, 77167 aha, that Shri Mukherjee was simply taken in 
us a trade learner on 6th August 1956 on the terms and conditions as Jaid 
down in the Training Contract Form accepted by him; that Shri Mukherjee 
neglected his work systematically, behaved unmannerly with his superiors, 
was guilty of frequent absence from his duty. Thus he was found 
absolutely ص00"‎ and incorngible and accordingly the training 
facilities were withdrawn from him with effect from 22nd January 1957. 


As regards the muintenance of Job Time Cards, the case of the Company 
is that these cards were introduced in 1952 for the benefit of both the 
workmen and the Company and this system was never discontinued. Some 
workmen all on a sudden on 11th February 1957 stopped posting Job 
Time Cards and incited other workmen not to post the same. Posting of 
Job Time Carda ts the normal duty of the workmen and obligatory on their 
part. 


As regards the strike, the Company’s case is that the strike was wholly 
illegal and unjustified as some representatives of the workmen insisted 
on (1) immediate reinstatement of Shri Mukherjee and (2) discontinuance 
of the system of maintaining Job Time Cards. As the strikers indulged 
in oll sorts of indiscipline and prejudicial activities inside the factory and 
as the atmosphere was tense and menacing, the Company had no alternative 
but to close. down the factory from 20th February 1957 for the 
aafety and security of the Company’s valuable plant and machinery. 
The 14 workmen who were under suspension assaulted ‘other workmen 
and staff and obstructed willing workmen to enter into the factory, 
threatened and intimidated them and they still continued the strike. In 
the circumstances the lock-out following the illegal strike was fully 0 
and Shri Mukherjee should he refused reinstatement and no relief should ما‎ 
erauted to the workmen and the writing of the Job Time Cards should be 
directed to be maintained. 

Decision 

As will appear from the order of reference there are 3 points for 

determination. 


lirstly, whether the dismissal of Shri Mukherjee is justified. Secondly, 
maintenance of Job Time Cards, and lastly, relief, 1f any, admissible to the 
workmen during the period of lock-out. Firat of all I would take the 
subject-matter of dismissal of Shri Mukherjee. 


issue No. 1٦ It is common ground that Shri Mukherjee was taken in 
as a trade learner on. 6th August 1956. The terms and conditions of his 
employment as a trainee or trade learner are set forth in Ext. A described 
as the “Contract Form Trainees’’. The Company relies on the condition 
No. | of the Trainees’ Contract Form for justifying their withdrawing the 


3460) THRE CALCUTTA GAZETTE SEPTEMBER 19, 1957 [Parr] 
| এরর ae! 
triining facilities from Shri Mukherjee. The evidences of Shri P. C. Nitra 
(Works Manager), 0O.P.W. 1, and the Senior Foreman Shri Ani] Chandra 
Biswas (O.P.W. 2) clearly establish that the Company found Shri Mukherjee 
unsuitable as a trade learner. غ1‎ is clear from their evidence that Shri 
Mukherjee frequently absented himself from his duty and his record of 
service was bad and he was further guilty of ill-behaviour towards charge 
hands. The warnings and instructions given to Shri Mukherjee were 
apparently lost upon him and he did not care to improve his unsatisfactory 
work and conduct as per reports Exts. E-E3. This is a conduct falling far 
short of the standard required of a trainee. A trainee must give a good 
account of himself during his training period and the Company expects 
him to learn his work properly, thoroughly and efficiently so that he may 
be usefully employed by the Company in future. The evidence in this case 
is that this trainee is a solitary instance of a trade learner being refused 
absorption. All other trainees before him without a single exception were 
absorbed. So the Company cannot be found fault with so far as their 
relation with trade learners ig concerned. Furthermore, he was unautho- 
risedly absent from his duty for the period from 19th January 1957 till 
Tuesday the 28rd January 19657 and reported himself for duty on the 24th 
when the Company in view of his previous conduct and work did not allow 
him to join. It ia admitted by Shri Mukherjee that he was absent on 
occasions and his attendance cards Exts. C-C4, were unsatisfactory, Shri 
Mukherjee, however, pleaded illness during that period but did not give 
any prior intimation to that effect. Tbe Company systematically found him 
unsuitable and so it had no alternative but to withdraw the training 
fucilities from him. Paragraph (1) of the Ext. A lays down that the train- 
ing period may be terminated earlier without assigning any reason if the 
trainee is not found suitable in the estimation of the Management. The 
Company has exercised the power vested in it by this clause. The Court, 
however, may serutinize whether the Company has arbitrarily exercised 
this power without any justification. In view of my observations above 1 
am unable ما‎ find that the Company capriciously dispensed with the training 
facilities hitherto extended to Shri Mukherjee. The Management has 
exclusive right in this behalf. If the Company found that this traimee was 
unsuitable, and thus terminated his training facilities the Court cannot 
interfere and foist this workman upon the Company. Be it said that no 
charter of demands was pending while Shri Mukherjee’s training facilities 
were withdrawn as it will appear from Government’s letter Ext. 1, dated 
2nd November 1956. I may further observe that the termination of the 
training period should not rightly be called dismissal. In view of my 
observations above, the termination of the training facilities of Shri Muk- 
herjee is justified and the Court will not interfere with it. 


issue No. 2: The evidence on this head is purely one-sided. The 
unchallenged evidence on this score is that the Job Time Cards have been in 
vogue since the year 1952. The Union has not adduced any evidence 
before me to show that the maintenance of these cards is superfluous. As 
testified to by oral evidence in this case on behalf of the Company, the 
various utility and benefits arising out of the maintenance of these cards 
are enumerated in their written statement and there are true records of the 
output of work, merit, efficiency and inefficiency of workmen. No evidence 
has been adduced on behalf of the workmen on the basis of which the Court 
can pronounce that the practice of maintaining Job Time Cards should be. 
discontinued. On behalf of the Union it is further urged that no other 
Company maintains Job Time Cards inasmuch as it involves additional 
labour on the part of the workmen without any further wages. Non- 
maintenance of such cards ১0৪৮৪], by other companies can he no ground or 


0 | THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 19, 1957 3461 
ee ee ees 


justifeation for un order asking the present Company to discontinue the 

\eystein. The system, as already said, seems to he very wholesome and 
~beneticial te both the Company and the workmen. Jn the circumstances, 
1 think, [ shall not be justified im finding that the system which has been 
iu vogue in the Company since 1952 should be discontinued. In a word, 
1 tind that the status guo so far as these cards are concerned should be 
maintained. 


issue No. 3: Now 1 take up issue No. 3, 1.e., whether the workmen are 
entitled to any relief during the stoppage of work (i.e., the period of lock- 
out), There is no dispute that the factory was closed from 20th February 
1957 tu 19101) April 1957 and the factory opened on 16th April 1957. The 
decision on the point hinges 00 whether the lock-out was justified. This 
necessitates the determination of the question whether the strike was legal 
or illegal. The Jaw 18 that the lock-out would be legal, if the strike was 
illegal ond unjustified, and if the strike was Jegal, lock-out would be 
egal and unjustified, but there are other considerations too. Thus the 
strikers would not be entitled to wages for the period of lock-out if the 
strike was Ulegal and unjustified. In this case no notice of the stay-in- 
strike by the workmen on 18th February 1957 at 2 p.m. was given to the 
Company. She Company was thus taken by surprise. The workmen went 
ou strike because the Company did not agree to reinstate this trainee and, 
secondly, because the system of maintaining Job Time Cards was not with- 
drawr in spite of concerted insistence of the workmen. The Company 
terminated the training faciliies of Shr Mukherjee because he was found 
—unsuituble and therefore the imaistence of the workmen to restore the train- 
ing facilities was fully unjustified and no less unjust was the demand of 
the workmen to insist the Company on their discontinuing the system of 
maintaining Job Time Cards which were found so useful. The utility of 
miintuining Job Time Cards is fully enumerated by the Company in para- 
graph 16 of their written statement which, in short, gives oa complete 
picture of the progress of work, efficiency and merit or otherwise of the 
workmen, ete. Thus no workman should have insisted on the Company’s 
withdrawing the system of maintaining these cards which were so useful 
to themselves. These cards are beneficial not only to the Company but 
also to the workmen themselves. Therefore their demand for discontinuance 
of Job Time Cards was also unjustified. It is argued before me on behalf 
of the Union that it is a fundamental right of workmen to go on stmke 
In assertion of their bargaining power and to back up their collective 
demands. In this connexion, a few lines may be quoted from the Full 
Bench decision in the case of Ramakrishna Iron Foundry and their workers 
(reported in 1964-17, 1.1۰.4. 372) which runa as follows: 


“Tne mpbt to atrike has been recognized by necessary implication in 
the industrial legislation in India and express statutory provisions 
have heen made for the purpose by regulating it. It is thus a 
recognized weapon of the workmen to he resorted to by them for 
usserting their hargaming power andl for backing up their 
collective demands upon an unwilling employer. During itr 
continuance, a strike has, however, an adverse effect upon the 
production and upon the industry. It is, therefore, to be used as 

a last resort where all other avenues for settlement of industrial 
disputes, as provided for in the statutory machinery, have rroved 
futile. Such being the position, it is desirable to discourage ita 
misuse and to control and minimise the beneful consequences of 
118 misuse in respect of the industry as far as possible and those 
objectives cay be obtained if suitable disabilities can be Jegitimate- 
lv imposed to prevent the misuse of that weapon.”’ 


3462 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE SEPTEMBER. 19, 1957 [Parr I 


he ct 


This Full Bench case has further held that in order to impose check: upon 
the misuse of the workman’s right to go on strike, the employer should 
have the right to didmiss a workman joining otherwise than bona fide an 
unjust strike and in the event of an unjust strike, an employer should have 
the right to terminate the service of a workman on the mere fact that he 
hus joined an unjustified strike. Judging in the light of the principles 
above the only irresistible conclusion is that these workmen resorted to an 
unjustified strike as it was resorted to by way of protest opainst the lawful 
dismissal of a trainee and the continuance of Job Time Carda which were 
really useful. ‘The stuy-in-strike waa also illegal as the workmen committed 
acts of criminal tresspass under section 447 of I.P.C. by not withdrawing 
themselves from Company’s premises which they occupied in order to 
intimidate and insult Company’s men without any desire to work. Thus 
the strike was both illegal and unjustified as the Company was all along 
upvresable to listen to workmen’s demands and anxious for a compromise. 
Further, there was no unfair labour practice on the part of the Commpany. 


The Company in this case has produced reports Exts. E series, notices 
.لا(‎ D series and other relevant papers to show how the Company patiently 
watched the conduct of the workmen and how sincerely and honestly they 
tried at every stage to avert the strike by means of persuasions and requests. 
All these pursuasions, however, fell on idle ears and the workmen remained 
adamant. There is further unchallenged evidence on the side of the 
Company to show that the workmen continued to be turbulent and their 
conduct seems to have been menacing as they went on shouting slogans and 
threatening the Company’s personnel with dire consequences similar to 
that which occurred in Jessop’s Factory. I think, public memory though 
proverbially short has not forgotten the inhuman and most diabolical 
murder of an Important officer of the Company by throwing him into the 
furnuce which was burning ablaze. In the circumstances no fault can be 
found with the Company if they locked-out the factory following upon the 
11110] and unjuatified stmke to which the workmen resorted over unjustified 
demands. The condition of the factory went from bad to worse ao police 
had to be informed and the Company rightly apprehended that there was 
potentiality for greater mischief if the factory were not closed, by destroy- 
ing the valuable machinery of the Company. In the circumstances, I must 
5:٤ that the stay-in-strike was illegally gnd unjustifiably staged by the 
workmen and the Company rightly und justifiably resorted to the lock-out 
of the factorv. That being so, the workmen cannot claim any relief during 
the period of lock-out when the factory had to he closed down under 
unavoidable circumstances yielding no production and thus involving the. 
Company in great loss. 


This is my award,

issue 
Is the discharge of Shri Tarapada Mullick justified ۶ To what relief 
by way of reinstatement and/or compensution he is entitled? 


AWARD 


This is a case arising out of the dismissal of a workman named Shri Tara- 


pada Mullick by Messrs. Bangodaya Cotton Mills. 


3464 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE SEPTEMBER 19, 1957 [Paar I 


The case of the Union in a nutshell is that this workman being an 
Assistant Secretury to Bangodaya Cotton Mills’ Mazdoor Union was. 
victimised by the Company on false allegation of his resorting to go-slow 
tactics and ineiting others to go-slow. This workman ig a piece-rated 
worker, in fact, his production fell because of inadequate supply of 
materials which was motivated by the Company who transferred him from 
(he section to another just to vietimise him The Company held a 
shum enquiry wherein principles of natural and social justice were violated. 
The Union therefore seeks his reinstatement with other incidental reliefs. 


The Company states that the workman was systematically giving less 
production since April 1956 and he was charge-sheeted for his go-slow 
tactics’ and using filthy language towards some female workmen. of shift 
‘A’? and insulting and intimidating the Manager when on 26th June 1956 
the charge-sheet was offered to him. <A proper enquiry was held into the 
charges wherein he participated and as the result of the enquiry he was 
dismissed. Thus there was no violation of the principles of natural and 
80017] justice. The workman can therefore get no relief. 


During argument two other technical objections were raised, viz., (1) 
that there can be no dispute between 11671152118 and the workman which 
should be between the proprietors of the Mills forming a limited Company, 
aud (2) that the workman tas not sigued the written statement. 
These two points will be taken up after the principal puint referred to is 
disposed of. | | 


Decision 


The main point is whether the discharge of the workman is justified. 
The Company held an enquiry and it has been argued by the learned 
Advocate for the Company that the enquiry was properly held in which 
the workman participated and was offered every facility, مھ‎ the termina- 
tion of his service is fully justified. If the argument could be accepted, 
there was an end of the Union’s case. To the contrary, the Union 
seriously challenges it as a sham enquiry. In deciding this point the 
Court is required to enter into details regarding the enquiry. First of all, 
a reterence need be made to the charge-sheets Exts. B, Bl and the work- 
man’s reply thereto. Charge-sheet Ext. B states two charges (1) that the 
workman had heen going slow since 1th April 1956 reducing production 
nnd (2) that on 24th June 1956 he used filthy language regarding some 
female workmen. Charge-sheet Iixt. 1(1 recites that on 26th Apri! (June ?) 
ut 6-30 p.m. he refused to accept the charge-sheet and insulted the 
Manager und threatened to kill him. In this charge-sheet he was asked 
to send in the reply within 24 hours of the receipt of the charge and there 
was a further order therein that he would remain suspended till the con- 
clusion of the euquiry, On the righthand margin ofthe charge-sheet 
there was the workman's reply of denials and he further asserted that he 
was not supplied with uecessary articles and equipments which explained 
less production and consequent reduction in his wages too and regarding 
the other allegations his reply is that he looks upon the female workmen 
as his mothers and sisters and upon the Manager as his father whom he 
could ever threaten. 


Next, the proceedings of the enquiry need be referred to. The enquiry 
was held by Shri Debabrata Chakravortw (0. P. W. 2), the Labour Officer 
of the Company. His deposition is that he held two enquiries the first 
enquiry was an er parte one held on 6th July 1956 and the second one on 
i6th July 1956 which was attended by the workman. The procesdinzy of 
the enquiry Ext. 1) are in the form of a narrative of the Enquiring Officer 


Pars 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 19, 1957 3465 
SE oe ee 


himself and it is clear that the statements of witnesses were not duly 
‘recorded. No importance need be attuched to the proceedings of the 
inquiry which were held ec parte. ا‎ the end of this report the Enquiring 
Ofliver recorded his finding that the charge regarding the filthy abuse to 
female workers was not proved, but that the other two churges were 
estublished. Let us now turn to the report Ext. D1 of the enquiry held 
on 16th July 1956. What the Enquiring Officer recorded is this, just to 
quote one instance, ‘‘Pyarelal was called then. He repeated what he told 
on Oth July 1956. Tarapada asked him to swear upon his religion whether 
all that he told was true and Pyarelal affirmed that the same was true. 
Tarapada said that this was not true. He was not given bobbins, so he 
had to remain idle for most part of his time. Chandramani did not give 
him the bobbins he required............ .۔''‎ The Enquiring Officer has recorded 
in the case of the majority of witnesses that they repeated what they stated 
on 6th July 1956, 7.e., the statements made by them during the ex parte 
enquiry. This has been extremely irregular. The Enquiring Officer 
should have recorded the statements afresh during the second enquiry 
attended by the workman. He should have abondoned' the statements 
made on the occasion of the er parte enquiry as those witnesses were not 
cross-examined on 6th July 1956 by the workman. The statements made 
during the first enquiry have been made to form a part of the second 
enquiry which has been irregular. The enquiry was thus vitiated [vide 
L. L. J. 1957(1), page 4949—Chaudhury A.R.S. & Union of India and 
others]. In that case the enquiry was held vitiated as the workman was 
confronted with evidence of witnesses recorded hehind his back’ and was 
not tendered for cross-exumination, 


Then again there are fundamental defects, namely, (1) the proceedings 
are recorded in Knglish and the workman does not know this language. 
There is nothing to indicate that the proceedings recorded in English were 
explained to the workman in Bengali, (2) there is no final order on the 
result of the enquiry. The Enquiring Officer submitted his report for such 
action as the Management deemed fit and the Management passed no order. 
Mismissal is communicated to the workman as per letter Ext. H, dated 
10th July 1956. ‘he Manager says that thev decided to dismiss him. The 
decision was practically of the Manager Shri Nagendra Mohan Dutta 
(O. P. W. 1). Thus he was himeelf the prosecutor and the Judge whereby 
the principle of natural justice has been violated and the enquiry must be 
held to be vitiated sem the case of Amalgamated Tea Estates Co., ۰ 
and Kerala Union Plantation Workers’ Union reported in 1956 ٠۰ 
(IL), page 433)]. In that case this principle was laid down. 


In the circumstances, I am unable to hold that there has been a proper 
enquiry in this case and the workman has been seriously prejudiced und 
the result of such a vitiated enquiry cannot be upheld. 


Next, I come to the charges. The Union seriously urges that the 
Company was lacking in bona fides in framing the charge of ‘‘go-slow’’ 
tactics. I must say that there is considerable force in this contention of 
ihe Union. In the first place, it is inconceivable that the workman who 
is » plece-rated worker will act against his own pecuniary interests in these 
critical days and produce less by resorting to go-slow tactics. His income 
fell considerably. He cried for more materials to produce more, but he 
could not make his voice heard, and he cried in the wilderness. The Union 
informed the Government (letter Iixt. le) and forwarded copies to the 
Company, but no improvement in the position of supply followed. The 
Company does not admit to have received copies of letters Exts. Lh, 10) but 


3466 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE SEPTEMBER 19, 1957 [Parr I 
না নত سسجت شیییئشیوشوےو_غںشسسششششسع‎ 
there is nothing to. suspect their genuineness. Rather suspicion falls on 
the Company that for his Union activities the Company tried to get rid of 
such disturbing element as this workman. There is no prescribed minimum 
of monthly or daily output required of a piece-rated workman, nor was 
: prescribed by the Company. The observations of their Lordships in 
the case of Ziakh vs. Firestone Tyre & Rubber Co., Ltd. and another 
reported in 1954 L.L.J-I, page 281, may be usefully quoted as follows: 
“It is perfectly true that a piece-rated worker may on occasion put into 
his work every ounce of energy that he possesses. He may reach heibts 
which it is not possible to reach every day, he may surpass himself on 
certain occasions, and nobody suggests that if a piece-rated worker does 
noi maintain the same standard throughout he could be guilty of slowing 
cown, But without reaching those heights it 1s expected even of a 
piece-rated worker that during that time that he is serving his employer 
he must at least use his normal skill and average speed......... Even though 
& minimum may not be prescribed. The conditions of service must require 
that during the time that employee is in the service of his employer he 
must at least give to the employer what he is entitled to, viz., the minimum 
of his ability and of his skill and of his time. If he deliberately refuses 
to give that minimum he is as much guilty of misconduct as he would have 
been if he did not come up to the minimum if such a minimum had been 
prescribed under the contract of service.”’ In this case the workman was 
not given adequate supply, how could he produce adequately? The 
Company has not produced any evidence regarding mode of supplies to 
such piece-ruted workers and the sweeper who mukes the supply is not 
examined. The workman produced his best according as supplies 
permitted. To add to that, this workman was eee দ্র subjected to 
iransfer without any ostensible reason from one section to another which 
clearly appears to be motivated to reduce his production and to victimise 
him for his activities in the Union matters. It may also be pointed out 
that there is no cogent evidence that he induced other workmen also to go- 
slow. Thus the জি of ‘‘go-slow’’ tactics is not substantiated beyond 
reasonable doubt in the enquiry held by the Court. The Court rather 
agrees with the Union that this workman who appeared to be a simpleton 
while in the witness box has been obviously victimised. In the 
circumstances, as there has been violation of the principles of natural 
justice and as there was want of bona fides on the part of tae Company and 
ne it 19 a clear case of victimisation and unfair labour practice, the decision 
of the Management cannot be accepted as a possible view and cannot be 
upheld, and a remedy is justly called for in the interests of justice. 


As regard the other charge of insulting and intimidating the Manager, 
the evidence on this head coming as it does from the Manager and the 
interested quarters seems to be more or less tutored and does not deserve 
full credence. The workman simpleton as he is might have exhibited his 
temper but that should not merit dismissal. Dismissul would be a punish- 
ment utterly disproportionate to his misconduct if any on this score. So 
he deserves relief. It may be observed that the charge about using filthy 
language towards some female workmen was neither established in the 
enquiry held by the Company, nor in the enquiry held by the Court. 


The normal relief is reinstatement in such cases of victimisation, but 
86 laid down in numerous reported cases the question of relief should not 
he viewed altogether subjectively from the point of view only of the 
employer or the employee but also objectively in the interests of the industry 
for bringing about harmony in the relationship between the two. In this 
case the Company’s Manager cannot be expected to accord just treatment 


1180 ]] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 19, 1967 3467 


tu such a workman, if reinstated, nor will the latter feel quite comfortable 
tc work amongst people whose aympathy he obviously alienated. On that 
ground reinstatement is refused. J think adequate compensation should 
meet the end of justice. A piece-rated workman as he is, he had no fixed 
wages. He entered the service of the Mills in 1952, so till his discharge 
on June 1956, he put in more than 4 years’ service. The allegation is that 
he slowed down from 16th April 1956. It is therefore directed that hia 
average monthly income should be calculated on the basis of his 3 months’ 
wages for the period from December 1955 to February 1956 and he should 
be paid as conpensation 4 months’ average monthly wages calculated on 
that basis for his 4 years’ service. T think this will quite meet the ends 
0: Justice in, this case, 


Next I take up the technical objections. The employer is described as 
Messrs, Bangodaya Cotton Mills. If there were no ‘“Messrs.’’ I think that 
would have been defective. What 18 meant is the employers ‘‘Messrs. 
Bangodaya Cotton Mills’. This objection therefore has no substance. 


The other objection is also without substance as the Union has properly 
signed ‘the written statement. If the workman would have signed the 
written statement, it would have been contended that the Union did not 
take up his case, so it is an individual dispute. Ordinanly the Union 
signs written statements. I therefore over-rule this objection. 


To sum up, the termination of the services of this workman is held 
to be unjustified and the Company will pay 4 months’ average income plus 
1). A. on the basis of the average income calculated for the period from 
December 1955 to February 1956 and arrear wages, if any, within a month 
uf the publication of the award. 


11018 is my award.

yranted leave with pay nor were they permitted to contribute to the Provident 
Fund which was a privilege or a condition of service available to a regular

rerwlar and permanent workman. They were treated merely as casual 
Labour. Now, whether a casual Inhour should be confirmed after a pre- 
scribed length of time was a matter pending for decision in the main case. 
So the Company should have taken the permission of the Tribunal before 
terminating the services of these casual workers, But, hecause these people

The Company’s claim that the workmen should not be paid any sub- 
ktantial amount as bonus in order to enable it to execute its schemes of 
expansion is not worthy of acceptance. The trading profits of the Company 
are not reaally the source from which expansion schemps of the Industry 
are to be financed. The Company should pay bonus to its workmen for the 
year ended 30th April 1995, on the basis of its prosperity in the year in 
question considered in the light of the decisions of the Full Bench of the 
Hon'ble Labour Appellate Tribunal in the case of Millowners’ Association, 
Bombay, reported in 1952 L.A.C., 435. 


The Company admits that the principles enunciated by the 6 
Labour Appellate [ribunal m the Full Bench case of Millowners’ Associa- 
tion, Bombay, are correct and should be made applicable to the present case. 
The Company also admits that these principles have been approved by the 
Hon'ble Supreme Court, a8 reported in 1955 L.A.C., page 1. 


The claim of some of the Unions fot Puja bonus of two months’ basic 
pay and ao customary bonus for ap unspecified period has not been sub- 
stantiated. Taking that the claim of the Puja bonus and the customary 
bonus means the bonus hy way of a condition of service, irrespective of the 
profit and loss of the concern, it may be observed that there 1s no evidence 
on record to justify the conclusion that there has been payment of any sum 
as bonus to the workmen unconnected with the profits earned by the Com- 
pany or as a condition of service. This claim is, therefore, rejected. The 
claim for bonus arises out of the claim and the right of the workmen to 
participate in the prosperity of the concern and on the trading results in the 
particular year. This year in our present case is the year 1954-55.

lu support of their case Hindusthan Gras Workers’ Union (hereafter 

called the Union) examined Shri Ami Srimam (1), 1) and Shri Narayan 

Choudhury (P.W. 2) besides proving documents Exts. 1 to 4; while 

Hindusthan Gas Oo., Ltd. (hereafter called the Company) exumined its 


officer Bejoy Kumar Jain (D.W. 1) besides proving documents Exts. A 
to Ol. 


Issue No. 1: The two workmen concerned, Shri Anil Srimani (P.W. 1) 
and Shri Narayan Chaudhury (P.W. 2) admittedly joined service respeo- 
tively us ao Welder and }‘itter in the present factory of the Company at 22 
New Tangra Road. Before this the factory of the টি was admittedly 
located at 42 Garden Reach Road. Keshoram Cotton Mills is also located 
in the said premises at 42 Garden Reach Road. 


The allegation in the written statement of the Union and the evidence 
of P.W. 1 that the workmen were transferred to Keshoram Cotton Mills are 
disproved by the joint application of the workmen (Ext. B). The work- 
men, it appears from Ext. B, were temporarily transterred to the old 
factory at 42 Giarden Reach Road for the purpose of dismantling old 
machinery lying over there. That the transfer was temporary is adinitted 
in the written statement of the Union itself. The employer has undoubted 
power of transferring an employee from one of his concern to another 
concern at a different place unless there be a contract or rule ٠٢ the 
contrary. As there has been no such contract or rule to the contrary, it 
is obvious that the order of transfer was in order and the workmen would 
have no justification to disobey the sume. As a matter of fact it appears 
that the workmen initially accepted the order of transfer and attended 
the old factory at 42 Garden Reach Road on 15th September 1955 and 16th 
September 1955. Although denied in the written statement the workmen 
adinittedly received conveyance charge for those days (165th September 
1955 and 16th September 1955) for going to the factory at Garden Reach 
Road from the factory at New T'angra Road by signing the receipts Exts. 
A to Al. 17th September 1955 was a holiday on account of Viswakarma 
Puja and 18th September 1955 was a Sunday when the factory was closed. 
On 19th September 1955 the two workmen (P.W. 1 and P.W. 2) came to 
the factory at New Tangra Road, recorded their attendance there and then 
met the Manager Shri Lakhotia. The Manager wanted the workmen to 
go directly to the factory at Garden Reach Road from the next day instead 
of coming to the factory at New Tangra Road and then going to the 
factory at Garden Reach Road. P.W. 2 in cross-examination admitted 
that on 19th September 1955 Shri Takhotia asked them to go directly to 
Garden Reach Road for work. He also said that thereupon they demanded 
conveyance allowance. According to the Company the Manager gave 
them an advance of Rs. 10 towards conveyance charge for a week on that 
date; while according to the workmen, Manager did not give such advance. 
From the evidence and circumstances I prefer to accept the Company’s 
version. Exhibit B though dated 17th September 1955 was not, in fact, 
written on that date but apparently written after the conversation with 
the Manager on 19th September 1955. In the said application objection 
was for the first time raised to such transfer to factory at Garden Reach 
Road. This was apparently done in order to counteract the direction of 
the Manager that the workmen should report directly to the factory at 
Garden Reach Road in order to avoid the time lost in the journey to come 
to the factory at New Tangra Rond and then going from there to the 
factory at Garden Reach Road. In their application Ext. B the workmen, 
however, insisted for allowing them to come first to the factory at the

who would obtain Ramplal’s recommendation in that regard. Lefranc 
submitted the statement Ext. A(47), characterising the allegations as falae. 
He gave evidence before the enquiry officer. So it appears that there was 
evidence 01) the basis of which the enquiry officer could hold the charges 
substantiated against these men. In the Buckingham and Carnatic Co.. 
Ltd. ease Their Lordships have laid down in clear terms that the Tribunal 
is to examine the finding of the management to assure itaelf that there is 
evidence to support the 9 and that the decision is a possible view on 
the evidence before it. The Tribunal cannot substitute its own judgment 
for the judgment of the management as in a matter of this kind the Tribunal 
does not act like a court of appeal but rather as a supervisory body. The 
decision of the management will not prevail if— 


(a) there is want of bona fides, or 


(b) it is a case of victimisation or unfair labour practice or violation 
of the principles of natural justice, or 


(৫) there is a basic error of facts, or 
(0) there has been a perverse finding on the materials. 


Our task is therefore is to examine if this enquiry has been vitiated by any 
of the elements enumerated above. On behalf of the workers two points 
৮৮6 pressed. One of the points is that these workers were ardent followers 
of the Mazdoor Union and on account of their Union activities the Company 
had hatched a plot to get them out of the way. The other point was that 
Rudal Routh having made allegations against the Foreman the latter bidded

his opportunity to retaliate and had taken advantages of the situation

There are internal dissensions amongst the workers. They have split 
into three or four camps and formed separate Unions. Shrijut Bhattacharjee

of which 18111001108] is the Secretary is favoured by the Company. Since the

Striking down bearers and messengers served no useful purpose. I am 
convinced that the allegation of victimisation on account of Union activities 
is entirely unfounded. 


There was no want of bona fides so far as the action of the management 
is concerned. Admittedly Rudal Routh wrote the letter containing imputa- 
tions against the Foreman and had stopped zinc washing on the plea that 
he must have the assistance of unother man all the time. The others had 
day after day refused to leave the line and take up alternative jobs. Their 
plea was that they were not surplus. The management is, in my judgment, 
the best judge whether workers in a particular job are surplus or not, On 
the 21st of December, the Company had made it known that piece rate would 
be introduced for nailing and wire-strapping of packing boxes. The staff 
engaged in the work was to be reduced and only six men were required 
(Ext. D3). The six men named in the order of reference were therefore 
considered surplus and they were informed accordingly. They protested 
that they were not surplus. The enquiry officer found on the evidence that 
their refusal to leave the line was a serious breach of discipline and merited 
the punishment of dismissal]. There was no error of facts and the finding 
on the materials available cannot be said to be perverse. It would appear 
that Rudal Routh and the other group were informed more than once by 
the Superior Officers verbally and also in writing that the attitude taken up 
was palpably wrong. They were advised to obey the orders but persuatfons 
produced no effect. Reference may be made to Exts. <A(4) to A(7). 
Exhibits J) and D1 are reports regarding Rudal Routh’s refusal to carry 
on the work of zinc washing unless he was given an assistant for the eutire

Rudal Routh was put to zinc washing work. The evidence shows that

in the solution bath, For the rest of a operation lasting 10 to 12 minutes

Rudal Routh had therefore no reason at all to refuse to do the work on the 
plea that the helper must stay with him throughout the entire operation. 
Both .the charges against him were proved. A point was raised that he 
suffered loss of remuneration on being diverted from his regular work to 
zinc-washing. The basic wages and دق‎ allowance of the workers 
remain fixed. On transfer from one section to another and one department 
to another the job premium or the incentive payable to time-rated and piece- 
rated workers respectively varies. <A grievance was made that Rudal Routh 
was drawing Res. 3-8 per day in his regular work but he was to get daily 
rate which was less by 25 per cent. on being put to zinc-washing work. This 
point was considered on more than one occasion by Tribunals on complaint 
being made that there was change in the conditions of service. The plea 
was repelled (ade Exts. G, G1, G2 and (G3). The workers have no vested 
right to the extra income. Even in one’s own section and department the 
quantum might vary from month to month. The Company has the right 10 
‘transfer the workers from one section or department to another even though 
it might entail reduction in the earnings by way of incentives. So far as 
T can see workers can raise no objection to such transfer on the ground of 
loss of income if the act of the Company is not tainted with ulterior motives 
or mgla fides. In this case [ am not satisfied that Kudal Routh was taken 
off from Bottom Soldering to zine-washing for any ulterior reusons. Jt was 
in the ordinary course of administration that his services were utilised for 
wince ‘washing. In such circumstances the worker cannot refuse to carry 
out the order sisnply because the 101) premium or incentive admissible in the

Shri Rayhubir and others refused to move out of the line on the ground.

2. The petitioner contends that he has been made to retire with effect 
রা the Ist June 1957 by a letter of*the Company, dated 25th April 1957. 
Tn that letter it is mentioned. that. the petitioner joined the service of the 
Company in June 1927 at the age of 22 years. So, on the 3lst May 1957, 
though he completed 30 years’ service under the Company, he was aged only 
52 years. [lis grievance iy that he should have been given extension of 
service, ond also that the Company ought to have taken permission of the 
Tribunal in causing his retirement before whom the main case of the indus- 
trial dispute between the present Company and its workmen was pending 
for adjudication. 


From the Standing Orders of the Company, which is not disputed, it is 
seen that that’ a man ts Jiable to retirement on completion of 30 years of 
service or on reaching the age of 55 yearn, whichever is earlier. In the 
present case the man completed his 3h years’ service on 3ilst May 19957. 
So, under the Standing Orders, though he might not have reached the age 
of 55 years, he was Hable to retirement on and from Ist June 1057. The 
Company, of course, should have taken permission of the Tribunal in writing 
before causing his retirement because this particular Standing Order was 
in taste before the Tribunal. So the petition under section 383A canuot be 
said to be not maintainable. But on the merits T find that the Company 
did not do anything wrong because what it did was in pursuance.of-the exist- 
ing Standing Orders. The existing Standing Orders would remain operative 
مھ‎ long they are not superseded or modified. In the circumstances, the 
ease under section 383A of the Industrial Disputes Act stands rejected on the 
merit.

THE COMMISSIONERS FOR THE PORT OF CALCUTTA 


Summary of the Minutes of the Proceedings of the 
Commissioners’ 7th Meeting, held on the 27th May 7 


AT the 7th Meeting of the Commissioners, held on the 
2711) May 1957, the following business was transacted:— 


(1) Construction of a new Tea Warehouse —Seoond Five- 
Year Plan.—The Commissioners decided that the Tea Board 
should be requested to furnish the necessary assurance for 
the full utilisation of the space provided and failing such 
occupation agres to the Commissioners’ terms for payment 
of ao mintmum rent for the accommodation. 


(2) Liability of the Trustees of Provident Funds under 
the Estates Outy Act, 1953.—The Commissioners approved 
the Chairman’s proposal in the matter. 


(3) Improvement of Quay Surfacing in Kidderpore and 
King George’s Docks and Garden Reaoh Jettles.—The 
Commissioners decided that concreting quay surfaces in 
Kidderpore Dock No. 1 should be 12101) preference and 
that the work should be taken in final when the quay 
walls were repaired. They 0150 decided that concreting the 
quay surface in Kidderpore Dock No. 2 should be taken - 
up as and when the need arose. 


(4) Port Development Scheme—-Second Five-Year Plan. 
—The Progress Report for the third quarter onding 3lat 
March 1957 was recorded, The Commissioners decided 
that the question of reducing the Plan expenditure should 
he considered sooner or later, unleas Government mean- 
while agreed to increase their share of asgsiatance for 
financing the projects. 


(5) Election of a Port Commissioner.—The Commia- 
sioners approved the appointment of Shri M, ا‎ Shah, 
Port Commissioner, as member of the Finance Exstablish- 
ment and Trafhe Committeo, vice Shri A, Rajagopalan 
deceased. : 

The Commissioners 7180 sanctioned routine establish- 
ment proposal4 and routine proposals relating to execution 
of works, purchase of materials, remission of charges, 
grant of leases, etc.

3862 THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., SEPTEMBER 19, 1957 [Parr I 
NE ھت ےج ےس‎ 


AWARD 


This is a case arising out of termination of services of 25 workmen of 
Messrs. Calcutta Porcelain Works with effect from Ist February 1957 on 
the basis of a notice, dated 9156 December 1920. 


The Company justifies the termination of the services of these work- 
men enumerated in the notice on the ground that their works were found 
unsatisfactory. 


On the other hand, the case of the Union is that the workmen have been 
victimised, pure and simple, and that this ta an extremely unfair labour 
practice. The Union further urges that the Company never found fault 
with their works; that they were not charge-sheeted, nor was any enquiry 
held, nor were they heard in their defence, and thus the principles of 
natural and social justice have been grossly violated. The Union therefore 
seeks reinstatement of the workmen with other incidental reliefs. 


Decision. 


The main pomt for consideration in this case is whether the termination 
of the services of these workmen is justified or not. 


{It is common ground that no charges were framed against these work- 
men, nor were they heard in their defence, nor was any enquiry held. 
Prima facie these workmen suddenly found themselves thrown out of their 
employment. The trump-card of the Company in the reports—Exts. A-A9 on 
the works of these workmen, The Union has examined some 4 workmen 
and there is nothing in the evidence to show that the full implication of this 
notice was brought home to the workmen who were going to be sacked. 
Curiously enough this Company has got no Standing Orders of their own 
laying down the terms and conditions of service of their workmen, so there 
is nothing before the Court regarding the minimum_ period of service a 
workman is required to put in before absorption. Few of these workmen 
as will appear from the tubular statement Ext. © put in by the Company did 
complete one year’s service more or less and the majority did Jess than a 
year. On behalf of the Union it is said that 6 months’ probationary period 
should be deemed sufficient for absorption. On the other hand, the 
Company urges that full probationary period for a year is necessary before 
absorption. As for myself in the absence of any definite rule regarding 
the probationary period necessary before confirmation, the Court is not 
competent to fix minimum probationary period either way. Be that as 
it may, now the Court proceeds to discuss in the state of evidence on 
record whether the termination of their services is justified. 


The Company has got undoubted authority to determine the strength of 
their labour force, and in common law, it has every night to discharge or 
dismiss an employee, which right is popularly called the “‘right to hire 
and fire’. But this mght is not un ae pr and is subject to certain 
statutory restrictions and দন্ড দা principles as enumerated in 1006 
L.L.J., Vol. I, page 325 (Lipton Limited and their workmen) :— 


(1) that an industrial worker must he placed in such a position that 
the security of his service may not depend upon the caprice or 
arbitrary will of the employer, 


(2) that industrial peace should be maintained, and 


(3) that industry should be efficiently managed.’’ 


Parr I] TUE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., SEPTEMBER 19, 1957 3863 


“In all these types of cases, however, the requirement of bona fides is 
essential 0 the termination of service in colourable exercise of 
the power or as a result of victimization or unfair labour practice 
or of caprice, should be prevented............... and that’ arbitrary 
conduct or wnnecessary hurshuess on the part of the employer, 
judged by the normal standard of a reasonable man, may be cogent 
evidence of victimization or unfair labour practice.”’ 


Judging by this standard, I am afraid, | am unable to uph®ld the action 
of the کت‎ in terminating the services of these workmen. Admittedly 
2 or 3 days after retrenchment of these workmen some 15/16 men were 
employed in the Kiln Department and these new men do the same job 85 the 
discharged ones. Likewise in the Sorting Department 2 or 3 days after 
their discharge some 0 new workmen were recruited. In the Saggar 
Department the unchallenged evidence is that the outturn of work increased 
from 130 to 150 pieces at the time of discharge. This is a distinct improve- 
ment on the quantity of production. So there is no cogent evidence before 
the Court to show that the quality or quantity of the works of these work- 
men suffered in. any way so as to justify the termination of services of these 
workmen. Secondly, it is significant to point out that neither the Manager 
who supervises the works of the workmen, nor Ganesh (Mistry), nor Pashu- 
pati Chatterjee, who is the depurtment-in-charge, has come forward to 
pledge his oath in this case. If the reports Exts. A-A9 be held sacrosanct 
there 38 an end of the case of the workmen but in the oircumstances set 
forth above these reports have practically no basis to stand upon and, I 
think, I shall not be justified in upholding the termination of the services 
of these workmen simply on the basis of such reports which are the hundi- 
work of Company’s men prepared behind the back of these workmen. ' ٥ 
Companv has tried to impress upon the Court their bona fides inasmuch as 
they re-employed two men Shri Debabrata and Shri Tribhuban even after 
the notice but the evidence on the side of the workmen is that after service 
of the notice, no enquiry was held in the meantime into the quality or 
quantity of their works and the re-employment of 2 men can be no shield 
against the unjustified termination of the services of the workmen. Trom 
the evidence on record coupled with the circumstances of this case bearing 
in mind the fact that in each department some new men were recruited 
soon after these workmen were thrown off, I cannot hold that the Company 
uccorded due treatment to these workmen and the Company’s action savours 
of an unfair labour practice which obviously resulted in their victimisation. 
Thus these Workmen were unjustly thrown out of their employment. 


As regards relief, the normal relief in such a case is reinstatement. So 
I direct that these 23 workmen should be re-employed but so far as 
incidental reliefs are concerned I think one month’s full wages should be 
granted to these workmen in each case. In this connexion I must state 
that I am not forgetful of the principle laid down in the case of Chopra 
Motors and their workmen reported in 1997 L.L.J., Vol. 11, page 162 
which runs as follows :— : 


‘“When it is clear that an employer cannot terminate the services of a 
workman except in a lawful manner and when the dismissal is not 
valid, the workman must be deemed never to have been dismissed 
at all and so continues in service, it is reasonable to hold that the 
norma] relief is reinstatement, subject, of course, to a condition 


that 1t might be ruled out in the circumstances of any particular 
case.’’ 


In the circumstances of this particular case as it appears from the records, 
the Company is not an affluent one. I therefore think that one month’s 


3864 THE CAL GAZ. EXTRY., SEPTEMBER 19, 1957 [Parr I 
০৯৯৯ 


full wages should be considered adequate compensation for their period € 
unemployment. 


In conclusion, the Company must reinstate these 23 workinen as per list 
except serial Nos. 8 and 23 of the Annexure A to the Compuny’s written 
statement (Shri Debabrata and Sbri Tribhuban) und pay to each of them 
their oue month’s full wages. The continuity of services of these work- 
men will be ০০161 as unbroken, The Company will reinstate these work- 
meno and pay them their wages for full one month as compensation within 
a month of the publication of this award. 


This is my award. 


Dictated and corrected hy me. 


N. C. CHATTERJEE, N. C. CHATTERJEE, 
Judge. Judge, First Labour Court.

This is an application under section 438A of the Industrial Disputes Act 
by Shri Rajen Biswas and 17 other employees of Messrs. National Motor 
(Works (hereinafter referred to as the Company), 65 Hazra Road, Calcutta, 
alleging wrongful dismissal from service on different dates without 
permission from this Tribunal when an industrial dispute between the 
parties was pending before it for adjudication. The applicants ask for 
reinstatement with compensation for the entire period of unemployment. 
The Company resists this application stating among others that the 
applicants were temporary and casual hands and, as such, no permission 
was required for termination of their services. Further, none of these 
employees was a protected workman within the meaning of section 33 of 
the Industrial Disputes Act. This case was taken up for hearing on 20th 
August 1907. Heard Shri Pathak for the applicants and Shri Manna, 
Counsel for the Company, The matter has been amicably settled between 
the parties, and a petition to this effect has heen filed by them in which 
the applicants sought to withdraw their petition under section 33A before 
the Tribunal on certain assurance from the employer. Heard both sides. 
The applicants are permitted to withdraw their application under section 
33. of the Industrial Disputes Act. ‘The case is thus disposed of,

Decision 


Issue No. 1: There were really 58 female workers and apprentices and 
not 59 as mentioned in the order of reference. The mention of Parul Duwi 
No. 22 of the list attached to the order of reference appears to be a mistake. 
Neither party claimed a workman of that name. The Union 9180 statea 
that there were only 08 female workers as mentioned in Annexure A to ita 
written statement filed on 6th September 1955 which was adopted by 018 
written statement filed before this Tribunal] on 29th March 1957. It is 
therefore accepted that only 58 female workers as per list attached to the 
order of reference, except 22 Parul Dui, are to be considered for the 
decision of the present issue. 


Evidenoe was adduced on both sides. 1১, W. 1 Pratima Na , P. W. 2

N irmal Chandra Sen, Works Manager, deposed for the Company. 
Documents Exts. A to P were marked for the Company. 


It appears from the evidence on record that there were seven female 
apprentices recruited by the Company and five of them were absorbed and

No. 27 Jharna Sen, No. 30 Rani Bose (Sarkar), No. 33 Sukumari Choudhurt

Matra respectively. Six of the  apprentfees had their. apprenricesbip 
extended at the date of hearing of the case and they were No. 43 Gayatri 
Biswas, No. 47 Niva (31081), No. 48 11:٢١١ Majumdar, No. 50 Annapurna 
Chatterjee, No. 54 Radha Sarkar and No. 59 Ava Dutta. At the date 
of the hearing of argument on 8th August 1957, the learned Advoeate of 
the Company informs me that out of these aix, five have since been 
absorbed as permanent employeea and only one, namely, Gayatri Biawas, 
is atill continuing as an apprentice. It appears that No. 45 Ranu Datta 
was dismissed for misconduct. It also appears that No. 63 Parul Majumdar 
who was an apprentice accepted an alternative job under the Company in 
the staff. She has therefore been absorbed in the staff and not in he factory. 
Four of the apprentices, namely, No. 7 Chhaya Dey, No. 2 Rina Dey,

8 lopg time, and they are no longer in the Company’s service. Five of the

Ne. 18 Smriti Ghosh, No. 12 Dali Mukherjee and No. 57 Gita Gupta, 
resigned the services of the Company. The rest of 34 have all been absorbed. 


It, therefore, appears that there is only one female worker who is retained 
مہ‎ apprentice and has not yet heen confirmed, All the workers who have 


heen confirmed are getting wages aos fixed by Major Engineering Tribunal 
for semi-skilled workmen. 


The who fixed for semi-skilled workinen is at the basic rate of Re. 1-5-6 
er day or Ra. 35 per month. The 1), A. for auch worker is of Ra, 81 or 
te, 1-3-3 per month. 


The learned Advocate for the Company stated that the female worker 
who was still continuing as apprentice will be confirmed when found 
suitable. This assurance is accepted. 


As to the service conditions of these female workera it 18 again assured 
by the learned Advocate for the Company that they will get the service 
conditions as laid down for workers of the Engineering industries hy the 
award of the First and the Second Major [nfMeering Tribunal. This 
‘ glatement is confirmed by me in this award. 


The Union claimed that the workers were allowed wages of Rs. 51 or مہ‎ 
per month till they were confirmed which was done some months after the 
worker gave full production aa is given by a permanent worker. The 
Union’s claim is that the workers should be paid full wages of Rs. 66 per 
month retrospectively since the day they gave full production. This claim 
is not covered, by the iasue as referred to this Tribunal. I do. not consider 
that the workers can be confirmed as permanent worker before he can give 
full production in the regular manner for some time. The claim for higher 
wages retrospectively should not be made only because the worker gave full

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 
OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF POLICE 
۱ ORDER 
Calcutta, the 24th September 1957. 


Whereas, I, H. S. Ghose Chaudhuri, Commissioner of Police, Calcutta, 
am of opinion thut it is necessary for the purpose of preventing annoyance 
19, and injury to the Health of, the public, and for the purpose of 
maintaining public peace and tranquility, to prohibit, restrict, regulate und 
impose conditions on the use or operution, in any area within the Town of 
Calcutta and the suburbs of Calcutta (as respectively defined in the Calcutta 
Police Act, 1866 and notification under section 1 of the Calcutta Suburban 
Police Act, 1866) or in any vehicle within such areas, of microphones, loud- 
speakers, or other apparatus for amplifying human voice or: amplifying 
music or other sounds; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred on me by section 431)- 
(1)(a) of the Calcutta Police Act, 1866 and _ section 17D(1)(a) of the 
Calcutta Suburban Police Act, 1866, read with West Bengal Ordinance 
No. IX of 1957 [The Caleutta and Suburban Police (Amel nont) 
Ordinance, 1957], I, the said H. S. Ghose Chaudhuri, Commissioner 01 
Police, Calcutta, do hereby order— 


(1) That no person shall use or operate in any area mentioned 0) the 
schedule below microphone, loudspeaker, or other apparatus for 
amplifying human voice or کک‎ music or other sounds 
without prior permission in writing of the Commissioner of 
Police, Calcutta, and subject to such conditions 118 the 
Commissioner of Police, Calcutta, may deem fit to impose. 


(2) That no person shall use or operate in any vehicle in any #-1ch area 
microphones, loudspeakers, or other apparatus for amplifying 
human voice or amplifying music or other sounds, without prior 
permission in writing of the Commissioner of Police, Caleutca. 


(3) Nothing in this order shall apply to any apparatus or vehicle 
belonging to Government or to such organisations as may {rom 
time to time be specified by the Commissioner of 1)01109) 
Calcutta, in this behalf. 

(4) Nothing herein contained in orders 1, 2 and 3 above shall affect the 
existing orders of the Commissioner of Police, Calcutta, prohibit- 
ing or restricting music and the making of other noises, before 
Hospitals or Mosques, or in areas where sounding of horns 18 
prohibit:d. 

Schedule 
The Town of Calcutta as defined in Calcutta Police Act, 1866, tozether 
with suburbs of Calcutta as defined by notification under section 1 of the 


Calcutta Suburban Police Act, 1866. 
H. ৪. GHOSE CHAUDHURI,, Commissioner.

Subject: Accounting of fees received from banks 
for safe custody of their duplicate keys in the 
Treasury, 


No. TM/635.—1]th September 1957.—A_ refer- 
ence 15 invited to Appendix 7-A of the Treasury, 
Rules, West Bengal, Volume IT, as inserted by 
the (tovernment of West Bengal, Finance Depart- 
ment, Audit Branch, notification No. 371F./ 
VIT-4(81)/55, dated 7th February 1957 and 
amended by their notffication No, 2068F., dated 
1901) July 1957, in terms of which banks are te- 
quired to pay fees for their duplicate keys lodged 
in the Treasury for safe custody. It has been 
decided that fees so received from the banks should 
he adjusted under the minor head “Other Fees, 
Fines and Forfeiturea” subordinate to the major 
head ‘*X1,V1—Miscellaneous’’ in the State Section 
of the accounts, 


All Treasury Officers in West Bengal are 
requested to note this for their guidance.

Agreement 


An agreement entered into between Greaves Cotton & (o., IJaimited, 
Calcutta, having its office at Ralli House, 16 Flare Street, Calcutta-1 
hereinafter referred to as the Compuny), and Greaves Cotton & Crompton 

arkinson (Private) Ltd. and Associated Concerns Workmen’s Union

Whereas the workers represented by the Union raised an_ industrial 
dispute which was referred to adjudication by the West Bengal Government 
order No. 4304Dis. /D/10L-107/58, dated 26th September 1956, and whereas 
the said industrial dispute was not taken up for hearing as compromise 
proceedings between the Union and the Company were in progress; 

Now, therefore, it 1s hereby agreed— 

(1) That the scales of pay shall be as in Schedule A attached to this 

Agreement. 

(2) The leave rules (casual, sick and privilege) shall be as in Schedule 
B attached to this agreement. 

(3) The tng da with regard to the reinstatement of Mrs. V. Haslam is 
withdrawn by the Union. The dispute with regard to the 
reinstatement of Shri Kartick Sen is also withdrawn, the 
Company gr to prv er gratia Rs. 700 (Rupees seven 

hundred only) to the ex-employee, Mr. Kartick Sen. 


This agreoment is entered into without prejudice to the Company’s 
contention that the Union is not recognised by the Company.

The Government of West Bengal, in the Department of Labour, by order 

No. 1047-1. It. /IR/111.-26/57, dated tha 22nd April 1957, referred under 
sections 7 and 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the 
industrial dispute between Messrs. Lipton Lamited, 0 Weston Street, 
Caleutta-13, and one of their workmen, Sk. Amjad Ahi, represested by the 
Lipton Mazdoor Union, 240-13 Bowbazar Street, Caleutta-12, regarding 
matters specified in the second schedule of the Act, to this Court for 
adjudication. 


Issue 
Whether the dismissal of Sk. Amjad Ali is justified? What relief is he 
entitled to? 7 
AWARD 


This 14 a case arising out of dismissal of Sk. Amjad Ali, 8, workman of 
Messrs. Lipton Ltd., on the allegation that he deliberately refused to carry 
out a reasonable. order of the Company and was thus found guilty of dis- 
obedience, insubordination and consequent misconduct meriting dismissal as 
per Company’s Standing Order. | 

The case of the Union, in short, is that Amjad Ali was recruited in 1949 
and that le was a vice-man fitter in the Company and it was not his duty 
to prepare ffelamp”’ which is a blacksmith’s job which he therefore rightly 
aa a to carry out. This followed a charge-sheet; a sham enqywiry was 
held denying reasonable facilities to the workman which thus resulled in 
violation of oll principles of natural and social justice and ultimately he was 
wrongfully dismissed. This workman is the Vice-President of the Union 
and he was victimised for his Union activities, pure and simple. 


3588 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 26, 1957 [Paar tf 


| ny সপ ০০৫০-২৯-১০ 


The Company, on the other hand, denies the material allegations in the 
written statement of the Union and contends, inter alia, that this Amjad 
Ali was engaged os a Mistry in the Company’s small Engineering repair 
shop on the 28th April 1949. On 27th April 1956, Mr. A. K. Biswas, one 
of the Company’s Engineering Executives, instructed Amjad Ali to make 
a clamp from mild ateel for the installation of a fan which he did to the 
ful) satisfaction of the Company; that on 2nd May 1956 he was asked to 
make a second clamp and was offered facilities and assistance from other 
Mistries, if necessary, but he refused to carry out this reasonable order of 
the Company saying that this was a blacksmith’s job and not that of a vice- 
hench fitter which he then claimed himself to be. This was followed by a 
charge-sheet to which he replied and an enquiry ‘was ultimately held on 
1911) Mav 1956 which was attended by all concerned including the workman | 
snd Shri Manindra Nath Das, his representative and member of the Works 
Committes, The Factory Manager duly held) an enquiry and offered all 
reasonable facilities to the workman to defend himself and ultimately 
found him guilty under section 18(d) and (0) of the Company's Standing 
Order. On these grounds, the Company contends that the workman is 
entitled to no relief. | 


Decision 


This Court is now called upon to decide whether the dismissal of 
Sk. Amjad Ali is justified or not, and, if he is entitled to any relief. 


The principal point of contention of the Union is that the preparation 
of a clamp is not the normul duty of a vice-bench fitter as this workman was. | 
So the Compuny had no justification for asking this workman to prepare 
2 clamp and, as such, this workman in refusing to edrry out this order was 
not guilty of disobedience of any lawful and rensonable order. On the other 
hand, the Company urges thot all Mistries at the time of their recruitment 
are intimated that they would be required to do all and sundry jobs as und 
when necessary while working in this Company. Admitted) , the main 
business of the Company is “packing and blending’’ for which the Mistries 
are required and there is also a forge in the Company which is used very 
scarcely, few and far between. At this stage, it need be said that there is 
no list defining the specified duties of Mistries in the Company. 


Now ٤ come to the facts. Admittediy this workman prepared a clamp 
which Mr. Biswas (O.P.W. 1), an 15560006156 of the Company, asked him 
to do. This clamp is a flat piece of rod, } inch thick and about 2 inches 
wide und is used for installing fans. Amjad Al) without any demur executed 
this work to the entire satisfaction of the Company. He was asked to make 
another clamp on 2nd May 1956 which he refused to do saying that it was 
not his duty but it was the job of a blacksmith. Mr. Biswas clearly brought 
home to lim repeatedly the consequences of refusal to carry out his order 
and gave him enough time, at least a mght, to reflect over the matter and 
to communicate to him the decision the next day. The workman neverthe- 
less informed Mr. Piswas on 3rd May 195¢ that it was not his job and he 
refused to prepare the clamp. This was followed hy a charge-sheet Ext. A. 
An enquiry was held on 15th May 1956 by the Factory Manager Mr. Stark 
O.P.W. 2), At this stage, the proceedings of the enquiry Ext. D1 and the 

ndings thereon Ext. D2 mav be referred to. I have gone through the 
proceedings very carefully. The proceedings give on honest picture of all 
that happened during the enquiry. Jt was attended by the workman, the 
Manager Mr. Stark, Mr. Biswas, the Labour Officer, Mr. Mahindra, and 
also by Manindra Nath Das and Vuiya Mistry on behalf of the workman. 
These proceedings read between the lines do not give slightest suggestion 
of any injustice rendered to the workman. It appears that the Enquirying 
Officer was permeated through and through by an honest desire to conduct the 


Part I} THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 26, 1957 3539 


++ = 


enquiry as conscientiously as possible and to held the scales of justice even 
between the Company and the workman and 1 have not the least hesitation 
in upholding this enquiry. Much has been made to malign this enquiry 
and the allegations that these were not explained to the workman who does 
not know English, nor was he offered facilities to cross-examine the witnesses 
ot to offer evidence on his side are absolutely unfounded. Mr. Biswas, it 
is evident, interpreted the proceedings of the enquiry in Bengali and the 
evidence of the Fiore Mannger is that the Labour Officer Mr. Mahindra 
also did this in part. So, it cannot be contended on behalf of the Union 
that this workman was innocent of the proceedings which were a domestic 
affair of the Company, and that he was denied reasonable facilities to defend 
himself. The proceedings cannot be held invalid merely on the ground that 
the workman did not know Knglish. The evidence clearly points to the fact 
that the same were explained to him in Bengal which he knew quite well 
and he was offered 91] reasonable and proper facilities to defend himself, 
It is not enouch to say that the workman did not subscribe his signature to 
the proceedings. Mere denial of the workman’s signature though he was 
asked to sign, does not go to invalidate the proceedings. 


The proceedings in this case give ample proof that the order on Amjad 
Ali to prepare a clamp was a reasonable order. Admittedly, he prepared one 
clamp and he was offered assistance of other Mistries as and when necessary. 
If it was not really his job as a vice-man or vice-bencl fitter as he designated 
himself he might have refused to carry out the first order. After having 
carried out the first order it did not Jie in his mouth to say that it was 
not his job. As regards his competency to prepare the clamp, that was 
proved because the first one was to the entire satisfaction of the authorities 
and in preparing the clamp he did not suffer any loss in prestige, status 
and emoluments, nor was his workload increased thereby. That being ৪০0, 
he was wrong in persisting in a wrong course in obstinately refusing to 
prepare the second clamp. The evidence as already said is that Mistries 
are at the time of their recruitment intimated that they would be required 
to do all and sundry jobs aos and when necessary and so the preparation of a 
clamp requiring the ৮10] slightly of a blacksmith was no wnjust or unreason- 
able order for the Company to pass and Amjad to carry out. What followed 
in cousequence is easily discernible. He had to face the enquiry which was 
very fair and the view that the Company took as the result of the enquiry 
can‘ never he said to be perverse or unreasonable. The evidence on record 
at the enquiry held by the Company and at the enquiry held by the Court 
leads to the same conclusion that this workman has rightly been dismissed 
for disobedience, insubordination and misconduct. The Standing Orders of 
the Company under section 18(d) and (0) and the latter inasmuch as his 
disobedience was an act subversive of discipline provide for the punishment 
of dismissal. The Court therefore cannot justifiably interfare with the 
result of the enquiry. 


The settled law as laid down in the case of Buckingham Carnatic Co. 
reported in 1952 L.A.C., page 490, is that the decision of the Management 
will not prevail: if— 


(a) there is want of bona fides, or 


(b) it is a case of victimisation or unfair labour practice or violation 
of the principles of natural justice, or 


(c) there is basic error on facts, or 
(d) there has been a perverse finding on the materials. 
The decision of the Management is also liable to be reversed if it 18 held 


by the Court that the punishment is so unjust that remedy 18 called for in 
the interests of justice. 


3540 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 26, 1957 | Pant 1 


a - . আও AOE پا‎ “i দল স্পা ee আল সত ৩৬ উস ডা পা এ It RRA পতিতার... ےکےکے۔وکدکک‎ 
পক পপ . নে সর 2 ৬ ০ ক সি ০ সপ ও সপ সা 
১১১০১ 


In this case us already scrutinised the decision of the Management is not 
tainted with any of the blemishes enumerated above. In the present case 
the ounishment of dismissal for the misconduct is also in accordance with 
Compuny’s Standing Orders and the Court has no power to substitute its 
own judgment in place of that of the Company and to reduce the punishment 
on the ground that it 18 excessive, unless the Management did exercise 
its discretion arbitrarily or legally. This is the Jaw laid down in the 
recent case of Bazpiai and others es. L.A.T. and another, reported in 7 
15150551৮01. If, pages 16-23. The Management found him guilty of mis- 
conduct on proper enquiry and awarded due punishment as per their 
Standing Order, مھ‎ the Court cannot interfere. 


The workman took a wrong stand and must bear the consequences that 
inevitably flow from it. He has been rightly dismissed. The Court cannot 
grant him any relief. His dismissal by the Company is justified and he is 
not entitled to any relief. 


This is my award.

ANNEXURE 


In the matter cf a complaint under section 33۸ of the Industrial Disputes 
Act, 1947, as amended by Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) 
Act, 1950, filed by Shri Sagar Kanu and Shri Punpun Coala, 
represented by Indian Chemical & Therapeutical Workers’ Union 1 Joy

BEFORE THE THIRD INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL

Sua J. N. MAITRA, Judge, Tlurd Industrial Tribunal. 


Miscellaneous Case No. 139 of 1956 under section 33A of the Industrial 
Disputes Act 


(1) Shri Sagar Kanu and (2) Shri Punpun 00019 ... Petitioners. 
VERSUS 


The Indian Chemical & Therapeutical Works Ltd., 9 Barrackpore Trunk 
Road, Calcutta-2  ... Opposite party. 


Present for the workmen: Shri Panchanan Bhattacharji. 


Present for the Company: Shri S. C. Sen, Advocate. 


AWARD 


This is a complaint under section 383A of the Industrial Disputes Act 
by two workmen, Of them Shri Sagar Kanu who serves in the Packing 
Section complained that he was employed as hand-cart puller from August 
1956 contrary to his normal duty as helper; while Shri Punpun Goala 
alleged that he was not granted increment although all other workmen 
were given increment in theeyear 1950-56. 


The Opposite party opposed the application. It contends that there 
has heen no contravention of provision of section 33 of the Act and as such 
the complaint under section 33A of the Act is not maintainable... The 
Company also pleads that Shri Sagar Kanu is not a belper but a cooly who 
is also to perform the duty of the hand-cart puller as and when necessary. 
Regarding Punpun Goala itt was alleged that he was on leave on medical 
grounds from 19th April 1955 and on the expiry of his leave on 23rd June 
1955 he remained absent without leave for more than a month. He then 
turned up on or about 38rd August 1955 and on furnishing medical 
certificate he was absent without pay till 18+ September 1955. He was 
allowed to work from 19th September 1955. The increment referred to was 
considered in the month of August 1955 when he was absent and so his 
00১৬ was left out. 

| Decision 


I agree that there has been no violation of the provision of section 93 
of the Act and accordingly the complaint is not maintainable. It 18 
admitted during hearing that there was no incremental scale of pay for 


3542 THE CAILUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 26, 7 [Paar 1 


eile ০. ও সা? ee 


workinen of the category of Punpun Goala and that the increment which 
was allowed to some workmen of that category was absolutely in the 
discretion of the Company. So, it cannot be said that there has been 
alteration of the conditions of service applicable to Punpun Goala. 
Besides he was admittedly absent for long due to illness and also in 
August 1955 when the question of increment was conidered. In the 
circumstances, the Company did nothing wrong in not giving him 
increment. ee Sagar Kanu the statement (Ext. A) filed in the 
main reference describes him Punpun: Goala and others as cooly. Punpun 
Goala (P.W. 2) admitted in his deposition that he has been doing the 
work of carrying bottles and also pulling hand-cart with packed medicines 
from one building to other. Sagar Kanu (P.W. 1) also admitted in cross- 
examination that ull the persons who are shown as coolies in the statement 
Ext. A do the work of pulling hand-cart as and when necessary. In the 
circumstances, his complaint that he was employed for 2/4 days in pulling 
hand-cart cannot be sustained. As a workman of the same category he 
should not grudge to pull hand-cart 1s and when necessary. The result is 
that the complaint must fail. 


Tt is awarded accordingly.

This is a case arising out of dismissal of Shri D. Ghosal of Messrs. Kirt

The case of the Union is that the workman Shri D, Ghosal, Assistant

3546 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 26, 1967 [Parr]
