3548 THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 26, 1957 [Pant I 


و سو یہ تو a‏ کو | eine‏ 


The original reference, out ‘of which the present’ application under 
section 33A arises, was made to this Tribunal by the’Government of Weat 
Bengal, Labour Department, under order No. S103Dis. ; 1D /81.-26/56, dated 
17th July 1956. The said reference has since been disposed of by this 
Tribunal and the award given«in this case has also been published in the 
Calcutta Gazette. 

AWARD 


The present application which has been made by as many as 80 workmen 
is a complaint under section,33sA of the Act. Their contention is that théy 
ure all permanent workmen at the Cotton ‘Waste Factory یسا‎ 
mentioned in the original reference, but during the pendency of the 
suid reference before this Tribunal they were all discharged verbally eon 
24th November 1956 without the express permission of the Tribunal. In 
the circumstances, they claimed reinstatement with full compensation for 
the [76710] of their forced idleness. 


The application was contested by the Company-Opposite Party. It 
contends that the present application under section 094 is not maintainable, 
11009111161) as the petitioners ere not employed in the Cotton Waste Fartory. 
The petitioners were employees in the Jute Press, which has no connection 
whatsoever with the ات‎ employed in the Cotton Waste Factory. The 
business of the Jute Press is separate from that of the Cotton Waste Factory, 
and both are independent and separate units. Besides, the Opposite Party 
contends that the petitioners were not discharged or dismissed them, but 
they were aimply 51-0 with effect from 24th November 1956 after due 
notice, and that such lay-off does not come unde® section 33 of the Act. 


So, the point for decision in this case is whether the application under 
section 338A os made by the petitioners is maintainable in Jaw. Both purties 
have adduced evidence. Besides oral evidence, the Opposite Party has also 
furnished documentary evidence. On a consideration of the evidence, I am 
of the view that the present application under section 33A is not maintain- 
able. It appears from Ext. J, which is the original order of reference made 
by the Government, that the industrial dispute that was referred to the 
Tribunal for adjudication, was between srs. Ladakchand O’ Vora, 3 
Gurgola Ghat Road, Salkia, Howrah, oatkl* their workmen at their Cotton 
Waste Factory at 3 Gurgola Ghat Road, Howrah. Thus, it is evident that 
in the original reference only the workmen working at the Cotton Waste 
Factory at 3 Gurgola Ghat Road, Howrah, were concerned in that dispute. 
But it has transpired from the evidence that the present petitioners were not 
employed in that Cotton Waste Factory at 3 Gurgola Ghat Road, but they 
were working in the Bandha Ghat Jute Preas, that is in the Press House 
Godown located at 4 11070111170] Shaw Road. Messrs. Ladakchand O’ Vora 
might be the owners of both the concerns—the Cotton Waste Factory at 
8 Gurgola Ghat Road and the Bandhaghaot Jute Press at 4 Hazarimnl Shaw 
Road. This does not matter much. But it has been satisfactorily proved 
that the Press House or the Press Godown is a separate establishment 
altogether from the Cotton Waste Factory at 3 Gurgola Ghat Road. In this 
view of the matter, it cannot he said that these petitioners, who were 
actually employed in the Press (todown, were the workmen in the Cotton 
Waste Factory at 3 Gurgola Ghat Road. Therefore, I hold that the present 
petitionera were not concerned in the dispute, which was the subject-matter 
of the reference. This heing the position, the present application under 
section 33A as made by them is not maintainable, and cannot be entertained. 

Furthermore, it appears from the materials furnished by the Opposite 
Party that these petitioners were not dismissed or discharged os alleged, but 
they were laid-off with effect from 24th November 1956 ,.for failure to 
procure quality cotton waste for export market for assorting. Such lay-off 


Part 1[ THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 26, 1957 3549 
cannot be treated as tantamount to an alteration of the conditions of service. 
Laying-off of the workmen is one of the normal conditions of service. So, 
it cuunot be s&id that the employer altered, to the prejudice of the workmen 
concerned, any condition bf service by such Jay-off. If during the pendency 
of the proeéeding before the ‘Tribunal any“employees are placed under lay- 
off, it cannot be said that their conditions of service have been changed 
prejudicially. It may react to their prejudice, but it is not an alteration 
in the service condition. Both the ingredients must be there, viz., altera- 
tion of the service condition as also prejudicial alteration. Section 33 has, 
therefare, no apploation where the action complained of is lay-off. So, 
in any view of the matter, it cannot be said that section 33 of the Act has 
been contravened. The application is accordingly rejected.

AWARD 


This is 0, complaint under section 83A of the Industrial Disputes Act 
by 38'permunent employees headed by Shri Birendra Nath Biswas. They 
ued that Puja bonus equivalent to one month’s wages was payable to 
them as a condition of service but the opposite party Company withheld 
such payment for the year 1956. Durtng hearing it wos contended that 
by such stoppage of payment during pendency of the adjudication 
proceeding in respect of industrial dispute between the opposite party 
Company and their workmen without permission from the said Tribunal, 
the opposite party contravened the provisions of section 88 of the Act. 
The empoyees accordingly prayed for an award directing the opposite party 
to pay one month’s wages as Puja bonus to them for 1996. 


The Company opposed the application. It contended that the 
complaint was not maintainable as there was no contravention of section 33 
of the Industrial Disputes Act. he Company denied that the payment of 
Puja bonus was ever a condition of service. 


3552 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 26, 1957 [Parr] 


a > ——_ 


eee ہلاو‎ 


گت ty‏ جم ےید اد ০ pee‏ زیہ و ও‏ یھ REM‏ لے دہ eee oe‏ ہدوہ و ع8 سلا۔ eg ee‏ 


Decision 


On giving careful consideration to the matter, I agree that the complaint 
ander section 388A of the Act is not maintainable. Foundation for 
complaint under section 33A is contravention of the provision of section 33 
of the Act. Conditions of service referred to in section 33(a) are such 
conditions of service which are either provided in. the standinig 
orders or decided by adjudication or about which there is no dispute 
between the parties and not those which are yet to be established by 
adjudication. In the present case when the Puja bonus claimed is not 
admitted hy the Company, it eannot be said there has heen contraven- 
tion of the provisions of section 388 by such denial of the right. The 
service condition mentioned in section 33(a) means a condition of service 
which is beyond doubt or dispute. Jf such condition of service it 
altered to the prejudice of the workmen without express permission of 
the Tribunal in writing before which the main case is pending, then 
only section 33 can be said to have been contravened and not otherwise. 
The letters of the Company which have been proved on the side of the 
petitioners سو‎ 1, l(a}, 100) and 106)] go to show beyond doubt that 
the claim of bonus as a condition of service was never admitted by the 
Company. Puja bonus as a condition of service can arise only from a 
epecific contract, express or implied. In the present case there was 
admittedly no express contract to pay Puja bonus every year. The 
petitioners relied on past payments for an jnference of implied contract 
to pay the Puja bonus as a condition of service. Before an implied 
contract can, however, be inferred from o course of conduct, one 18 to 
be sure that there is nothing in the course of conduct which is inconsistent 
with the contract proposed to be inferred from it. In the present case 
not only the payments were not made at uniform rates but also in some 
year it was admittedly given originally as advance making it recoverable 
in five equal instalments such as in 1953 [vide Ext. l(a)]. The evidence 
of P.W. 1, Rabindra Nath Mukherji, further reveals that advances so 
paid in respect of workmen getting more than Rs. 100 were recouped in 
full. Then he had also to admit in cross-examination that in the ت۷6‎ 
1361 B.S., the Company refused to pay bonus and ultimately agreed to 
pay it on the workmen approaching for the same as a ‘“‘relief’’ in 
connection with the Puja expenses. All thege do not indicate that the 
workmen can claim Puja bonus مد‎ a matter of right. Be that as it may, 
when the cluim is not admitted but has yet to be established, I find that 
such incoherent right cannot be treated as a condiion of service within 
the meaning of clause (a) of section 33 of the Act. In a case like this 
remedy lies under section 10 of the Act, and not by complaint under 
section 338A. In this view of the matter I find that the complaint 1s not 
maintainable and 1t must fail. 


It 1s awarded accordingly.

Issues 
(1) Is the dismissal of Shri Bhikan Roy and 5hri Haricharan Kurmi 


justified ? 
(2) To what relief are they entitled ? 


AWARD 


The case of the Union is that the driver Shri Bhikari Roy and the cleaner 
Shri Haricharan Kurmi appointed in 1954 were all at once asked by the 
Company to make a deposit of their two months’ wages each, which not 
having been complied with, their services were terminated without any 
notice, justification and enquiry. 


3554 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 2, 1957 [Panr] 


The Company contends in reply that it is not a case of dismissal but. 
that the two workmen took out the lorry for the last time on the 28th J-ly 
10050, removed Tarpaulin, Tyre, R.T.A. Road Permit, Insurance token, tax 
token, etc., and thereafter did not turn up. Accordingly, the two work- 
1781) have been found guilty of grave misconduct for musappropriating 
these valuable articles of the Company and no question of their reinstate- 
ment arises. 

Decision 


I must say that in this case the evidence on behalf of the Company, both 
oral and documentary, proves its case: to the hilt. The oral evidence is oft 
Mahaguj Singh, a brother of Rameswar Singh, one of the proprietors of the 
Company. It is in evidence that the Company on the failure of the driver 
to return the Tarpaulin and Tyre lodged information with the Police (7449 
a copy of G. D. Entry, dated 30th July 1956, Ext. B). The Company 
further produced a copy of an application Ext, C submitted to the Motor 
Vehicles authorities praying for a duplicate of R.T.A. permit for the lorry 
No. WBL 9404 which the রি used to ply. The Garage Register Ext. A 
elso goes to show that this lorry was taken out by the driver on 28th July 
1956 for the last time and there is no entry to indicate that the lorry was 
taken out thereafter. Besides that, the Insurance token, Tax token, eta., 
were also not returned. I have no reason to suspect the bona fides of the 
Company in lodging information with the Police and applying for a dupli- 
cate road permit, etc., as was done. Jt 1s indeed very ditticult to believe 
11181 the Company would stoop so low us to falsely implicate these two poor 
employees for nothing. The driver, it is significant to note, set up a false 
excuse that he left the Tarpaulin with the firm to which he delivered the’ 
Se for the last time. That ia nothing short of a lie. Qn behalf of the 

nion, there are bare statements of these two workmen which do not 
certainly outweigh the cogent evidence adduced by the Compnay. 


In the circumstances, I find that this is a case wherein the 2 workmen 
left the job heing guilty of crimmally misappropriating the valuable 
articles of the Company and so there can arise no question of granting re- 
Instatement or any other kind of relief. | 


Next, it was alleged on behalf of the Union that their wages for June, 
July, 1956 are withheld. But it has been proved by the production of the 
Accounts Book (Ext. D) of the Company that each of them rather took an 
excess of Rs. 10 in July 1956 and their wages for June 1956 were fully paid 
to them. 


pia in fine, it Is found that these 2 workmen are not entitled to nny 

relief, রর |

Dearness allowance payable to steamer and flat clerks was Rs. 80 which 
wos later raised to Rs. 36. The Unions’ grievance is that while the 
clerical and non-clerical staff of the head office and Ghat office of the Joint 
Companies get dearness allowance according to Bengal Chamber of Commerce 
rate, the flat and steamer clerks are paid nt a much lower rate for no appre- 
ciable reason. On behalf of the Companies it was pointed out that the 
rate of dearness allowance paid to flat and steamer clerks is not low by any 
standard. The Labour Appellate Tribunal sitting in appeal over the Third 
Major Jute Tribunal award fixed dearness allowance at Rs. 32-8 for the 
clerical staff. In the Titaghur Paper Mills Rs. 35 is the amount of dearneas 
allowance. Citing these instances Shrijut Bose, Counsel for the Companies, 
maintained that the flat and steamer clerks are not being given a raw deal 
sv far as dearness allowance is concerned. In his view these clerks cannot 
be treated as Calcutta clerks inasmuch as they are away for most of the time 
sailing in the vessels where they are ollotted. Dearness allowance paynble 
to Calcutta clerks cannot legitimately be laid claim to on their behalf. In 
this connection I may advert to the summary of the details of the award 
made by Shri A. Das Gupta at page 1736. Dearness allowance for the 
staff in the Calcutta offices and Ghats was fixed at the Bengal Chamber of 
Commerce rate. The same rate was applicable to T.D. Inspectors and Audit 
Inspectors when they are in Calcutta. Admittedly flat and steamer clerks 
are directly under the control of the head office in Calcutta. In all fairness 
they ought to be treated as belonging to the Calcutta staff. Their families 
must necessarily be left in Caleutta when they are on duty in a flat or steamer. 
Dearness allowance is a contrivance to neutralize the high cost of living at 
u certain percentage. The neutralization is intended for the ٤ 
not only of the employee but also of the members of his family. 
Simply, because the employee happens to be on board a_ vessel 
in course of performance of his duties, it cannot be said that 
the cost of living so far as the family is concerned: must صا‎ 
judged by other standards. In my view the Bengal Chamber 
of Commerce rate is due to these clerks as well. They are equally affected 
by the rise in the cost of living as the head office and Ghat clerks to whom 
the Company has granted the Bengal Chamber of Commerce rate. I find 
no cogent reason for making a distinction between other clerks and the 
flat and steamer clerks. On behalf of the Company reliance wag placed upon 
a decision of the Supreme Cort reported in 1956¢ 2 L*l.J., page 450. In 
that case the Caleutta Tramwat? Company, Ltd., though a mgmber of the 
Bengal Chamber of Commerce Ye 106 allow dearness"allowanco’ to clerks 
and depot cashiers on the rates deeided upon by the Bengul Chamber of 


Commerce. Their Lordships df the Appellaje Tribunal had held that the

issue No. 3--Revision of working hours of Chat employees: ‘The work- 
tng hours in the Ghat office are not the same as the working hours in other 
offices of the Companies. The workers in the Ghat office are accordingly 
smarting under a sense of injustice. By the award made in 1949 by Shri 
A. Das Gupta the working hours fixed for the clerical staff were as 
follows :— 


10 a.m. to 6 ag with mid-day recess for one hour from Monday to 
Friday. On Saturday 10 a.m. to 2 or 3 p.m. if the state of work 
permitted earlier closing. 


On applications made by some members of the Ghat staff they were permitted 
(0 work from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. without any interval for tiffin and leave 
office at 9 p.m. The workers have produced evidence that they have been 
working from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. with half an hour’s break for tiffin without 
exception being taken by the authorities. The witnesses for the Company 
denied that any right was given to the members of the staff to take half (1) 
hour’s time off for tiffin when they work from 10 a.m. 60 8 p.m. They might 
take their tifin while working in their seat but they were supposed to be 
‘fon call’? and no excuses could be made that they were having a tiffin 
break. J am satisfied that the company did not relax the stringency of the 
rule for work from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. with one hour’s recess for refreshment. 
On their own prayer some of the clerks were allowed to work from 10 a.m. 
to 5 p.m. at a stretch without any tiffin interval. This privilege was shown 
to those who for their own reasons wanted to leave office at 5 p.m, and were 
0 a prepared to forego the period of midday rest. The Unions can- 
not claim as a matter of right that reduction of the working hours made by 
the clerks without authority from the employers should be regularised by 
an award of the Tribunal. Working hours a& fixed for the clerical staff by 
the earlier award should not be interfered with. They must remain the 
same as awarded by Shri A. Das Gupta. 


An apprehension was entertained thut on Saturdays the discretion to 
permit early departure may not be exercised in a [জর spirit. 58 
may be made to deny the indulgence available under the award. A safe- 
guard may accordingly be provided. It is directed that clerks detained after 


38 p.m. on Saturdays will get half day’s wage in addition to their normal 
wages. 


With regard to the.gubordinate staff an award was made in 1956 by this 
Tribunal which was published in Calcutta Gazette, dated the 4th October 
1956. at. 3761. At 97180 this Tribunal gave directions that the working 
hours woujd be 8 hours in a day in a straight shift and 48 hours in a week, 
i.e., from Monday to Saturday both days inclusive. This award made only 
the other day must be allowed to have its full scope. No revision is called 
for so soon after the. last adjudication.

issue No. 1—Roevision of Leave Rules of non-clerical staff: The non- 
Clerica) staff are at present allowed to enjoy 16 days’ privilege leave on full

The Inland Stearn Navigation Workers’ Union demands privilege leave

The Paschim Bengal Mazdoor Congress lays claim to one mounth’s

ment the non-clerical staff will have privilege leave on full pay for 16 days

nyreement) for 15 days which may be accumulated up to a maximum of not 
more than 60 days. There ought to be provision for casual leave as well. 
I award casual leave on full pay for 10 days in a year. The leave rules 
will come into effect from October 1967. 


Ten days’ notice must be given by the applicant for privilege leave.

So no further increase in the dearness allowance can be given. The 
Company is faced with keen competition in the market, ang so it is 
unable to allow any ‘further increase in the dearness allowance. It 
further adds that the Union had started a hunger-strike as a result of 
which the Company had no other choice but to grant a flat increase of 
Rs. 2 in deurness allowance to all employees with effect from Agrahayana 
1363 B.S., over and above the existing dearness allowance. So the question 
of dearness allowance should be taken as finally settled and concluded, 
says. the Company. 


I refer to the agreement between the parties, dated 1811) September 
1954, which is not disputed. Under this agreement the grades ا‎ scales 
as mentioned therein were agreed upon to work for 3 years. In this 
agreement, as per the paragraph 11, I find the following: 


‘The existing rate of dearness allowance will prevail unless there is a 
substantial change in the working 01838 cost of living index, in 
which case the rate will be suitably adjusted.”’ 


So it is cleur that in the matter of dearness allowance, there should be 
no change unless the working class cost of living index shows a 
substantial change. It is clear that the Company did not shut the door 
for increase in dearness allownnce under any circumstances. The pay 
scales would not be revised under that agreement in course of coming 
3 years from 15th September 1954, but the question of dearness allowance 
was kept open for revision in case the working .class cost of living index 
showed any substantial change. So the Company’s contentton fails when 
it says that because the pay scales and grades were revised, “it 48 not 
open for the Union to agitate for increase of the dearness allowance. 
Snnilarly,,-the other contention of the Company cannot be, -sestained, 
because the settlement in question was agreed upon subsequent to the 
judgment of the Labour Appellate Tribunal. The position indicated by 
the said judgment of the Appellate Tribunal was revised by the agreement 
of 15th September 1954. So it is not open to the Company to go 
beyond this agreement. Thus the clear position is that if I find that the 
working class cost of living index has substantially increased, then 
the dearness allowance would be liable to be increased.

جم سیت‎ EE 


_ Now, turning to the Ext. 3, I get that the Secretary of the Union has 
given the indiver of the working class cost of living ‘since August 1904 
up to March 1957, with their base at 100 points in 1939. 1 was uaked to 
refer to the figures of the cost of living index given by the State 
Statistical Bureau, West Beagal. On referénee — to heen figures of the 
state Statistical Bureau, J find that the Ext. 3 was not. fully correct 
having in it inaccuracies in certain figures. I have got the Ext. 3 
corrected accordingly. I get that in August 1954, the working class cost 
of living index stood at 344-1, In August 1955, it went down to 338°4. 
In August 1966, it jumped up to 3914. In May 1957. it bas reached 
4006 points. So 1 get that from 3441 in August 1974) it “has come up to 
400-6 in May 1957. So, 1s this not a substantial” change in the cost of 
living index? There has bean a rise of 56 pofhts. Accor ing to the 
ugreement as per the Ext. D, the Union ip entitled to claim নিল 
of dearness allowance on the basis of rite in the coat of working class 
living index. 


Next, tho question 18, what should be the quantum of increase in 
dearness allowance on the basia of the aforesaid rise in the cost of living 
index¥ At 344 points in September 1955, at the time of the agreement in 
question, dearness allowance stood at Rs. 30 per month. I remind that 
there is no dearness allowance up to 180 points of the cost of living index. 
0 Rs. 30 in Septem ber 1954, represented (10181181455 160 for the 
excess points above 180 points, 1.e., for 164 points. So, roughly, rupee one 
is the amount for rise in dearness allowance for every 5} points. So, to 
cover 56 points (400 points minus لاخ‎ points), the amount of rise in 
dearness allowance would be Rs. 10 and odd. Now, this quantum of rise 
in dearness allowance can be legitimately cluimed by the Union, and it 
has been so claimed by it in the present case. But [ must point out that 
the rise in the cost of living index is not fully compensated in any 
concern, It is seen from the trend of decisions that 75 per cent. is the 
maximum neutralisation done of the rise in the cost of living index in 
any concern in India. The reason is not far to seek. The নী are, 
no doubt, hit by the rise in the cost of livinig index. So, are the 
consumers, the people of the country. If the سرد مرا‎ allowunce is 
increased, the prices of materials are liable to be increased in consequence 
thereof. That will have a repercussion on the consumers in general in 
the long run. Besides, workmen in_ service of Companies being people 
of this land, should be prepared to share with the rest of the people 
sufferings on account of the rise in the cost of living. In that view also, 
there should not be full neutralisation of the rise in the cost of living. 
The question of the سو‎ also deserves consideration. By the rise 
in the cost of living index, if dearness allowance has got to be increased, 
it is likely to hit the employer in its profits. So, unless he has the 
freedom to raise the prices of commodities, he produces just to maintain 
his quantum of profits, he will be hard hit. This chemical industry, 
along with other auch industries, is faced with keen competition in the 
market. There is no monopolistic market. Foreign competition 18 
growing in” volume. Imports and exports are restricted. So the industry 
ig in کہ‎ tight corner. In this state of things full neutralisation of the 
deficiency #s a result of rise in the cost of living index by dearness 
allowance cannot be permitted, So, I allow Ra. 7 as increase in dearness 
aHowance on the pay 80816 up to Rs. 50. Thereafter dearness allowance 18 
increased by Rs. 5 for a rise of Rs. 50 in the pay scale as in the existing 
scale. So, in place of the present dearness allowance which is Rs. 30 for 
pay range up to Rs. 60, it would now stand at Re. 37. In place of the 
existing dearness allowance of Rs. 35 meant for the pay range up to Rs. 100, 
Rs. 42 will be available under this award. Rs. 47 will take the place of the

For the pay range above Rs. 2(M), the dearness allowance which now exists

range up to Rx. 50 mndstly come from the working class people. They are 
in need of increase in dearness allowance because they are hardest hit as a 
result of the rise in the cost of living index. The rise tn the prices of 
principal and essential commodities, viz., rise, oil, Hour, fuel, ete., is most 
perceptible. Even if [ consider the case of the middle-class people who are 
supposed to belong to the pay range above Rs. 50, ۱] find that the increase 
in dearness allowance to the extent of Rs. 7 will to a great extent mitigate 
their sufferings on account of the rise in the prices of essentin] commodities, 
The Company should not prudge this increase in dearness allowance becenuse 
under the verv agreeinent of 1954 the door for such legitimate increase m 
dearness allowance was left open,—and quite advisedly. It 1s no use 
blinking at facts of such stupendous rise in the coat of living and t6 remain 
quiescent. Phe workinen are bound to be ill at ease unless their elementary 
needs are attended to. So this increase in deerness allowance 18 only 
legitimate and proper. The Company has the undoubted capacity to pay 
this increased dearness allowance (ride the balance-sheet). 


The increase of dearness allowance as ordered above will be reduced by

ANNEXURE 
In the matter of a complaint under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes 
Act filed by Rampujan Shaw and three others 010. Dishergarh Power 
Workers’ Union, P.O. Sunderchak, district Burdwan, ali employees of 
Messrs. Dishergarh Power Supply Company, P. 0. 01517988111) district 
Burdwan, against the aforesaid Company. (Case No. 6 of 1957.)

Union. 


AWARD . 


he original reference out’of which this case has arisen was made under 
(Jovernment order 10. 3953Dis. /1)/100-120/56, dated 5th September 1956. 


2, Tt is the contention of the petitioners that they have been discharged 
by the Power House Superintendent saying that their services were no 
longer required by the Company, and that this has been done without the 
express ৮ nee of the Tribunal in writing, before whom the main cuse 
was pending for adjudication. 


The Company contends that the petitioners were casual employees em- 
ployed, for a job requiring a specified period of time, and that they were 
given to understand this position of employment at the time of appointment. 
As the said job was completed, and the specified period was over, these people 
had their services automatically terminated. So, no permission of the 
Tribunal under section 33 of the Act was required, and the case under 


section 3931 doea not ۰ 


The Company has filed several documents showing appointment of these 
four persons. From those documents it is clearly seen that these men were 
appointed for casual work, and for a specified period of time, and that there 
men had accepted the job on conditions mentioned therein. 


8568 THE CAIXUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 26, 1967 [Pant I 


From the evidence of Rampujan, P.W. 2, I get that they had put in 
services much longer than what was stipulated. But they have admitted 
that their services were not continuous, but with breaks. It is also admitted 
that they were never given any leave with pay, nor were they allowed to 
continue to the Provident Fund which were the conditions of service of the 
permanent employees. So, it is clear that these people were treated as 
casugl employees. Now, whether they should be made permanent after the 
prescribed length af service was an isaue befure the Tribunal in the main 
cause. It was settled by u compromise between the parties on the issue that 
the Company would absorb 20 such casual labours into ita permanent 
vacancies, and that they would be treated as probationers in the beginning, 
andl after six months the Company would confirm them. So, that agreement 
also shows that casual labours could not claim any lien on the service or 
any permanency in service. So, if the Company has terminuted their 
services, it cannot be said that the Company has infringed section 33 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act. So the case under section 33A does not he. The 
petition uccordingly stands rejected.

COVERNMENT OF RAJASTHAN 
Home (D) Department 
NOTIFICATION 
Dated Jaipur, the dth August 1957. 


No. F.26(9)Hb/56.—Wherens it appenrs to the State Government that 
the books, pamphlets and documents mentioned below contain matter which 
ig intended to promote and does promote feelings of enmity and hatred 
between different classes of citizens of India and is deliberately and 
muliciously intended to outrage the religious feelings of the Jain (Bania) 
community by insulting the religion and the religious beliefs of that class 
and the publication of which is punishable under sections 153A and 295A 
of the Indian Penal Code; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred by section 99A of 
the Code of Crimigal Procedure, 1898 (V of 1898), the State Government 
does hereby declare every copy of the aforesaid books, pamphlets and 
documents to be forfeited to Government: 


Books, Pamphiets and Documents 


(1) Volume entitled “186 Witkarni’’ in Hindi written by Sadhu 
Anoop Das and printed by the Shri Venkteshwar Steam Printing Press, 
Bombay, in Somvat year 1868: This is full of venomous propaganda 
against the ‘‘Bunia’’ community. 


(2) Book entitled ‘‘Nyay Chintamani’”’ in Hindi written by Soni Har- 
chand of Sirohi, published in Samvat year 1982. This again is full cf 
vicious propaganda ugainst the ‘‘Bania’’ (Jain) community and attacks 
on the Jain religion, 


(3) Book entitled ‘‘Kitab Mufid Am Muusumweh’’, published in Samvat 
year 2013 and 1956 A.D. and printed at Shri Kamla Printing Press, Katla 
Bazar, Jodhpur, by Bansi Lal Solanki. ‘This is an extract from the bigger 
volume ‘‘Jagat Flitkarni’’ of Anoop Das. : 


(4) ‘‘Atm VPuran’’ in Hindi written by Soni Harohand and published 
at the Kamla Printing Press, Katla Bazar, Jodhpur. This is also written to 
outrage the religious feelings of the Bania community and incite other 
elusses against them. | 


(5) Printed leaflets in Hindi entitled— 

(i) “Shri Anoop Swamiji-Ki-Artik’’ printed at Shri Ramayan 
Printing Press, Darhyapur, Badigaon, Badi Pasi, Ahmedabad, 
and published by President, Anoop Mandal, Sirobi. 

(ii) ‘“‘Dukhiyon-ki-Pukar’? published by Manager, Bharat Policy Form 
Company, Government Sarkar Hall, or President Anoop Mandal, 
Kishinagar, and printed at the Saryodaya Press, Jodhpur. Both 
are written with the view to promote class hutred and malhgn 
the Bania community. 


By order of the Governor, 


[ILLEGIBLE], Dy. Secy.

Notification 


IN accordance with the provisions of sub-section (4) of 
wetion 126 of the Calentta Port Act, 1890 (Bengal Act 
[1] of 1890). the following New By-laws Nos. 4B and 52A 
which the Commissioners propose to incorporate in the 
By-laws for the Port of Calcutta are heroby published for 
general information :--- 


Proposed New By-laws Nos. 4B and 52A 


“‘4B.—Restriction of entry of vehicles in Docks and 
Jetties: (i) ‘The Troftic Manager may, on application in 
prescribed form from the owners of lorries, carts including 
handcarts, bullock earts and buffalo carts and other 
vehicles, issue an annual permit for entry into and exit 
from the Docks and Jetties on such terms and conditions 
a8 he may lay down frorn time to timo. 


Gi) The Traffic Manager reserves the right to refuse 
the 12781) of any such permit and to cancel or withdraw 
@ny permit already granted at uny time he thinks fit and 
proper without assigning any reasons, 


Gin) The Trafe Manager may also take all necessary 
stepe to ensure:— 


(a) The proper entry into and exit from the Docks and 
Jetiies of loaded or empty lorries. carts includin 
handcarts, bullock carta and buffalo carte anc 
other vehicles. 


(b) The oxclusion of all persons who enter or attempt 
to enter into Docks and Jetties with any lorry, 
cart including handcart, bullock cart and buffalo 
cart or any other vehicles without any valid 
permit, or in respect of which the permit has been 
refused, or cancelled, or withdrawn, or in respect 
of which the period of the permit has expired. 


(c) The prosecution of such offenders and dotention 
for the purpose of heing handed over to the Police 
of such offending lorries, carts including hand- 
curts, bullock carts and buffalo carts and other 
vehicles ag the case may 08.) 


‘‘62A.—Entry of ۷۸۱٢۰۱۵۶ in Docks and Jettles without a 
valid pormit: No person shall enter mto the Docks and 
Jetties with any lorry, cart including handcart, bullock 
cart and buffalo cart or other vehicle without any valid 
permit as 10010 down in By-law No. 41; and any person 
found contravening the provision of the said By-law is, 
without prejudice to the provisions of By-law No, ITI, 
liable to prosecution as a trespasser, and his lorry, cart 
including handcart, bullock cart and buffalo cart or 
vehicle, as the case may be, shall also be liable to detention 
jor being handed over to the Police.” 


The proposed By-laws will be submitted to the Govern- 
ment of India for confirmation on the expiry of fourteen 
days after the first publication of this notification in the 
State Gazette und comments or criticisms if any, with 
regard thereto received by the undersigned within that 
period will be considered.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 


In order to assist the handloom industry, the Government of India had 
issued in December, 1962, a notification under the Cotton Textiles (Control) 
Order, 1948, restricting the production of dhoties by a mill or a group of 
mills to not more than 60 per cent. of the average quantities of dhoties 
packed for sale per month tor internal consumption during the year April, 
109] to March, 1982, It was, however, not always possible under this 
notification to penalise the offender for infringement of its provisions. To 
remove this disability, the Dhoties (Additional Excise Duty) Act, 1953, was 
passed providing for the imposition of a penal excise duty on a regulated 
80019 on mills infringing this restriction. | : 


2. In order to clarify beyond doubt that a group of mills under the 
saine ownership or cammon management could combine their quotas of 
dhoties fixed under section 3, it 1s proposed to amend the said Act to enable 
the Government to fix a collective quota wherever necessary for a group 
of mills. under the same ownership or common management. The Bill is 


designed to achieve this object. 


MORARJI DESAI. 


NEw Deir; 
The 4th July, 1967. 


MEMORANDUM REGARDING DELEGATED LEGISLATION 


Clause 601 the 13111 seeks to amend section 5 of the principal Act to 
enable the Central Governmnt to make rules to provide for the form and 
manner of application for the fixation of permissible quota for any group 
of mills and the procedure to be followed in relation to. such fixation. These 
are matters of procedure and minor detail which may be entrusted to the rule 
making power of the Central Government. The. proposed delegation of 
legislative power is of a normal character. 


M. N. KAUL, Secy.

It is hereby notified for general information that the Corporation of

Gupte Lane in Ward No, 2 under section 357(1) of the Calcutta Municipal 
Act, 1951.

Ou 26th June 1957 the workmen through their Union placed o charter 
of demands before the Proprietor of Sk. Nasiruddim Bidi Factory at 146

missioner, West Bengal, Calcutta-1. 


On 26th June 1957 Sk. Abdul Ghaffoor, the Proprietor of the concern 
and Jonab Md. Ismail, President of the Union, agreed that a Committee be 
formed with three members from the Munayement, three members from the 
Union and Shri K. .کا‎ Kapani, Industrial Relations Adviser of Industrial 
Relations Bureau, 138 Canning Street, as Chairman and the Committee 
should consider the charter of demands after hearing both parties. 


Accordingly, a Committee was formed with Jonab Abdul Baqi, Jonab 
Abdul Razzak and Jonab Abdul Hamid as Management's nominees and 
Shri Robin Chakraverty, Joint Secretary of the Union, Jonab Zakir Hussain, 
(Jeneral Secretary of the West Bengal Biri Mazdoor Federation and 
Mohammed Sammi, worker-member of the Factory Committee, os ngminees 
of the workmen, with Shri .کا .کا‎ Kapani as the Chairman. |

188 Canning Street, Calcutta, on 6th July 1957 at 1-30 p.m. and proceed-— 
ings were drawn. The demands put forward in the Union’s letter were 
taken up ad seriatum from Nos. 1 to 6. At this stage Management nominees

15586 No, 1: Wage structure—(a) Time rates, (b) Piece rates.—The 
Union’s demand is as follows :— 


Time rate minimum Ra, 74, maximum Rs. 150 for time-rated monthly 
paid workers,

The Management contended that time-rated workers of thé Bakin 
Packing, Administration and Sales Departments are no doubt monthly paid 
workers but not monthly rated as they are on & 400 work no pay” basis. 
The Board agrees with this contention. Management further contended 
that time rates paid by them are fairly in comparison with those paid by 
other Biri manufacturers in the Calcutta Industrial Belt. There is no 
asgument about this. On the other hand, the Union contends that Sk. 
Nasiruddin is the biggest manufacturer in Calcutta area and as such his 
workers must be better off than others. Birt manufacturing 18 u cottage 
induatry and the wages therein cannot be compared with large organised 
industries in the Calcutta Industrial Area. In a buyers’ market with a 
keen competition a particular establishment cannot be burdened with higher 
wages as compared to those paid elsewhere in the area in similar concerns. 
AT the same time it cannot he agreed that workers should be paid at a low 
rate because others are paying low wages. We, therefore, strongly feel 
that the present wage structure needs revision and we fix the following 
graded scalea of cunsvlidated daily wages :— 


Time rates.—With 52 Sundays and 6 Festival holidays the number of 
working days in a year comes to 307, i.e., a working month of 20.0 
days. The Board takes it at 25 days for the purpose of fixing and 
computing the time rates awarded as under:— 


Effective from Ist July 1957 the graded scale of daily consolidated 
wages shall be 105. 2.40—12 nP—Rs, 3.60. 


All time-rated workers now on the rolls of the employer will be fixed in 
the above scales at the next higher point on Ist October 1957.

Labelling any other brand with 4 labels—Rs. 5-4 (5.25) per lakh.

issue No. 3: Leave and HMolidays.—Yaking into consideration the

Issue No. 4: Security of Service. —There are no Standing Orders in this 
establishment though the number of workmen normally employed in the 
Manufacturing Process and Administrative and Sules Departments are 
more than 50. It is recommended that immediate steps should be taken to 
have Standing Orders framed under the Industrial Employment (Standing 
Orders) Act, 1946. In the meantime it is, however, essential that there 
must be some security of tenure and workers should not be allowed to work 
under an apprehension uf being removed at any time. As a safeguard the 
employment of any workman shall not be terminated without assigning 
any reason thereof and without giving him sufhicient chance and time to 
explain his couduct in the event of any alleged misconduct against him, 
save and except when he is unauthorisedly absent for more than 6 days; 
when he will be considered to have left his job of his own accord; and shall 
lose the lien on his employment with the Compuny. 


Normally any worker who has completed one year’s continuous service 
from the date of his first joining the Company and/or who hag put in 240 
days’ actual work in any working year (lst October to 30th September) 
will be considered as a permanent workman, may he be on time and/or piece 
rates und shall have title to all the benefits laid down in Chapter IVA of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and to one month’s notice or wages in leu 
thereof in the event of terrMination of his employment for reasons other than 
dismissal for gross misconduct and/or voluntary resignation. 


Workman on roll who hus rendered more thun 6 muntls but less than 
one year’s continuous service up to the date of this award, shall be consi- 
dered as temporary and who have not so far completed even 6 months’ 
service shall be treated us daily or casual. ‘They shall have no title to any 
notice or wages in lieu of notice and/or to any other compensation in the 
event of termination of their employment save and except any dues earned 
but unpaid wages and earned leave at one day for 20١ days worked prior 
to such terinination.

lettera SKN and a number.

bearing the letters SAN and a number.

event of abnormal absentee amongst the Bakers, Packers, workers of the

and Packing Departments us a permanent leave reserve who shall be 
required to do any work that may be assigned to him at the discretion of 
the Management when he 1s not engaged as a substitute in the leave vacancy 
of the department to which he is assigned. Where on any day absentation 
in any of these departments is abnormal Management should recruit Badlis 
instead in case such absenteeism 18 likely to continue for more than 2 days 
at a atretch. This method 1f adopted and implemented will allay all fears 
and upprehensions of the Label Departinent workers on piece rate and will 
ensure reasonable flow of work for them to carry on. ۱

The Government of West Bengal, in the Labour Department, by order

award on the said industrial dispute and this award was published in the 
“Calcutta Gazette, Hatraordinary, dated 15th March 1956. In the

(9) Should increment for the year 1954 be granted? Jf so, at what

The parties filed a joint petition of compromise on issue Nos. 2 and

terms of the setllement in regard to issue No. 3 was as follows: 


‘The claim on issue No. 3 of the achedule of order of reference is

ANNEXURE 


In the matter of an industrial dispute between Messrs. Hindusthan Lace 
fAanutacturing Corporation Ltd, (Head Office at 8.1 Esplanade East,

facturing Corporation Ltd. Mazdoor Union, 47/۸ Rashbehari Avenue,

BEFORE THE SECOND INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL

শি1 (1. 1১, MUKHERJEE, Judge, Second Industrial Tribunal 


Appearances ; 
For the employees; Shri Kiran Chandra Mitra, Advocate. . 


Kor the Company: Shri N. K. Mukherjee, Advocate. 


The Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, by ita order 
No. O08-1.R./D/111-806/06, dated “010 February 1957, referred the above 
dispute to this Tribunal for adjudication. 


The issue as contained in the schedule to the order of reference in as 
follows :— | 


Are the workers named below entitled to any compensation for lay-off 
for varying periods claimed by them from 9th November 1956 
onwards, and yf so, the amount in each case: 


(1) Shri Sunil Sarkar. 

(2) Shri Gobinda Lal Banerjee. 
(3) Shri Ajit Das. 

(4): Shri Santosh Banerjee. 

(8) Shri Mukul Kumar Dey. 


AWARD 


Tt is the case of the Union that the workmen mentioned in the issue are 
permanent employees of the Company. but all on a sudden, they were laid- 
off with effect from 9th November 1956 until further notice. The said lay- 
off has been characterised to be unjust and unfatr, inasmuch as the Company 
instead of laying-off the temporary employees, laid-off these 5 workers who 
were permanent. The ground as assigned by the Company for lay-off had 
also no basis. Accordingly, compensation for the entire period during 
which these 6 workers were laid-off has been claimed. | 


The Company in reply stated that the lay-off of these workers was justi- 
fied, as there was huge accumulation of finished stock in the section, in 
Which these workers were emplayed. It has further contended that the 
question of payment of any compensation for the period of lay-olf to these 
workers does not arise, becuuse this concern is an industrial establishment in 


Part I] THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., SEPTEMBER 26, 1957 89139 


which only 20 workers worked on an average per working day in the month 


of October 1906, that is the calendar month preceding the month they 
were laid-off. 


Adimittedly, these 0 workers were 1810-0 by the concern, and there 1s 
no dispute or coutroversy between the parties over this. But the parties are 
at variance regarding the period of lay-off. It is urged on behalf of the 
Company that the present 5 workers ure not entitled to get any lay-ofl com- 
-pensation, because this concern is an industrial establishment in which less 
than 50 forkmen on an average per working day were employed in the 
calendar month preceding the month they were laid-off. اسم‎ Advocate 
appearing on behalf of the Company in support of this contention took his 
stand on section 256A of Chapter VA of the Industrial Diaputea Act, 1947. 
This Chapter relates to Jay-off and retreuchment. Sub-section (1) of section 
256A says that sections 206 to 261 inclusive shall not apply to industrial 
establishments in which less than 50 workmen on an average per working 
day have been employed in the preceding calendar month. Kxplanation to 
section 25۸ provides that in sections 226, 257) aud 25K “industrial estab- 
lishment” means a factory as defined in clause (m) of section 2 of the 
Factories Act, 1948. “Factory”? as defined in clause (m) of section 2 of the 
Factories Act, 1948, means any premises including the precincts thereof— 


(i) whereon ten or more workers are working, or were working on an 
day of the preceding twelve months, and in any part of দা 
a manufacturing process is heing carried on with the aid of 
power, or is ordinarily so carried on, or 


(ii) whereon twenty or more workers are working, or were working on 
ony day of the preceding twelve months, and in any part of 
which a manufacturing process is being carried on without the 
aid of power, or is ordinarily so carried on,— 


but does not include a mine subjeot to the operation of the 
Mines Act, 1952 (XXXV of 1952), or a railway running shed. 


Admittedly, the workmen concerned were laid-off from the month of 
November 1956 onwards. So, tho preceding calendar month as mentioned 
in clause (a) of aub-section (1) of section 25۸ of the Act was the month of 
October 1956. It has been saitefactorily proved by the evidence—both oral 
and documentary—as furnished by the Company, that in this industrial 
eatnblishment Jess than 50 workmen on an average per working day were 
employed in October 1956. The above evidence also goes to show that at 
the relevant time only 15 or 16 workers were employed in this concern, 
which is even less than the number required for a factory as defined in sub- 
cluuge (11) of clause (m) of section 2 of the Factorigs Act, 1948. This being 
the position, I am of the view that these workers are not entitled to get “ 
lay-off compensation under the law, even if it be assumed that their lay-o 
was unjustified. Chapter VA of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, as 
stated above, relates to lay-off and retrenchment. It will be clear from 
section 257 of the Act that the rights and liabilities of employers and 
workmen in so far as they relate to lay-off and retrenchment shall be deter- 
mined in accordance with the provisions of that Chapter alone. In such 
circumstances, the Tribunal cannot rise above the law, and grant compensa- 
tion to these workers from the point of equity, in utter disregard to what 
has been provided by Statute or codified law. The Tribunal must respect 
and follow the law as made by the Legislature. It is not open to the 
Tribunal to dispense compensation to the warkmen concerned, if it is not 
in accordance with the provisions laid down in the Act. Learned Advocate 
appearing for the Union has voiced an argument that the limitation as 
provided in sub-section (i) of section 26A can have no application to the 


5985. THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., SEPTEMBER 26, 1957 (0৬2 I 


Torneo ৯‏ جچالجے 


সি 

present case, inasmuch as this concern has not standing orders making pro- 
vision for such lay-off. I must say stroightway that I was not at all 
impressed by this argument. The absence of standing orders is immaterial, 
where clear and explicit provisions have been made in Statute for lay-off 
and retrenchment in industrial establishments. Standing orders cannot- 
certainly over-ride what has been provided in law. Thus, the legal objec- 
tion as raised on behalf of the Company succeeds. 1 therefore, ‘hold that 
the workers concerned are not entitled to get any compensation whatscever 
for the period of their lay-off. This issue is answered accordingly.

dn the matter of a complaint under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes 
Act, 1947, filed by Abdul Gaffur, an employee of Messrs. Victory Jute 
products, represented by Bengal Chatkal Mazdoor Union, Carden 
Reach, 1.1 Carden Reach Road, Calcutta-24, against the said Company. 
(Case No. 162/56 under section 33A.) 


BEFORE THE SECOND INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL 


PRESENT : 
১৮৮ 07. P, MUKHERJEE, Judge, Second Industrial Tribunal. 


Appearances : 
For the employee: Shri Patit Paban Pathak. 
For the Company :Shri P. R. Mukherjee, Advocate. 


AWARD 


This is an application under section d3A of the Industrial Disputes Act 
1947, that was presented on 29th October 1956 before the First Indusrial 
Tribunal by Shri Abdul Gaflur, one of the employees of Mesers. Victory 
Jute Products, Ltd., on the ground that during the pendency of the 
original reference before that Tribunal, the Company terminated his 
aervice with effect from Ist September 1956 without taking express 
permission from the Tribunal. By Government order No. 798 1.R./D/7L- 
37/56, dated 9th March 1957, subsequently passed, the original reference 
which was pending before the Firat Industrial Tribunal was withdrawn 
from that Tribunal, and assigned to this Tribunal for disposal. Accord- 
ingly, the First Industria] Tribunal sent to this Tribunal the application 
“under section 33A that was filed by the applicant concerned before that 
Tribunal. It may be stated in this connection that the main reference is 
atill pending before this Tribunal. 


A preliminary legal objection has been raised on behalf of the Company- 
opposite party regarding jurisdiction of this Tribunal to deal with the 
present application under section ddA. I have heard the learned 
representatives on both sides on this point. If what is alleged in the 
application under section 383A be true, 1t can be said that there was 
contravention of the provisions of section 33. Section 034 of the Tudustrial 
Disputes Act lays down that a contravention of the provisions of section 38 
must take place during the pendency of proceedings before a Tribunal to 
attract the operation of that section. It 1a alleged in the application 
that the said contravention took place on Ist September 0. But the 
fact remains that the industria] dispute, which was the subject-matter of 
the main reference, was referred to this Tribunal by Government order, 
dated 9th March 1957, in supersession of the order, dated 12th June 1966, 
by which the said dispute was referred to the First Industrial Tribunal. 
Thus it is apparent that there could be no pendency of the adjudication 
proceedings বস this Tribunal prior to 9th March 1957. Contravention 
of section 33 as alleged by the applicant had taken place, when the 
reference was pending before the First Industrial Tribunal. Section ۸ 
lays down in و‎ and unequivocal terms that where an employer contra- 
venes the provisions of section 33 during the pendency of proceedings 
before a Tribunal, any employee nygrieved by such contravention may 
inake a complaint in writing in the prescribed manner to such Tribunal, 


$913t THE CAL. GAZ. EXTRY., SEPTEMBER 26, 1957 [Part 4 


سے ےج ہے ںہ سض کے یس قسم سے এ ETE RT a হাসি উর‏ شش ہج ہے : ২_-২-_. শ্রঁউ‏ مو چھ .ہے রে tT SETUP EN et ee eh ee‏ 
tree: পে‏ ہس ا- وو + بے ے ہے ہے ee on‏ ھے সস‏ 


and on receipt of such complaint that Tribunal shall adjudicate upon the 
complaint, as if it were a dispute referred to or pending hefore it. So, 
the First Industrial Tribunal was alone competent to decide the present 
application. Hence, ou a plain construction of section 383A, this Tribunal 
bas no jurisdiction to deal with the present complaint under section ۰ 
This is the view that I have taken in a cause published in the Calcutta 
Gazette, dated 28th February 1957, at page 823 (825). Shr Pathak 
appearing on behalf of the workman has contended that the present 
rroceeding should be treated as being in continuation of the proceeding 
سو‎ the First Industrial Tribunal, Hut I am unable to accept the view 
propounded by Shri Pathak. The language of the order, dated 9th March 
1957, makes it perfectly clear that a fresh reference was made to this 
Tribunal in supersession of the previous reference to the 11751 Industrial 
Tribunal, So, it must be treated og a new reference made by the 
Government, and in no sense can this Tribunal be regarded as a successor 
to the First Industrial Tribunal. This Tribunal is altogether a different 
Tribunal. In the light of above, 1 accept the preliminary legal objection 
as raised on behalf of the opposite party, and hold that the alleged contra- 
vention compluined of by the applicant occured not during the pendency of 
the adjudication উওর before this Tribunal. 


_ In this view of the matter, this Tribunal has no jurisdiction to deal 
with the present application under section 33A. The case is thus disposed

scales ux under that agreement. There could not have been any reasonable 
objection to Company's mentioning, m the fresh appointment letters, the 
pay-scales nlong with the starting salary and dearness allowance, if the 
Company in fact adopted it. It is ‘just possible that the employees thought 
that the ‘ucceptance of the starting salary in the pay-scales amounted to 
introduction of the pay-scales under the agreement. The agreement of 1945 
was hetween the employees’ Union and the Motion Pictures Asseciation. 111 
the absence of evidence showing details about the nuthority of the parties 
to enter into a contract, it caunot be said that this agreement is an agree- 
ment relating to individual cinema houses and their employees, and is 
legally binding as such. It is said that the Association made عۃ‎ recom- 
mendation to its constituent members to follow this agreement, and in that 
view of the matter, the terms of settlement appears to be of a recommenda- 
tory nature. 11 is up to any individual cinema house to accept the recom- 
mendation or refuse it. Whether the refusal would be proper or not is o 
domestic iskue between the Association and its members, Nothing turns on 
that in adjudicating the present dispute. Admuttedly, there are no incre- 
mcntal pay-scales in existence in this Company and, 85 such, the 
employces cannot, as of right, demand increment year after year, much less 
any ‘cumulative arrears’, of increment for the past eight years. No 
eustom or implied contract has been attempted to be proved in this case 
1৭ support of the claim. In my opinion, the agreement of 1948 has no legal 
binding effect on the parties before this Tribunal unless they themselves 
udopt it. No part of the present claim can.succeed on equitable principles 
or on principles of natural justice, It has been suggested by the Company 
that the present pay, in many cases, is higher than what has heen’ recom- 
mended in the second agreement of 1956. That may or may not. be true. 
As there are no incremental scales in force in this Company, and as there is 
no binding agreement between the parties allowing annual increments to 
the employees, the employes, IT am afraid, are not entitled to, any arrears 
of increment for the past eight, years in this dispute. This issue is thus 
decided against the employees. | : 


This is my award,

ORDER 
New Delhi, the 9th September 1957 
§.R.0. 2861..-In exercise of the powers conferred hy section 3 of the 

Essential Commodities Act, 1995 (10 of 1955), the Central Government 

hereby makes the following Order, namely :— 

1. Short title, extent and commencement.—(1) This Order may be 

called the Wheat Roller Flour Mills (Licensing and Control) Order, 1957. 

(2) It extends to the whole of India oxcept the State of Jammu and 


Kashmir. 
(3) It shall come into force on the Ist October 1957. 


- 9  Definitions.—In this Order, unless the context otherwise requires,— 

(a) ‘form’? means a form set out in the Schedule to this Order; 

(b) ‘‘inspector’’ means any officer appointed as such by the Central 
(fovernment to exercise the pcwers and perform the duties of an 
Inspector under this Order; 

(০) “licensing authority’? means an officer appointed = the Central 
Government to exercise the powers and perform the duties of ٭‎ 
licensing authority under this Order; ۱ 

(৭) ‘roller mill’? means a flour mill in which disintegration of wheat 8 
done by grooved steel or iron rollers worked by power, and 

(e) “wheat products’ includes maida, atta, suji, rawa, resultant atta 
and bran.

0. Licences required for roller flour mill8.—No owner or person in 
charge of ند‎ roller mill shall manufacture, or cause to be manufactured, any 
wheat product except under and in accordance with the terms and conditions 
of a licence issued under this Order. 


4. Issue of ficences.-—(1) Every application for a licence under this 
Order shall be made to the licensing authority in Form I. 


(2) A licence issued under this Order shall be in Form IT. 


5. Poriod of validity of licenc®.--A licence issued under this Order 
shall be valid until the 13158 December of the year in which it is issued and 
may be renewed for one year at a time. 


6. Fee for ticencé.—The fee payable for a licence shall be Rs. 5 and 
that for renewal of a licence, Its. 2. 


7. Duplicate licence.—If the licensing authority is satisfied that a 
licence issued under this Order is defaced, lost, destroyed or otherwise 
rendered useless, the licensing authority may, on application made in that 
behalf and on payment of a fee of Rs. 10 issue a duplicate licence. 


8. Maintenance of accounts.—Every licensee shal] maintain correct and 
true accounts in respect of his business in such form and manner as the 
licensing authority may specify. 


9, Returns.—kvery licensee shall submit on the Ist and 1661) of every 
month to the licensing authority and to any other authority specified by 
the licensing authority, a return in Form III. 


10. Powers of licensing authority to issue directions to licensees. — (1) 
The licensing authority may issue directions to licensees in regard to— 


(a) the purchases. of wheat for the purpose of manufacture into wheat 
products ; 


(b) the proportion in which different kinds of wheat products shall be 
produced or manufactured; and 


(c) the disposal of wheat products. 


(2) Every 119970889 shall be bound to carry out the directions of the 
licensing uuthority under sub-clause (1). 


11. 58899615101) or cancellation of licences.—If any licensee contravenes 
any of the provisions of this Order or any of the conditions of the Licence, 
then, without prejudice to any other action that may be taken ayainst him, 
the licensing authority may, after giving him an opportunity of making his 
objections, suspend or cancel the licence. A copy of the order suspending 
or cancelling the licence shall be communicated to the licensee. 


12. Appeal.—Any person aggrieved by an order of the licensing 
authority under clause 11 may, within two months from the date of receipt 
7 him of the order, appeal to the Secretary to the Government of India, 

inistry of Food and Agriculture, Department of Food.

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 
DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH 
Public Health. 


NOTIFICATION 


No. P.H./4776/2R-45/57.—27th September 1957.—Whereas the Gover- 
‘is satisfied that areas in the districts of Burdwan, Birbhum, Bankura, 
Inapore, Llooghly, Howrah, 24-Parganas, Murshidabad, Malda, Weat 
jajpur, Nadia, Cooch Behar and Darjeeling, not constituted muni- 
lities under the Bengal Municipal Act, 1932 (Bengal Act XV of 1932), 
-inafter referred to as the said areas are threatened with an outbreak of 
luenza being a dangerous epidemic disease; 


; And whereas the Governor is satisfied that the ordinary provisions of 
رہ‎ for the time being in force in the suid areas, are insufficient for the 
‘vpose of preventing the outbreak and spread of the said disease ; 


. Now, therefore, in exercise of the power conferred by section 2 of the 
+¢.idemic Diseases Act, 1897 (ITI of 1897), the Governor is pleased to 
“ascribe for a period of three months the following temporary regulations 
‘vo be owerved by the public and by all persons affected thereby for prevent- 
‘ne the outbreak and spread of the said disease in the said areas: 


Regulations 


1. (1) These regulations shall apply to the areas in the aforesaid 
districts, not constituted municipalities under the Bengal Municipal  Aot, 
1932 (Bengal Act XV of 1932). 


(2) They shall come into force at once. 


2. In these regulations, unless there is anything repugnant in the 
subject or context : سے‎ 


(a) ‘‘Board’’?’ means a District Board constituted under the MHengal 
Local Self-Government Act of 1885 (Bengal Act III of 1885);
